title: Unlike needy Keir, trash-talking Andy speaks a language Trump understands | John Crace | The Guardian
description: Burnham has nothing to hide as he prepares to meet president he once called poisonous. It may actually win him more respect
Author: John Crace
Headline: Burnham has nothing to hide as he prepares to meet president he once called poisonous. It may actually win him more respect
Content: ‘He wasn’t going to apologise to The Donald for what he had said. Not least because he had meant every word.’Composite: Kin Cheung/Getty; Tasos KatopodisView image in fullscreen‘He wasn’t going to apologise to The Donald for what he had said. Not least because he had meant every word.’Composite: Kin Cheung/Getty; Tasos KatopodisThe politics sketchAndy BurnhamUnlike needy Keir, trash-talking Andy speaks a language Trump understandsJohn CraceBurnham has nothing to hide as he prepares to meet president he once called poisonous. It may actually win him more respectThu 27 Aug 2026 10.47 EDTFirst published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 10.30 EDTShareIt makes a pleasant change. Not so long ago,Keir Starmerwas falling over himself in his efforts to keep things sweet with Donald Trump. Offering the US president a second state visit within minutes of meeting him. Everyone knows you should never put out on the first date: it only makes the other person think you’re a pushover. Sure enough, The Donald banked the marching bands and the Windsor silver service, made polite conversation for three days and then went back to trash-talking him.Yet still, Starmer just sat there and took it. As if one word of criticism would be too much. Wittering on about the “special relationship” as if Trump gave a moment’s thought to the UK before he did anything. The rest of us wouldn’t have put money on the US president even being able to locate Britain on a map. It was only latterly, when The Donald chose to bomb Iran, that the penny finally dropped for Keir. And even then he looked pained by the apparent betrayal, as he resisted the calls of Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage to join in the war.UK officials prepare for potential Trump talks as Burnham plans New York tripRead moreNo such misgivings forAndy Burnham. This week, the prime minister was reminded that when he had been mayor of Greater Manchester, he had said The Donald wouldn’t be welcome in his city and that he could take his poisonous politics elsewhere. Words that had been loudly cheered at the time by many in Britain who had had enough of all the toadying. After all, it wasn’t as if the Trump-whispering had made any difference. If anything, it had only added to his contempt for us. You’ll never get any thanks from a narcissist.Nor did Andy have any regrets now that he was prime minister and was likely to meet Trump in person for the first time at the UN general assembly in New York at the end of next month. Far from it. “Shit happens” was pretty much his precis of what had gone down. He wasn’t going to apologise to The Donald for what he had said. Not least because he had meant every word.This was the real world. Politicians say stuff. Trump had said all sorts of things about him, too. That he had beenmayor of “some town”. To be fair to Agent Orange, it’s quite likely he had never heard of Manchester before. Neither geography nor an interest in other people have ever been his strongest suits. All he had known about Andy was that he was “extremely liberal”. Which in Maga language is the same as saying he’s a “Commy bastard”.So here was Burnham’s deal. He wasn’t planning to go out of his way to insult the US president, but neither would he be offering unexpurgated sycophancy. Instead, we would be getting a very British type of pragmatism. He would do what was necessary in the UK’s interest but not much more. They would be polite and try not to accentuate their differences, but there would be no pretence of any lasting friendship. Just stick to the matters in hand and get the hell out. After New York, Andy wouldn’t be sending weekly WhatsApps. Out of sight, out of mind.Weirdly, this performative show of an ersatz friendship – the US and UK are meant to be more or less on the same side, after all – is likely to be far more effective than Keir’s more needy approach. Because this is the type of language The Donald understands. Although he craves the fawning, he has no respect for those who offer it. He takes it as a sign of weakness. Equally, no amount of flattery is ever enough. There is a hole in Trump’s psyche that can never be filled.With Burnham, there is going to be more a meeting of equals. Two world leaders who are doing what it takes to get along with each other. It’s as close to respect as a sociopath like Trump can get. Andy hasn’t taken a backward step, or attempted to deny his previous comments. More that that was then and this was now. Just get used to it.View image in fullscreenNo amount of flattery from Keir could ever be enough. There is a hole in Trump’s psyche that can never be filled.Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersYou can say one thing one day and the opposite the next. It’s up to the other person to work out which one was the truth. Or maybe neither, or maybe both. After all, that’s precisely what The Donald does. Contradiction is his modus operandi. And it’s got him to the White House. So if it works for Trump, why not for Burnham? Sincerity can be an overrated virtue for a world leader. You don’t always need a Love, Actually moment to make your feelings known.“So I’m looking forward, actually, to my first meeting [with Trump],” said Andy. And he probably is. His cards are on the table and he has nothing to hide. Plus, he has a sense of humour and self-deprecation, which also might confuse the US president, who has neither.It also feels as if there’s less at stake with this meeting than there was with many of Starmer’s. Back in the early days of Trump’s presidency, it was as if much of the world was holding its breath for what he might do next. Now, not so much. We’ve all learned to adapt to The Donald. Even to his never-ending war with Iran, which has jacked up the cost of living. All his bad habits are now priced in. And suddenly he looks more vulnerable. A man who has found the world doesn’t automatically bend to his will. A man who is under pressure on the domestic front, with many Americans fed up with his foreign wars and angry at the cost of petrol (never get between an American and their car). A president facing tricky midterm elections and in danger of becoming a lame duck.For Burnham, it’s also the home front that is occupying most of his attention. Good vibes are a decent start, but sooner or later he has to do something different to Starmer while boxing himself in with the same fiscal rules. So who knows? The meeting between Andy and The Donald may be less tricky than first imagined. A welcome distraction for both of them.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamThe politics sketchDonald TrumpKeir StarmerForeign policycommentShareReuse this content

title: Like a rhinestone cowgirl – Dolly Parton’s most glorious, joyful and meta looks | Fashion | The Guardian
description: Across six decades, the late country singer and pop culture icon turned self‑presentation into a flamboyant art form
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Across six decades, the late country singer and pop culture icon turned self‑presentation into a flamboyant art form
Content: The hair, the curves, the rhinestones … Dolly Parton.Photograph: Michael Ochs Archives/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe hair, the curves, the rhinestones … Dolly Parton.Photograph: Michael Ochs Archives/Getty ImagesFashion Statement newsletterFashionLike a rhinestone cowgirl – Dolly Parton’s most glorious, joyful and meta looksAcross six decades, the late country singer and pop culture icon turned self‑presentation into a flamboyant art formDon’t get Fashion Statement delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereGuardian writersThu 27 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 13.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDolly Parton may have had a record 25 US country No 1 singles, released 66 studio albums and earned six Golden Globe nominations, among manyother achievements, but the Tennessee-born star also had an incredible number of fashion moments. “It costs a lot of money to look this cheap”, she famously quipped when asked about her style. As we bid her farewell, six Guardian writers reflect on their favourite Dolly looks.‘About as far from the Glastonbury aesthetic as it is possible to get’View image in fullscreenBejewelled … Glastonbury, 2014.Photograph: Alamy/PAHead-to-toe white rhinestones, long red fingernails strumming a matching white bejewelled guitar. Teased platinum wig, blue eyeshadow. About as far from the Glastonbury aesthetic as it is possible to get, but on that Sunday afternoon in 2014, a 180,000 strong crowd fell in love with Dolly. Her charm, her wit, her voice, and just the pure ballsy goodness of her. In her own words: “Don’t judge me by the cover, ’cause I’m a real good book.” Amen.Jess Cartner-Morley, associate editor (fashion)‘She proved the best way to live is in a look you love’View image in fullscreenRock’n’roll … with Miley Cyrus, 2022.Photograph: NBC/Vijat Mohindra/Getty ImagesWhile Parton wore a plethora of looks, sometimes up to 10 a day, you always knew what you were going to get. For over 60 years she held firm to her signature style – a silhouette that emphasised her tiny waist, along with high heels, higher hair and a heavy sprinkling of sparkle. In today’s world of image architects and constant reinvention, her continuity felt even more refreshing.Speaking toVoguein 2023, Steve Summers, Parton’s longtime stylist and creative director said: “Designing for Dolly is great, because there are so many [Dollys].” “I’ve got the philanthropist, the singer, the actress, the theme-park owner. The canvas is always very broad.” Here we have godmother Dolly, at the age of 76, performing with her goddaughter Miley Cyrus in 2022. And her look perfectly captures her attitude to style, as well as her outlook on life. Belting out I love Rock ‘n’ Roll, Parton didn’t have time to entertain any boring discourse about age-appropriate style. She was too busy living. And as Parton proved, the best way to live is in a look you love.Chloe Mac Donnell, deputy fashion and lifestyle editor‘It’s almost meta’View image in fullscreenNot dumb … the grand opening of Dolly Parton’s Trinkets and Treasures in 2010.Photograph: Taylor Hill/FilmMagicAmong Dolly Parton’s greatest quotes, the most iconic must surely be “I’m not offended by dumb-blonde jokes because I know I’m not dumb … and I also know I’m not blonde.” So much has been said about Parton as an artist who took her craft seriously but not herself, and this rhinestone-embellished, yellow “dumb blonde” top is emblematic of that. It’s almost meta. Every bit of her aesthetic, modelled after a bold, flamboyant and glamorous woman in her local Tennessee who was derided as the “town tramp”, was intentional. Art not artifice. A paean to women who wouldn’t make themselves smaller, who would not only wear society’s prejudices but throw them back with a lip-glossed kiss.Jason Okundaye, assistant opinion editor‘Formed the blueprint for everything I thought was glamorous’skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenRed carpet done right … New York in 1989.Photograph: Ron Galella, Ltd./WireImageI first watched Steel Magnolias aged 7 and Dolly’s glamorous style was instantly seared into my brain. It is still my favourite film (I’ve always loved a tearjerker) and Truvy’s rose pink nails and blonde puffball permed hair made their way from the big screen to the red carpet for the film’s New York premiere in 1989, alongside a healthy dose of crystals and décolletage. It formed the blueprint for everything I thought was glamorous.Melanie Wilkinson, styling editor‘Her authenticity was almost medicinal’View image in fullscreenA little bit country … posing with her tour bus, 1977.Photograph: Donaldson Collection/Getty ImagesNot to miss the point about Dolly – itwasall about the rhinestones, the teetering heels and the long red fingernails. But the point was also that, whether in a milky way’s worth of sparkles or a pair of jeans and a knotted shirt, it seemed she couldn’t help being authentically herself. Her looks, though often flammable, never felt artificial, and she wore them like a second skin. In a world of algorithmic, Pinterest-board taste, where it can be hard to tell whether your style is even your own, there’s something almost medicinal in that.Ellie Violet Bramley‘Each rhinestone became a diamond under her touch’View image in fullscreenRadiating joy … Los Angeles, 1978.Photograph: Harry Langdon/Getty ImagesMy favourite Dolly Parton look is every Dolly Parton look – each rhinestone became a diamond under her touch.The day I met her, we were both wearing matching shades of purple (further evidence that she’s my higher power). But I especially loved this 1978 canary yellow dress and bubble wig. This is how I’ll imagine Dolly now that she’s left us; orbiting the cosmos radiating joy.Joe Stone,lifestyle editor, Saturday MagazineTo read the complete version of this newsletter – complete with this week’s trending topics in The Measure –subscribe to receive Fashion Statementin your inbox every Thursday.Explore more on these topicsFashionFashion Statement newsletterDolly PartonnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Robert Carlyle: ‘When we did The Full Monty strip, the reaction from the crowd was terrifying’ | Movies | The Guardian
description: The actor on which star he’d devour first on a lifeboat, why he prefers pigeons to dogs and how Trainspotting put the Scottish accent on the map
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: The actor on which star he’d devour first on a lifeboat, why he prefers pigeons to dogs and how Trainspotting put the Scottish accent on the map
Content: ‘When I was starting off, you rarely heard a Scottish accent on TV or film, other than Sean Connery’ … Robert Carlyle.Photograph: Alana Paterson/The ObserverView image in fullscreen‘When I was starting off, you rarely heard a Scottish accent on TV or film, other than Sean Connery’ … Robert Carlyle.Photograph: Alana Paterson/The ObserverFilm & Music reader interviewMoviesInterviewRobert Carlyle: ‘When we did The Full Monty strip, the reaction from the crowd was terrifying’As told toRich PelleyThe actor on which star he’d devour first on a lifeboat, why he prefers pigeons to dogs and how Trainspotting put the Scottish accent on the mapThu 27 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou’re stranded on a lifeboat withEwan McGregor,Ewen Bremner,Jonny Lee Miller,Kevin McKidd,Peter Mullan,James Cosmo,Keith AllenandIrvine Welsh. Who do you eat first?DarkAnaemicI77I suppose you have to think about who’s the healthiest and has looked after their body best. I reckon Ewan would be a wee bit too chewy, and Irvine a wee bit pickled. I’ll go for Kevin McKidd because he’s been out in LA for 20 years, eating good food.Did you really not likeZippytheWest Highlandterrierwho playedWee JockinHamish Macbeth?Campbell97View image in fullscreen‘There must have been 10 Wee Jocks’ … with  Ralph Riach in Hamish Macbeth, 1996.Photograph: Alan Wylie/AlamyI’m sure this will disappoint people, but there must have been 10 Wee Jocks. I just don’t like working with animals because they don’t know they’re acting, so it can take them 10 takes to cross a road. The best animals I’ve ever worked with were the pigeons onThe Full Monty TV show, which we had to chase. I thought: “This is never going to work.” But they just did what they were told and would fly out of their box and land on your shoulder. I love pigeons now. Dogs, not so much.I was in theYouth Opportunities Programmetouring theatre company atGlasgow Arts Centreshortly after you in the early 80sand itshaped my future. How important was the experience for you – and do you think it’s even harder now for people from working-class backgrounds to get into the arts?ChorazonandEastJamMy experience was fantastic. If I hadn’t found that place, I definitely wouldn’t be speaking to you today. It was certainly hard when I was starting off, especially because of the accent. You rarely heard a Scottish accent on TV or film, other than Sean Connery. But things changed and Trainspotting had quite a lot to do with that, when the Scottish accent became more familiar to people. I think you see far more working-class actors in TV and film nowadays than you did back in the 80s, which is good.View image in fullscreen‘Things changed’ … from left: Ewen Bremner,  Jonny Lee Miller, Ewan McGregor, Carlyle and Kevin McKidd in Trainspotting.Photograph: Moviestore/Rex/ShutterstockWhat was it like to look in the mirror and seeJohn Lennonstaring back at you inYesterday?MegMayI don’t particularly look like John Lennon, but apparently there’s something about the bridge of my nose that looks a bit like his, which is what the wonderful prosthetics people focused on. When they were putting it all on, I’d sunk quite low in the chair, so I could only see the top of my head in the mirror. When they finished and I sat up, it was quite freaky.View image in fullscreen‘Incredibly moving’ … Geraldine Somerville, Robbie Coltrane and Carlyle in Cracker, 1994.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockI really enjoyedThreeat theEdinburgh international film festival. When youdirect, do you draw morefrom directors you’ve worked with or on your own instincts as an actor?PettyDabblerI’ve been phenomenally lucky to work with some fantastic directors such as Ken Loach, Danny Boyle and Alan Parker, who you would be foolish not to learn from. Directing myself in The Legend of Barney Thomson was certainly different to just acting, because directors have 500 fires to put out each day, so I was thinking more about the directing than the performance.Your performance asAlbie KinsellainCracker, a man traumatised byHillsborough, wasterrifying and incredibly moving. How did you go about creating him?LiffeyBearI remember watching the Liverpool game at Hillsborough on TV back in 1989, but not fully appreciating what had happened. Certainly, the way the Sun reported it was disgusting, accusing Liverpool fans of pissing on police officers and stuff like that. I took those terrible stories and the behaviour of the police as my starting point, along with the anger people across Liverpool felt at what had happened.Did you all really show everything to the audience at the end of The Full Monty?WomanofWolfvilleYes, we did. What a shocker that was! We only did the entire strip once and it was shot from the back, thank God. It took two and a half days to shoot. We’d come on, take off our ties, the audience would get excited and then we would cut for half an hour to set up the next shot. We took off our shirts, then our hats. By the end, the audience must have thought: “This isn’t going to happen.” So when it did, the reaction from the crowd of mainly women was terrifying.View image in fullscreen‘What a shocker that was!’ … in The Full Monty, 1997.Photograph: Cinetext/20th Century Fox/AllstarTheatre is clearly important to youand you’re an immensely versatile actor. Is there any particular reason why we don’t see you treading the boards?NepthsolemI worked in Scottish theatre for years and later had my own theatre company. But then TV and film came into my life and I’ve gone down that road ever since. I’m constantly offered theatre and West End shows, and always take it to the brink before running away again. You’ve got toreallylove theatre to do it. It’s easy for a lot of actors to put on rose-tinted specs about theatre, but it’s incredibly hard work. I wouldn’t want to short-change the audience by going into a piece that I had to do twice a day for months, and that I didn’t really love.What happened to you recommending new bands every week on your Saturday Tunes on Twitter/X?FFreundThat began during the pandemic. I know a lot of young musicians through my kids, and I became acutely aware that there were no gigs, no money, no music. I tried my best to say: “You should listen to stuff you’ve never heard.” I was easily listening to 200 tunes a week. I loved a band calledMoonlight Parade, this guy calledNick Shanefrom Dundee, andSkylightsfrom Leeds. I kind of fell out of love with Twitter, and it’s more difficult to do it on Instagram. But I’m trying to think of a way to bring it back.Did Blur get cross when you werein an Oasis video?TopTrampYes. I know Damon very well. Afterwards, he said: “Why did you do that? Why have you never done one of ours?” I said: “Because you never asked me!” I was gutted that I didn’t get to see Oasis last year, but my wife and kids were there on the first night at Heaton Park, and my wife said she saw people crying all over the place. They recorded a bit of Little By Little – the video I’m in – and when they showed me, it almost made me cry, too.View image in fullscreenFilming the video for Oasis’s Little By Little with Liam Gallagher, in 2002.Photograph: Ken McKay/ShutterstockIt’s shite being Scottish! Discuss.TheReturnOfDrWhatsonIt’s shite being from any country really, isn’t it? I think it depends on your lot in life. You could equally say it’s beautiful and fantastic being Scottish. You see that when the Scottish national team play, the pride people have – they just love being Scottish. But it depends on your social circumstances. If life is socially difficult for you, then of course it’s shite being Scottish. But equally, it can be a brilliant thing, too.Three, directed by Robert Carlyle, will have its North American premiere at Edmonton international film festival, which runs from 24 September to 3 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmFilm & Music reader interviewRobert CarlyleIrvine WelshScotlandTelevisioninterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Race to get aid into Nepal and Tibet amid warnings flood lake could burst | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Flash floods have killed at least 469 people while homes and infrastructure have been swept away
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Flash floods have killed at least 469 people while homes and infrastructure have been swept away
Content: The aftermath of the floods in Nuwakot, Nepal. More than 1,300 people are missing.Photograph: Skanda Gautam/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe aftermath of the floods in Nuwakot, Nepal. More than 1,300 people are missing.Photograph: Skanda Gautam/SOPA Images/ShutterstockNepal-Tibet flood disasterRace to get aid into Nepal and Tibet amid warnings flood lake could burstFlash floods have killed at least 469 people while homes and infrastructure have been swept awayNepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updatesWhat caused the flash flood in Nepal and Tibet?Hannah Ellis-PetersenandGaurav Pokharelin Kathmandu,Sam JonesandAmy HawkinsThu 27 Aug 2026 14.03 EDTFirst published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 12.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe international community was scrambling to get aid into flood-stricken parts of Nepal andTibeton Thursday as authorities warned that a lake ⁠formed at the ⁠site ⁠where the ​deadly torrents occurred ⁠was rising and ⁠at risk ​of ‌bursting.The catastrophic flash floods that hitNepaland Tibet on Wednesday, thundering down valleys and obliterating entire villages, killed at least 469 people and left more than 1,300 missing.Efforts to locate those unaccounted for – including hundreds of tourists from India, the US, Britain, Australia and Canada – have been complicated by the destruction of dozens of bridges and 25 miles (40km) of roads in the mountainous region, which is popular with trekkers and pilgrims.Satellite images showing before and after collapseRescue teams reported finding bodies hundreds of miles downstream from the disaster zone in the Chitwan district of Nepal, near the Tibetan border. Dozens of injured people were transported to Kathmandu for advanced medical care and more than 100 people were rescued by Nepali army personnel in helicopters.Videos from Wednesday’s disaster showed amassive wall of water crashing down on the borderas people tried to flee. The power, volume and speed of the floods gave little time for escape.Trucks were overturned and houses, roads ⁠and power plants were swept away in Nepal, while ​officials in Tibet said they feared “major casualties” after a mudslide hit a border crossing.How the deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – a visual guideRead moreTom Fletcher, the UN’s humanitarian chief, described the flood as “horrifying”. He said emergency teams had been mobilised and an initial $2m (£1.5m) of disaster funds allocated to cover emergency medical care, shelter and water.9:21‘Tsunami from the sky:’ floods leave trail of devastation in Nepal and Tibet - The LatestNepal’s disaster authority warned of continuing danger on Thursday, appealing to residents and rescuers to stay away from a swelling lake that had formed at the flood site. Chinese authorities said a barrier lake at the confluence of the Tsogyal and Purupqiangzangbu rivers was overflowing and could burst.Girilal Budhathoki, 36, who lives in the Rasuwa district of Nepal’s Bagmati province, said the flood waters swept away his wife and four children while he was away from the family home.“A huge surge of water came,” he said. “Everything turned completely black, and I couldn’t understand what was happening. Suddenly, something heavy crushed me and I fell down.”Budhathoki realised what had happened only when he returned to the place where his house had stood. “I searched desperately for my wife and children but I couldn’t find them,” he said. “They didn’t make it out. My wife was swept away too. I am all alone now.”Map showing location of the disasterKamal Kharel, who works at a hydropower plant in Chilime, also in Rasuwa district, was in the office when the floods hit. “The whole place shook as if there had been a huge earthquake,” he said. “But when I went outside, I saw everything a storm and raging water.”Kharel and some of his colleagues managed to climb a hill, where they stayed until they were rescued by the army on Thursday morning. He said: “I had never seen waves crashing that high. You only see waves like that in the sea.”People from the hard-hit districts of Nuwakot and Dhading, in Bagmati province, were seen gathering outside an army training centre – the base for helicopter rescue operations – seeking information about missing family members.Police were recording the names of the missing outside the barracks gate. Mobile phone torches were their only source of light as the area remained without electricity because of damaged hydroelectric infrastructure.View image in fullscreenFlooding has caused widespread damage to homes, roads, bridges and other infrastructure in Nuwakot, Nepal.Photograph: Ap Tolang/Nexpher/Zuma Press/ShutterstockThe village of Soley, in Nuwakot, which had about 25 homes, was almost wiped out, according to Nirajan Paudyal, a Kathmandu-based journalist whose parents and other relatives lived there. Desperate for information, he had travelled to the area on Thursday for news of his family. “There is no update till now,” he said. “I fear there won’t be any update.”More than 500 foreigners were among 826 people missing in Nepal, police and tourism ⁠officials said. Among those unaccounted for were 177 from India, 90 from the US, 34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 25 from Canada.Chinese state media said at least 558 were missing on the Tibet side of the border, of whom at least 260 were foreign nationals.Many of the victims were on a pilgrimage to Kailash Mansarovar, a high-altitude site in ‌Tibet revered by Hindus and Buddhists among others.Early reports from Nepali ​officials suggested an earthquake could have caused the lower part of a glacier to collapse and trigger ‌the floods. But the US Geological Survey later said what was initially reported ‌as a 4.4-magnitude earthquake was a seismic shock generated by glacial rock and ice collapsing, and the flow of debris. “No earthquake had occurred,” it said.A graphic showing how the situation unfolded.Srijana Gurung, the acting Nepal director for the international NGO Plan International, said communities across the Himalayan country were facing “climate shock after shock” with hardly any time to recover.“Floods and landslides have always happened in Nepal but the climate crisis is making them far more frequent and intense,” she said. “The priority now must be reaching those affected, supporting families searching for loved ones and ensuring vulnerable communities have the assistance they need.”Gurung said children and families who had lost their homes and livelihoods would be in urgent need of medical help, food, shelter and hygiene kits. “There is also a risk of waterborne disease as access to clean water and sanitation is likely to have been damaged,” she said.View image in fullscreenPeople look at the devastation left by flash flooding in Nepal’s Nuwakot district.Photograph: Rajesh Kumar Singh/APScant information has emerged from the Chinese authorities about the scale of the destruction. Tibet is the most tightly controlled part ofChinaeven under normal circumstances. Foreign journalists cannot visit the region unless they are part of a government-controlled tour and the authorities have cracked down harshly on calls for greater autonomy from the Tibetan people. Tibetans have almost no contact with the international media because of fears of retribution.Only brief, state-controlled media reports about the floods have been allowed to circulate in China and the authorities have confirmed only three deaths. Chinese reports have focused on rescue efforts.Locator map for the wider regionMaya Wang, the deputy Asia director at Human Rights Watch, wrote on X: “The floods raise questions about whether Chinese authorities could’ve done more to reduce disaster risks, given longstanding concerns from Tibetan diaspora groups & experts about rapid, state-led development in areas where Tibetans have little say.”She called on Beijing to “allow Tibetans access to information and international researchers and journalists unfettered access to the region, and conduct a rigorous investigation into the disaster”.Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalTibetChinaSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Thousands of UK women have undiagnosed PTSD after childbirth each year, study finds | Women's health | The Guardian
description: Experts call for joined-up support through the postnatal period amid concerns GPs are not trained to spot symptoms
Author: Denis Campbell
Headline: Experts call for joined-up support through the postnatal period amid concerns GPs are not trained to spot symptoms
Content: Research has estimated that either 5% or 5.9% of women giving birth in the UK suffer PTSD.Photograph: KatarzynaBialasiewicz/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenResearch has estimated that either 5% or 5.9% of women giving birth in the UK suffer PTSD.Photograph: KatarzynaBialasiewicz/Getty ImagesWomen's healthThousands of UK women have undiagnosed PTSD after childbirth each year, study findsExperts call for joined-up support through the postnatal period amid concerns GPs are not trained to spot symptomsDenis CampbellHealth policy editorThu 27 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThousands of UK women develop undiagnosed post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) after childbirth every year, research has found.The frightening and dangerous condition is being missed in at least 15,000 women a year across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, and the true toll could be double that or more, according to the authors of research in a leading medical journal.The gap in maternal mental health care is revealed in an evidence review published on Friday by doctors at the University of East Anglia’s medical school who specialise in women’s health.Many GPs mistake PTSD forpostnatal depression, which means women who urgently need specialist help for the former receive treatment that is not appropriate, it found.The NHS’s widespread failure to identify PTSD in women who recently had a child has prompted concern because undiagnosed mental ill health among them has been linked to relationship problems, long-term suffering and a high risk of suicide.The research, published in the British Journal of General Practice, is the first attempt by experts to quantify how many cases of childbirth-related PTSD in the UK are diagnosed or not. The NHS does not collect such figures, despite the fact up to one in 16 mothers develop the serious mental health condition, often because they had a traumatic experience while giving birth.The leader of the UK’s 50,000 GPs admitted that cases of PTSD were going unrecognised and untreated because of “an important gap” in family doctors’ ability to recognise the symptoms, which include nightmares, flashbacks, anxiety and persistent negative thoughts, including hopelessness.Research has estimated that either 5% or 5.9% of women giving birth suffer PTSD and also that fewer than half of those who get it are diagnosed and receive NHS care. In some cases it can occur even when the woman has had a medically uncomplicated birth.“The Office for National Statistics figure for the 2025 live birthrate in England and Wales, not including Scotland and Northern Ireland, was 585,396. This figure does not include stillbirths and miscarriages, which are significant risk factors for childbirth-related PTSD,” said Dr Megan Foreman, the lead author of the paper, who is also a GP.“Therefore, at 5% of the 2025 ONS birthrate for England and Wales (29,269), combined with the evidence from Moran et al that less than 50% of women with PTSD symptoms postnatally are referred for specialist perinatal mental health support, a UK figure greater than 15,000 women, but potentially in the tens of thousands, would be justifiable based on the available evidence,” she added.Many cases of PTSD are being missed when new mothers go to see their GP for the NHS-wide checkup of their own and their baby’s health six weeks after the birth, the six co-authors say. That is particularly because, although there is NHS guidance on what should happen in those consultations, there is no approved framework for assessing women’s risk of having PTSD.The fact that six-week checks are meant to cover the health of newborns as well as their mothers, including immunisations the baby needs, means the child’s situation can “dominate the consultation … [which] can make assessing the mother’s mental health challenging, particularly if they attend alone with the child”, the study found.“In addition, some women may not feel able to discuss a traumatic birth immediately as it may be retriggering,” the paper points out.“A UK study demonstrated that, despite half of GPs recognising trauma-related features when reviewing case vignettes describing childbirth-related PTSD, their most common diagnosis was postnatal depression,” it adds.Misdiagnosis can be detrimental to women with PTSD because they are then prescribed antidepressants, which are not as effective for treating it as psychological therapy, and also because the evidence shows that “treating depression alone may not improve coexisting childbirth-related PTSD”, the authors say.AI can detect heart disease in women using mammograms, study suggestsRead moreFailure to correctly identify PTSD also matters because it and postnatal depression increase the risk of suicide, which is the commonest cause of death among women in the year after giving birth.“Untreated childbirth-related PTSD can have profound effects on women and families”, including needing further NHS care, avoiding contact with doctors and hospitals or choosing to have an elective caesarean or home birth with future pregnancies, the paper adds.Angela McConville, the chief executive of the NCT parenting charity, said the findings were worrying and showed that NHS postnatal care needed to focus more on mothers’ emotional wellbeing.“The possibility that so many women could be living with undiagnosed PTSD after birth is deeply concerning. PTSD after birth is a serious and often overlooked condition that can have a profound impact on women and new mothers, as well as those around them. No one should have to reach crisis point before they are listened to and able to access support,” she said.“These findings are a powerful reminder that birth trauma does not end when care in hospital ends. When trauma goes unrecognised or unsupported, the effects can be felt across relationships, family life and wellbeing for months or even years.“A traumatic experience [of pregnancy or childbirth] can affect [mothers’] mental health, relationships and confidence at a time when people are adjusting to life with a new baby,” McConville added.The authors based their conclusions on analysis of existing official data on the numbers of women giving birth, known prevalence of PTSD among them and six-week checkup GP appointments.“This paper highlights an important gap in how we identify and support women experiencing PTSD following childbirth,” said Prof Victoria Tzortziou Brown, the president of the Royal College of GPs.Recognition of the condition was vital, given the trauma involved, but the six-week check was not enough for a GP to adequately assess their mental health, she said.Tzortziou Brown added: “The six-to-eight-week postnatal check is an important opportunity for GPs to discuss a woman’s physical and mental wellbeing, as well as the health of her baby. But childbirth-related PTSD can be complex to identify.“Symptoms may overlap with depression, anxiety and other postnatal mental health problems, and may not become apparent until months after the birth.“Recognition therefore cannot depend on a single consultation. Women need joined-up support throughout the postnatal period, across maternity services, health visiting, general practice and specialist mental health services.”In the UK, the charityMindis available on 0300 123 3393 andChildlineon 0800 1111. In the US, call or textMental Health Americaat 988 or chat 988lifeline.org. In Australia, support is available atBeyond Blueon 1300 22 4636,Lifelineon 13 11 14, and atMensLineon 1300 789 978Explore more on these topicsWomen's healthHealthMental healthNHSChildbirthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ratko Mladić, the ‘Butcher of Bosnia’, dies in The Hague | Ratko Mladić | The Guardian
description: Bosnian Serb commander responsible for Srebrenica massacre dies in prison while serving life sentence for genocide
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: Bosnian Serb commander responsible for Srebrenica massacre dies in prison while serving life sentence for genocide
Content: Bosnian Serb army commander Gen Ratko Mladić  addresses his troops in the eastern Bosnian town of Vlasenica in December 1995.Photograph: Oleg Stjepanovic/APView image in fullscreenBosnian Serb army commander Gen Ratko Mladić  addresses his troops in the eastern Bosnian town of Vlasenica in December 1995.Photograph: Oleg Stjepanovic/APRatko MladićRatko Mladić, the ‘Butcher of Bosnia’, dies in The HagueBosnian Serb commander responsible for Srebrenica massacre dies in prison while serving life sentence for genocideFrom the archive:Fourteen years a fugitive: the hunt for the Butcher of BosniaRatko Mladić will die in jail. But go to Bosnia: you’ll see that he wonPeter BeaumontSenior international correspondentThu 27 Aug 2026 12.12 EDTFirst published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 10.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRatko Mladić, the infamous Serbian general who was serving a life sentence for genocide committed during the Bosnian war, has died in prison in The Hague.Mladić had been one of the main architects of the policy of ethnic cleansing during the Bosnian war. He wasconvicted of genocidefor orchestrating the 1995killing of at least 8,000 Muslims in the UN-designated “safe area” Srebrenica, the worst massacre in Europe since the second world war.Mladić, who was nicknamed the “Butcher of Bosnia”, had been in ill health after having a series of strokes.A UN international tribunal confirmed Mladić’s death, saying he had died in hospital in The Hague earlier in the day.“Mladić passed away today while hospitalised in The Hague,” the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals said in a statement, adding that judge Graciela Gatti Santana had ordered “a full inquiry into the circumstances” of his death.Described by the former UN rights chief Zeid Ra’ad al-Hussein as “the epitome of evil” after his conviction,Mladić was one of the most notorious figuresof the war that killed more than 100,000 people and left more than 1 million homeless.View image in fullscreenThe Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadžić (right) with Mladić in 1995. Karadžić was also sentenced to life imprisonment for genocide and war crimes.Photograph: Ranko Cukovic/ReutersHe commanded his troops to “scorch the brains” of Bosnian Muslim people and had boasted of being a “Serbian god”.The news of Mladić’s death was first broken on Serbian state television after his son, Darko, had spoken earlier about his father’s declining health.‘The voices of our dead have not faded away’: the fight for the memory of genocide in SrebrenicaRead moreMladić was sentenced by a UN tribunal to life imprisonment in 2017 over genocide and war crimes committed during Bosnia’s 1990s war. He was arrested in Serbia in 2011 after 16 years on the run.The slaughter in Srebrenica was the culmination of a brutal war that had lasted more than three ⁠years, during which Mladić oversaw the siege of Bosnia’s capital, Sarajevo, which was pounded daily by artillery, tank and sniper fire, killing 10,000 people.The goal of the Serbian leadership, which Mladić was tasked with implementing – as determined ⁠by the UN’s international criminal tribunal for ⁠the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) – was the forcible expulsion of ​Bosnian Muslims, Croats and other non-Serbs to clear Bosnian land for the creation of a greater Serbia.The tribunal found that Mladić, together with the late Serbian president Slobodan Milošević and the Bosnian Serb political leader Radovan Karadžić, were part of a criminal conspiracy to implement the plan.View image in fullscreenSlobodan Milošević.Photograph: Srdjan Ilic/AP“I do not recognise this court,” Mladić said at an ⁠ICTY hearing on his case in 2014. When he was sentenced, he shouted: “This is all lies, you are all liars!”The Serbian campaign culminated in the horror of Srebrenica when, after the withdrawal of Dutch UN peacekeeping forces, thousands of Bosnian men and boys were rounded up, killed and their bodies bulldozed into mass graves.View image in fullscreenMladić (front left) entering Srebrenica in 1995.Photograph: Sipa Press/Rex ShutterstockMladić had the siege filmed to show him praising his “lads” and haranguing the UN peacekeepers who misguidedly accepted his solemn word that the inhabitants would be safe in his hands.“We give this town to the Serb people as a gift,” Mladić said to the camera, claiming the victory as revenge against Muslim Turks, who had once held the area as part ‌of the Ottoman empire.The next day, Mladić’s forces were filmed handing out sweets to children, promising their safe passage. Meanwhile, thousands of men and boys were being readied for slaughter.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA screengrab from 12 July 1995 shows Mladić speaking to a young Muslim boy after he had assured residents of Srebrenica they would be safe.Photograph: APWhen Nato tried in 1995 to rein in his forces with the threat of limited airstrikes, his troops seized UN peacekeepers as human shields, chaining them to likely targets.14 years a fugitive: the hunt for Ratko Mladic, the Butcher of Bosnia | Julian BorgerRead moreThe son of a second world war partisan fighter killed in 1945, Mladić was, according to his family, born in March 1943 in the tiny Bosnian village of Bozinovici, putting his age at death at 83 (though official documents recorded his date of birth a year earlier, in 1942).Mladić was an officer in the communist Yugoslav People’s Army (JNA) when Yugoslavia’s disintegration began in 1991.When Bosnian Serbs rose in 1992 against Bosnia’s Muslim-led secession, Mladić was chosen to command the new Bosnian Serb army that swiftly overran 70% of the country.Dozens of towns were besieged with heavy weapons that once belonged to the JNA and villages were burned down, as 22,000 troops with the UN Protection Force stood by, more or less helplessly, under orders not to take sides.View image in fullscreenEdiba Salihović raises her hands as she reacts with other Bosnian women upon hearing the sentence at the end of Mladić’s trial in Potočari, near Srebrenica, in November 2017.Photograph: Amel Emrić/APA combination of western pressure, Nato strikes and covert US arms and training for Croats and ⁠Muslims gradually turned the tide against Mladić’s army. After the war, Mladić went into hiding, with the reformists ruling post-conflict Serbia not daring ​to move against a man who was a hero to a core of nationalist Serbs.Mladić continued to insist he was “a simple man” chosen to protect his people. When he was finally arrested in 2011, he put up no resistance. He had a heart ​attack in 2013 and seemed older than his years. By his own account, he felt like a frail old man.This month, a UN doctor said Mladić’s death “may occur at any time”, possibly within weeks, but his application for release was again rejected.View image in fullscreenMunira Subašić (pictured in 2019), from the Mothers of Srebrenica group, said she deplored that Mladić’s crimes were still being denied by many Bosnian Serbs.Photograph: Anadolu Agency/GettyMunira Subašić, from the Mothers of Srebrenica group, said she deplored that Mladić’s crimes were still being denied by many Bosnian Serbs. “Today, a major war criminal died, the criminal of the Balkans,” Subašić said. But while 31 years later mothers of victims were “still carrying the pain in our souls … we are still listening to denials, we are still listening to how Ratko Mladić was a hero for the Serbs”.Elizabeth Evenson, the international justice director at Human Rights Watch, said: “The death of Ratko Mladić, the former Bosnian Serb army commander found guilty of genocide, including the massacre of up to 8,000 Bosnian men and boys after the fall of Srebrenica, Bosnia, in July 1995, is a reminder of the ongoing need for justice, truth, and reparations in the western Balkans.“Full accountability for such terrible crimes, in Bosnia and elsewhere, demands commitment by governments to justice, even decades after the events themselves.”Explore more on these topicsRatko MladićSerbiaBosnia and HerzegovinaEuropeSrebrenica massacreRadovan KaradzicnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham accused of U-turn after initially backing political donations cap to fall below £500k | Party funding | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Campaigner says PM wrote in email he believed £500k cap should be reduced over time to guard against undue influences
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Exclusive: Campaigner says PM wrote in email he believed £500k cap should be reduced over time to guard against undue influences
Content: Other campaigners, including the broadcaster Carol Vorderman, are urging Andy Burnham not to back down over a donations cap in the face of opposition from trade unions.Photograph: WPA/GettyView image in fullscreenOther campaigners, including the broadcaster Carol Vorderman, are urging Andy Burnham not to back down over a donations cap in the face of opposition from trade unions.Photograph: WPA/GettyParty fundingBurnham accused of U-turn after initially backing political donations cap to fall below £500kExclusive: Campaigner says PM wrote in email he believed £500k cap should be reduced over time to guard against undue influencesKiran StaceyPolicy editorThu 27 Aug 2026 14.51 EDTFirst published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 14.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham recently supported an even lower donations cap than previously reported, according to correspondence seen by the Guardian, as the row over next week’s elections bill escalates.The prime minister wrote to a campaigner in May outlining his support for a £500,000 individual donations cap, which he said would “guard against the perception of any one party being unduly influenced or swayed by one person or organisation”.In a follow-up email seen by the Guardian, Burnham went on to say he believed the cap should gradually be reduced – a proposal now being put forward by the Labour MPStella Creasy.Campaigners are accusing Burnham of a U-turn afterthe Guardian reportedthe prime minister had decided not to back the attempts by Creasy and others to introduce a donations cap in next week’s elections bill.In his first message to Shaun Bowler, who runs the websitewakeupgb.co.uk, Burnham wrote: “I do think there should be a cap on political donations. This would guard against the perception of any one party being unduly influenced or swayed by one person or organisation.“As to the level, I think that would have to be subject to wider review of political funding but my gut feeling would suggest somewhere in the region of £500k.”In a second message, the then would-be MP for Makerfield said: “[I] would definitely want to see that reduced over time. I am in complete agreement that there needs to be wholesale culture change in Westminster.”Bowler has now written to the prime minister accusing him of abandoning his previous commitments. He wrote: “It appears you are going to break your promise to me – and the nation …. Weeks after being elected, you have made your first major U-turn.”Burnham drops support for political funding cap aimed at curbing mega-donorsRead moreHe added: “This is your chance to actually deliver the start of that cleanup. Show us that politics can be clean and trustworthy. Don’t surrender to the mess.”Other campaigners, including the broadcaster Carol Vorderman, are also urging the prime minister not to back down in the face of opposition from trade unions, who havewarned that a donations cap could undermine their ability to contributeto the Labour party.Senior figures at groups including Transparency International, Spotlight on Corruption and Greenpeace have also written to Burnham. In an open letter, they call for a “low and hard cap on all political donations”, adding: “We know you agree that politics should not be for sale. Please take action now to ensure it will not be under your leadership.”The issue will come to a head next week when MPs debate the next stage of the elections bill. The bill will lower the voting age to 16 and cap donations by Britons based abroad, but not on domestic donations.Creasy had put forward an amendment to cap domestic donations at £100,000, while her colleague put forward an amendment to cap them at £1m.Creasy has now changed her amendment to set the cap at £500,000, reducing in the second year to £100,000 unless ministers intervene to set it at a different level. The proposal, which has cross-party backing, mirrors what Burnham told Bowler he would support in May.The prime minister’s aides say that while he is not backing a donations cap next week, he is not ruling one out in the future. ALaboursource said: “This bill was designed to deliver our manifesto commitments on votes at 16 and to strengthen political donation rules to guard against foreign interference and that’s what the government is prioritising. But we’re not ruling out taking further steps to protect our democracy in the future.”Officials also said the government would not support an attempt by the Labour MP Anneliese Dodds to reduce the amount political parties can spend during an election campaign after the limit was raised by the previous Conservative government.Explore more on these topicsParty fundingLabourAndy BurnhamElectoral reformStella CreasyTrade unionsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Russia says UK ‘playing with fire’ amid reports CIA chief has warned Kremlin not to attack Nato | Russia | The Guardian
description: Moscow threatens retaliation after Andy Burnham says UK will help Ukraine start producing long-range missiles
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: Moscow threatens retaliation after Andy Burnham says UK will help Ukraine start producing long-range missiles
Content: Vladimir Putin in Moscow this week. Russia has made frequent threats against Ukraine’s western allies.Photograph: Mikhail Metzel/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenVladimir Putin in Moscow this week. Russia has made frequent threats against Ukraine’s western allies.Photograph: Mikhail Metzel/AFP/Getty ImagesRussiaRussia says UK ‘playing with fire’ amid reports CIA chief has warned Kremlin not to attack NatoMoscow threatens retaliation after Andy Burnham says UK will help Ukraine start producing long-range missilesPeter BeaumontandJessica ElgotThu 27 Aug 2026 15.26 EDTFirst published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 07.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussia has said it could retaliate against the UK for its support of Kyiv by striking military targets inside and outsideUkraine, amid reports that the director of the CIA warned the Kremlin against attacking Nato during a secretive visit this week.Andy Burnham, Britain’s prime minister, said on Monday the UK wouldallow Kyiv access to classified technologyto start ⁠its own production of Storm Shadow ​long-range ​cruise missiles. France has also agreed to supply missile technology. Maria ⁠Zakharova, Russia’s foreign ministry spokesperson, said on Thursday Britain and France were “playing ⁠with ​fire”.Responding to the latest Russian threats, a Ministry of Defence official reiterated UK support for Ukraine. “Britain stands shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine and we are committed to providing the equipment Ukraine needs to defend itself against Putin’s illegal invasion.Russiashould be in no doubt about the resolve of this government to stand against Russian aggression, in Ukraine and against the UK and our allies,” they said.The Wall Street Journal reported thata visit by John Ratcliffe, the CIA chief, to Moscowon Tuesday had followed a US intelligence assessment that Russia could be planning to test Nato with a limited assault on an allied country. This could range from a cyber-attack to a small-scale incursion, probably in a Baltic nation.Russia has made frequent threats against Ukraine’s western allies during the war, including thinly veiled nuclear threats and others apparently aimed at diplomatic missions in Kyiv.View image in fullscreenK2 Black Panther main battle tanks will be deployed by Poland near the border with Russia’s Kaliningrad region as Nato countries neighbouring Russia move to increase their military readiness.Photograph: Roman Koziel/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockAsked ‌to comment ‌on the reports of Ratcliffe’s visit – and despite Thursday morning’s threat against UK targets – Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin spokesperson, said: “A lot of this kind of scare-story material is being published right now. Of course, it has ‌nothing to do with reality and nothing to do ​with the intentions of the Russian Federation.”The intense scrutiny around the Ratcliffe trip and Russia’s intentions comes amid a new report over shortfalls of missile interceptors available inEurope.A report by the Associated Press says the US military is experiencing a “beyond critical” shortage of advanced missile interceptors in Europe largely driven by Donald Trump’s war with Iran, according to a US defence official in Europe and aNatoofficial, raising concerns about vulnerabilities in Nato countries to a potential Russian attack.The US defence official said the most concerning shortfall involved Patriot missile interceptors, which can shoot down Russia’s high-speed ballistic missiles. The Nato official confirmed the low inventories of Patriots among American and Nato forces in Europe. Both spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military matters.Russia is believed to be contemplating a further escalation of its war with Ukraine after months ofescalating Ukrainian attackson Russia’s oil refining infrastructure and other sites, which are imposing an increasing economic toll.View image in fullscreenA Japanese government sign in Tokyo says ‘the Northern Territories are an inherent part of Japan’s territory’, referring to the Russian-controlled Southern Kuril Islands. Russia has invoked its nuclear threat against Japan over the claim.Photograph: Yuichi Yamazaki/AFP/Getty ImagesThe Kremlin has adopted ever more bellicose rhetoric, much of it aimed at a domestic audience, as the war in Ukraine has been brought to its doorstep.In the space of a few days Russia has invoked the threat of its nuclear arsenal against Japan over its territorial claim to the disputed Kuril Islands. It has described relations with the US as a “crisis” and at a historic low point.Ratcliffe’s reported warning mirrored onemade by his predecessor, William Burns, in 2021before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine – which Moscow also denied it was contemplating.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionConcerns over Moscow’s intentions have been increasing amid a rise in incidents of Russian hybrid warfare attributed to Moscow across Europe, from cyber-attacks and drones to arson, at facilities associated with supporting Ukraine’s war efforts.Russia and the US have tried to play down Ratcliffe’s meeting with his Russian counterparts: Trump on Wednesday described the visit as “semi routine”. However, the unusual nature of the encounter has caused intense speculation in the west and Russia.The US president continued to play down the encounter on Thursday, telling Axios that Ratcliffe had arrived in Moscow with “no message” and claiming there was “nothing unusual” about the meeting.Asked later by reporters about reports about the CIA director Ratcliffe had delivered a warning to Russia, Trump replied: “I don’t want to comment on that, but they’re not going to attack.”Nato countries neighbouring Russia have moved quickly to increase their military readiness.Polandthis week announced it had taken delivery of its first shipment of South Korean Black Panther main battle tanks, which will be deployed near the border with Russia’s Kaliningrad region.Cezary Tomczyk, Poland’s deputy defence minister, said this month Warsaw was preparing for the possibility of a full-scale conflict.Tomczyk toldSuper Express media: “We are preparing for war, hoping it never happens.”Explore more on these topicsRussiaUkraineNatoPolandEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Actor Peter Cullen, voice of Optimus Prime and Eeyore, dies aged 85 | Movies | The Guardian
description: Montreal-born actor also voiced KARR in Knight Rider and the monster in Predator, having started his career on Canadian TV and radio
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Montreal-born actor also voiced KARR in Knight Rider and the monster in Predator, having started his career on Canadian TV and radio
Content: Peter Cullen was best known as the voice of Optimus Prime in the Transformers franchise.Photograph: E Charbonneau/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeter Cullen was best known as the voice of Optimus Prime in the Transformers franchise.Photograph: E Charbonneau/Getty ImagesMoviesActor Peter Cullen, voice of Optimus Prime and Eeyore, dies aged 85Montreal-born actor also voiced KARR in Knight Rider and the monster in Predator, having started his career on Canadian TV and radioNadeem BadshahThu 27 Aug 2026 14.56 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 16.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePeter Cullen, the actor behind the voice of characters including Eeyore in Disney’s Winnie the Pooh franchise and Optimus Prime in Transformers, has died aged 85.He died on Wednesday at his home inLos Angeles, a statement said.The Canadian actor began his biggest role – as Optimus Prime, the honourable leader of the Autobots – for the Transformers TV series in 1984. He returned for seven Hollywood Transformers films from 2007 to 2023 and other spinoffs.Cullen voiced the melancholic donkey Eeyore in The New Adventures of Winnie the Pooh TV series from the late 1980s as well as numerous related shows, films and games.View image in fullscreenPeter Cullen, seen here in 2014, voiced Optimus Prime from 1984.Photograph: Jim Ruymen/UPI/ShutterstockHis other notable roles included the roars of King Kong for the 1976 remake, and KARR – Knight Automated Roving Robot, the evil counterpart to KITT – in the Knight Rider series in 1982 and 2009.The actor is also credited with coming up with the eerie clicking sounds that emerged from the mouth of the monster in the Arnold Schwarzenegger film Predator in 1987.His family said: “Peter Cullen passed away peacefully, surrounded by his loving family – and held in the hearts of his many friends and countless fans worldwide.“His family asks that you honour his remarkable legacy by serving your communities and leading others with compassion, integrity, and loyalty and always remember, ‘be strong enough to be gentle’.”The Montreal-born actor began his career on Canadian TV and radio and was then a regular on programmes including The Sonny & Cher Show and The Smothers Brothers Comedy Hour before deciding to concentrate on voice acting.Cullen said Optimus Prime’s resonant and authoritative voice was inspired by his older brother Larry, a retired captain in the US Marine Corps who had served in the Vietnam war, who suggested he should play the character as “a real hero, don’t be a Hollywood hero”.“He said, ‘Don’t go yelling and screaming. He’s strong enough to be gentle’,” Cullen recalled. “And that resonated with me, and I could hear his voice all the way to the audition. When he drops down, when he gets serious, is where I found Optimus Prime.”Cullen gave Larry a cut of the wages he received for playing Optimus Prime until his brother’s death in 2011.In a 2014 NPR interview, Cullen acknowledged that he initially approached playing Optimus Prime with puzzlement. “I auditioned like everybody else,” he said. “I was told it was a hero, and I was told it was a truck.”The actor’s performance earned him a Daytime Emmy nomination for outstanding performer in an animated programme in 2011, and he was honoured with a lifetime achievement award at the Children’s & Family Emmy Awards in 2023.When the director Michael Bay resurrected the Transformers franchise for a film in 2007 starring Shia LaBeouf, Cullen told IGN: “I describe it as kind of slipping into an old pair of very comfortable shoes that you haven’t worn for a while. I just slipped right into them, and they felt as good as the last time I put them on.”Explore more on these topicsFilmTelevisionLos AngelesCanadanewsShareReuse this content

title: Uefa raises stakes with criminal complaint in battle to unseat Infantino | Uefa | The Guardian
description: Uefa has begun a legal process against the embattled Fifa president but it will still be an uphill struggle to remove him
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Uefa has begun a legal process against the embattled Fifa president but it will still be an uphill struggle to remove him
Content: The Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, with his Uefa counterpart Aleksander Ceferin in 2021. The two organisations are locked in a war of words over Fifa’s abandoned FFE proposal.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAView image in fullscreenThe Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, with his Uefa counterpart Aleksander Ceferin in 2021. The two organisations are locked in a war of words over Fifa’s abandoned FFE proposal.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAUefaAnalysisUefa raises stakes with criminal complaint in battle to unseat InfantinoMatt HughesUefa has begun a legal process against the embattled Fifa president but it will still be an uphill struggle to remove himThu 27 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 16.58 EDTShareAnyone who interpreted Uefa’s decision to withdraw a proposed boycott of Fifa competitions,revealed by the Guardian on Wednesday, as a backward step in the attempt to remove Gianni Infantino as Fifa’s president has been quickly disabused of that notion.In a stunning development that overshadowed one of the biggest days in the European football calendar as national football federation and club executives gathered for the Champions League draw in Monte Carlo, Uefa announced it waspreparing to make a legal complaintagainst Infantino in Switzerland alleging “criminal mismanagement” for his role in the failed World Cup sell-off plan.Uefa, having removed the immediate pressure on Fifa on one front bypermitting European teams to playin next month’s Under-20 Women’s World Cup and October’s senior Women’s World Cup qualifiers, has dramatically increased the stakes on another.The first step in that legal process is seeking disclosure in the United States of documents relating to the abandonedFifaForward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, which Uefa described in a 56-page document sent to three US courts as having an “absurdly low enterprise value of only approximately $20bn” (£14.7bn).From the moment it became clear Infantino would not resign after withdrawing the FFE plan four days after it became public,Uefahas been pursuing the valuation issue, which if the sale had progressed would have enabled Joshua Kushner’s Thrive Capital to buy 21% of future Fifa revenues in perpetuity for $4.2bn.The Guardian revealed on 6 August that Uefa was commissioning an independent valuation of FFE amid concerns Infantino was planning to sell off football’s crown jewel on the cheap, a feeling exacerbated by the fact Fifa’s sales deck did not contain any information on the valuation process or evidence of a competitive tender.As one source who questioned Fifa’s valuation said this month: “We need to find out if they were selling the World Cup at a knockdown price.” The intention to bring a criminal complaint is the logical extension of this process.View image in fullscreenThe four-year cycle leading to this summer’s World Cup yielded $15bn in revenue for Fifa.Photograph: Claudio Thoma/EPAEven the most cursory of inquiries over the past few weeks vindicated Uefa’s concerns. Fifa’s revenue for the four-year cycle that culminated in this summer’s World Cup was $15bn, leading market analysts to suggest that $20bn was a low valuation, particularly as the proposal did not appear to include provisions to prevent expansion and the creation of new tournaments.Kushner’s subsequent purchase of the LA Lakers with the former Disney chief Bob Iger for $12.5bn further convinced Uefa that Thrive Capital had been given a sweetheart deal by Infantino, a conviction underlined by its suspicion that Infantino was lining up a lucrative role worth tens of millions of pounds a year as FFE’s chair after standing down as Fifa’s president, which he plans to do in 2031 if he wins a further, final term.Infantino’s determination to cling to office – demonstrated by his decision to enter campaign mode byattending a meeting of the Caribbean Football Unionlast weekend in the Dominican Republic where, as the Guardian revealed, he suddenly approved several funding projects – emboldened Uefa further.Uefa has taken the legal route after being thwarted in numerous requests to Fifa to disclose documents. It has made court filings in New York, Florida and Colorado to obtain papers it may submit to Swiss courts seeking criminal charges.Just as significant as the attempt to take Infantino to court in his adopted country is Uefa’s attempt to rally Fifa members behind it in its attempt to unseat him via March’s presidential election.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor all Uefa’s public bullishness that Infantino’s race is run, several senior figures there and among its allies at Concacaf – the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation – have admitted concerns to the Guardian that they are struggling to get many member associations outside Europe to turn against him.Over the past few weeks several FAs have privately indicated it may take evidence of criminal activity, or at least proof that Infantino would have been personally enriched by the FFE venture, for them to abandon him.Even those with a brief knowledge of Fifa’s history would agree that the rebels concerned about momentum to unseat Infantino stalling have a point. Although he loves to paint the world governing body as the ultimate democracy underpinned by a one-member, one-vote system, the reality is anything but. Although elections are held every four years there have been only three permanent presidents in the past 52 years, and the last to leave office after a vote was England’s Sir Stanley Rous in 1974.Rous’s conqueror, the Brazilian João Havelange, resigned after 24 years and was later found to have accepted bribes related to the sale of media rights by a Fifa ethics committee. His successor, Sepp Blatter, stood down after winning five elections in the midst of an FBI investigation in 2015, which has resulted in more than 20 criminal convictions in the US and could lead to more.Any hope among the rebels that the Swiss authorities will come to their aid and bring Infantino to court should be tempered by those authorities’ long history of turning a blind eye to Fifa corruption, which meant intervention from the FBI was required to expose and punish it.Explore more on these topicsUefaFifaGianni InfantinoFootball politicsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Fightland review – 50 Cent’s farcical boxing show is featherweight at best  | Television | The Guardian
description: This boxing drama wants its sex, drugs, bling and violence – but isn’t willing or naughty enough to truly go for it. Instead, it ends up as just a long, bruising slog
Author: Jack Seale
Headline: This boxing drama wants its sex, drugs, bling and violence – but isn’t willing or naughty enough to truly go for it. Instead, it ends up as just a long, bruising slog
Content: Far too good for this material … Howard Charles, right, as Duke Kilroy in Fightland.Photograph: Fightland 2025 Starz/PAView image in fullscreenFar too good for this material … Howard Charles, right, as Duke Kilroy in Fightland.Photograph: Fightland 2025 Starz/PATV reviewTelevisionReviewFightland review – 50 Cent’s farcical boxing show is featherweight at bestThis boxing drama wants its sex, drugs, bling and violence – but isn’t willing or naughty enough to truly go for it. Instead, it ends up as just a long, bruising slogJack SealeThu 27 Aug 2026 17.05 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 20.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFightland is what you might, for a joke, have calleda drama that’s like MobLandbut with boxing. That they have gone with that as the title of the new show from G-Unit Film & Television, the production company founded by the rapper Curtis “50 Cent” Jackson, is an immediate warning that this is not a series that bursts with originality, passion or technical finesse. At best, Fightland asks whether what it’s got will just about do, and hopes you’ll distractedly say yes.Howard Charles is Maduka “Duke” Kilroy, a British boxer who, when we first meet him, is in Las Vegas, winning the world heavyweight championship. Everything’s going for him: he’s the champ and Joy (Deborah Ayorinde), the woman he enjoys a post-bout warmdown with on the silk sheets of a penthouse suite, seems receptive to his plan to take their relationship further. It’s a risky goal given that Joy’s husband is Kingsley Marshall (Nicholas Pinnock), Duke’s manager, who is also London’s top drug dealer; we’ve seen him brutally break the leg of a journalist who asks him about the secret drug-based wing of his empire.View image in fullscreenRisky business … Deborah Ayorinde as Joy with Nicholas Pinnock as Kingsley.Photograph: Starz/PASure enough, later that evening Duke is set on by goons, presumably hired by Kingsley after discovering that his golden boy has double-crossed him. The resulting fracas leaves Duke bereaved and, after he fights back a little too much, in prison. On his release six years later, he returns to London, bent on revenge. His plan is to pose as a penitent lost son, rejoin the Marshall crime/boxing family and bring it down from the inside. But Kingsley has gone awol, so instead Duke is up against the big man’s two heirs, who are a two-for-one cliche of a gangster patriarch’s pampered adult children: Zeek (Charles Babalola) is weak, vain and impetuous, while Cece (Anita-Joy Uwajeh) is smart, ruthless and overlooked.View image in fullscreen‘A two for one cliche of a gangster patriarch’s adult children’ … Charles Babalola as Zeek and Anita-Joy Uwajeh as Cece with Pinnock as their father.Photograph: Fightland 2025 Starz/PAThe setup sounds simple enough, but Fightland fumbles it on account of its fundamental flaw, which is that nobody’s motivation for anything is ever clear. Perhaps because it’s banking a big twist for the back half of the season, the show is coy to the point of outright confusion on who knows what about the affair and the attack on Duke, what the repercussions of his imprisonment were, and where Kingsley might be. In scenes in which characters ought to discuss these things, they awkwardly don’t, although if there’s a plot point the show wants to remind us of, oh boy does it crowbar that into the dialogue. You are evidently meant to let it wash over you; viewers who have a tendency to say, “Wait, why did they do that?” or “Hang on, that isn’t going to work because …” are in for a long, bruising slog.Fightland wants its violence, sex, bling, betrayals and bricks of illegal powder, and isn’t too fussed how it gets there. Except, it’s not interested enough in any of those things. If we’re going to do a sex-and-violence crime caper, let’s get properly naughty with it. But Fightland has almost no bedroom mojo and the fight scenes are perfunctory and weirdly short. They often offer tantalising premises – a duel to the death with a coked-up, machete-wielding strip club owner, for example, whose blade keeps clanging against the stage’s chrome pole – before petering out. If you can’t be excellent, at least be excessive; Fightland constantly holds back. Even boxing, which offers all kinds of ready-made metaphors for the power games played by businesspeople and criminal kingpins, is relegated to the background. The scenes in boxing gyms could be taking place anywhere.View image in fullscreen‘Drug Connect???’ … Howard Charles as Duke Kilroy.Photograph: Fightland 2025 Starz/PACharles is a formidable presence but he’s far too good for this material, as is Pinnock, which makes the decision to quickly remove the latter from the action even more bewildering. They are both more than capable of fronting a rich, layered character drama, which Fightland doesn’t attempt, or a knowingly camp romp, which it can’t muster the energy for either. The script is deliberately funny on occasion, but so rarely that you almost question whether it is deliberate; it’s not as unintentionally funny as you’d hope, either, although Duke’s homemade photoboard of the Marshalls and their acolytes, featuring the scrawled caption “DRUG CONNECT??”, is one highlight.Fightland moves quickly and smoothly enough that all this may not matter too much. Maybe Cece’s nonsensical plan to make millions by introducing casino sportsbooks to the UK, a country that already has an established betting shop/online bookmaker industry, will somehow work. Maybe the South American cartel Duke is in league with will conquer London, despite their British operation apparently consisting entirely of Duke and one guy they have sent over. Maybe Fightland will survive and be allowed to rumble on for three or four seasons. But it’s a featherweight contender.Fightland aired on Sky Atlantic and is on Now in the UK and Stan in AustraliaExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewBoxingreviewsShareReuse this content

title: AI-proof? Younger workers desert the digital world for traditional crafts | Work & careers | The Guardian
description: In a disrupted job market people are turning to heritage crafts such as bookbinding, metalwork and boatbuilding
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: In a disrupted job market people are turning to heritage crafts such as bookbinding, metalwork and boatbuilding
Content: Eryn Lawley, Imogen Carney and Harriet Bone, apprentices at Ludlow Bookbinders in Shropshire.Photograph: Andrew Fox/The GuardianView image in fullscreenEryn Lawley, Imogen Carney and Harriet Bone, apprentices at Ludlow Bookbinders in Shropshire.Photograph: Andrew Fox/The GuardianWork & careersAI-proof? Younger workers desert the digital world for traditional craftsIn a disrupted job market people are turning to heritage crafts such as bookbinding, metalwork and boatbuildingLauren AlmeidaThu 27 Aug 2026 09.38 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 14.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s a bleak moment for young peopleentering the workforce for the first time. For decades, a university degree seemed to promise a stable career – but entry-level white-collar jobs across almost all sectors arebeing disrupted by AI. Budding accountants, software engineers and junior lawyers increasingly find themselves displaced by cheap automation.Even creative fields are struggling against AI tech that can produce artwork, lengthy prose or complex design briefs in seconds.But many young workers have responded by turning to what they see as “AI-proof” heritage crafts. These are the centuries-old, hands-on jobs, such as boat-making, metalwork or bookbinding, that require specialist knowledge built on creative judgment and dexterity, skills not yet mastered by AI.Eryn Lawley, a 27-year-old politics graduate, said future-proofing her career meant walking away from the digital world. She is now a second-year bookbinder apprentice at Ludlow Bookbinders in Shropshire, learning a trade whose core techniques have not changed for centuries.“Even just staring at a screen too long was bad for me,” she said. “I always wanted to do something more material, and I think there is something more inherently valuable to something when it is made by a person.”The work at Ludlow is slow, detailed and tactile. Thebookbinding processis almost entirely by hand, using Victorian-built presses, foil-blocking machines and glue brushes.“People are discovering that, as everything is already decided for you by a computer or algorithm, being able to make or own something physically is good,”Lawley said. “And it is very satisfying to repeat a task to perfection. It is meditative as a job so it is extremely low-cortisol.”View image in fullscreenLucky Emerson, a Cox London apprentice.Photograph: Inge Clemente/Cox LondonPaul Kidson, Ludlow chief executive and a fourth-generation bookbinder, said an influx of interest from young people represented a lifeline for a rapidly shrinking industry.
