He estimates there are now fewer than 50 handcraft-operating bookbinders in Britain today.“British bookbinding has a terrific reputation across the world, but like so many things in the 50s, 60s and 70s, the training just started to dry up,” Kidson said. “All the formal apprentice schemes collapsed in the early 1980s, and the industry got no training at all.“We have to train our own people because you can’t recruit at volume because there aren’t any [courses]. Fortunately there is now a desire among a lot of people to want to have the satisfaction of actually making something.”There is no lack of commercial demand. High-end publishers are betting that shoppers will pay a premium for objects that are crafted by human hands. Joanna Reynolds, chief executive of the Folio Society book publisher – which partnered with Ludlow for a limited edition release of a Game of Thrones book – said the company rejected generative AI tools in its creative processes.“We do not use AI in terms of our art,” she said. “We believe in the importance of supporting the creative world, and we know there is huge pressure on them at the moment. Their skills and their abilities need to be supported by as many people as possible.”The number of young people hoping to fill these creative posts is growing rapidly. Cox London, a design house that specialises in artistic metalwork, started its apprenticeship scheme last year. Nicola Cox, a co-founder, said this year the company received more than 160 applications for two apprenticeship places.“People want to make things and work with materials, [to] have that closeness with it,” she said. “There is AI-proofness about art that is made with someone’s hands. There is a real resonance in something that has a mark and the energy of human hands.”For Lucky Emerson, an apprentice at Cox London, there is a “worrying feeling” that AI is taking over the creative world.“The physicality of actually making things is incomparable, especially when people crave originality. Even though technology has advanced, handcrafted art is considered a lot more valuable and will always remain that way.”View image in fullscreenNazifa Tabassum, an apprentice at Cox London.Photograph: Inge Clemente/Cox LondonNazifa Tabassum, also an apprentice at Cox London, said she did not think AI would replace her work, but that it could change it.“For me it isn’t just about making things with my hands,” she said. “It’s about continuously developing my skills, and using technology where it adds value, while still providing the expertise and craftsmanship that people can’t easily automate.“I see AI as a tool that can assist, but not something that replaces, the satisfaction and value of skilled manual, handcrafted work.”At the National Theatre in London, technical apprenticeships span everything from IT to traditional wig-making, costume design, prop-making and metalwork.“Our apprenticeships are partly about the need to create a more representative workforce, both for the National Theatre and for the [wider] creative sector,” said Kath Geraghty, head of technical qualifications.“It is also about plugging the skill gap. These theatre crafts are dying out – our metalworkers are all over 50, wig-making as a skill is really dying. There’s a real need to create our own talent.“And it’s always been about creating a skilled workforce for the wider creative sector beyond theatre, such as film, TV and broadcast.”View image in fullscreenSarah Ray-Dobson, an apprentice prop-maker at the National Theatre.Photograph: Cameron SlaterSarah Ray-Dobson, a 27-year-old apprentice prop-maker at the National Theatre, said she felt her practice had been shielded from AI disruption that affected other creative pursuits.“Everything I’ve been doing for the past two years is very hands-on,” she said. “At my level, it has not been affected by AI.”But Geraghty adds that, like many employers, the National Theatre is struggling with the huge number of AI-generated applications for its apprenticeship programme.“We used to think that 100 applicants was a popular apprenticeship,” she said. “In this most recent round of recruitment, we had 728 applications for one role.“We haven’t yet worked out how to manage it, because it’s not viable for our staff to read 700 applications with care and attention. But the job market that young people are in is difficult, and they are applying for anything they can.”Explore more on these topicsWork & careersCraftEmployabilityAI (artificial intelligence)ApprenticeshipsManufacturing sectorGraduate careersfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Marketing meltdown: why has Andrew Garfield’s new film suddenly added Robin Hood? | Andrew Garfield | The Guardian
description: Paul Greengrass drama The Uprising was supposed to be a historical epic about the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381 – but a strange new campaign has inserted a surprising figure
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: Paul Greengrass drama The Uprising was supposed to be a historical epic about the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381 – but a strange new campaign has inserted a surprising figure
Content: Andrew Garfield in The Uprising.Photograph: Entertainment Pictures/AlamyView image in fullscreenAndrew Garfield in The Uprising.Photograph: Entertainment Pictures/AlamyAndrew GarfieldMarketing meltdown: why has Andrew Garfield’s new film suddenly added Robin Hood?Paul Greengrass drama The Uprising was supposed to be a historical epic about the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381 – but a strange new campaign has inserted a surprising figureStuart HeritageThu 27 Aug 2026 09.58 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 14.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNobody likes to have the full plot of a movie spoiled before they’ve even seen it. However, sometimes this can be taken to the extreme. Take the newPaul Greengrassmovie, The Uprising, for example. It is two weeks away from its US release and not only does nobody know the plot, but nobody seems to know what it is even about. Seriously, nobody at all. The film’s distributors just spent yesterday squabbling in public about whether Robin Hood was in it or not.Here’s what we know so far. Initially, all the trailers and promotional materials made The Uprising look like a film about the Peasants’ Revolt that tore through England in 1381. And this was very exciting, since the revolt was a thrilling moment in history that has been bizarrely underserved by Hollywood over the years. Most exciting of all, though, it sounded like it fit exactly into Greengrass’s wheelhouse: full of action and realism and political awareness.Hollywood encore: how ‘pro-shot’ Broadway shows became a major draw on the big screenRead moreBut that all changed this week, when the film’s US distributor, Focus Features,announcedthe film’sfull title on social media. What had once simply been The Uprising was now The Uprising: The Rise of Robin Hood. It added a new synopsis, reading: “Set against the true events of the Uprising that helped inspire the legend of Robin Hood, [Andrew Garfield’s character] forms an army of the people to face the King’s might in a fight for justice.”Needless to say, this was both confusing and frustrating. Frustrating because it sounded like a historically grounded and socially relevant film would now contain a character best known for once being played by a cartoon fox, and confusing because the stories of Robin Hood were set during the reign of Richard the Lionheart, who died nearly two centuries before the Peasants’ Revolt took place.Andrew Garfield’s character seemed to be at the centre of the mix-up. Officially credited as “The Ploughman”, we can assume that he has been named after William Langland’s poem Piers Plowman, which was written in the years leading up to the revolt. The poem is known for containing the first unambiguous literary reference to Robin Hood. It is also worth pointing out that, in 2022 when the film was firstannounced, The Uprising was set to be called The Hood.Realistically, several things might have happened here. The first is that Greengrass took a deeply uncharacteristic swing while making this film, and decided to augment the story of Wat Tyler with a time-traveling Robin Hood, blazing into the future to help the downtrodden people of England in their hour of need. The second is that he’s suggesting the Peasants’ Revolt helped reshape a mythical figure into a symbol of working-class resistance, at which point the distributors figured, “Screw it, let’s just tell everyone that Robin Hood is in it.”The Death of Robin Hood review – Hugh Jackman darkens a heroic tale in grim dramaRead moreThis backfired immediately. Not only because people were exasperated by the thought of yet another Robin Hood movie – not for nothing did this year’s A24 movieThe Death of Robin Hoodflop hard, recouping less than half of its production budget worldwide – but because the film’s UK distributor is adamant that the film has absolutely nothing to do with the guy at all.Contacted byMetroyesterday, Entertainment Film Distributors issued a statement reading: “The Uprising is a historical epic about the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381, not Robin Hood. The UK marketing campaign does not make any reference to Robin Hood. Marketing materials posted by other countries that may appear in the UK online and on social media referencing Robin Hood are not issued or approved by us.”Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onplatform.x.com. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueWhat we’re left with is a film that urgently needs to define exactly what it is before it comes out. As things stand, somebody is almost certainly going to feel conned.If the UK distributor is right, there will be those who hear this week’s new title, rush to the cinema in the hope of watching a Robin Hood film and leave disappointed because they were actually presented with a muddy meditation on class warfare based on a 700-year-old allegorical poem.But if the US distributor is right, then there will be those who rush to the cinema to watch a historically rigorous reenactment of one of the most important moments in British history and leave disappointed because Garfield turns up in a DeLorean halfway through, winks directly at the camera and then gets off with a busty maiden.The Uprising might be one of those things. It might be both. For all anyone knows, given the utter ineptitude of its own communications, it could even turn out to be Cloverfield 4 and climax with a scene where the peasants, the aristocrats, Robin Hood, King Arthur and Paddington Bear all team up to defeat a howling kaiju. At this point, who would even care?Explore more on these topicsAndrew GarfieldPaul GreengrassAction and adventure filmsDrama filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The best mattress for side sleepers – and how to choose one, according to doctors and osteopaths | Sleep | The Guardian
description: Do you need a soft mattress if you sleep on your side, or are firm models better for your back? And what about pillows? Here’s what the experts say
Author: Jane Hoskyn
Headline: Do you need a soft mattress if you sleep on your side, or are firm models better for your back? And what about pillows? Here’s what the experts say
Content: Side sleeper? The right mattress can make all the difference.Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSide sleeper? The right mattress can make all the difference.Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterSleepThe best mattress for side sleepers – and how to choose one, according to doctors and osteopathsDo you need a soft mattress if you sleep on your side, or are firm models better for your back? And what about pillows? Here’s what the experts sayThe best mattresses, testedThe best mattresses for back painJane HoskynThu 27 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMost of us, me included, sleep on our sides. Drooling into yourpillowand giving yourself a dead arm may not be as photogenic as Sleeping Beauty lying prettily on her back, but it’s probably better for you. Studies have found that sleeping on your left side can help reducesnoring,sleep apnoeaandacid reflux, and the experts I spoke to for this article say side sleeping is good for your back and your sleep.Side sleeping brings its challenges, though, and I don’t just mean the drool. The curves of your body need somewhere to go. If yourmattressisn’t cushioning your hips and shoulders, or your knees are pressing against each other, you may struggle to sleep well andexperience aches and pains. An overly soft surface can also cause problems, as you’ll know if you’ve ever spent the night on a friend’s concave sofa.To find out why, I asked osteopaths, doctors and sleep experts what’s going on at a musculoskeletal level when you spend the night snoozing on your side. Here, I’ll reveal how their advice can help you find your ideal mattress – and the pillow that’ll make it even more comfy.Not too firm, and not too softView image in fullscreen‘You need enough cushioning for your pressure points, without sinking in too far.’Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianAs a side sleeper, you’re already doing well. “It’s the best sleeping position for back pain, as it encourages a neutral spine,” says Michael Fatica, osteopath and co-founder of theBack in Shapeprogramme for pain relief. It doesn’t guarantee it, though.To demonstrate, lie on the floor. First lie flat on your back, and then on your side in your usual sleeping position. When you’re on your side, your “pressure points” – hips, shoulders and knees – bear more load than when you’re on your back, and this pushes your spine into a curve instead of letting it lie straight, or “aligned”.“Spinal alignment is even more crucial for side sleepers,” says Dr Deborah Lee, who works with online pharmacyDr Foxand bed retailerComfybedss. “On your side, there’s a natural tendency for the spine to curve or twist if the mattress isn’t providing the right support. This contributes to backache, neck soreness and general disrupted sleep, affecting your mood and energy levels the next day.”Your first priority, then, is to make sure you have enough cushioning to accommodate your pressure points. “If your hips can sink a little bit [into the mattress], that helps to keep your spine steady,” says Fatica. “Women may need a softer or a more forgiving mattress, because they tend to have a more exaggerated hips-to-waist ratio than a guy. One of the things we suggest to patients, especially women, is to put a little towel or cushion in their side at waist level to even out their spine if their mattress is too hard.”Too much cushioning is not the answer, though. “Don’t go to the opposite extreme and buy a super-soft mattress,” says Barry Rickhuss, sleep product specialist at Mattress Next Day. “If your shoulders and hips are sinking too deeply, that pulls your spine out of alignment, too.”How to choose the best mattress for side sleepingView image in fullscreen‘Rather than trust the medium-firm tag, try a mattress for yourself.’Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianAll the experts I spoke to recommended a medium-firm mattress for side sleepers. As I’ve discovered by testing dozens of mattresses, though, that description is a broad church. A couple of “medium-firm” models were so firm they gave me lumbar (lower back) pain, and one or two were so soft they left me with neck ache because my neck was craning upwards on to my relatively firm pillow. Rather than trust the medium-firm tag, try a mattress for yourself.Start with your own mattress, to see if it’s still working for you. Lie on it in your usual sleeping position and ask someone to look at your back. “They’ll be able to see if your pelvis is sitting too high or low and putting a bend in your spine,” says Fatica. If your spine is neutral, it should form a relatively straight line from your neck through your back to your pelvis when viewed from behind. If your tailbone curves up, the mattress is too firm. If your bum sinks, it’s too soft.It’s useful to be able to lie on a mattress in a showroom, especially if you take your trusty spine-checker along to check for that line when you’re lying down, but a two-minute test isn’t really long enough to judge a mattress. “You might lie down and say, ‘oh, this is comfy’,” says Fatica, “but will it be comfy after eight hours? A lot of mattresses now come with long trial periods, and that tends to be the best approach.”Most of thebest mattresseswe’ve tested have free trial of 100 nights or more, and a couple (such as theSimba Hybrid Probelow) stretch to double that. In my experience the brands keep their word on these trials, collecting your mattress for free if you don’t get along with it. Just make sure to keep it in good condition: a mattress protector is essential during any trial period.Hybrid mattresses proved particularly popular with the experts I spoke to. “A hybrid mattress, with traditional springs for support and a layer of foam for cushioning, offers the right amount of sink for your hips and shoulders when you sleep on your side,” says Rickhuss. A foam layer is also recommended by Hannah Hayden, mattress and bedding buyer at Dreams. “Memory foam is particularly effective in adapting to body contours and relieving pressure,” says Hayden, “although hybrids with a plush comfort layer provide good support while maintaining some responsiveness.”The prices below reflect current bank holiday offersBest hybrid mattress for side sleepers:Otty Original HybridOttyOriginal Hybrid, double£540£540 with code FILTER10 at OttyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianDouble, £540 with code FILTER10 at OttyOtty’s flagship hybrid mattress combines tall pocket springs with layers of foam to create a delicious balance of support and cushioning. As with most of the hybrids I’ve tested, the Otty is a “bed-in-a-box” mattress that comes vacuum-shrunk, so you can get a king or even a super king size up narrow stairs before you open it.Read our fullOtty Original Hybrid reviewOttyOriginal Hybrid, double£540£540 with code FILTER10 at OttyBest mattress for side sleepers with a 200-night trial:Simba Hybrid ProSimbaHybrid Pro£909.30£909.30 at SimbaView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianDouble, £909.30 at SimbaSimba’s luxurious hybrid mattress was love at first sleep for me. It was just soft enough to accommodate the curves of my small side-sleeping body, but had enough pushback to make my back feel well supported. It may be a little too soft for some side sleepers, but the 200-night free trial gives you ample time to find out.Read our fullSimba Hybrid Pro reviewSimbaHybrid Pro£909.30£909.30 at SimbaBest mattress topper for side sleepers:Simba Hybrid mattress topperSimbaHybrid mattress topper£296.65£296.65 at SimbaView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianDouble, £296.65 at SimbaIf you have a firm pocket-sprung mattress that’s still in good nick but need a little more cushioning, a mattress topper could prove to be an excellent buy. Simba’s topper contains a layer of micro-springs as well as foam, so it feels wonderfully responsive and robust. It comes with a 10-year guarantee, too.For more, read our guide to thebest mattress toppersSimbaHybrid mattress topper£296.65£296.65 at SimbaIt’s not just about your sleeping positionView image in fullscreen‘Panda’s memory foam topper is an excellent buy for adding softness to a mattress that feels too hard.’Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianThe way you lie in bed is an important factor when choosing a mattress, but not the only one. Your body size, for instance, has a big (or petite, if you like) impact on how firm your mattress should be. Generally speaking, the lighter you are, the less firmness you need, especially if you sleep on your side.If you have joint pain, particularly at side-sleeping pressure points such as hips, shoulders and knees, you may find relief in a well-cushioned mattress. “Pressure relief should be a top priority when choosing a mattress [if you have joint pain],” says Lisa Artis, deputy CEO of theSleep Charity, which partners with Simba. “Materials that adapt to your body’s shape can be particularly helpful.”Memory foam is notably adaptive and pressure-relieving, although if you choose a foam mattress you’ll want to make sure it’s supportive enough for you. In my experience, soft and “sinky” memory foam is wonderful for relieving pain, but can aggravate lower back pain and neck ache if you sink too far into it. The best foam and hybrid mattresses have plenty of support in the form of pocket springs or dense support foam, especially if you’re a larger sleeper.Adaptive foam is also brilliant at absorbing movement (motion isolation), so it’s a great choice if you share with someone who tosses and turns in bed. As a fidgety side sleeper who shares with another fidgety side sleeper, I can confirm that a sufficiently supportive foamy mattress can help prevent arguments as well as discomfort.Best mattress for side sleepers with joint pain:Tempur Pro Plus SmartCoolTempurPro Plus SmartCool£2,399£2,399 at TempurView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianDouble, £2,399 at TempurMemory foam cradles your body in a low-pressure way that almost feels like being suspended. The medium edition all-foam SmartCool left me craving more firmness, but it could be ideal for you if pressure relief is a priority.Read our fullTempur Pro Plus SmartCool reviewTempurPro Plus SmartCool£2,399£2,399 at TempurBest mattress topper for pressure relief:Panda Bamboo mattress topperPandaBamboo mattress topper£125.96£125.96 at PandaView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianDouble, £125.96 at PandaPanda’s 5cm memory foam topper is an excellent buy for adding softness to a mattress that feels too hard. It’s brilliant for motion isolation, too, and its cooling foam and bamboo fabric cover are designed to help control your body temperature when the nights get too warm.Read our fullPanda Bamboo mattress topper reviewPandaBamboo mattress topper£125.96£125.96 at PandaFor more, read our guide to thebest mattresses for back painThe best pillows for side sleepersFinding the perfect mattress and then slapping a lumpy old pillow on top is like covering a gourmet meal with ketchup. Sure, you might likeketchup(and you may love your lumpy old pillow), but it defeats the point. If you’re putting effort and money into getting the best mattress for your body, give your sleepy head the same honour, too.It’s not just your head that benefits from a good pillow, or even just your head and neck, but your whole body – especially if you sleep on your side. “A pillow gives more than comfort; it provides support between your head and mattress,” says Louise Silver, a product technologist at the bed brandFeather & Black. “Side sleepers shouldn’t go without a pillow altogether, as it creates an immediate issue with alignment. When you lie on your side, there’s a natural gap between the ear and the outer shoulder. Without a pillow to support that space, the head drops down towards the mattress, the shoulder rolls forward and the spine curves out of its neutral position. This puts strain on your neck, shoulders and upper back, which can lead to stiffness, tension and poor-quality sleep over time.”How should you choose the ideal pillow, then? “A pillow that’s too flat, particularly if you’ve overused it, can cause a drop and strain the neck muscles,” says Dr Deborah Lee. “A pillow that’s too thick can push the head upward, though, creating the same problem but in the opposite direction.“Side sleepers should look for pillows labelled medium to firm, with enough loft to maintain the natural alignment,” says Lee. “Many side sleepers also find that placing a pillow between the knees can reduce hip and lower back strain.”Best pillow for side sleepers:Otty Deluxe Pure pillowOttyDeluxe Pure pillow£69.99£69.99 at OttyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Edward Munn/The Guardian£69.99 at OttyIn his test to find thebest pillows, Edward Munn hailed Otty’s memory foam pillow as “supportive and bouncy, but not excessively tall, which means it works best for those who sleep mainly on their back and side, as I do.”OttyDeluxe Pure pillow£69.99£69.99 at OttyBest adjustable pillow for side sleepers:Emma Comfort Cooling pillowEmmaComfort Cooling pillow£59.25£59.25 at EmmaView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Edward Munn/The Guardian£59.25 at EmmaIf you find Otty’s pillow too boxy, perhaps because you’re on the small side like me, here’s a great idea from Emma: an adjustable pillow containing layers that you can add and remove until you find the ideal height for your neck and shoulder. The filling is microfibre rather than memory foam, so it feels a bit less dense and closer to the cloud-like sensation of feathers.EmmaComfort Cooling pillow£59.25£59.25 at EmmaFor more ways to sleep better with the Filter:The best mattress toppers for every sleeperThe best pillows – testedThe best duvets for every seasonJane Hoskyn is a features journalist who’s spent three decades rearranging bookshelves and “testing” products while deadlines loom. title: ‘She should have been queen of the world!’ Readers remember Dolly Parton | Dolly Parton | The Guardian
description: From quiet acts of generosity and life-changing gigs to singing for a professional puppeteer, Dolly Parton has had a profound impact on readers’ lives
Author: Nicola Slawson
Headline: From quiet acts of generosity and life-changing gigs to singing for a professional puppeteer, Dolly Parton has had a profound impact on readers’ lives
Content: ‘She made a sound that I could see’… Dolly Parton performing in 1973.Photograph: Alamy/PAView image in fullscreen‘She made a sound that I could see’… Dolly Parton performing in 1973.Photograph: Alamy/PADolly Parton‘She should have been queen of the world!’ Readers remember Dolly PartonFrom quiet acts of generosity and life-changing gigs to singing for a professional puppeteer, Dolly Parton has had a profound impact on readers’ livesPhoto gallery: fans pay tribute to Dolly PartonGuardian readers andNicola SlawsonThu 27 Aug 2026 09.02 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 10.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘She was as genuine as they come’I had the opportunity to meet her when I volunteered to work the Country Music Awards in the late 70s. Me and three other kids had Dolly all to ourselves for about 20 minutes. I remember with disbelief how she took several unhurried minutes with each of us and gave us her undivided attention for that time. She had no reason to do this. She was just as genuine as they come. Her philanthropy was exceptional. Her talent speaks for itself. I miss her already.Larry Lipman, Tennessee‘We were not ready to let her go’I always said Dolly should have been queen of the world. She was a natural unifier, humanist and all-round good egg. She never alienated anyone and, given the chance, could have solved any political problem. She was unique. Her magnificence is reflected in the outpouring of shock and grief at her passing. The world still needed Dolly and we were not ready to let her go yet. You will be sorely missed, Dolly.Ruth, LondonView image in fullscreenDolly Parton performing with Elton John at the 39th Annual Country Music Association Awards at Madison Square Garden in 2005.Photograph: Scott Gries/Getty Images‘I have yet to hear a person make a more beautiful tone’I’m not usually terribly affected when famous people pass away. But this one took the wind out of my sails. I’m a puppeteer and actor and I worked with her for a week in 1987 on her variety TV series. It was the Christmas episode, and they had hired a group of character puppets to fill out the sketches and musical numbers.Normally, when you get to a song in a table read, you just skip over it. But Dolly was in a mood to start singing the song herself, a cappella. When Dolly began to sing, all the other people disappeared. There was just Dolly, me and The Voice in that room. She made a sound that I could see. It was as if the ceiling had vaporised and the room filled with a golden light. I was mesmerised. She sang only the beginning of the song, and though this was almost 40 years ago, I have yet to hear a person make a more beautiful tone.Allan Trautman,CaliforniaView image in fullscreenParton and Katy Perry perform Coat of Many Colors at the 51st annual Academy of Country Music Awards in 2016.Photograph: Matt Sayles/Invision/AP‘I thought about her Coat of Many Colors when I had to wear hand-me-downs to school as a kid’Growing up as another hillbilly, I used to think about Dolly and Loretta Lynn when a few folks made fun of me for my incorrect pronunciations. I thought about her Coat of Many Colors when I had to wear hand-me-downs to school as a kid. But I pursued my dreams, stiffening my spine, as she did. I remember the very first time she appeared with Porter Wagoner and I have loved her music ever since. Her Smoky Mountain Christmas CD was only sold at Cracker Barrel but it is one of my favourites. She had such talent, such grace and goodness. She was so comfortable and authentic in her own skin. There will not be another like her.Anonymous, South Carolina‘More of us could stand to model Dolly’s bravery and kindness’Dolly Parton stood up for women, Black people and LGBTQIA people, and she did so in a region and industry where it was not trendy. On the one hand, I identify as Black and gay, and I appreciate being stood up for. But I think the more important element is the way she modelled speaking up for all her values, including those, in a culturally conservative part of America where doing so requires vastly more grit and risk than it does in regions like the east or west coast. She stood up anyway in the face of a potentially overwhelming backlash to those causes on her own turf.She also supported HIV/Aids treatment access, the development of the Moderna Covid vaccine, and she gave numerous children a chance to develop literacy skills by donating books.In the southern USA, where I am from, Dolly Parton will go into the pantheon of heroes. In this modern day world where cruelty and injustice are far too common, more of us could stand to model Dolly’s bravery and kindness, and I hope to see us do that.Antonio, Hanoi (originally from Kentucky)View image in fullscreenParton during a concert at Théâtre Mogador, Paris, in 1978.Photograph: Christian Rose‘She presented me with a pair of boots after a day spent shopping’I met Dolly in November 1978 when she came to perform in Paris at the Théâtre Mogador. I had just started to work for RCA records as a junior publicist. On the day before the concert, my boss called me at 7am saying she was sick and I had to replace her. I had to pick Dolly up at the George V hotel, with a chauffeur and limousine and take her everywhere she wanted to go.So there was young me, heart beating fast, meeting my first American artist, setting foot in a palace hotel and sitting in a limousine for the first time in my life. Her first request was to go to Christian Dior, which was another first for me. Due to the snobbish attitude of the shop assistants, who did not even bother to speak to her, we quickly retreated. Their mistake, she could have bought the building.When we returned to the George V she presented me with a box containing a pair of boots. I later realised she had carefully planned this as her assistant had asked about my shoe size and what style I liked when we were at the Galeries Lafayette. I was absolutely gobsmacked. Over the years when I would hear about all her good deeds, I was never surprised, having experienced her generosity first-hand.Fabienne Drinkwater, Australia (originally from France)View image in fullscreenDolly Parton in 2022.Photograph: NBC/Katherine Bomboy/Getty Images‘As a singer, I appreciated her incredible range and expressive quality’In the mid-early 1970’s when I was still in high school in Ohio, my brothers and I went to see Merle Haggard at the Akron Civic theatre and were blown away by the warm up act, which was Dolly Parton. We went home and worked out a few of her songs in our basement “studio” and years later one of my brothers formed a Dolly Parton tribute band in San Francisco called Parton Me. When Merle died in 2016 my brother said it felt like a member of our family had passed away. I have that same sense today hearing of Dolly’s passing. As a singer, I appreciated her incredible range, expressive quality, choice of songs in a set, her songwriting, and her interpretation of covers.Kathy Adams, UtahView image in fullscreenDolly Parton reads her book Coat of Many Colors, at the Library of Congress in Washington in 2018.Photograph: Andrew Harnik/AP‘Thanks to her, my son receives one book per month’I didn’t know much about Dolly Parton apart from Jolene. But thanks to herImagination Library, my 18-month-old son receives one book per month. I think it’s an amazing project and I hope it will survive her.Antoine, London‘She made me feel better about myself’As a trans girl growing up in rural Australia in the 1970s and 1980s, Dolly was one of the few celebrities who really made me feel better about being trans. Well before it was the thing to do, she made positive and supportive comments about trans women and LGBT people more generally. Her approach to life was also something that helped me through. In the early 1980s, a friend had one VHS tape and it was 9 to 5. We must have played it a thousand times until we didn’t need the sound any more to act out the movie from end to end.I was also a very freckled redhead, and I was bullied a lot for it. The lines from Jolene: “Your beauty is beyond compare / With flaming locks of auburn hair” also made me feel better about myself. It would have been great if she’d got her wish and died on stage at 120, but the 80 years she did give us were beyond compare.Maya, Australia‘A monumental loss for us all’How is it possible to cry for the loss of someone I’ve never met? Dolly’s kindness and sheer decency just shone from her. A monumental loss for us all but what a legacy she leaves behind.Jackie McDee, ScotlandExplore more on these topicsDolly PartonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I fight pain and fear with art’: how Yayoi Kusama blazed a trail for neurodivergent artists | Yayoi Kusama | The Guardian
description: The pioneering Japanese artist talked openly about how her mental health and neurodivergence informed her creativity, paving the way for the likes of Turner prize winner Nnena Kalu
Author: Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Headline: The pioneering Japanese artist talked openly about how her mental health and neurodivergence informed her creativity, paving the way for the likes of Turner prize winner Nnena Kalu
Content: ‘Her art shaped a sometimes overwhelming world of intensity, pattern and form’ … Yayoi Kusama, Tate Modern, London, 2012.Photograph: Ray Tang/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘Her art shaped a sometimes overwhelming world of intensity, pattern and form’ … Yayoi Kusama, Tate Modern, London, 2012.Photograph: Ray Tang/ShutterstockYayoi Kusama‘I fight pain and fear with art’: how Yayoi Kusama blazed a trail for neurodivergent artistsThe pioneering Japanese artist talked openly about how her mental health and neurodivergence informed her creativity, paving the way for the likes of Turner prize winner Nnena KaluRhiannon Lucy CosslettThu 27 Aug 2026 08.42 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 18.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYayoi Kusama –who has died at the age of 97– was 10 when she first started experiencing vivid hallucinations consisting of visual and aural disturbances, which she described as “flashes of light, auras, or dense fields of dots”. A drawing from 1939, of a woman in a kimono assumed to be her mother, shows her obliterated by those dots; they would become Kusama’s artistic obsession. She hallucinated flowers, too. “I was looking at the red flower patterns of the tablecloth on a table, and when I looked up I saw the same pattern covering the ceiling, the windows and the walls, and finally all over the room, my body and the universe”, she once said, when asked about that recurring motif. “I felt as if I had begun to self-obliterate, to revolve in the infinity of endless time and the absoluteness of space, and be reduced to nothingness.”For Kusama, art making was a means of survival. “I fight pain, anxiety, and fear every day, and the only method I have found that relieved my illness is to keep creating art. I followed the thread of art and somehow discovered a path that would allow me to live”, she saidin a 2012 interview. In so doing, she became one of the most acclaimed and admired contemporary artists, staging happenings and influencing the pop art movement as a pioneering figure in the New York avant garde. Her exhibitions and major retrospectives draw huge crowds. In 2022, due to enormous public demand, Tate Modern in London extended her Infinity Mirror Rooms show for a whole extra year (it ended up running until 2024).View image in fullscreenNnena Kalu, winner of the Turner prize 2025.Photograph: James Speakman/PAKusama leaves a planet that is far more enlightened about mental illness and neurodivergence than that which she entered. Different ways of seeing are increasingly embraced by the art world, which is beginning to understand how the brilliant, beautiful diversity of the human brain can feed into groundbreaking artistic practice. Neurodivergent, disabled and autistic artists are nominated for major prizes, and last year Nnena Kalu, who is autistic and has a learning disability,won the Turner prize. Furthermore, artists such asLouis Wain, who was schizophrenic, and Andy Warhol – who had traits consistent with autism – are increasingly viewed through the lens of neurodiversity.“Artists like Kusama, much like our own Nnena Kalu, have shown that great art does not come from a single source or follow a traditional route,” said a spokesperson forActionSpace, a London organisation who support and facilitate work by learning disabled artists. “The art world is richer for it, and their work continues to challenge us to recognise and celebrate the many voices that shape it.”Despite the historically unfair stigma of mental illness, Kusama was always vocal about her struggles and how they fed into her work, in the 1970s voluntarily checking herself into a mental-health facility in Tokyo and working in a studio nearby. Processing the “obliteration” she experienced involved repetitive ways of working – those signature dots and flowers covering everything including her own clothing – while her extraordinary infinity rooms installations of mirrors and lights took the concept of sensory overload and turned it into something magical and all-encompassing. In this way, we were granted a powerful glimpse through Kusama’s eyes.“Kusama’s practice seemed to channel the intrinsic auditory, repetitive and hallucinatory compulsions that she experienced,” says Kate Adams, director and co-founder ofProject Art Works, a collective of artists with complex needs, and their collaborators who were nominated for the Turner prize in 2021. “Rather than create an escape from these, her installations shaped and described for others a sometimes beautiful, sometimes overwhelming world of intensity, pattern and form.View image in fullscreenAn enduring influence … Yayoi Kusama as a young woman.Photograph: Magnolia Pictures/Everett/Shutterstock“This has parallels with the way in which stimming, hyper focus and innate sensory sensitivities find a way into the rich practices of neurodivergent artists and makers,” she continues. Adams points out that mental illnesses such as OCD are not necessarily the same as neurodivergence – we should be wary of grouping them all together. There can be parallels though, in Adams’ words “when anxiety overwhelms wellbeing”. Often diagnoses can overlap.This is true of my brother, who is profoundly autistic: non-verbal, with OCD. Although he is unable to tell me, I have always instinctively known that he sees the world differently. He had a childhood fascination with the way light is reflected on water, and his fear of the dark knots in the wood of the pine bathroom’s walls saw my mother frantically painting them over the moment she realised what was going on. That ASD comes with sensory differences has long been known in the autism community, but awareness has now reached a point where sensory rooms are cropping up in schools, hotels and airports. Exploring Kusama’s infinity rooms at Tate Modern with my son, who was then a baby, was a meaningful moment for me. The older children at his nursery had also been to visit, and for a while the walls were covered with pictures of dots that they had made as a tribute to Kusama.Kusama often referenced how art had saved her, saying: “If it were not for art, I would have killed myself a long time ago.” Although disabled and neurodivergent artists still face major barriers, and still experience moments of sadness and despair that are shared by those of us that love them, Kusama’s work and enduring influence stand as a lasting tribute to the complex magnificence of human perception and experience.Explore more on these topicsYayoi KusamaMental healthArtPaintingInstallationNeurodiversityHealthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The flat-pack skyscraper: how wood can shape the cities of the future | Green building | The Guardian
description: The long read: Our buildings are monuments to extraction and extreme emissions. But what if we turned from destructive concrete to timber?
Author: James Crawford
Headline: The long read: Our buildings are monuments to extraction and extreme emissions. But what if we turned from destructive concrete to timber?
Content: The long readGreen buildingThe flat-pack skyscraper: how wood can shape the cities of the futureOur buildings are monuments to extraction and extreme emissions. But what if we turned from destructive concrete to timber?Last chance to buy the summer issue of The Long Read magazine, now with 15% off.Click hereto orderJames CrawfordThu 27 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 11.15 EDTShareView image in fullscreenMjøstårnet, the world’s tallest wooden skyscraper.Photograph: Voll Arkitekter/Ricardo FotoI travelled to Oslo in the early autumn. It felt like arriving into the future. Or, at least, a fragment of a possible future. I drove north in the quiet digital bubble of my electric rental car. In 2024, Norway became the first country in the world where electric carsoutnumbered petrol cars.A smooth, pristine motorway unfolded between farmlands and low hillsides of dense green forest. Long tunnels carried the route up above the banks of Lake Mjøsa, Norway’s largest lake. After a little more than an hour, the road curved downward to run parallel to the lakeshore.Through gaps in a line of golden birch trees, a tall, slim structure broke the horizon. It rose from the water’s edge, topped by a triangular crown of bare, interlocking beams. Against the heavy grey sky and the enfolding mist, it radiated a gentle warmth from its pale burnt-orange exterior. The only building of any height anywhere in the surrounding landscape, it is known as Mjøstårnet, the “Tower of Mjøsa”: an 18-storey, 277ft (84m)-high wooden skyscraper. The tallest all-timber building in the world.Mjøstårnet occupies a slice of shoreline next to the small town of Brumunddal. It incorporates offices, apartments, and a 72-room hotel. I was staying on the 11th floor, and I rode up in an elevator shaft fabricated entirely of wood (although the elevator cabin itself was made of steel and glass).View image in fullscreenThe interior of Mjøstårnet.Photograph: Voll ArkitekterTwo sides of my corner room had large picture windows, one looking west across the lake and the other north along the shore. There were wooden floors throughout, wooden tables and lamps, a wooden bed, and pair of low swivel chairs formed out of thin slats of bent pinewood.Most striking of all was the huge wooden column that formed both the corner piece of the room and – extending in segments above and below me – one of the four edge-points of the whole tower. It looked reassuringly sturdy, as if it were the trunk of a massive tree that had been stripped of its bark and worked into a smoothed organic approximation of a geometric strut of steel or concrete. Which is almost exactly the case: except that it is not just one tree but many – a series of blocks of timber that are precision cut and then pressed and held together using extremely strong glue, creating what is known as mass timber, or glulam (short for “glued laminated timber”).The piece in my room was the largest of its kind in the building, its cross-section measuring some 2ft wide by 5ft (0.6m by 1.5m) long. Although coated in a pale wax laminate, you could still see the unique knots and whorls running across its composite slices of wood.Through the window, mist slipped in waves down the forested slopes of the far shore. Gusts of wind blew fine rain against the glass. Inside, there was no sound. The view shifted from white, to grey, to the encroaching blue of night. Eventually I settled down to sleep in what, I realised then, amounted to something of a childhood fantasy – a giant treehouse in the sky.Mjøstårnet began its life as a sketch on a napkin. Two rectangular boxes marked out in blue ballpoint pen: one lying flat, the other standing on end, on top of the first. The actual finished structure is not far removed from this original draft – except that the second rectangle kept elongating farther and farther upward. “Height was very important here,” Arthur Buchardt, the developer who drew this sketch, told me. “It had to be a signal. To show what is possible. And I think now it has made a lot of people wake up.”I met Buchardt the day after my arrival, on the 18th floor of the tower, where he keeps his own penthouse apartment. Now in his late 70s, he has the look of a Bond villain – tall, broad, vigorously healthy, perfectly bald – and the demeanour of a favoured great-uncle, quick to laugh and possessed of a twinkling, boyish enthusiasm. We sat at his living room table – wooden, of course – drinking black coffee and looking out through the floor-to-ceiling windows that form the entire western face of the penthouse.All of the wood, Buchardt told me, gesturing around the apartment, and more generally at the whole building, came from the immediate landscape. In the centre of the room was an L-shaped pillar of grey marble containing a gas fire. That stone, he said, was taken from the surrounding hills. Even the art on the walls was local. “So this was a political statement,” he said. “To use all this local material.”Buchardt moved to Brumunddal as a boy and spent most of his teenage years in the town. After graduating in business – studying at Oslo and Edinburgh universities – he returned to take over his father-in-law’s plumbing company. In a few years he sold it on, using the proceeds to move into property development, and then, when the 1994 Winter Olympics came to Lillehammer and the town needed brand-new accommodation for athletes and visitors, he built his first hotel. He has built 23 more since, all across Scandinavia. And, increasingly, he has built them out of wood.“About 10 years ago I had to wake up a little bit myself. About the importance of the environment, about what we are doing to it,” he told me. It was the announcement of the Paris climate agreement in December 2015 – with its transnational pledge to reduce global emissions and shift toward net zero emissions – that prompted Buchardt into action. “Politicians talked about the need for a ‘great green change’. And I thought, how can I answer those political signals?” All he really knew how to do was make buildings. But what if he made them differently?“It was right then, in 2015, that I put some drawings on this napkin. And I took it to an architect” – the Trondheim-based firm Voll Arkitekter – “and asked them, ‘How big is it possible to go with a high-rise wooden building?’ Because you can’t make large modern structures without steel or concrete entirely. But you can reduce how much you use. You can reduce that a lot.”View image in fullscreenThe view from the top of Mjøstårnet.Photograph: 360Cities.net/AlamyThis is the thing about concrete. Not only is the world running short of the sand we need to make it – and having to consider extreme alternatives to meet demand, from removing and crushing entire mountaintops to dredging Greenland’s silt-plugged fjords – but its intensifying use also causes spiralling feedback loops. The built environment accounts for 37% of all global emissions, coming from the combination of the construction process itself and the energy required for heating, lighting and maintaining buildings over time. Between 7 and 8% of these total emissions are from concrete manufacturing alone. Since 1960, concrete use in construction has grown tenfold. Less than 1% of this concrete is produced from recycled materials. Instead, we just keep making more and more of it, requiring more and more sand – a projected 50% more by 2060 around the globe.In effect, almost all of our modern towns and cities are formed out of materials that have been extracted, smelted, superheated or synthesised through the intensive use of fossil energy. Cities are, literally, monuments to extraction and emissions, the focused expressions of mining, burning, melting, sintering and moulding the mineral contents of the Earth. It would be hard to invent a more efficient machine for the concentrated emission of CO2if you tried.But what if you imagine replacing the superstructure of our homes and workplaces and offices – even our high-rises – with wood? Trees take carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere and store it inside their bodies. Cut them down, and they retain the CO2rather than releasing it. Build with them, and they still keep holding that carbon. When you fabricate a typical mid-rise building out of steel and concrete, its construction alone generates around 1,500 to 2,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions. That same building, when made out of wood, sequesters anything from 600 to 1,000 metric tons of CO2. And that is before you even factor in the additional absorption that comes with the planting and regrowth of the harvested trees.For just one building, the difference is remarkable. What about an entire city? You turn dense population centres, some of the most concentrated emitters of greenhouse gases, into massive carbon sinks. You invert the equation, make buildings not part of the problem but part of the solution. You shift from a construction economy that is mineral based, requiring the ever more widespread depletion of finite resources, to one that is forest-based and endlessly renewable. Wood as an urban antidote to sand and steel and cement. From the concrete jungle to the timber city.That, at least, is the vision. The reality, of course, is not quite so simple. Right now, for instance, construction with mass timber is expensive. The cost of Mjøstårnet came to around £100m. The same tower, built entirely of steel and concrete, would have been £10 to £15m cheaper.Much of this, however, is a matter of perspective. Studies looking at the knock-on effects of global concrete production estimate that the associated damages it causes to health and the environment have a quantifiable financial value, a value that is almost equivalent to – or by some estimates may even exceed – the value of the entire concrete industry itself. A shifting, climate-focused economics can quickly change the parameters of cost efficiency. As can transparency over environmental impacts. “Ten years ago, I didn’t read what the CO2footprint was of a car,” Buchardt said to me. “No one was that interested. Now the first thing you look at is the CO2. And I think that is how it will go with buildings.”View image in fullscreenMjøstårnet, on the banks of Lake Mjøsa.Photograph: Voll Arkitekter/Ricardo FotoAs he put it, “we will look at a certificate of each building, and you will see its CO2emissions, its energy consumption, what it is made of. You will look at a particular hotel and say, you know, there’s steel, there’s glass, it’s using so much electricity, it’s like a beacon of emissions, and so you won’t stay there. While those who have low-carbon-emission buildings will go to the market, and they will tell you about it. Maybe it starts as a marketing tool, but then it becomes a standardisation.”Brumunddal and its surrounding district of Ringsaker has always been logging country. Earlier on the morning I met Buchardt, I had visited the sawmill and factory of Moelven, a local company that has grown to become one of Scandinavia’s largest wood processors, and which supplied the materials for Mjøstårnet.The head of its building systems division, Rune Abrahamsen, showed me the glulam production line. He led me from huge warehouses of newly sawn and delivered timber, stacked in neat piles like bundles of giant matchsticks, to a factory floor where computer systems cut, bent, pressed and glued the wood into any shape a client required. Everywhere was redolent with the smell of pine and spruce. Finally we came to a loading bay, about the size of an aircraft hangar, where finished glulam beams wrapped in blue tarp awaited transport all across the country.Rune worked as the structural engineer on Mjøstårnet – tasked with turning Buchardt’s napkin drawing into a solid reality. “To be honest,” he said, “my first thought when Buchardt called me about this project was ‘Is he playing with me here, or is he for real?’”Rune has always had a passion for timber construction. When he was a student in the 1990s, he said, everyone was focused on designing structures in concrete, steel and aluminum. “And there were very few people studying or searching for solutions in wood. And I thought, why do I need to be like all the other 250 students that I’m graduating with? Let’s try something else.”He first began working with glulam about 30 years ago. The concept itself was actually more than a century old, but while the basic idea of cutting up logs and then gluing them together to increase stiffness and strength is the same, what has changed is the technology: the precision and speed with which you can now shape and manipulate the wood.View image in fullscreenGlulam being manufactured in Germany.Photograph: Zoonar GmbH/AlamyBuilding high, however – as high as Buchardt wanted Mjøstårnet to go – was something that no one had tried before. Timber buildings, Rune explained, are very light compared to concrete and steel structures. “And remember that buildings are vertical cantilevers. So when the wind blows at the top, it multiplies the forces, creating horizontal accelerations higher up.” It is, he said, like being in the crow’s nest at the top of a ship’s mast. Down on the deck, you may only feel the gentle rocking of the sea. Up on the mast, however, every pitch and roll becomes hugely amplified. Structurally, the wood can handle these forces easily – but those people actually staying on the higher floors might not.To dampen the sway and remove the risk of “sea sickness” they had to weigh the building down – turning, in the end, to laying layers of concrete on the decks of the upper floors. This was a fraction of what most tall tower blocks would use, and the minimum they needed to meet “comfort” standards, but it was still there, nonetheless.For the construction of the building itself, they used a novel and untested assembly technique. The hundreds of glulam beams, columns and trusses that formed the superstructure were processed and shaped to millimetre accuracy at the nearby factory, and then transported individually to the site without any trial fitting. In effect, Mjøstårnet was like a flat-pack skyscraper, its simple timber skeleton rapidly rising piece by piece and floor by floor – at the rate of almost one floor per week – all installed by a tower crane, with no need for any external scaffolding. Far faster than building with concrete.View image in fullscreenMjøstårnet under construction.Photograph: Øystein ElgsaasWith an all-timber structure, Rune said, there is one question that everyone asks: What if it catches on fire? From the spark that ignited and then consumed the “forest” of roof beams in Notre Dame Cathedral in 2019 to the great conflagrations in cities throughout history, wood’s capacity to burn is a major reason it has been largely phased out as a modern urban building material.“Most people would think that this is a catastrophic thing to do,” Rune said, “to build such a tall timber building. But probably it is about the most fire-safe building in Norway.” The glulam had to undergo rigorous testing. “We made samples that we took to a fire laboratory in Trondheim. We burnt the glulam columns – and they do burn, but eventually they stop burning. It’s like if you go to the woods and you make a bonfire and you put a big log on late in the night. You go to sleep, and then the next morning, everything around the outside of the log is gone, the bark and such, and the log itself is deeply charred, but it’s still solid. So if a column in the building burns, it chars the surface but that charring protects the inside – and it is still strong enough to carry the load of the building.”In this respect, Mjøstårnet has received a rather ringing endorsement. Norway’s largest insurance company insures the building – and also takes up two of its office floors. “You can prove as an engineer and a manufacturer that something is going to be safe,” Rune said, “but you need to have the insurance company with you.”If you want to scale up the number of mass-timber buildings to replace concrete and steel, you have to substantially increase the number of trees you cut down. The wood for Mjøstårnet was produced by harvesting more than 16,000 spruce and pine trees from the forests that surround Brumunddal. Given that the world has lost one-third of its forests since the end of the last ice age, with half of this loss occurring in the last century alone, it isn’t surprising that for some, the prospect of removing even more trees is alarming. As a 2018 open letter from a consortium of US environmental groups put it to the mayor of Portland, Oregon, the increased demand for mass timber “may provide a perverse incentive to shorten logging rotations and more aggressively clearcut”.Rune, for his part, seemed acutely aware of this tension. “For wood to be a good part of the solution, you need to take into consideration that you’re not harvesting more from the forest than actually grows back.” Currently, he said, for every tree cut, they plant two more.View image in fullscreenA rendering of the planned W350 tower in Tokyo.Photograph: Sumitomo Forestry Co“Here, in our part of Scandinavia, it takes about 80 years for a tree to grow. But we have enormous amounts of forest. So, even though our industry has expanded a lot in recent years, we’re still only harvesting about 30% of the annual growth. We’re still getting more and more trees, even though we are harvesting more. There’s a big scalability within the resource right now.”This, ultimately, was Buchardt’s goal with Mjøstårnet – to make it “just the beginning of bigger wooden buildings”. He was, he said, already working on an even taller all-wood building in Sweden. At the same time, the urban developer Atrium Ljungberg had recently announced the construction of Stockholm Wood City, a new 250,000 sq metre neighbourhood of offices, homes, shops and apartments, all created out of timber. In Winterthur, Switzerland the 100-metre-tall wooden “Rocket” apartment block is soon to arrive on the skyline, while in Perth in Western Australia a project is under way to almost double that height again, with a 191-metre-high “half-wood” tower.View image in fullscreenA rendering of Atrium Ljungberg’s Stockholm Wood City proposal.Illustration: White Arkitekter/Atrium LjungbergSimilar developments are cropping up all acrossEurope, North America and Asia. Most ambitious of all is the Japanese timber company Sumitomo Forestry’s master plan for a 350-metre-high wooden skyscraper. When completed, sometime around 2041, it will become not only the tallest wooden building in the world (by some distance) but also the tallest building of any kind in Japan.Buchardt was going to Helsinki the following week, to give a speech. He opened his notebook – he does not use computers if at all possible, he said – and showed me the title he had chosen, which he had written out in English: “How difficult is it to make things easy?” It was going to be about Mjøstårnet, and wood – about using local materials, local people, local expertise. More broadly, I asked, was it about climate change? We know the basic equation; we know what drives emissions – we know that extraction underpins all of our lives. That’s easy. What we don’t seem to know, fundamentally, is how to change that.In response, he took me to the corridor of the penthouse and showed me a framed original manuscript by a famous Norwegian poet, author and musician, Alf Prøysen, who was born near Brumunddal in 1914. It included some lines from Prøysen’s most celebrated folk song, A Day Tomorrow. Buchardt offered me a rough translation. “You shall have a day tomorrow,” he said, “that stands clean and unused; with blank white sheets and fresh new crayons; and you can correct the errors of the day before; and you’ll face tomorrow’s evening with joy.”The sentiment is clear. That there is always a chance to start anew, to make amends, to try again. Either in your own life, or from one generation to the next. The problem now, of course, is that the sheet is not blank, nor clean nor unused. It bears the inky stain of the last few centuries – the still-fast-accumulating, unerasable errors of the day before.Concrete: the most destructive material on EarthRead moreLater that afternoon, I drove to the far side of the lake and hiked up through an old forest of spruce and Scots pine. From a clearing at the top of the hill I could see Mjøstårnet on the far shore – soft, wooden, rooted. A tower envisioned as the concentrated expression of this landscape. Or this landscape, as it is for now.Rune said that the forest environment in Norway was changing. As the weather warmed, the treeline was moving higher up the mountain slopes, offering even greater space for growing. But at the same time, they were experiencing more landslides and wildfires. The rising temperatures were also bringing new species, new insects, into the region, including spruce beetles, which can cause huge damage across large areas of forestry.Perhaps the reason it is “difficult to make things easy” is because we are always trying to fix ourselves in place and in time, while the environment – eroding, prograding, warming, waning – continually migrates all around us. It is the story of sand, forests, deserts, ice and glaciers too. When we build, we think we are looking to the future. But really, we are always drawing from the past. Making our homes from centuries-old trees or millennia-old sand – all powered by eons-old fossils.Adapted fromThe Vanishing Earth: A Journey Through the Last Days of Abundance, which will be published by Scribe on 10 September.Listen to our podcastshereand sign up to the long read weekly emailhere.

title: Food allergies when flying are no joke. That’s why nuts should be banned on planes | Lucy Pasha-Robinson | The Guardian
description: People with allergies must be able to travel without fear, and a compassionate society should respect that, says Lucy Pasha-Robinson, an assistant Opinion editor at the Guardian
Author: Lucy Pasha-Robinson
Headline: People with allergies must be able to travel without fear, and a compassionate society should respect that, says Lucy Pasha-Robinson, an assistant Opinion editor at the Guardian
Content: ‘Most airlines will make an announcement asking passengers to avoid consuming nuts if you let them know that somebody in your party has a severe nut allergy.’Photograph: Nigel Blake/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Most airlines will make an announcement asking passengers to avoid consuming nuts if you let them know that somebody in your party has a severe nut allergy.’Photograph: Nigel Blake/AlamyOpinionAllergiesFood allergies when flying are no joke. That’s why nuts should be banned on planesLucy Pasha-RobinsonPeople with allergies must be able to travel without fear, and a compassionate society should respect thatThu 27 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 13.59 EDTShareWhat are you most scared of? Perhaps snakes send a chill down your spine. Or heights leave your knees weak. Peanuts may sound like an odd source of phobia, but they have taken on an absurd bogeyman quality for me since my daughter was taken to hospital by ambulance after eating peanut butter when she was six months old. Just the sight of a bowl on a pub bar, or their shells discarded on the pavement, can raise my heart rate – even when I’m not with her.Nowhere is the sight of peanuts more confronting than at 30,000ft, especially now when millions are jetting back from their holidays. Travelling with a severely allergic child can be a nightmare for all sorts of reasons, but the idea you could be sat next to a passenger consuming the very thing that has hospitalised them is its own kind of hell.Most airlines will make an announcement asking passengers to avoid consuming nuts if you let them know that somebody in your party has a severe nut allergy. But I brace for impact when these announcements are piped out. On almost every flight there is at least one passenger who sighs or makes some inane comment, loud enough for everyone to hear, about how annoying it is.Oh, I’m sorry – is not being able to eat nuts for a few hours inconveniencing you? Does one passenger’s desire to consume peanut M&M’s trump someone else’s right to stay alive? I didn’t realise the right to eat nuts was a civil liberties issue. How utterly absurd.And yet, people get disproportionately upset about being told not to eat things. Chloë Dickson, who runs the Instagram accountpeanutfreezone,recently posted a horrifying video of her experience flying with a severe peanut allergy and a man behind her responding, “Really?” to an announcement asking passengers not to eat nuts. He “then proceeded to make comments throughout the entire journey about eating peanuts around me, along with two other people nearby,” the caption reads.I am mystified by this mean-spiritedness. Allergies are not a lifestyle choice but a medical condition. And yet, they seem to inspire a lack of empathy in the public consciousness. Perhaps it’s due to a misunderstanding of what allergy actually is. For people such as Chloe and my daughter, we’re not talking about skin irritation or a dodgy stomach, however unpleasant that might be.Anaphylaxisis a severe, potentially life-threatening allergic reaction that can affect multiple body systems and commonly impacts breathing or consciousness. The primary treatment is adrenaline via an EpiPen and it requires immediate medical attention.But I suspect many people do know what severe allergy can look like, they just think this level of caution is overblown and are frustrated by having to make accommodations. Take a look at some of the comments under Chloë’s post and you’ll see what I mean. They are staggering in their stupidity. “Fly private or DON’T FLY AT ALL. Don’t make other people’s lives miserable just to please yours!” one reads. “I travel with a bag of peanuts for these moments,” says another. There really are people who seem to believe that those with allergies should just not travel at all. Or not go out to eat. Or not be able to participate fully in life outside their own homes. I wonder if they would feel that way if it was their children who were diagnosed.Allergic people can’t be wrapped in cotton wool. Some of the best advice I got when my daughter was small, from an angelic NHS allergy nurse, was that you do your very best to keep her safe and then you carry EpiPens as your insurance policy. That’s given me lots of comfort over the years when gauging risk. But when you’re trapped in a metal tube in the sky with no possibility of medical attention, the stakes feel much higher.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionExperience: I’m allergic to nearly everythingRead moreWhat scares allergic people most is not necessarily the risk of an airborne reaction, which isvanishingly rare, it’s the possibility of cross-contamination. That peanut dust on someone’s fingers could then spread to the tray table, the seat, perhaps the toilet door. That a rogue peanut from a previous flight has fallen between the seats or touched the seatbelt. On quick turnaround budget airlines with minimal cleaning, the risk you may come into contact with the allergen starts to feel frighteningly high. And even tiny amounts of nut protein can trigger a life-threatening reaction for some people.Banning nuts on planes seems like a no-brainer. And I say nuts because of all the common allergens, they are the least likely to beoutgrown in childhoodand have ahigher rate of causing severe reactions. That means telling passengers not to bring nut products on board. But even just stopping the practice of serving them on flights would drastically reduce the risk of cross-contamination when travelling. And it would take the pressure off anxious, allergic passengers to advocate for their safety. Of course, no ban could be watertight, which is why airlines should make a blanket rule that anyone with severe allergy should be offered priority boarding to clean their own seats before takeoff as a precaution.Allergic people shouldn’t have to justify their medical needs to people who don’t understand them. Banning nuts on planes could send an important message to the broader public. That people with allergies should be able to travel without fear. That compassionate societies make accommodations.Lucy Pasha-Robinson is a Guardian assistant Opinion editorDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
