title: A Britain of wildfires and flood risks: be sure, the climate crisis is real, and we will deal with it  | Angela Eagle | The Guardian
description: Reform and the Conservatives are willing to mislead the public, but as environment secretary, I believe we must be honest – and act boldly, says Angela Eagle
Author: Angela Eagle
Headline: Reform and the Conservatives are willing to mislead the public, but as environment secretary, I believe we must be honest – and act boldly, says Angela Eagle
Content: Smoke rising from burning homes in Stourbridge, West Midlands, 13 August 2026.Photograph: WEST MIDLANDS FIRE SERVICE/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSmoke rising from burning homes in Stourbridge, West Midlands, 13 August 2026.Photograph: WEST MIDLANDS FIRE SERVICE/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionExtreme weatherA Britain of wildfires and flood risks: be sure, the climate crisis is real, and we will deal with itAngela EagleReform and the Conservatives are willing to mislead the public, but as environment secretary, I believe we must be honest – and act boldlyThu 27 Aug 2026 08.05 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 13.32 EDTShareThis long, hot summer has brought our third drought in five years and thedriest July in almost two centuries. We’ve seenwildfires burn down homesand now face the risk of flash floods as we move into autumn. It should be a wake-up call for those saying that concerns about the climate crisis are overblown; that we should simply sit back and do nothing; or row back on attempts to restore our natural environment. As the new environment secretary, I won’t let that happen.No one who has experienced this summer in the UK should be in any doubt that our climate is already changing. We know the future holds warmer, wetter winters, hotter, drier summers, and more extreme weather.Honesty about what is required to deal with this changing reality is the least we should expect from our politicians. But last week we saw an astonishing response from Reform UK’s deputy leader,who told peopleto “enjoy” the scorching heatwaves and described this government’s efforts to combat the climate crisis as “arrogant”.This response isn’t just ignorant; it is insulting.From bone-dry to soaked to the bone, welcome to the age of climate whiplash | Aditya ChakraborttyRead moreInsulting to the firefighters risking their lives to fight blazes up and down the country. Insulting to the public whose lives are disrupted by scorching temperatures that were once a rare occurrence. And insulting to our farmers struggling to turn a profit as drought damages their crops.This government’s response is not to throw in the towel and accept the chaos caused by extreme weather. It is to work to build and manage landscapes so they are resilient enough to withstand it and recover.We know that healthy ecosystems retain more water and can help act as natural firebreaks. That resilience does not just protect us from the impacts of wildfire. It guards against flooding and pollution, too.But some, including the Conservatives, have made the argument thatrewilding lowers resilience to fireand that we should reverse restrictions on burning heather on our moors and peatlands. The exact opposite is true.The evidence clearly shows that wetter, healthy peatlands hold more water and are less likely to develop species that are vulnerable to fires. The damage that has been done to these vital habitats by decades of burning has made them more vulnerable to wildfires in the long term, not less.The solution to raging wildfires is not more burning of our countryside. It is to restore and better manage our environment.Where rewilding has been prioritised, as at the National Trust’s Holnicote estate, you can clearly see the stark difference that it makes to the ability to withstand extreme weather. In areas where rivers and wetlands have been restored, the plants are green and blooming. Elsewhere, the ground is brown and dry.As environment secretary, most of what comes across my desk is underpinned by the need to adapt to our changing climate – and this government is taking these challenges head on.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat’s why the prime minister this month convened anemergency Cobra meeting, bringing together senior ministers, firefighters, weather forecasters and other experts to make sure we’re doing all we can to keep the country safe from wildfires. That includes a temporary ban on the sale of disposable barbecues.We arespending almost £100mto strengthen the country’s capacity to respond to wildfires and extreme weather.And we are backing our farmers during the droughtwith a £65m funding boost, rule changes to make building on-site reservoirs easier and the largest nature-friendly budget in history to make our farms more resilient to extreme weather and to protect our food security.Adapting to our changing climate demands sustained attention, effort and investment. Others may simply deny the problem or stick their heads in the sand, but this government will rise to the challenge.Angela Eagle is the secretary of state for environment, food and rural affairsExplore more on these topicsExtreme weatherOpinionClimate crisisWildfiresDroughtLabourcommentShareReuse this content

title: An $18bn settlement is a drop in the ocean for Meta – but the tide will still come for it | Chris Stokel-Walker | The Guardian
description: This week’s settlement without liability was pragmatic, but it doesn’t change the inevitability of further lawsuits around the world, says technology writer Chris Stokel-Walker
Author: Chris Stokel-Walker
Headline: This week’s settlement without liability was pragmatic, but it doesn’t change the inevitability of further lawsuits around the world, says technology writer Chris Stokel-Walker
Content: Mark Zuckerberg arrives at a court in LA for a trial over whether social media platforms deliberately addict and harm children, 18 February 2026.Photograph: Ryan Sun/APView image in fullscreenMark Zuckerberg arrives at a court in LA for a trial over whether social media platforms deliberately addict and harm children, 18 February 2026.Photograph: Ryan Sun/APOpinionMetaAn $18bn settlement is a drop in the ocean for Meta – but the tide will still come for itChris Stokel-WalkerThis week’s settlement without liability was pragmatic, but it doesn’t change the inevitability of further lawsuits around the worldThu 27 Aug 2026 09.11 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 13.59 EDTShareNot many people would count paying $18bn they didn’t expect to when they woke up that morning as a victory. Yet for Meta, the owners of Facebook and Instagram, the agreementwith 52 US attorneys generalto settle claims that it designed its products to be addictive to children, and misled people about their safety, could be described as a win of sorts.Meta denies wrongdoing, and the amount it plans to pay will be spread over a decade. Some of it is contingent on other big tech firms not named in its case coughing up too. The cash is chump change forMeta, which made around $60bn in profit last year. More damaging to the tech giant in the long run could be the agreement to unwind some of the mechanics it has spent two decades perfecting to keep us on its platforms.Under-18s in the US will face a default two-hour daily limit on Facebook andInstagram, with access blocked overnight – unless a parent changes the setting. Teachers will be glad to hear notifications will be muted during school hours, while teenagers will be nagged as much by the platform itself as their parents about exactly how long they have spent staring at their screens.All of these are significant changes that materially change how the company’s products work – and all of them should be welcomed. But in lots of ways, Meta has got off lightly with this agreement, both in what it’s been asked to do and the fine it must pay.What the decision shows, just months after Meta chose to fight its corner in court, and lost significantly, is how the economics of fighting social media litigation have changed. This settlement signifies an important and deliberate shift in strategy. In August, Meta went to court in New Mexico – a decision that cost it dearly. The judge thereordered the firm to pay $942m and overhaul some protections for children– a decision it is appealing. The fact that Meta lost that case, and was found to have done wrong, was far more damaging than this week’s settlement without liability, even if the amounts involved were smaller. Still,thousands more cases involving social media addiction claims are still wending their way through US courts.And chastened by a couple of losses, it looks – at least in this instance – like Meta has taken the approach that a pyrrhic victory is better than the risk of another real loss. Settlements without admission of fault avoid judgments and a legal situation that could quickly spiral out of control for Meta’s product offering.While Meta has had to make significant changes to its platforms as a result of this week’s settlement, it still ultimately has control over what changes are made, and has sought to limit them to the bare minimum. Settling, however expensive, is a way of protecting its core business proposition.Meta now faces a Hobson’s choice when it comes to litigation. It can gamble on a jury and risk vast damages, damaging internal disclosures and a judge deciding which parts of Instagram orFacebookmust change. Or it can pay an eye-watering but manageable sum to settle, negotiate the product changes on its own terms and staunch the bleeding.That $18bn is certainly more than most companies could pay, but it pales in comparison with the $1.5tn Meta’s own PR team warned the case could cost it had it gone through the courts – and the more realistic $200bn the prosecuting lawyers sought to squeeze from the firm. And even more than that, Meta has managed to make some of the bill somebody else’s problem. About a third of the settlement it has agreed to pay is conditional on TikTok and YouTube introducing similar restrictions and each making matching payments. Meta ispublicly calling on both companiesto sign up.As this is a negotiated settlement–and one in which no one wins, but Meta certainly doesn’t lose–not everyone has been won over. While attorneys general from 48 US states agreed to Meta’s proposition, Florida’s representative has publicly rejected the deal and intends to continue pursuing Meta. James Uthmeierdismissed the settlementas “peanuts” and said “We’ll see them at trial.”Nor is this necessarily just an American story. The settlement formally applies only to the participating US states and territories. A Meta spokesperson told me it already offers strong protections for teenagers elsewhere. It will watch how the new measures work before deciding what comes next internationally.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut running substantially different versions of Facebook and Instagram around the world is hardly attractive. And Meta has now demonstrated putting these restrictions in place is possible. Given the drive towards child safety online in the UK and Australia, it seems likely that politicians will soon ask why American teenagers get them and children in their own countries don’t. The UK’s own Online Safety Act is a useful stick for the government to wield in this instance, adding extra leverage to bring those changes here, too.And it’s that which may prove the settlement’s biggest consequence. Meta has paid billions to manage to duck liability in one court case. But in doing so, it may have opened up the possibility of change in a raft of other countries.Chris Stokel-Walker is the author of TikTok Boom: The Inside Story of the World’s Favourite AppDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: If MPs want to take on Nigel Farage over his dodgy finances, they need to clean up their own act | Frances Ryan | The Guardian
description: It’s hard to beat back charges that MPs are ‘all the same’ when they have accepted £400k in freebies this year, says Guardian columnist Frances Ryan
Author: Frances Ryan
Headline: It’s hard to beat back charges that MPs are ‘all the same’ when they have accepted £400k in freebies this year, says Guardian columnist Frances Ryan
Content: Illustration: Eleanor Shakespeare/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Eleanor Shakespeare/The GuardianOpinionPoliticsIf MPs want to take on Nigel Farage over his dodgy finances, they need to clean up their own actFrances RyanIt’s hard to beat back charges that MPs are ‘all the same’ when they have accepted £400k in freebies this year – £100k up on last yearThu 27 Aug 2026 06.03 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 13.59 EDTShareHow has your summer been? Done anything nice? As MPs prepare to head back to parliament next week, you’ll be relieved to hear that some of the most prominent figures in British politics have been enjoying the season’s cultural highlights – and without paying a penny. MPs throughout the Commons havereceived £400,000 of “freebies”to concerts, sports matches and other events so far this year, according to the most recent disclosures.Over the summer alone, Wes Streeting, now the defence secretary, enjoyed the Chelsea flower show thanks to Lloyds Banking Group covering the £1,839 cost, as did the shadow chancellor, Mel Stride. Lucy Powell, who has since become deputy leader of theLabourparty and education secretary, accepted £858-worth of tickets to a Harry Styles concert at Wembley from the PRS for Music industry group. Meanwhile, the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, nabbed seats at Wimbledon worth £1,360 from the All England Club.Totalled up,MPs have been gifted£100,000 more so far this year than in the whole of 2025, with recipients seemingly learning few lessons from Keir Starmer’s“passes for glasses” scandal, in which a Labour peer gifted the then prime minister designer eyewear and clothes before being spotted in Downing Street with a temporary security pass.Like many of these types of stories, there’s some nuance lurking behind the headlines. MPs quite rightly go to events linked to their constituency or local area. Andy Burnham accepting £3,800 tickets to the Brit awards in Manchester – when he was the regional mayor – to spotlight the city hosting the event for the first time is not the same as Streeting presumably just really wanting to meet Monty Don.The increase can also partly be explained by the fact MPs have become more consistent about declaring hospitality on the parliamentary register after Starmer changed the rules, while ticket prices are well known to have gone up across the board. And yet, wade through the details of gigs and horse racing and it’s hard not to conclude some MPs are simply practising blatant grifting. Call it a treat for a seat, where our elected officials are enjoying must-see shows as a kind of unofficial bonus.That much of this stuff was gifted by big business, including gambling firms and banks, makes the whole thing feel considerably grubbier. Why did the betting company Flutter want to shower then local backbencher and now chief whip, Anneliese Midgley, with high-priced tickets to the Grand National and Cheltenham?Public perception of such luxury perks will be even more unforgiving against a backdrop of an ongoing cost of living crisis. A night at the Ivor Novello awards may not be theduck house-level opulenceof 2009’s expenses scandal,but the optics are little better. While much of the population are struggling to pay their electric and food bills, MPs are getting out the fascinators for Ladies’ Day at Aintree.View image in fullscreenHarry Styles on stage at Wembley this year.Photograph: Anthony Pham/Live Nation/PAPoliticians, of course, are human. Who among us wouldn’t be tempted by Harry Styles? The electorate, for its part, tends to want leaders to connect with everyday life. There’s a reason why Malcolm Tucker in The Thick of It – based on the rumour Alastair Campbell got Tony Blair clips of EastEnders and reality shows – makes a “zeitgeist tape” to help his useless ministers seem “in touch”. But it would be disingenuous to pretend MPs are driven to accept hospitality gifts as a bid to be down to earth,or that balancing such demands from the public is somehow a complex, grey area. Most people like to see their MP letting loose at a concert – they just want them to have paid for their ticket.With the standards watchdogdue to question Nigel Faragewhen parliament reopens – an inquiry he temporarily dodged by calling a byelection – the coming weeks will very likely see a renewed focus on what MPs receive and the transparency around it.On paper, Farage’s gifts are in another league to his colleagues’ freebies: forget a ticket to the tennis, we’re talking£5m from a crypto billionaire and further “financial support” from a convicted fraudster. And yet to a public who have for decades seen front-page stories about politicians’ finances – from expenses and second jobs to tax avoidance – the idea that the Reform UK leader is an outlier worth investigating rather than one of a bad bunch can feel at best a hard sell and, at worst, hypocritical.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRupert Lowe set to be paid as much for divisive posts on Elon Musk’s X as for being MPRead moreIf MPs wish to be able to hold Farage to account with credibility, they will need to show they care about cash and transparency in every form. That means the government looking harder into how some MPs are using their influence to make extra money, not least when it’s linked with the growth of the far right. Just this week it emerged that the Restore leader, Rupert Lowe, is set to earn as much from his –anti-migrant– posts on X as he does from his MP’s salary (which he gives to charity) since Elon Musk took over and financially rewarded some high-reach posts. “Gifts” come in many forms.Winning public trust will also require MPs to be squeaky-clean themselves and stop accepting hospitality unless it’s linked to their constituency – even if that means watching the Chelsea flower show on iPlayer like the rest of us.Because every time an MP goes to an event for free, it comes with a hidden cost: a public with ever-decreasing faith in the political class, who are more likely to greet outright corruption or cronyism with a weary shrug. “They’re all the same” is a dangerous public mood for a democracy and one that, once embedded, can be deeply hard to dislodge.Frances Ryan is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Jon Ossoff went low on Natalie Harp. The plan worked | Moira Donegan | The Guardian
description: The senator’s remarks reflect a turning point in Democrats’ attacks on the president. What should we make of them?
Author: Moira Donegan
Headline: The senator’s remarks reflect a turning point in Democrats’ attacks on the president. What should we make of them?
Content: ‘What is the moral consequence of this kind of sexism, the kind that Ossoff evoked – obliquely, subtly, but definitely – with his remark?’Photograph: American Photo Archive/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘What is the moral consequence of this kind of sexism, the kind that Ossoff evoked – obliquely, subtly, but definitely – with his remark?’Photograph: American Photo Archive/AlamyOpinionTrump administrationJon Ossoff went low on Natalie Harp. The plan workedMoira DoneganThe senator’s remarks reflect a turning point in Democrats’ attacks on the president. What should we make of them?Thu 27 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 13.36 EDTShareApparently, he likes to say her namewith a French accent. “Na-tah-lee!” the president cries out, in that affected tone of faux-formality that one might use with a person they love but do not quite respect, and she comes running, her thin legs teetering on her heels.Natalie Harp, Trump’s 35-year-old “executive assistant”, was an odd recurring character in the latest blockbuster Trump administration book, Regime Change, by the New York Times’ Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan. In the book, Harp features like a silent sentinel, ever present but eerily quiet as Trump rants and raves. It’s not exactly clear what the scope of her responsibilities are; though, asJamelle Bouiepoints out, the fact that she evidently helps run the president’s social media accounts, which can sway markets and influence his foreign counterparts, makes her one of the most powerful people in the federal government.But the dignity of Harp’s character does not often seem to equal the gravity of her influence: once, she wascaught on videosprinting across a golf course on foot, chasing the golf cart that was speeding the president away to the next hole. For a while, she wascalled the “human printer”among Trump aides, in reference to the portable printer that Harp carries around with her: one of the primary ways she spends her time appears to be searching for flattering news stories and social media commentary about the president online, and printing it out to nourish his self-regard. But from Haberman and Swan’s reporting, it was not always clear exactly what Harp was thinking. Though many Trumpworld insiders are clearly identifiable as off-the-record sources in their book, Harp does not seem to be among them.It’s a miracle: Natalie Harp has turned Republicans into feminists | Arwa MahdawiRead moreBut recently, more of Harp’s own words have come to light. The Daily Beast published the full text of two letters from Harp to Trump, whose existence had previously been reported by Haberman and Swan. In the letters, Harp is rapturously worshipful, sycophantic, almost slavish. “You are all that matters to me,”she wroteto Trump. She called him her “Guardian and Protector in this Life”. (The capitalization is in the original.) It’s long been known that Trumpprizes devotionamong his underlings, that he seeks out flattering commentary about himself, and that he is surrounded, particularly in his second term, exclusively by the kind of people who will never tell him anything that he does not want to hear. Still, the spectacle of Harp’s obsequiousness – her willingness to debase herself for an 80-year-old man whose vulgarity, misogyny, racism, narcissism and impulsiveness have damaged her country in ways it will probably never recover from – is disturbing and grotesque.Still, Harp herself might be less unsettling than the near certainty that there are others like her – White House staffers and federal bureaucrats and petty functionaries of the Maga machine – who have made flattery of Trump a large portion, if not the entirety, of their jobs. Probably, few Americans would ever have heard of Harp if it were not for Jon Ossoff, the Democratic Georgia senator running for re-election and widely assumed to be mulling a presidential bid, who mentioned Harp in a pointed barb in a campaign stump speech in Atlanta. Trump,Ossoff said, doesn’t want to do the job of president; he wants, instead, to “build his ballroom and travel with Natalie”.We do not need to be stupid: it strains credulity, and discredits the considerable savvy of Ossoff’s team, to claim that this remark was not meant to arouse salacious suspicion about the nature of Harp’s relationship with the president, and speculation that it might be sexual. Ossoff’s wording retained plausible deniability; still, I think he knew exactly what he was doing. Ossoff, in his campaign, has styled himself as firm-minded, resolute and morally ambitious – aninheritor to Barack Obama. But in this remark, he diverged noticeably from Michelle Obama’s famous mantra “when they go low, we go high,” which has long been a shibboleth for the kind of Democratic politicians who have preferred dignity over effectiveness in the Trump era. Ossoff was going low.It is shocking how well it worked. The evocation of Harp in Ossoff’s speech triggered a slew of news stories about the aide, delivered by White House reporters who seemed almost giddy to be able to cite as newsworthy something that before had been merely creepy. Asked about Harp on television, Habermanreferred toher as Trump’s “binky” and “comfort blanket”, infantilizing him in humiliating terms. Trump surrogates were dispatched todefend Harpwith a ferocity and insistence that couldn’t help but suggest that the president himself was angered. Ossoff, it seemed, had struck a nerve. At the beginning of Trump’s rise to power, many in politics gawked at his seemingly sui generis ability to dictate the news cycle: to say outrageous things, or make bizarre provocations, and send reporters, commentators, surrogates and his opponents into a frenzy trying to respond to them. The effect was that Trump determined the subject of discourse; everyone else responded to him. Ossoff turned the tables, and he made it look easy.Unhinged White House response shows senator’s ‘Natalie’ barb struck a nerveRead moreOne of the allegations that Trump’s aides spewed in their responses to the remark was that in insinuating that something inappropriate was afoot between Trump and Harp, Ossoff was being sexist. Those on the left rushed to discount this: no one, after all, really believes thatDonald Trump, he of “grab ’em by the pussy”, is leading a movement that has serious or sincere concerns for women’s dignity. But to say that Ossoff’s remark contained no misogyny would be naive, if not dishonest: if his suggestion was made deliberately, then he was using Harp’s gender to undermine her professionalism, and to evoke a sex scandal. Of course there is misogyny in this gesture, the suggestion that a young woman is not entirely serious. That Harp’s character and conduct suggest this much more than her sex does need not force us to pretend not to see things that we do.What is the moral consequence of this kind of sexism, the kind that Ossoff evoked – obliquely, subtly, but definitely – with his remark? For my part, I do not see any equivalence between the misogyny imposed on American women by the Trump regime – or, for that matter, the misogyny imposed on American women by Trump personally – and the minor distastefulness of Ossoff. It’s like comparing a dropper of water to the Pacific Ocean. Every woman, every feminist, knows that she has accepted things out of necessity or convenience that the most stringent adherence to principle would require her to reject. And I confess, I am more encouraged by Ossoff’s pugnaciousness than I am put off by the gendered undertones of the remark. After all, it is a grim reality of our gendered world that wherever there is a straight man who esteems himself to be godlike and extraordinary, there will be a straight woman somewhere not far behind who inexplicably believes him. We must work on building a world where this is not true. The first step might be getting this guy out of the White House.Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnistExplore more on these topicsTrump administrationOpinionUS politicsWomenDonald TrumpGenderDemocratsNatalie HarpcommentShareReuse this content

title: Does Nigel Farage know what people really think of him? I do – and he won’t like it | Aditya Chakrabortty | The Guardian
description: An anti-Farage army of voters is there to be galvanised, as exclusive data shows. But getting them out will be tricky, says Guardian columnist Aditya Chakrabortty
Author: Aditya Chakrabortty
Headline: An anti-Farage army of voters is there to be galvanised, as exclusive data shows. But getting them out will be tricky, says Guardian columnist Aditya Chakrabortty
Content: Illustration: Bill Bragg/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Bill Bragg/The GuardianOpinionReform UKDoes Nigel Farage know what people really think of him? I do – and he won’t like itAditya ChakraborttyAn anti-Farage army of voters is there to be galvanised, as exclusive data shows. But getting them out will be trickyThu 27 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 09.52 EDTShareWho can stopNigel Farage? Which voters would actually dig out their ID and schlep down to the polling booth to fight him?Over the past year, these two questions have come to shape British politics. From Runcorn and Helsby to Caerphilly and Aberdeen South, via countless flimsy leaflets claiming “Only X can win here”, parties have jostled for the part of his majesty’s opposition to Reform. Those battles have given us Hannah Spencer and Andy Burnham; they have bulldozed Labour in Wales and forcedKeir Starmerout of No 10.Those questions hang over Britain even now, in what is easily Farage’s summer horribilis. He faces a shiny new prime minister and fronts a team that keeps scrapping with itself, while ahead looms a parliamentary investigation into whether he should have declared a £5m gift from agenerous crypto billionaire from the other side of the world. Look at these turquoise clowns, chortle the Westminster commentators. Check out that Burnham bounce, marvel analysts.And despite it all, Farage’s side are almost neck and neck in the polls with Burnham’s. Constituency-level analysis suggests that, were an election called tomorrow, Reform would leap from eight to somewhere between 100 and 200 seats. Among thoseLabourMPs swept out by a turquoise tide could easily be the party chair, Bridget Phillipson, the chancellor, John Healey, and the justice secretary, who is in charge of the prisoner release programme, Alex Norris.A hard-right organisation thatexerts a mysterious yet reliable pull on former membersof theBritish National partymay have a lower electoral ceiling than many feared; but its floor remains high enough to help deny Burnham an outright majority. A party that wants Trump-style deportation squads on British streets, to curb further the right to protest and to slash social security might still lead the next government, or at least become the official opposition.Anyone worried by that prospect needs to understand who those anti-Farage voters are and what could get them off their sofas at an election. That’s why I was glad to have an exclusive look at the first-ever study of the anti-Reform electorate.Published today by anti-racist campaigners Hope Not Hate, it is based on a large survey by Focaldata of nearly 9,000 Britons. These are people who, if a snap election were called tomorrow, could be persuaded to go out and put their “x” against an opponent to Reform. They are some of the most important voters in the country and they are probably not who you think.If I say “anti-Reform army”, who do you see? Perhaps a bunch of leftwingers who live in cities, haver between Zack Polanski and Andy Burnham and ask their baristas for exotic milks. That’s half of them, and, the study shows, they skew young, minority ethnic and graduate. But the other half aren’t on the left at all. The joint-largest group in the Farage resistance is what Hope Not Hate describe as “rightwing on cultural issues and very rightwing on economics”. Think driveways, tidy lawns, a fondness forLudwig. Their worry isn’t that the turquoise troops will be conservative – it’s that they won’t be conservative enough, instead bringing chaos. One other key demographic fact in the fight against Farage: women just don’t like what he stands for. That weak spot has been known to analysts for years and it’s partly why in Makerfield theReform candidate’s saloon-bar sexismhelped torpedo his chances.Perhaps you too have spotted the curious omission in this little list of black marks against Farage’s name. To any question in Britain today, Reform reliably provides one answer: it’s the immigrants’ fault. Housing? Immigrants. Welfare? Immigrants. Oh, and small boats. Yet many who dislike Reform don’t object to its anti-migrant rhetoric. Those comfortable rightwingers I’ve just mentioned were vital in denying GB News regular Matt Goodwin a victory in Gorton and Denton earlier this year, according to one local campaigner who spent weeks doorknocking there – but not for the reasons lefties might think. “Racism doesn’t offend them; they just think it’s vulgar.”In that one-liner lies a grave fault in mainstream politics and media: they have made racism more socially acceptable than at any point in the past 40-odd years. Keir Starmer and his flags, Yvette Cooper and the British bunting she says she used for home decor, Shabana Mahmood telling“white liberal hecklers” to “fuck right off”: look on your works, ye mighty, and despair.I draw two big conclusions from this important study. The first is that what works against Reform in one seat will almost certainly not work in others. At the time of the Caerphilly showdown, Cardiff University’s Dr Jac Larner was regularly rung up by the London-based media: what lessons should they learn from Plaid Cymru’s success? He doesn’t think there are many. “Plaid can provide an alternative political identity for voters: progressive, working class – and Welsh. In Scotland, the SNP can still do that.” But in England, the nationalist politicians wear red corduroys and are bankrolled by foreign billionaires while bleating on about remigration for brown and black people.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHere’s the other conclusion: opponents of Reform share with its supporters an utter abhorrence of Westminster. By two to one, the pollsters find, they are deeply unhappy with mainstream politicians and media. Writing aboutHope Not Hate’s analysis last yearinto Reform voters, I noted that very few of them were unreachable by other parties – it’s just that most politicians didn’t bother to reach out. In the case of Starmer’s Labour it was a patronising pat on the head, and next to no attempt to tackle urgent problems such as the cost of living.Farage returns to our screens next week, as the Reform party conference kicks off. One imagines there will be the mandatory triumphalism and speeches promising that tomorrow belongs to them. It isn’t true, of course. Voters might back Farage or Burnham, but they are mainly lending their support, not committing it. The kind of compromises that the new prime minister has begun making this week oncouncil housebuildingand needless dithering on nationalising Thames Water will arouse little ire now. The people who will mind are those leftwingers who helped get Burnham into parliament, and for now they may be mollified by a couple of token gestures. But if Labour’s strategy is essentially to do what Starmer did, but with better comms and more social-media dopamine, it will get the same result as he did: a disaster, not just for Labour, but for the rest of us.Aditya Chakrabortty is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsReform UKOpinionNigel FarageAndy BurnhamKeir StarmerLabourcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on the Nepal-Tibet floods: prepare for more climate-linked disasters | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Medicine, food and other supplies are the urgent priority. But the rising risks from shrinking glaciers must be faced too
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Medicine, food and other supplies are the urgent priority. But the rising risks from shrinking glaciers must be faced too
Content: Buildings and roads are buried in mud and debris following flash floods at Devighat in Nuwakot district, Nepal.Photograph: Skanda Gautam/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenBuildings and roads are buried in mud and debris following flash floods at Devighat in Nuwakot district, Nepal.Photograph: Skanda Gautam/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockOpinionNepal-Tibet flood disasterThe Guardian view on the Nepal-Tibet floods: prepare for more climate-linked disastersEditorialMedicine, food and other supplies are the urgent priority. But the rising risks from shrinking glaciers must be faced tooThu 27 Aug 2026 13.40 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 13.46 EDTShareThousands of people in Nepal and Tibet are in desperate need of emergency assistance following Wednesday’s disaster. With360 peopleconfirmed dead, more than 1,300 others are still missing as search and rescue operations continue. The precise sequence of events linking glacier collapse to flash floods is yet to be confirmed. But there is no doubting the enormous destructive power of the brown torrent that can be seen on video clips surging down the steeply sided Himalayan valleys, sweeping away everyone and everything in its path.Testimony from survivors about terrifying near-escapes and losses is reminiscent of previous disasters, including the 2004 tsunami. With some of the worst-affected areas still cut off and accessible only by helicopter, there is a high level of uncertainty about the total number of people who have died or homes that have been destroyed. Existing medical, food, shelter and sanitation supplies will need to be replenished. Pledges of help for locally led relief efforts from foreign governments and agencies, following reports that hundreds of those missing weretouristsor pilgrims, must lead to swift action. People need basics including electricity and clean water before they can start to rebuild and recover.Satellite images of the glacier and affected rivers are among crucial pieces of evidence used by scientists to piece together an account of what happened. Initial reports of an earthquake were later discounted, with seismic activity instead attributed to theimpact of the glacier collapseand ice-rock avalanche. Nepalese authorities have issued warnings about the high risk of further floods. Women and children who have been displaced are particularly vulnerable to further harm, including disease and trafficking.As with other disasters that are widely recognised to be climate-related, it is unwise to jump too swiftly to conclusions.Tectonic movement, which leads glaciers to change their shape over time, is a natural process. But already, multiple glaciologists and other earth scientists have pointed to global heating as a crucial destabilising factor. Higher temperatures are well established to be altering mountain environments worldwide, with the Himalayas warmingtwice as fastas the global average. As the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has pointed out, this puts the region and its people at heightened risk not only from avalanches,landslidesand floods, but also from freshwater shortages caused by retreating glaciers.The implications of this may seem overwhelming. While millions – and perhaps billions – of people around the world accept that greenhouse gas emissions have altered the Earth’s atmosphere, the impact of human activity on the geology of mountains is a less familiar idea. Once the immediate humanitarian crisis inNepalhas eased, and survivors have been helped to safety, this is the reality that must be addressed.Mitigation of the climate threat through the transition away from fossil fuels remains essential. But resilience andadaptation measuresalso offer vital protection, particular to communities in exposed locations. As mountains become more dangerous, early-warning systems must be strengthened. Disaster preparedness should be prioritised at a national level and in aid budgets so that agencies are better equipped to react. Governments must rally round the people of Nepal and Tibet, and prepare to support similarly afflicted parts of the world in future.Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterOpinionFloodingAvalanchesExtreme weatherClimate crisisNepalTibeteditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on energy costs: vulnerable households need help with their bills | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Soaring prices are plunging struggling families into debt. The government must support them in the short term as it invests in a clean energy future
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Soaring prices are plunging struggling families into debt. The government must support them in the short term as it invests in a clean energy future
Content: ‘The government is right to stress, as the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, did again this week, that completing the transition away from fossil fuels holds the key to bringing future costs down.’Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The government is right to stress, as the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, did again this week, that completing the transition away from fossil fuels holds the key to bringing future costs down.’Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesOpinionEnergy billsThe Guardian view on energy costs: vulnerable households need help with their billsEditorialSoaring prices are plunging struggling families into debt. The government must support them in the short term as it invests in a clean energy futureThu 27 Aug 2026 13.39 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 00.17 EDTShareFuelled by the consequences of Donald Trump’s disastrous war on Iran, household energy debt in Britain is continuing to soar,risingto a record £6bn by the end of June. That figure is set to hit £7bn by the end of the year, as the government’s cap on gas and electricity pricesgoes upto a three-year high in October. The human cost among the less well off will be more people regularly choosing whether to skip meals, ignore other bills or stay cold this winter.Such is life at the sharp end of the cost of living crisis, which Andy Burnham has made it his priority to address since arriving in Downing Street. The day after he became prime minister, Mr Burnhamannouncedthat VAT would be removed from electricity bills from the beginning of October. But the Middle East-related rise in the price cap, announced on Wednesday, more than wipes out the effect of his cut. In an era of geopolitical volatility, high energy costs have become the new normal.The government is right to stress, as the energy secretary,Miatta Fahnbulleh, did again this week, that completing the transition away from fossil fuels holds the key to bringing future costs down. As well as being the right thing to do, clean renewable energy will eventually deliver cheaper bills and end Britain’s exposure to fluctuations on international gas markets. But as families’ finances are tipped over the edge by fuel prices they simply cannot afford, short-term solutions are needed if Mr Burnham is to deliver on his pledge to give them “breathing space”.The warm-homes discount for vulnerable households was set at £140 in 2011; it has gone up by a miserly £10 since then. A new social discount scheme is desperately required, which can properly insulate the less well off from financial pressures that neither they nor the government can control. Emergency crisis and resilience funds run by local councils need to be boosted.Gordon Brown hassuggestedthat the latter could be done through the introduction of a new betting and gaming tax. The Trades Union Congress haslobbiedfor the financing of a new social tariff through a windfall tax on banks. Flexibility, as Mr Brown has also observed, can be sought within the fiscal rules Mr Burnham has inherited. With the requisite political will, the money can be found.At the same time, the government needs to drive the necessary investment in the green transition and find a way to shift more of its financing on to the broadest shoulders. In part, that should mean switching more environmental costs away from household bills and into general taxation. Researchindicatesthat some low-income households spend three times more of their net income on levies than wealthier ones. Britain’s climate goals make moral and economic sense, and are supported by the public. But an overly bill-focused approach to green investment helps those seeking to present net zero as the problem rather than the solution.Following Ofgem’s announcement of the price cap rise, Mr Burnhamacknowledgedthe impact it would have. A further, bigger spike in January ispredictedif market volatility continues. The prime minister’s VAT cut on electricity bills was welcome. But as the Conservatives and Reform UK exploit high energy costs to create dividing lines over the green transition, the government’s approach needs to become bigger and bolder.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: We need new reservoirs – and it’s a job for the state, not private companies  | Water | The Guardian
description: Letters: David Griffiths says mayors could be empowered to build water infrastructure, while Kevin Whately suggests incorporating communal storage into new housing estates
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: David Griffiths says mayors could be empowered to build water infrastructure, while Kevin Whately suggests incorporating communal storage into new housing estates
Content: The reservoir at Scammonden dam, West Yorkshire, which opened in 1971.Photograph: Don McPhee/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe reservoir at Scammonden dam, West Yorkshire, which opened in 1971.Photograph: Don McPhee/The GuardianWaterLettersWe need new reservoirs – and it’s a job for the state, not private companiesDavid Griffithssays mayors could be empowered to build water infrastructure, whileKevin Whatelysuggests incorporating communal storage into new housing estatesThu 27 Aug 2026 12.37 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 13.15 EDTSharePete Ford (Letters, 20 August) rightly reminds us that “The Victorians … built reservoirs, aqueducts and local water-storage infrastructure.” But who were these “Victorians”? Generally speaking, they were local councillors and their professional engineers.Taking my own town as an example, within 40 years of its incorporation as a borough in 1868 it had built five new reservoirs, as well as taking over others previously provided by ad hoc groups of commissioners, with water delivered through 240 miles of mains. By 1897 it was one of 610 urban councils with their own water undertakings.As recently as 1971, Queen Elizabeth opened Scammonden dam (a joint project of Huddersfield Corporation Waterworks and the Ministry of Transport, which also carries the trans-Pennine M62 motorway). With new reservoirs now urgently needed, perhaps the Burnham government will see this once again as an appropriate role for mayors and combined authorities, rather than failing private companies.David GriffithsHuddersfield, West YorkshireI so agree with Sheila Carey-Thomas’s suggestion that communal underground water storage could be incorporated into new housing estates to take advantage of our wet springs (Letters, 20 August).Similarly, heat-exchange shafts could be sunk and shared to tap heat from underground. Surely, too, by locating any planned datacentres near new housing estates, the cooling water could be piped to centrally heat the houses, rather than wasted. All of the above could be incorporated into estates during the construction phase without adding hugely to the cost of each individual house.Kevin WhatelyAspley Heath, BedfordshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Students are being set up to fail by compulsory GCSE resits | GCSEs | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to Polly Toynbee’s article calling for mandatory exam resits to be scrapped in a first step towards education reform
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to Polly Toynbee’s article calling for mandatory exam resits to be scrapped in a first step towards education reform
Content: ‘It is no surprise that the number of those not in education, employment or training has risen in an age of compulsory resits.’Photograph: Caiaimage/Chris Ryan/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreen‘It is no surprise that the number of those not in education, employment or training has risen in an age of compulsory resits.’Photograph: Caiaimage/Chris Ryan/Getty Images/iStockphotoGCSEsLettersStudents are being set up to fail by compulsory GCSE resitsReaders respond to Polly Toynbee’s article calling for mandatory exam resits to be scrapped in a first step towards education reformThu 27 Aug 2026 12.38 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 13.13 EDTShareI was delighted to read Polly Toynbee’s demolition of compulsory GCSE resits (How can we stop destroying the prospects of a generation? Scrapping compulsory GCSE resits will be a start, 24 August). Of course, level 2 qualifications in maths and English should be accessible to all school leavers who need them. However, the depressing treadmill of resitting resits is thin educational gruel and Michael Gove should be ashamed for espousing such a killjoy policy.As a governor at a large further education college in Bedford, I find it depressing to receive data at every single board meeting focusing on GCSE resit results for thousands of students who “failed” maths and English just a few months previously. Speaking to students and staff, it is apparent that resitting exams is counterproductive. Compulsory GCSE resits are a negative learning experience, offering no reflection on how to improve. In most cases students merely fail again.It does not have to be this way. The potential stepping-stone qualifications are a positive idea and lessons from the past need to be considered. I began my career teaching mature students (aged 17 to 70) GCSE English at evening classes in the 1980s. We did not force them to do the same course over and over. Rather, we offered “mature” syllabuses, avoiding the repetition of school failure and using more creative approaches to learning and assessment. It is no surprise that the number of those not in education, employment or training has risen in an age of compulsory resits.John ButcherEmeritus professor of inclusive teaching in higher education, The Open UniversityPolly Toynbee’s excellent article describes just how damaging our exam system has become. Failing the 11-plus in 1960, when only one boy from my large working-class West Yorkshire primary school class passed, negatively affected the rest of my life. I eventually got to university, but was unable to do a BA, which I wanted to do, because of a lack of an O-level foreign language – it was not taught at my school. I struggled through a BSc.I subsequently had a career as a secondary school teacher and have been appalled by how Tory governments negatively affected the educational experience of students from the late 1980s, starting with the absurd “quart in a pint pot” Kenneth Baker national curriculum and marketisation of schooling. More recently, the manic Michael Gove “reforms” have destroyed local education authority control and accountability, wasted colossal amounts of money on “free schools” and academy chain bureaucracies, imposed a punitive inspection system, narrowed the 14-16 curriculum and turbocharged norm-referenced overassessment. All these changes have been driven by a nostalgia for a selective and academic elitist education that is unsuited to modern times.The third of students unable to pass maths and English GCSE and condemned to the resit treadmill are victims of Tory arrogance and folly, and will feel this “failure” just as I did with the “stupid” (invoking Govian terminology) 11-plus for the rest of their lives.Philip WoodKidlington, OxfordshirePolly Toynbee’s article should be read alongside Pete Crockett’s letter on the same date (Let’s focus on what people with special needs can do, rather than what they can’t, 24 August). Grades 1 to 3 are not “fails” for many students with additional needs – they are successes, built on the hard work of students, teachers and teaching assistants, often against the odds.Ruth EversleyPaulton, SomersetHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Surprising AI breakthroughs raise soul-searching questions for mathematicians | Mathematics | The Guardian
description: Letters: Whether mathematics thrives or perishes in the age of AI depends on what it is that society values in the human intellect, writes Dr Henry Bradford
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Whether mathematics thrives or perishes in the age of AI depends on what it is that society values in the human intellect, writes Dr Henry Bradford
Content: ‘The development of AI will stimulate debate about the value of mathematics as practised by human beings.’Photograph: Igor Mojzes/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘The development of AI will stimulate debate about the value of mathematics as practised by human beings.’Photograph: Igor Mojzes/AlamyMathematicsLettersSurprising AI breakthroughs raise soul-searching questions for mathematiciansWhether mathematics thrives or perishes in the age of AI depends on what it is that society values in the human intellect, writesDr Henry BradfordThu 27 Aug 2026 12.37 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 12.40 EDTShareI share Kasra Rafi and Bruce Schneier’s impression that recent mathematical breakthroughs by AI consist in clever recombination of existing ideas, not development of truly novel theory (No, AI doesn’t mean the end of mathematics – at least not yet, 25 August). The question is: what happens to mathematics if this changes?Like many mathematicians, I have done much soul-searching in recent weeks, especially since a key problem in my own field of group theory (the existence of non-sofic groups) was solved this month by OpenAI’s Astra model. Astra’s proof consists largely in a slight twist on theorems by my colleagues Gabor Kun and Andreas Thom. That said, even a few months ago I would have found the idea that AI was capable of such a breakthrough incredible, so it seems foolhardy now to bet against AIs achieving superhuman capabilities in all areas of mathematical thought in the coming years.This forces the question: what is the purpose of mathematical research? Is it simply to prove new theorems (at which task future AIs may be far better than humans)? The great American mathematician Bill Thurston thought not: in his1994 essayOn Proof and Progress in Mathematics, he wrote that mathematicians “discover ... that what they really want is usually not some collection of ‘answers’ – what they want isunderstanding”. In other words, mathematics consists in the ideas living in human brains, with new theorems serving as markers for our progress in understanding and sharing these ideas.This matters, because the development of AI will stimulate debate about the value of mathematics as practised by human beings. If AI can churn out research papers faster and cheaper than humans, then administrators within cash-strapped universities will surely be tempted to regard their mathematical researchers as superfluous. On Thurston’s view, this would be a mistake, because the value of those researchers’ work consists less in the papers they write than in their contributions to the preservation and furtherance of mathematical knowledge amongpeople.Whether mathematics thrives or perishes in the age of AI is not merely a technical question about the capabilities of future machine intelligences. It is a collective decision that society makes about what it is in the human intellect that we choose to value.Dr Henry BradfordFellow of mathematics, Christ’s College, University of CambridgeHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Government must prioritise heat pump installation to tackle climate chaos | Environment policy | The Guardian
description: Letter: Colin Hines says Andy Burnham’s focus should be on drastically cutting fossil fuel use in a way that reduces bills and generates secure jobs
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Colin Hines says Andy Burnham’s focus should be on drastically cutting fossil fuel use in a way that reduces bills and generates secure jobs
Content: The installation of heat pumps – which can also provide cooling in summer – in all properties would making buildings more energy-efficient, says one reader.Photograph: Pancake Pictures/Getty Images/Image SourceView image in fullscreenThe installation of heat pumps – which can also provide cooling in summer – in all properties would making buildings more energy-efficient, says one reader.Photograph: Pancake Pictures/Getty Images/Image SourceEnvironment policyLettersGovernment must prioritise heat pump installation to tackle climate chaosColin Hinessays Andy Burnham’s focus should be on drastically cutting fossil fuel use in a way that reduces bills and generates secure jobsThu 27 Aug 2026 12.37 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 12.40 EDTShareIt is hardly surprising that many who were optimistic and supportive of Andy Burnham becoming prime minister, but who also prioritised tackling climate chaos, are becoming increasingly unsure about him, given his tardiness in emphasising this threat as an overriding policy objective (Labour ‘could lose up to 50 seats’ to Greens if new drilling in North Sea approved, 19 August).One of the problems he faces is that the political debate around energy is obsessed with relatively short-term fossil fuel supplies. Instead, the focus should be on drastically and rapidly cutting fossil fuel use in a way that reduces bills and generates secure jobs through a devolved energy programme for every postcode.Key to this must be a public commitment to rapidly “get off gas”. This must prioritise a rapid nationwide programme of increasing the installation ofheat and cooling pumpsin all properties and making buildings more energy-efficient.An immediate source of labour could come from giving work to existing workers made redundant by Keir Starmer’s ill-thought-out policy to cut energy billsbydropping investmentin energy saving. Nothing concrete was put in its place and Andrew Warren, chair of the British Energy Efficiency Federation,has pointed outthat a staggering 12,100 skilled professionals have already been made redundant, with a further 80,000 estimated to be made redundant in the next 12 months.A final social advantage to this approach would be that the future labour force could come from apprenticeships that create the skilled workers required and would help tackle today’s youth unemployment problem.Colin HinesConvener, Green New Deal GroupHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Liverpool need midfield nous, Michael Carrick is already under pressure and Villa can bid farewell to Enzi Konsa
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Liverpool need midfield nous, Michael Carrick is already under pressure and Villa can bid farewell to Enzi Konsa
Content: Left to right: Arsenal’s Ezri Konsa, Manchester City’s Marc Guéhi and Forest’s Morgan Gibbs-White.Composite: EPA, GettyView image in fullscreenLeft to right: Arsenal’s Ezri Konsa, Manchester City’s Marc Guéhi and Forest’s Morgan Gibbs-White.Composite: EPA, GettyTen things to look out for this weekendPremier LeaguePremier League: 10 things to look out for this weekendLiverpool need midfield nous, Michael Carrick is already under pressure and Villa can bid farewell to Enzi KonsaGuardian sportThu 27 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 19.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google1Guéhi versatility crucial as Bouaddi arrivesEnzo Maresca hasa shiny new £85m midfielderhe could select for a debut but, at 18 years old, he may want Ayyoub Bouaddi to have a bit of time watching on from the bench to learn about the Premier League from his elders. The Moroccan may not have anticipated one of those to be a centre-back by trade. Marc Guéhi will be eager to make a triumphant return to Crystal Palace and may well have the opportunity to do so from central midfield, where he played last weekend in the victory over Bournemouth, scoring the equaliser. The centre-back was a surprise selection in the blocker role next to Elliot Anderson, but equipped himself admirably and was not limited to the dirty work, often being found in more advanced positions in open play and happy to have the ball at his feet. His long-term future is unlikely to be outside of defence but further proof of Guéhi’s adaptability will be a positive for Maresca, as a long season awaits.Will UnwinCrystal Palace vManchester City, Friday 8pm (all times BST)2Liverpool need to stop Gibbs-White“It is just not personnel,” insisted Andoni Iraola in response to Liverpool conceding two goals to quick Newcastle transitions in his first Premier League game as the club’s head coach. Some long-term faults can not be rectified overnight – although that did not prevent some hysterical reactions to the performance at St James’ Park – and with Liverpool prioritising wingers in the final days of the transfer window the answer to this particular weakness, as Iraola indicated, lies on the training ground. Morgan Gibbs-White revelled in the spaces behind Liverpool’s midfield last season as he – and set-pieces – helped Nottingham Forest toa second successive league win at Anfield. Iraola does not want to curb Ryan Gravenberch’s attacking instincts but greater tactical discipline and willingness to do the dirty work from the entire Liverpool midfield will be needed to stop Gibbs-White producing a repeat performance. Forest’snew record signing, Liam Delap, has also been registered in time to play.Andy HunterLiverpool vNottingham Forest, Saturday 12.30pm3Everton note Cherries’ set-piece strugglesThere were so many encouraging takeaways for Bournemouth despite an agonising late defeat at Manchester City. The catalyst for City’s turnaround was Marc Guéhi’s 84th-minute equaliser, the England defender heading in unmarked at a corner, after wasting a near-identical earlier chance. For Bournemouth, it was a familiar source of pain; only Liverpool conceded more set-piece goals in the top flight last season (20), with the Cherries and Crystal Palace both conceding 18. Bournemouth sought to address their vulnerability in the summer by hiring their first dedicated set-piece coach in Nicolas Gagnon, who worked with Canada at the World Cup and previously at Southampton and in Saudi Arabia. Only Arsenal, Manchester City,Manchester Unitedand Aston Villa claimed more points away from home than Everton last season and David Moyes’s centre-backs, Jarrad Branthwaite and James Tarkowski, will be licking their lips if Bournemouth do not sharpen up their act.Ben FisherBournemouth v Everton, Saturday 3pmView image in fullscreenBournemouth were again undone by a set-piece goal as they lost 2-1 at Manchester City.Photograph: Darren Staples/AFP/Getty Images4Too early for a relegation six-pointer?Contrasting opening weekends for Coventry and Hull, harsh reality dealt out against the dream scenario lived out. AtArsenal, Coventry were well beaten by the champions, while in East Yorkshire, Manchester United were soundly, deservedly defeated. Despite contrasting starts, both teams remain warm favourites for relegation. Two defeats in a row for Frank Lampard’s team would dim the optimism of a summer of anticipation. Hull seek to extend the reverie of last week though Coventry are unlikely to be caught as cold as United last week, and surely cannot defend set pieces so badly. The last three Championship matches between these two teams ended in draws, last season’s meetings goalless, although both squads have since been upgraded by brisk transfer business. At Hull, much is expected of Lucas Herrington who missed Australia’s fateful penalty against Egypt at the World Cup. The teenage defender shone against Stoke in the Tigers’ successful midweek Carabao Cup assignment.John BrewinCoventry v Hull, Saturday 3pm5Tottenham keen for Tonali to tickIt has not taken long for Sandro Tonali to be reunited with his former teammates. After succumbing 3-0 on the opening weekend atBrentford, a home victory will be the minimum requirement for Tottenham. Roberto De Zerbi and his players will be desperate to show that things have changed after a busy summer in the transfer market. Tonali will be a key part of that; he was the only central midfielder who made it past half-time in west London, so at least has minutes in his legs to build on. The Italian will be eager to not suffer at the hands of a team that served him well after bringing him to England. Tonali is supposed to make his new team tick and a rousing home debut would do a lot for everyone’s confidence, while defeat will bring plenty more questions.WUTottenham v Newcastle, Saturday 5.30pmView image in fullscreenSandro Tonali (left) faces his old club Newcastle after a difficult debut against Brentford.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian6Acheampong fights to stay with BluesThis is an important moment in Josh Acheampong’s development. The 20-year-old academy graduate did not have many opportunities last year but he started in Xabi Alonso’s back three whenChelseabeat Fulham on Monday. It was a big vote of confidence from Alonso in the young defender, who played well, and may indicate that Acheampong will stay at Stamford Bridge this season. Several clubs are interested in the England youth international and there is talk of a loan before the transfer window shuts, but Acheampong would strengthen his position further if he is selected again for Sunday’s home game against Brighton.Jacob Steinbergskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChelsea v Brighton, Sunday 2pm7Carragher comments can fuel Black CatsOn Monday night, Jamie Carragher told a Sky Sports audience that he thought Sunderland might be relegated this season. The former Liverpool defender compared Régis Le Bris’s team to the Sheffield United side managed by Chris Wilder that went down in 2020-2021 – their second season after promotion – and suggested Sunderland were “arrogant”. How will Le Bris’s players respond against Fulham at the Stadium of Light on Sunday? Has the moment arrived to end a winlessPremier Leaguerun against the west London side stretching back 12 years? If there are legitimate concerns about the ability of Le Bris’s players to cope with a Europa League campaign, regular Sunderland watchers struggle to buy into the accusations or arrogance, let alone the analogy with a very different Sheffield United side. Nonetheless, last Saturday’s 2-1 defeat at Ipswich has prompted a certain anxiety, leaving Wearsiders hoping Nordi Mukiele is fit enough to raise defensive standards.Louise TaylorSunderland v Fulham, Sunday 2pmView image in fullscreenSunderland fans have bristled at Jamie Carragher’s prediction for their team’s season.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/Reuters8Leeds look to strengthen as Bees buzzSub-plots abound at Elland Road as Leeds and Brentford meet after two wins apiece from their first competitive matches of the season. There is the goalkeeping beauty contest between Daniel Farke’s showpiece summer signing, James Trafford – who has registered two clean sheets in his opening games – and Brentford’s Caoimhin Kelleher. Further forward, fans can ponder the question of which centre forward, the Leeds favourite Dominic Calvert-Lewin or his opposite number Igor Thiago will prove the more incisive. Similarly the technical area tactical duel involving Daniel Farke and Keith Andrews looks extremely hard to call. Away from the pitch, Farke is hoping to win a race with Sunderland to sign Marseille winger Igor Paixão for around £30m as the Leeds manager urges his board to strengthen. “I’m happy with my group and my signings so far,” said Farke. “But we know we can definitely improve our squad. That is what Leeds supporters andLeeds Uniteddeserve.”LTLeeds v Brentford, Sunday 2pm9Carrick under pressure to deliverManchester United are bloody-nosed andIpswich Towndefinitely delighted after the tale of each team’s results on the opening weekend. At Hull City, Michael Carrick’s team played with zero cohesion and conviction and went down to a miserable 2-0 loss. At Portman Road Gary O’Neil’s side hosted Sunderland and claimed a rousing late 2-1 win, so arrive at Old Trafford with a bounce in the step. Carrick has to lift his men and get a result – preferably victory. A loss, at home, to another promoted team, would begin the latest inquest into a United No 1: a predicament suffered by every manager post-Sir Alex Ferguson.Jamie JacksonManchester United v Ipswich, Sunday 4.30pm10Villa fans bid farewell to KonsaAt a time when the manner of a player’s departure feels particularly pertinent, especially atAston Villa, Ezri Konsa can expect a warm reception on his return to the club. Konsa could make his Arsenal debut at Villa Park against his former club, where he excelled across seven seasons. A £12m buy from Brentford in 2019, Konsa surely represents one of their finest signings in the Premier League era. He joined fresh from a single season in the Championship with Brentford and left as an England regular and Europa League winner. Konsa’s role in Villa’s recent success should not be overlooked. Unai Emery can be judged by Villa’s extraordinary run of league finishes – seventh, fourth, sixth and fourth – but also his track record of turning promising talents, like Konsa, into fully-fledged internationals.BFAston Villa v Arsenal, Monday 8pmPosTeamPGDPts1Brighton1432Arsenal1333Brentford1334Everton1235Hull1236Chelsea1137Ipswich1138Man City1139Leeds11310Liverpool10111Newcastle10112Fulham1-1013AFC Bournemouth1-1014Sunderland1-1015Nottm Forest1-1016Crystal Palace1-2017Man Utd1-2018Coventry1-3019Tottenham Hotspur1-3020Aston Villa1-40Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueTen things to look out for this weekendArsenalManchester CityManchester UnitedTottenham HotspurLiverpoolChelseafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Broad and Anderson lament ‘extreme and tiresome’ off-field incidents involving England players | Stuart Broad | The Guardian
description: Stuart Broad and Jimmy ­Anderson have criticised the ‘extreme and tiresome’ flood of negative ­stories around the England cricket team’s drinking and socialising habits
Author: Simon Burnton
Headline: Stuart Broad and Jimmy ­Anderson have criticised the ‘extreme and tiresome’ flood of negative ­stories around the England cricket team’s drinking and socialising habits
Content: A portrait of England bowlers James Anderson and Stuart Broad in the Long Room at Lord’s.Photograph: Gareth Copley/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA portrait of England bowlers James Anderson and Stuart Broad in the Long Room at Lord’s.Photograph: Gareth Copley/Getty ImagesStuart BroadBroad and Anderson lament ‘extreme and tiresome’ off-field incidents involving England players‘Mind-numbing that people end up in these positions’Brydon Carse incident is the latest in a long lineSimon Burntonat Lord'sThu 27 Aug 2026 16.46 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 19.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStuart Broad and Jimmy Anderson have criticised the “extreme and tiresome” flood of negative stories around the England cricket team’s drinking and socialising habits, with Anderson – England’s all-time leading wicket-taker – saying it is “just mind-numbing that people can still be putting themselves in these positions”.The latest scandal involving members of the Test squad involved the bowler Brydon Carse, who was pictured being led away from a Derby bar in handcuffs in the early hours of Sunday morning. The 31-year-old was briefly arrested by police on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly before being “de-arrested”, though they continue to investigate an allegation of assault in connection with the incident. Carse was dropped from the squad for the second Test against Pakistan that started at Lord’s on Thursday, buttook two wickets for Durhamon the first day of their County Championship game against Gloucestershire.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAbbas dusts himself down to dominate England – and close in on the honours board | Simon BurntonRead more“Eight of the 30 centrally contracted players have now been reprimanded or involved and that is quite extreme and actually quite tiresome,” Broad said, at the unveiling of a joint portrait of himself and Anderson at Lord’s on Wednesday night. “Joe Root spoke beautifully on this and is a brilliant example of how to do it. If you won’t listen to him and follow him, then this is not for you. South Africa away [this winter] and Australia at home [next summer] – if you can’t commit every bit of your mind and body to wanting to perform on this field, then I don’t understand.”Anderson was one of several players fined for a breach of discipline at a nightclub in St Lucia during the 2007 World Cup, when he was 24. “I learned my lesson the hard way early on,” he said. “You learn from it and I said to myself: ‘Right, I’m not going out for the next two years.’ It was a massive wake-up call. You can make a mistake when you’re young, but you have to learn from it and grow up fast. So it’s just mind-numbing that people can still be putting themselves in these positions when there is so much attention around it.”Anderson went on to play 401 games for England across all formats, before retiring from international cricket in 2024 aged 41. He continues to play for Lancashire. “We went through our careers. People messed up and we were no angels – we enjoyed a beer and celebrated victory as hard as anyone,” he said. “But when we were successful, we had players who did that sort of policing. Someone would say: ‘Just come away, you don’t need another drink, you don’t need to go to a nightclub,’ and if someone wasn’t training properly someone would say to them: ‘You tossed off that net session, you didn’t practise properly.’ This is a young team and they’ll get there.”Explore more on these topicsStuart BroadJimmy AndersonEngland cricket teamEngland v Pakistan 2026CricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: Champions League draw: Arsenal face Real Madrid, Man City get Barcelona and PSG | Champions League | The Guardian
description: Arsenal will host Real Madrid and visit Bayern Munich, Aston Villa entertain PSG and Liverpool face Inter at San Siro
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: Arsenal will host Real Madrid and visit Bayern Munich, Aston Villa entertain PSG and Liverpool face Inter at San Siro
Content: The Champions League draw takes place in Monte Carlo, with Thierry Henry and David Villa among in attendance.Photograph: Manon Cruz/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe Champions League draw takes place in Monte Carlo, with Thierry Henry and David Villa among in attendance.Photograph: Manon Cruz/ReutersChampions LeagueChampions League draw: Arsenal face Real Madrid, Man City get Barcelona and PSGManchester United will host Bayern MunichAston Villa welcome PSG; Liverpool go to InterNick Amesin Monte CarloThu 27 Aug 2026 13.44 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 17.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArsenal face mouthwatering assignments against Real Madrid and Bayern Munich as they bid to go one better than last season’s agonising near miss and win a firstChampions Leaguetitle.Mikel Arteta’s side werepipped on penalties by Paris Saint-Germain in the final three months agoand will be expected to cruise through this season’s league phase. The bulk of their draw appears kind but they are tasked with a visit to the Allianz Arena to play Bayern, whom theybeat 3-1 at the Emirates Stadium last November, and host Real, who are once again under the charge of José Mourinho. Two seasons ago, Arsenalbeat the Spanish giants 3-0 at home in a quarter-final first leg, Declan Rice scoring two memorable free-kicks.Champions League 2026-27 league phase draw: Arsenal to play Real Madrid, Manchester City face PSG and Barça – as it happenedRead moreArsenal will also welcome Borussia Dortmund, Lille and the Azerbaijani debutants Sabah to north London. Their other away fixtures involve trips to Napoli, Slavia Prague and a reunion with their ex-player Héctor Bellerin at Real Betis.Manchester City will swiftly renew acquaintances with Rodri when they visit Barcelona during Enzo Maresca’s first Champions League campaign in charge. They will greet Kevin De Bruyne and Napoli at the Etihad Stadium, just as they did last season incruising to a 2-0 win. Their other home ties bring an enticing meeting with the reigning champions, PSG, a tie against Sporting and a visit by AEK Athens. Trips to Porto, RB Leipzig and Lens will round off their schedule.The return ofManchester Unitedto Europe’s elite competition throws up home games with Bayern, Roma, RB Leipzig and Sabah. Michael Carrick’s team will travel to Como, who are managed by Cesc Fàbregas, along with Atlético Madrid, Sporting and Villarreal.Liverpool will host Atlético, Porto, Villarreal and Lens. They visit Lask, the newcomers whosensationally beat Celtic on Tuesday, along with Club Brugge, Fenerbahce and Inter in a relatively kind-looking set of games.Aston Villa, ravaged in recent weeks by the departures of key players, will hope to have strengthened sufficiently for a home tie with PSG and a visit to Barcelona. They will be heartened by astirring performance in their recent Super Cup defeat to Luis Enrique’s side in Salzburg. Borussia Dortmund, Fenerbahce and the Norwegian new boys Viking Stavanger will also visit Villa Park. Unai Emery will also take his team to Club Brugge, Galatasaray and Slavia Prague.Quick GuidePremier League teams' UCL opponentsShowManchester City:PSG (home), Barcelona (away), Sporting (h), Porto (a), Napoli (h), Leipzig (a), AEK Athens (h), Lens (a).Liverpool:Atlético Madrid (h), Inter (a), Porto (h), Club Brugge (a), Villarreal (h), Fenerbahce (a), Lens (h), Lask (a).Arsenal: Real Madrid (h), Bayern Munich (a), Borussia Dortmund (h), Real Betis (a), Lille (h), Napoli (a), Sabah (h), Slavia Prague (a).Aston Villa: PSG (h), Barcelona (a), Dortmund (h), Club Brugge (a), Fenerbahce (h), Galatasaray (a), Viking (h), Slavia Prague (a).Manchester United:Bayern (h), Atletico (a), Roma (h), Sporting (a), Leipzig (h), Villarreal (a), Sabah (h), Como (a).Order of fixtures to be confirmed by UefaWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.While Chelsea did not qualify for European competition this season, their home will still host Champions League football. The Ukrainian champions, Shakhtar Donetsk, still unable to play continental matches in their homeland, will stage home games there. Real Madrid are the most high-profile of their four visitors, meaning Mourinho will return to his old stomping ground.PSG’s bid to win a third successive Champions League title involves home league games against Barcelona, Roma, Galatasaray and Slovan Bratislava, as well as trips to Villarreal, Como, City and Villa.The first set of fixtures will be played on 8 and 9 September. title: US Open: Carlos Alcaraz to face Safiullin on return as Sabalenka gets tricky draw | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: Carlos Alcaraz faces the in-form Russian Roman Safiullin in the first round of the US Open while Aryna Sabalenka will take on Camila Osorio at Flushing Meadows
Author: Tumaini Carayol
