Headline: Carlos Alcaraz faces the in-form Russian Roman Safiullin in the first round of the US Open while Aryna Sabalenka will take on Camila Osorio at Flushing Meadows
Content: Carlos Alcaraz returns to competitive singles action for the first time in fourth months to defend his US Open crown.Photograph: Marcin Cholewinski/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenCarlos Alcaraz returns to competitive singles action for the first time in fourth months to defend his US Open crown.Photograph: Marcin Cholewinski/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockUS Open Tennis 2026US Open: Carlos Alcaraz to face Safiullin on return as Sabalenka gets tricky drawAlcaraz back in action after four-month injury layoffNovak Djokovic faces Mariano Navone in first roundTumaini Carayolin New YorkThu 27 Aug 2026 14.34 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 16.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCarlos Alcaraz has been handed a tough draw on his return to singles competition after a four-month injury layoff as he faces the in-form Russian Roman Safiullin in the first round of the US Open.‘Grand slams are the engine to make a living’: Mackenzie McDonald on why players still compete when injuredRead moreAlcaraz, the defending champion in New York, has not competed in singles since sustaining a right wrist injury at the Barcelona Open in April, with the Spaniard missing the French Open, where he was also the defending champion, and Wimbledon. He was understandably rusty and tentative with his first serve when making his first competitive appearance since the injuryalongside Serena Williams in the mixed doubles eventon Tuesday, with the pair losing in the quarter-finals and the 44-year-old Williams even outperforming him during large parts of their time on court. His opening match against the world No 98 Safiullin, who has risen more than 100 places in the world rankings this year after returning from injury and defeated Alcaraz indoors at the Paris Masters in 2023, will be a significant first challenge.Between the uncertainty surrounding Alcaraz due to his lack of match play and the absence of the world No 1, Jannik Sinner,who was forced to withdraw due to a knee injury, the men’s Flushing Meadows draw is as open as it has been in years. As the second seed, Alcaraz’s section includes both the eighth seed, Ben Shelton, and the 10th seed, Arthur Fils, the winners of the Canadian Openand Cincinnati Openrespectively, the two ATP Masters 1000 events leading up to the US Open. Fils will face a high-profile first-round opponent in the former world No 3, Stefanos Tsitsipas.The four-time champion Novak Djokovic will begin his latest attempt to become the oldest singles grand slam champion in the open era as the fourth seed in Alcaraz’s half of the draw. He faces Mariano Navone in the first round with the out-of-form seventh seed Daniil Medvedev the highest-ranked seed in the Serb’s quarter. Alexander Zverev, the French Open champion, is the top seed at a grand slam tournament for the first time and faces the Italian Lorenzo Sonego in his opener.While a large group of players have an opportunity to make a career-defining breakthrough in the men’s draw, it will be difficult for the rank-and-file competitors to stop the strong group of elite players at the top of the women’s draw despite their differing form. Aryna Sabalenka, the defending champion, will begin against Camila Osorio as she tries to hold on to her No 1 ranking after a difficult few months.View image in fullscreenAryna Sabalenka (left) and Jessica Pegula may meet in the semi-finals, a potential rerun of the 2024 final that Sabalenka won.Photograph: Frank Franklin II/APThe highest ranked players in Sabalenka’s half are the in-form third seed, Jessica Pegula, a potential semi-final opponent, the Wimbledon champion and sixth seed, Linda Noskova, and the seventh seed, Karolina Muchova, the runner-up at Wimbledon. However, considering Sabalenka’s recent results, even a potential third-round match with the two-time grand slam champion and 27th seed, Barbora Krejcikova, cannot be taken for granted.The strong bottom half of the draw, meanwhile, is overflowing with title contenders.. Elena Rybakina, the second seed, seemed to be in an ideal position to usurp Sabalenka at the top of the rankings but her form is uncertain after she was forced to retire from her quarter-final against Iga Swiatek in Cincinnati last week due to a leg injury.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSwiatek, the eighth seed, and the fourth seed, Coco Gauff, were the two most notable performers in the buildup to the US Open, winning in Toronto and Cincinnati respectively. Swiatek could face Rybakina in the quarter-finals, while the highest ranked player in Coco Gauff’s section is the French Open champion and fifth seed, Mirra Andreeva. Other contenders include the 13th seed and two-time champion Naomi Osaka, who could face Rybakina in round four, and last year’s runner-up Amanda Anisimova.Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026US Open tennisTennisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Women’s Super League 2026-27 preview No 7: Crystal Palace | Crystal Palace Women | The Guardian
description: Jo Potter’s side charged to promotion and have brought in striker Bethany England as they bid to stay up
Author: Sophie Downey
Headline: Jo Potter’s side charged to promotion and have brought in striker Bethany England as they bid to stay up
Content: Aimee Everett celebrates promotion to the Women's Super League after Crystal Palace’s victory over Portsmouth in May. Photograph: Eddie Keogh/WSL/Getty ImagesJo Potter’s side charged to promotion and have brought in striker Bethany England as they bid to stay upBySophie DowneyThu 27 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 19.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGuardian writers’ predicted position:13th (NB: this is not necessarily Sophie Downey’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)Last season’s position:2nd (WSL2)ProspectsCrystal Palace have been on arollercoaster over the past few seasons. An inaugural Women’s Super League campaign in 2024-25 brought relegation and the club secured top-flight football again a year later. They will hope their WSL experience gives them an advantage with important lessons learned.The nature of their promotion push under Jo Potter was nothing short of remarkable. An indifferent start had them languishing near the bottom but 12 wins in their last 14 games enabled them to pip Charlton to the second automatic promotion spot on the final day.They have recruited intelligently over the summer. The arrival of the prolific Bethany England was a statement, as was the loan signing of the France goalkeeper Pauline Peyraud-Magnin, and Molly Bartrip brings considerable defensive acumen. In Shannon O’Brien and Lexi Lloyd-Smith, Potter has brought in two young attacking players who have caught the eye and Teyah Goldie and Fuka Tsunoda arrive on loan with the hope of kickstarting their careers.Faith has also been put in the core of the side that got them back to the WSL, many of whom have been through all the ups and downs. Abbie Larkin, Ashleigh Weerden, Shae Yanez and Molly-Mae Sharpe are a few of those who have stuck by the club and been rewarded. There was, however, a blow at the start pre-season when it was revealed My Cato had sustained an anterior cruciate ligament injury.Palace’s start is a tricky one. Everton, Arsenal and Tottenham make up their opening three games, a real chance to test themselves against seasoned WSL sides and see where they are at.How they finished in the past five seasonsOff-field pictureThe women’s team have been fully integrated into Crystal Palace FC since 2022, rather than being made into a separate entity like some of their WSL counterparts. Woody Johnson, David Blitzer, Josh Harris and Steve Parish continue to invest in and support the women’s side. There is a little uncertainty around the whole club after reports in June that Johnson, Blitzer and Harris are keen to sell their combined stake of 79% but nothing has come to fruition.The managerPotter is widely regarded as one of the brightest young managers. The 41-year-old arrived at Palace last summer, joining from Rangers, where she had hit the ground running in her managerial career, winning back-to-back cup doubles and narrowly missing out on the SWPL titles on two occasions. She was widely credited at Rangers for the integration and development of several academy players into the senior setup. Potter had a prolific playing career. She won the FA Cup with Birmingham in 2012 and was part of the England squad that secured bronze at the 2015 Women’s World Cup.View image in fullscreenJo Potter is seen as one of the brightest young managers in the game.Photograph: Nigel Roddis/WSL/Getty ImagesStar signingEngland’s arrival was a significant coup. The 32-year-old striker brings a wealth of experience, leadership, quality and goals that will surely be invaluable to the team’s chances of survival. England is an out-and-out goalscorer and her WSL tally sits at 87 after spells at Doncaster Belles, Chelsea, Liverpool and Tottenham. She won nine major trophies during her seven-year stint at Chelsea and sparked life into Spurs, proving pivotal to their successful attempt at avoiding relegation from the WSL in 2023.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionStat attackPalace won one home match in 2024-25 when they finished bottom of the WSL. They maintained more of a fortress last season, topping the second tier for points won at home. Keeping something of that form going will be crucial if they are to stay up.Graphic showing Crystal Palace had the best home record in Women’s Super League 2Set for a breakthroughLloyd-Smith will be one to keep an eye on, the England youngster adding more firepower to the team. The 23-year-old gets her first shot at top-flight football, signing a three-year deal after a successful two years with Bristol City, where she finished last season as the WSL 2 top scorer and the club’s young player of the year. A versatile and speedy attacking player, she can thrive anywhere across the frontline.What they say“Palace are an ambitious club. They’ve been in the WSL before, they’ve had two amazing promotions now, and I think you can see their investment in thewomen’s game. They’re really pushing to want to be among the best, and they’ve got amazing facilities … It’s a place where I hope that I can make a lot of good memories, score a lot of goals, and make some good history for the football club” –England on signing for PalaceWhere are they playing their home games?The Eagles will continue at Sutton United’s VBS Community Stadium, where they have played since the 2023-24 campaign. The club continue to work hard to make it an entertaining and affordable matchday for supporters, with a fan zone before the game, affordable pricing and alcohol allowed in the stands, with a dedicated drink-free zone. Select games will be played at Selhurst Park, the first coming against Tottenham on 20 September.Explore more on these topicsWSL season previews 2026-27Crystal Palace WomenfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: USA’s Russell and Brazil’s Dos Santos smash world records on ‘crazy’ night in Zurich | Athletics | The Guardian
description: Masai Russell and Alison Dos Santos broke world records as Mondo Duplantis prevailed in a historic pole vault duel on a remarkable night in Zurich
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Masai Russell and Alison Dos Santos broke world records as Mondo Duplantis prevailed in a historic pole vault duel on a remarkable night in Zurich
Content: Masai Russell celebrates after winning the women’s 100m hurdles in a world-record 12.09sec at the Diamond League meeting in Zurich.Photograph: Claudio Thoma/EPAView image in fullscreenMasai Russell celebrates after winning the women’s 100m hurdles in a world-record 12.09sec at the Diamond League meeting in Zurich.Photograph: Claudio Thoma/EPAAthleticsUSA’s Russell and Brazil’s Dos Santos smash world records on ‘crazy’ night in ZurichDos Santos and Russell smash hurdles world recordsWerro comes within 0.42sec of 800m world recordBednarek and Wanyonyi clock world-leading timesAgenciesThu 27 Aug 2026 17.05 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 17.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMasai Russell and Alison Dos Santos each set a world record while Mondo Duplantis won a historic pole vault on a frenetic Thursday night in Zurich.The Letzigrund Stadium had a raucous sell-out 25,000 crowd and the still, balmy weather conditions helped the athletes no end.Brazil’s Dos Santos was the first to make a mark, clocking a sensational 45.80 seconds in the 400m hurdlesto beat the previous mark of 45.94secset by Norway’s Karsten Warholm in the final of the Tokyo Olympics.“I have been showing great form throughout the season – that I am fast, I am strong,” said Dos Santos, with Warholm finishing second and dubbing their discipline a “crazy event”.“As soon as I knew I was coming here, I was excited. The weather’s good, the track’s amazing,” the Brazilian added.Then came US star Russell, the Olympic champion, timing 12.09sec in the 100m hurdlesto beat the previous best of 12.12secset by Nigeria’s Tobi Amusan at the Eugene world championships in 2022.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueDos Santos and Russell will leave Zurich with a cheque each for $80,000 for having broken their respective records.The world records were punctuated by a scintillating competition in the pole vault, eventually won by double Olympic and triple world champion Duplantis. The US-born Swede came under real pressure from Greek rival Emmanouil Karalis, who vaulted a personal best of 6.20m. Duplantis cleared 6.25m for victory, while both vaulters tried a possible world record 6.32m, in a truly thrilling showdown that gripped the stadium’s attention.It was the first time in vaulting history that two athletes had gone beyond the 6.20m mark.“It’s not every day two people go for the world record, so that was nuts,” said Karalis.The icing on the cake came in the women’s 800m, with the star attraction Switzerland’s own Audrey Werro. Werro also did not disappoint, registering the third fastest time ever in the two-lap race, 1:53.70, as she edged ever closer to Jarmila Kratochvilova’s Cold War world record of 1:53.28 set in Munich in 1983.“It was crazy, I am very proud. Thank you everybody!” the 22-year-old said.Femke Broeders-Bol finished second as she continues to improve in her transition from the 400m hurdles in which she was twice a world champion.“Being in a great event with a great time – amazing,” the Dutch athlete said.View image in fullscreenA fan holds a sign urging Armand Duplantis towards a world record as the Swede attempts 6.32m after winning the men’s pole vault at the Diamond League meeting in Zurich.Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty ImagesKenya’s world and Olympic champion Emmanuel Wanyonyi held off Algeria’s Djamel Sedjati for a nail-biting victory in the men’s 800m.Wanyonyi has said that going for David Rudisha’s world record of 1:40.91 is like running a marathon under two hours, and the mark once again proved elusive as he timed a world lead of 1:41.76 for the win. Sedjati was just 0.07sec adrift.“When I see the world records being broken, I know my time will come. There is time for everything,” said Wanyonyi.Explore more on these topicsAthleticsUSA Olympic teamUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: Wigan rise to occasion against Hull KR as town unites to remember Sir Billy Boston | Super League | The Guardian
description: Liam Marshall bagged a hat-trick of tries as Wigan Warriors routed Hull KR 46-0 on a night when fans came together to remember Sir Billy Boston
Author: Aaron Bower
Headline: Liam Marshall bagged a hat-trick of tries as Wigan Warriors routed Hull KR 46-0 on a night when fans came together to remember Sir Billy Boston
Content: Wigan Warriors pay tribute to Sir Billy Boston before completing a record 13th straight Super League win.Photograph: Paul Currie/SWpix.com/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenWigan Warriors pay tribute to Sir Billy Boston before completing a record 13th straight Super League win.Photograph: Paul Currie/SWpix.com/ShutterstockSuper LeagueWigan rise to occasion against Hull KR as town unites to remember Sir Billy BostonSuper League: Wigan Warriors 46-0 Hull KRLiam Marshall bags hat-trick of tries in routAaron Bowerat the Brick Community StadiumThu 27 Aug 2026 17.40 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 19.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the night whenWigan Warriorscelebrated one of their greatest entertainers, perhaps it was fitting that Matt Peet’s class of 2026 produced a performance Sir Billy Boston would have been proud of on their charge towards, potentially, another Super League title.There are some nights where the result is dwarfed by the occasion. Where sport, in truth, comes second. This was undoubtedly one of those, as what felt like the entirety of this town where rugby league is more akin to a religion than a pastime came together in grief to remember the life and career of their most cherished adopted son.Prime minister Andy Burnham ‘heartbroken’ after death of rugby league legend Billy BostonRead moreIn the week Boston passed away at the age of 92, Wigan’s players were challenged by Peet to deliver a performance rugby league’s first knight would have adored. At times, it was a game played in conditions that Boston himself would have been familiar with during the sport’s winter seasons; biblical rain and utterly horrendous weather.But Wigan, just like Boston did in his own career, made light of those difficulties to register a 13th consecutiveSuper Leaguevictory, extending their own modern era record and returning to the top of the table. Leeds Rhinos will get the chance to return serve on Friday when they face St Helens, but it is obvious it will take some team to stop Wigan this year.Few are better placed than the ever-eloquent Peet to put this night into perspective, though. “It was for Sir Billy,” he said. “Tonight was about more than just two points. I loved the crowd, the event the club put on and the performance too.”That event Peet mentions was incredibly moving. From the rows of flowers that lined the stadium to the pre-match ceremony, right down to the little touches – best epitomised by Wigan leaving the usual seats of Boston and his late wife, Lady Joan – who herself only died last month – empty. It moved many inside the venue to tears.On the pitch, Wigan were given a helping hand by the defending champions. At the end of a run of four games in 14 days, Willie Peters chose to leave out many of his big-hitters and blood youngsters. The end result was perhaps entirely expected, with an under-strength Robins failing to score for the first time in Peters’ glittering and trophy-laden reign.Behind 28-0 at half-time, his young side dug in after the break but this was still a brutally one-sided affair. “I expected it to be that tough,” Peters said. “I’m proud of the effort; we hung in there and it could have gone out to a massive scoreline. It could have got a lot worse.”Fittingly, it was Wigan’s wingers who shone in appalling conditions in the first half. Zach Eckersley and Liam Marshall both crossed for wonderful braces and with the outstanding Jai Field adding a try, the Warriors had a commanding lead by half-time.In truth, Rovers could muster little in terms of a meaningful response.View image in fullscreenLiam Marshall dives in for the first of his three tries.Photograph: Paul Currie/SWpix.com/ShutterstockHull KR now know that if St Helens win on Friday, they will be level with the seventh-placed Saints with two games left: and they meet on the final day. It could yet be a shootout for the final play-off place. Peters will argue he was looking at the bigger picture, and games against Huddersfield and the Saints, in passing up a chance to compete here.The best sides do not let such opportunities pass by without being clinical.Wigan’s defence was as strong as their attack, and with Marshall completing his hat-trick before further tries for Adam Keighran and Jake Wardle, it always felt about how many Wigan would declare on, rather than whether the Robins would hold them at bay.These two sides have contested the last two Grand Finals with one win apiece. The odds against a third are lengthening by the week, with only one of them looking like they will be at Old Trafford.Explore more on these topicsSuper LeagueWigan WarriorsHull KRRugby leaguematch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Tadej Pogacar battles back from scare on descent to win stage six of Vuelta a España | Vuelta a España | The Guardian
description: Slovenia’s Tadej Pogacar recovered from veering off the road at a corner to win stage six of the Vuelta a España as Britain’s Josh Tarling retired from the race
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Slovenia’s Tadej Pogacar recovered from veering off the road at a corner to win stage six of the Vuelta a España as Britain’s Josh Tarling retired from the race
Content: Tadej Pogacar moved one step closer to completing a Grand Tour slam when winning stage six.Photograph: Alexander Hassenstein/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTadej Pogacar moved one step closer to completing a Grand Tour slam when winning stage six.Photograph: Alexander Hassenstein/Getty ImagesVuelta a EspañaTadej Pogacar battles back from scare on descent to win stage six of Vuelta a EspañaSlovenian leader recovers after misjudging cornerBritain’s Josh Tarling pulls out of event mid-stageAgence France-PresseThu 27 Aug 2026 12.31 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 18.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTadej Pogacar outsprinted Enric Mas to claim victory in stage six of theVuelta a Españaon Thursday, his third stage win of the race.The Slovenian and Mas outshone their rivals on the gravel in the stage’s final climb, and Pogacar held off the Spaniard when arriving in Castellón de la Plana to extend his general classification lead. The five-time Tour de France winner Pogacar, the overwhelming favourite for the Vuelta, is aiming to complete a Grand Tour grand slam.Tadej Pogacar looks unstoppable as he sets sights on another slice of history at VueltaRead moreRamses Debruyne grabbed the third spot on the podium, finishing in a group including Primoz Roglic, Richard Carapaz and Felix Gall, 46 seconds behind the leaders. UAE Team Emirates’ Pogacar, who had a brief scare as he came off the road on the final descent, now leads Movistar’s Mas by 3min 34sec and his compatriot Roglic by 4min 21sec overall.There was a big battle to get into the break but it took a long time for an escape to form. Finally 15 riders moved clear and established a two-and-a-half minute gap on the peloton with 40km remaining. The final climb of Puerto El Bartolo split up the break and then peeled on to a gravel road, where Pogacar attacked and picked off the riders ahead of him. Mas was hot on his tail and the Spaniard dug deep to charge past Pogacar and come over the top of the climb ahead. Pogacar came off the road and into a grassy section after misjudging a corner, but he swiftly recovered to get back on Mas’s trail. The four-time Vuelta winner Roglic, Gall and Debruyne were chasing the front two, but Pogacar and Mas worked well together to keep their advantage. Pogacar led out towards the finish line and Mas could not catch him.It was a bad day for Oscar Onley, who lost more than a minute and a half on his general classification rivals.Earlier in the day, the Netcompany Ineos rider Josh Tarling abandoned the race with around 120km of the stage left, with his team not giving a reason. The Briton’s brother Finlay Tarlingdied in the Tour of Portugalafter a crash with a vehicle, but Josh decided to race in Spain in honour of his sibling. “Josh Tarling’s brave La Vuelta has come to an end and he’s decided to stop. We couldn’t be prouder,” said Netcompany Ineos on social media.Tarling produced a strong display in the first stage individual time trial, coming third behind Pogacar and Ethan Hayter.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOn Friday, riders travel 149.8km from Vall D’Alba to the race’s second summit finale at Aramón Valdelinares.Explore more on these topicsVuelta a EspañaTadej PogacarCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Twickenham £660m makeover plan hit as locals push back against concert scheme | Rugby Football Union | The Guardian
description: Local councillors have said the RFU’s plan to increase the number of non-sporting events at Twickenham does not address the effect on residents
Author: Gerard Meagher
Headline: Local councillors have said the RFU’s plan to increase the number of non-sporting events at Twickenham does not address the effect on residents
Content: The RFU want to increase the number of concerts at  Twickenham.Photograph: Adam Davy/PAView image in fullscreenThe RFU want to increase the number of concerts at  Twickenham.Photograph: Adam Davy/PARugby Football UnionTwickenham £660m makeover plan hit as locals push back against concert schemeCouncillors say plan does not tackle effect on residentsRFU want to increase number of non-sporting eventsGerard MeagherThu 27 Aug 2026 11.12 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 00.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Rugby Football Union’sbid to stage more concerts at Twickenhamhas been delivered a blow after local councillors insisted planning permission should not be awarded until the proposal further commits to limiting the impact.The RFU hassubmitted its planning applicationto Richmond council to use the stadium for non-sporting events for up to 15 days a year, with a decision due in October. Public consultation was due to end on Thursday with 240 submissions in favour and 456 against at the time of writing.RFU expects £10m loss off the back of England’s worst Six Nations campaignRead moreWhile the ward councillors based in neighbouring Whitton, St Margarets and North Twickenham do not oppose the idea of the stadium hosting more concerts, they make clear in comments on the application they believe the plan does not do enough to guarantee improvements in infrastructure to cope with the “intensification of use” or mitigate against the effect on local residents.The councillors, who do not sit on the planning committee that will make the decision, highlight transport, road closures and the cumulative effect of more concerts in addition to the sporting events held at Twickenham. They suggest the RFU should fully fund “additional public realm impacts”.The letter, signed by councillors Katie Mansfield, Maria Margiotta and Jo Humphreys, says: “We recognise the stadium’s importance to Twickenham and accept that some increase in non-sporting events can be appropriate. […] However, we do not believe that the application yet provides sufficient assurance that this intensification of use will be matched by the infrastructure and mitigation necessary to accommodate it, or that all necessary measures will be sufficiently specific, funded and enforceable.”The RFU can host three non-sporting events per year, but has applied for a phased increase to eight, spread over 15 event days, and to increase the maximum capacity from 55,000 to 75,000.The union points out it is a phased increase, with six non-sporting event days in year one and only one in midweek initially. The RFU says Richmond council would have the chance to introduce further mitigation measures as part of an annual operational review that would act as a failsafe mechanism.The union believes theadditional revenue would be crucialin helping to fund the planned £660m overhaul of Twickenham and has previously threatened to relocate if Richmond council does not grant the necessary permission. A document submitted as part of the planning application reads: “if the RFU is unable to generate the revenues required to support the continued development of the game through its activities at Allianz Stadium, it would place increasing pressure on the long‑term sustainability of remaining in Twickenham”. The RFU has also said hosting more concerts would underpin a £500m investment into rugby over the next five years and would generate an extra £86m for the UK economy as well as increase spending in the local area by £28.5m.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRunning dry: drought-hit UK sporting venues and parched pitches – in picturesRead moreThe submission by the councillors, which is neither in support nor opposition, but rather an observation, concludes that “we are not opposed to the stadium evolving its role as a major venue, and recognise the significant economic, cultural and wider benefits that this can bring […] However, the current proposal does not demonstrate how the proposed intensification of use will be mitigated by robust, enforceable and funded infrastructure improvements.“At present, the commitments offered do not provide sufficient confidence that Twickenham’s infrastructure and residential environment can sustainably support the proposed increase in non-sporting events.”The councillors go on to list a series of commitments they want made before adding: “We believe this would enable the stadium to continue to play an important role in Twickenham while ensuring that the needs of the local community and the capacity of the infrastructure supporting it are properly recognised. It should not be approved without the commitments necessary to achieve that.”The RFU points to how Wembley and Tottenham stadium can host 54 and 30 concerts a year respectively while Twickenham is limited to three. Opponents cite the example of the Emirates Stadium, however, and how Arsenal lost a high court battle in 2014 when attempting to increase the number of concerts a year from three to six.Much of the opposition centres around antisocial behaviour experienced on England matchdays as well as concerns over transport, air quality and noise disturbance. One local resident details in a planning submission how “four aggressive, inebriated gentlemen” stole a For Sale sign from her front garden after a recent England match and, while two reluctantly returned it, they shouted insults as they did so.A petition against the proposal has reached 4,000 signatures, but the west London chamber of commerce has come out in support along with a number of local businesses, demonstrating how polarising the issue is.“Allianz Stadium generates about 85% of the RFU’s revenue, but needs significant investment to meet the expectations of a modern world-class venue, at a time when rugby itself needs a stronger financial footing,” said a RFU spokesperson. “Our planning application is about making better use of this national asset to unlock that investment.“The application is now with Richmond council and we are encouraged that more than 200 local residents and businesses have already written in support. We look forward to continuing to work closely with residents, the council and other local stakeholders throughout the process.”Explore more on these topicsRugby Football UnionRugby unionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s war on Iran is rapidly draining US navy budget, documents and interviews reveal | US military | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Experts and former officials say accounts are running dry, and funding a war with no clear endgame is the main challenge
Author: Aram Roston
Headline: Exclusive: Experts and former officials say accounts are running dry, and funding a war with no clear endgame is the main challenge
Content: US navy sailors on the flight deck of the USS Abraham Lincoln as part of Operation Epic Fury, on 28 February 2026.Photograph: US navy/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenUS navy sailors on the flight deck of the USS Abraham Lincoln as part of Operation Epic Fury, on 28 February 2026.Photograph: US navy/Getty ImagesUS militaryTrump’s war on Iran is rapidly draining US navy budget, documents and interviews revealExclusive: Experts and former officials say accounts are running dry, and funding a war with no clear endgame is the main challengeAram RostonThu 27 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 13.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump’swar on Iranhas driven the US military into a severe financial crisis, with the US navy forced to transfer money from its payroll and other sources to cover the costs of combat, according to documents obtained by the Guardian, and interviews with navy officials, contractors and defense analysts.The US-Israeli operation, which has depleted US munitions stockpiles and prompted retaliatory Iranian strikes that have wrecked strategic bases across the Middle East, is piling pressure on budgets across the military.One Pentagon memo about navy funding seen by the Guardian warns that there are “shortfalls in payroll” accounts due to the department “raiding” them to fund combat operations.View image in fullscreenUS navy sailors on 3 March 2026 in the Mediterranean Sea.Photograph: US navy/Getty ImagesExperts and former officials say the accounts are running dry. “The piggy bank is broken,” said Harlan Ullman, a retired naval officer. Ullman is a member of the National Commission for the Future of the Navy but he said he is not speaking on the commission’s behalf.One official and one navy contractor said non-emergency maintenance on shore-based facilities has been deferred because of the cash crunch.USS Abraham Lincoln to visit port in Thailand after more than 250 days at seaRead moreWhen Trump started the war on 28 February, it quickly strained the military’s existing budgets – particularly that of the navy, which not only helped launch the initial wave of attacks but was later responsible for an extensive naval blockade. The White House eventually asked Congress for emergency funding to pay for the war efforts, but prospects that the request will be approved are dim amid the unpopularity of the war.A navy official who was briefed on how the service is planning to address the shortfalls said money is shifted around in imaginative ways. “The money for payroll,” he said, “was robbed to pay for overseas contingencies and is being backfilled by money that hasn’t been spent. They are backfilling payroll so we get enough money in our paycheck.”The navy’s budget for 2026, almost $300bn, has different batches of money allocated by Congress for various requirements: personnel, shipbuilding, procuring specific weapons systems and “operations and maintenance”, the day-to-day running of the fleet and its bases. The law limits how money can be rejiggered throughout all those batches of money.The issue has occasionally surfaced in some hearings on Capitol Hill. Susan Collins, in a 21 July hearing of the Senate appropriations committee, said: “I’m told some military services face near-term solvency challenges.”A staffer said the navy was one of the services Collins was referring to.In a statement, a navy spokesperson said maintenance and operations funds have not been depleted. “The Department of the Navy,” the statement said, “is actively managing its resources to meet current pay obligations on time. We continue to work closely with Congress to address ongoing operational demands and sustain our personnel and readiness throughout the fiscal year.”Inside the service, the cash shortage is no secret. “They’re just not speaking publicly about it,” said Todd Harrison, a defense analyst at the conservative American Enterprise Institute. “And I suspect that is a deliberate decision of the civilian leaders in the Pentagon, starting at secretary, that this is for political reasons, that they don’t want to look like they’re damaging future military readiness over a war that is becoming increasingly a political liability.”‘We face critical shortfalls’The military knew the crisis was coming. In mid-May, Adm Daryl Caudle, chief of naval operations, cautioned Congress that the crunch would hit in July. “The FY ’26 budget didn’t bake in Epic Fury,” he said. “I do fear that I’ll have to start making decisions in the July timeframe on how I do force generation. That could make differences between how I do exercises, how I do routine operations in order to make sure that I … have the funds necessary to continue the war effort for Epic Fury.”Pete Hegseth has pushed Congress for emergency funding, without which, he said in July, “we face critical shortfalls”. The defense secretary testified that the Iran war cost $35.7bn, but it’s unclear if that is a full accounting of the war’s costs.View image in fullscreenA Tomahawk missile is launched from the USS Thomas Hudner in Mediterranean Sea on 5 March 2026.Photograph: US navy/Getty ImagesWhen the Trump administration asked Congress for $67bn in emergency funds for the defense department, it didn’t break down how much would be for the navy.The House passed a $1.15tn defense billin July and a separate budget authorization that would provide $73bn for the war in Iran, but it’s unlikely either will become law.Ullman noted that during the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, funding was more forthcoming from Congress because those conflicts were authorized by a resolution. “There is no authorization to use force in this case. Is Congress obliged to pay for a conflict it did not authorize?” he said.‘They ran out of their money’The fact that the navy is broke – or at least out of money for now – may be something of a slap in the face for Trump.The president has often evoked what he sees as his affinity with Theodore Roosevelt, who was president from 1901 to 1909 and presided over the expansion of the US navy, deploying the so-called “Great White Fleet” that steamed around the world. Instead of a Great White Fleet, Trump’s administration has embraced the term “Golden Fleet”. Among his naval ambitions: plans for mammoth “Trump class” ships – the largest battleships in US history.Trump’s micromanagement has included directing the navy to redesign an aircraft carrier so it launches jets with a steam and hydraulic catapult system rather than by an electromagnetic system. Asthe Guardianreported, every year since 2017 he has opined about his preferences in carrier launch catapults.At this point, however, funding a war with no clear endgame is the main challenge. A former military officer now working for a navy contracting company, who has been briefed on the shortfalls, said: “They’re fucked. They shot all their weapons; they trashed all their ships; they ran out of their money.”Explore more on these topicsUS militaryDonald TrumpUS-Israel war on IranTrump administrationUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Woman found guilty of indecent assault against two pupils at London boys’ school in 1980s | Crime | The Guardian
description: Sally-Anne Bowen, now 65, convicted of assaulting boys at Christ’s College, Finchley, where she was chemistry teacher
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Sally-Anne Bowen, now 65, convicted of assaulting boys at Christ’s College, Finchley, where she was chemistry teacher
Content: Sally-Anne Bowen arriving at Harrow crown court.Photograph: James Manning/PAView image in fullscreenSally-Anne Bowen arriving at Harrow crown court.Photograph: James Manning/PACrimeWoman found guilty of indecent assault against two pupils at London boys’ school in 1980sSally-Anne Bowen, now 65, convicted of assaulting boys at Christ’s College, Finchley, where she was chemistry teacherCaroline Daviesand agencyThu 27 Aug 2026 13.23 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 15.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA chemistry teacher has been found guilty of indecently assaulting two teenage pupils at an all-boys school in the late 1980s.Sally-Anne Bowen, who taught at Christ’s College in Finchley, northLondon, assaulted the teenage boys when they were aged around 14 to 15 and she was in her mid-20s.Bowen, of Hemel Hempstead, Hertfordshire, did not appear to show any emotion as a jury at Harrow crown court returned majority verdicts finding the 65-year-old guilty of seven counts of indecent assault after six hours and 29 minutes of deliberations.One complainant told jurors he had sex with the teacher “about 20 or 30 times” over several months. He would visit Bowen’s home, considered her to be his girlfriend and had fallen in love, the court heard.In his evidence, the man – who cannot be named for legal reasons – said he kept their relationship secret because he felt compelled to protect the teacher, who he said had drummed it into him that he was not allowed to tell anyone.“I never, ever spoke to anyone about it,” he said. “I was always really aware, she drummed it into me.” He added: “Years she got to teach because I remained silent.”He said in a police interview that the experience had been “the destruction of my education”.Madeleine Wolfe, prosecuting, told jurors in her closing speech that the man’s evidence had “a real visceral quality to it”. She said: “There can be no doubt that there was a lasting impact on him. It’s not a schoolboy fantasy, is it? He’s started this account in 2014 – this has real-life implications for him, remained with him for decades.”It was not until he became a parent himself that the man began to realise what had happened to him, Wolfe said.The second complainant said he and Bowen kissed once in a cafe when he was goaded into it by other boys.Another former pupil at the school, Tobias Oliver, said during the trial that Bowen acted as if she was in “a Sabrina Carpenter video” while in the classroom, and “dressed and behaved more like my teenage female friends than the other teachers”.Oliver, who did not know the two victims, told jurors: “The topics of conversation in class often strayed away from chemistry and became quite sexual.”Bowen had no boundaries and “felt more like trying to be one of us, like our friend, than a teacher,” he said. Bowen was “very flirtatious” in class and told them how she enjoyed giving oral sex to her boyfriend, he said.He recalled an occasion when a boy in Bowen’s class was reading a “sex manual”, which he believed to be the Kama Sutra. He said Bowen went through the book and discussed “the merits of different sexual positions” with the students.Oliver also described how on another occasion Bowen sat on a desk and caught the attention of the class before slowly opening her legs, revealing her underwear.Richard Luker, who was head of science at the school in the late 1980s, told the court he remembered a complaint from the first victim’s mother that she was concerned the boy was planning to travel abroad with Bowen at the end of term.During the trial, Bowen claimed the allegations were “total fabrication”. She said she had had a medical condition that in the late 1980s had not been diagnosed and had made sexual intercourse difficult and painful for her.Her partner of 36 years, Darren Scotchbrook, giving evidence, said Bowen had not been aware of her condition when they met in 1990, and sex had been “clearly not enjoyable for her” as a result.Asked under cross-examination how she had dressed in the classroom, Bowen replied that she “wasn’t going to dress like Margaret Thatcher” in her mid-20s. She told the court she did not flirt with students and was “just friendly”.She denied having a relationship with the first complainant. “Absolutely not, no relationship whatsoever. Student-teacher,” she said.She denied knowing the second complainant, saying she did not remember him even after seeing him give evidence in court.Allegations against Bowen featured in the Tortoise Investigates podcastLucky Boylast year.Bowen was granted bail until her sentence hearing on 20 November.Explore more on these topicsCrimeLondonEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: USS Abraham Lincoln to visit port in Thailand after more than 250 days at sea | US military | The Guardian
description: Thai navy says ‘routine’ visit’ will allow personnel to rest and recuperate amid reports of poor conditions onboard
Author: Anna Betts
Headline: Thai navy says ‘routine’ visit’ will allow personnel to rest and recuperate amid reports of poor conditions onboard
Content: In a photo supplied by the US navy, the USS Abraham Lincoln is seen in the Indian Ocean on 22 August.Photograph: Zoe Simpson/US Navy/Handout Via ReutersView image in fullscreenIn a photo supplied by the US navy, the USS Abraham Lincoln is seen in the Indian Ocean on 22 August.Photograph: Zoe Simpson/US Navy/Handout Via ReutersUS militaryUSS Abraham Lincoln to visit port in Thailand after more than 250 days at seaThai navy says ‘routine’ visit’ will allow personnel to rest and recuperate amid reports of poor conditions onboardAnna BettsThu 27 Aug 2026 11.05 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 12.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier is set to make a temporary stop inThailandnext week as it heads back to the United States, Thai navy officials said, after spendingmore than 250consecutive days at sea supportingUS operationsagainstIranamid recentreportsof poor living conditions and low morale onboard the vessel.The Lincoln left the Middle East several days ago after being relieved by theUSS George Washington, and is now headinghometo San Diego. A Thai navy official toldReutersthis week that the carrier was expected to make a brief port visit in Thailand next week for the crew to rest and recuperate before continuing their journey home.“The stop is ‌a ⁠routine port visit intended to allow personnel to rest and recuperate … as well as to receive logistical support,” the spokesperson for the Thai navy said.Earlier this week, the Thai navysaidthat three ships from a US navy carrier strike group would be making a brief port call in eastern Thailand to allow personnel to rest. No military exercises would take place during the visit, the statement added. The Thai navy did not identify ​the vessels or provide a date.Families of US sailors denounce Trump and Hegseth for ‘dismissing their experiences and calling them liars’Read moreThe planned stop comes as the Lincoln’s deployment has faced scrutiny in recent weeksamid reportsof poor living conditions onboard among its crew. Family members of sailors have described shortages of supplies and water, plumbing problems, low morale, andworsening mental healthamong the roughly5,000 personnelon the carrier. TheNavy Timesalso reported that there had been several attempts by sailors to jump overboard.On Wednesday, the wife of a sailor who jumped overboard toldMS Nowthat her husband, who she said had since returned to the US, was now facing disciplinary action from the navy.Charging documents viewed by MS Now reportedly accuse the sailor of violating Article 83 for “malingering”, which isdefined assomeone who, “with the intent to avoid work, duty, or service”, fakes “illness, physical disablement, mental lapse, or mental derangement” or “intentionally inflicts self-injury”.The document also reportedly accuses the sailor of violating Article 86 for “absence without leave” whichis whenthe service member, without authority, “fails to go to his appointed place of duty at the time prescribed”, “goes from that place” or “absents himself or remains absent from his unit, organization, or place of duty at which he is required to be at the time prescribed”.The couple, both 19, have a three-year-old son and welcomed a daughter in February while he was deployed. His wife told the outlet that he had requested paternity leave but was denied.The sailor is now reportedly facing non-judicial punishment, which MS Now notes is typically used by commanding officers to address minor rule-breaking without a court martial.The navy did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the Guardian. In a statement to MS Now about the decision to pursue a non-judicial punishment for the sailor, a navy official said that “the Navy is fully committed to the health and wellbeing of every Sailor”.“We strive to foster environments that support mental health by removing barriers to seeking help, increasing awareness of resources, and taking appropriate action when someone is in need,” they added. “Mental health resources are available to our Sailors 24/7, and asking for help is a sign of strength.”The Lincoln left San Diego on 21 Novemberbound for the Pacific, but was redirected to the Middle East. It has since spent more than250 consecutivedays without a significant port visit.Reports about the conditions onboard havepromptedseveral Democratic lawmakersto demandanswers from the Pentagon.Explore more on these topicsUS militaryThailandAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Three UK airports hit by cyber-attack with data of 8.7m customers accessed | Airline industry | The Guardian
description: Company that runs Manchester, Stansted and East Midlands hubs says passenger safety is unaffected
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Company that runs Manchester, Stansted and East Midlands hubs says passenger safety is unaffected
Content: Manchester airport. Most of the accessed data related to wifi sign-ups in the three airports’ terminals.Photograph: AP S (uk)/AlamyView image in fullscreenManchester airport. Most of the accessed data related to wifi sign-ups in the three airports’ terminals.Photograph: AP S (uk)/AlamyAirline industryThree UK airports hit by cyber-attack with data of 8.7m customers accessedCompany that runs Manchester, Stansted and East Midlands hubs says passenger safety is unaffectedBusiness live – latest updatesLauren AlmeidaThu 27 Aug 2026 10.53 EDTFirst published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 08.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester, London Stansted and East Midlands airports have been hit by a cyber-attack in which hackers accessed the data of about 8.7 million customers.The incident involved data related to “car park, lounge and fast-track bookings and in-airport wifi sign-ups”, and the hackers obtained email addresses, phone numbers, vehicle registration numbers and postcodes, said Manchester Airports Group (MAG), which operates the three hubs.The company said that “at no point has passenger safety or aviation security been compromised” during the incident and operations at the airports were unaffected. The hacked system did not hold customers’ bank or payment details.View image in fullscreenAn email sent to an affected customer from London Stansted airport.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAIn an email to customers, London Stansted said: “We would urge you to be particularly cautious of unexpected emails, calls or text messages claiming to be from us. We will never contact you unexpectedly to ask for payment or banking information. We apologise for any inconvenience or concern this may cause.”The cyber-attack hit the airports during the peak summer travel season. Many families are flying back into the UK this week before the start of the new school year. Fifty-four million passengers flew through Manchester, London Stansted and East Midlands airports combined last year.A MAG spokesperson said the company had “immediately contained the risk” from the incident and was “working with specialist advisers and taking appropriate steps to protect our customers and systems”.“We have informed and are working with the relevant authorities. At no point has passenger safety or aviation security been compromised,” they said. “Airport operations remain unaffected and customer parking services continue to operate normally.“We would like to reassure customers that Manchester Airport Group takes the security of customer information extremely seriously and we apologise for any inconvenience or concern caused.”Lauren Wills-Dixon, a partner at the law firm Gordons, said the scale of the attack was notable.“Airports sell a number of services including lounge access, parking and fast-track bookings. Wi-fi access also requires customers to input their data,” she said. “As a result, operators will hold large amounts of customer data and this, together with the increased use of technology, only increases the threat of a cyber-attack.”The incident comes as pressure grows on suppliers and operators of national infrastructure to improve their cyber-defences.Flights were delayed and cancelled last year at three major European airports – including London’s largest, Heathrow – after thecompany behind the software used for check-in and boarding said it had been hit by a cyber-attack.Hackers linked to Iran were blamed earlier this monthfor a cyber-attack that caused the temporary shutdown of a British power plant. The government said the incident involved a small-scale generator and that at no point was there a risk to the wider energy system.There was a wave of high-profile cyber-attacks against British companies last year, ranging from one thatshut down the operations of Jaguar Land Rover for weeksto others targetingMarks & Spencer,Harrodsand theCo-op food chain.Explore more on these topicsAirline industryCybercrimeHackingStansted airportManchesterDerbyshireTransportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Broadcaster Jenni Murray died days after north London car crash, inquest hears | Jenni Murray | The Guardian
description: Coroner is told BBC veteran was dazzled by headlights before collision and her injuries led to bronchopneumonia
Author: Kevin Rawlinson
Headline: Coroner is told BBC veteran was dazzled by headlights before collision and her injuries led to bronchopneumonia
Content: Jenni Murray was best known as the voice of BBC Radio 4’s Woman’s Hour, which she hosted for three decadesPhotograph: Gary Doak/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenJenni Murray was best known as the voice of BBC Radio 4’s Woman’s Hour, which she hosted for three decadesPhotograph: Gary Doak/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.Jenni MurrayBroadcaster Jenni Murray died days after north London car crash, inquest hearsCoroner is told BBC veteran was dazzled by headlights before collision and her injuries led to bronchopneumoniaKevin Rawlinsonand agencyThu 27 Aug 2026 08.44 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 15.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe broadcasterJenni Murraydied days after being involved in a car crash that happened when she was dazzled by headlights, a coroner has heard.Murray, 75,was best known asthe voice of BBC Radio 4’s Woman’s Hour, hosting the programme for three decades and becoming the longest-serving presenter in its history.Shedied on 12 March this yearafter the collision in north London eight days earlier, the inquest into her death heard on Thursday.Dame Jenni Murray obituaryRead moreThe northLondonarea coroner Tony Murphy ruled Murray’s cause of death was bronchopneumonia caused by fractures to her rib and sternum sustained in the crash.At the inquest at Barnet coroner’s court, Murphy read a statement from Dr Clare Morkane, a consultant at the Royal Free hospital, where Murray died after being admitted on 4 March.“Jennifer had been driving when she became dazzled by vehicle lights and collided with two stationary vehicles. Following the collision, Jennifer was unable to recall events, exited the vehicle independently and she was conveyed to hospital,” Morkane said.The collision took place on Wildwood Road, adjacent to Hampstead Heath, shortly before 8pm, the inquest heard. It caused “multiple rib fractures”, a fracture to her upper sternum and a collapsed lung.In hospital, Murray was placed on non-invasive ventilation and moved to intensive care but developed bronchopneumonia. Morkane said that after a significant deterioration on 10 March, a decision was made to focus on palliative care. “Jennifer died peacefully on 12 March 2026 at approximately 15.45 hours,” she said.The Metropolitan police investigated the crash but closed their inquiry.Murray’s husband, David Forgham-Bailey, attended the hearing via video link.After Murray’s death, the former Labour deputy leader Harriet Harman called her “the broadcasting wing of the women’s movement”.Murray announced on Woman’s Hour in 2006 that she had been diagnosed with breast cancer and began raising awareness of the condition as a vice-patron for Breast Cancer Now, a position she held for almost 20 years. She was made a dame in 2011 in recognition of her contribution to broadcasting.Murray was a noted feminist and a celebrated broadcaster. Her final episode of Woman’s Hour in 2020 ended with Helen Reddy’s feminist anthemI Am Woman. Woman’s Hour won the Television and Radio Industries Club award for best radio programme in 2004, and Murray was honoured with Sony awards in 2010 and 2011.Explore more on these topicsJenni MurrayRadio 4BBCLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Climate crisis could be destabilising mountain areas like Nepal, experts warn | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Unusual heat this year may have melted ice and thawed bonds that hold glaciers in place – leading to catastrophe
Author: Jonathan Watts
Headline: Unusual heat this year may have melted ice and thawed bonds that hold glaciers in place – leading to catastrophe
Content: Nuwakot in Nepal. The UN’s scientific advisory body warned in 2023 that ice-bound landmasses would become more unstable.Photograph: Sanjit Pariyar/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenNuwakot in Nepal. The UN’s scientific advisory body warned in 2023 that ice-bound landmasses would become more unstable.Photograph: Sanjit Pariyar/NurPhoto/ShutterstockNepal-Tibet flood disasterClimate crisis could be destabilising mountain areas like Nepal, experts warnUnusual heat this year may have melted ice and thawed bonds that hold glaciers in place – leading to catastropheNepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updatesWhat caused the flash flood in Nepal and Tibet?Jonathan WattsThu 27 Aug 2026 14.25 EDTFirst published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 14.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe devastating flash flood that has ripped through the border communities of Nepal andTibethas heightened fears that the climate crisis is destabilising the geology of mountain and polar regions, threatening millions of people.Satellite imagery suggests a glacier collapse high in the Himalayas was the primary cause of the deadly torrent of mud, water and ice that tore along the Bhotekoshi River on Wednesday. It swept away buildings and roads and left at least 360 dead and 1,400 missing.A magnitude 4.4 earthquake was initially blamed for the collapse. However, it is now thought to have been caused by the huge wall of ice that crashed down on to the north slope of Langtang Lirung, a 7,000-metre (23,000ft) mountain, the impact of which registered a magnitude of 5.2.“Additional analysis of long-period seismic waves indicates that the seismic energy was instead generated by a glacial collapse and debris flow,”the US Geological Survey said.A map showing the area where the flash flood hit.The ice-rock avalanche pushed boulders and other debris into the Lhende Khola River, a tributary of the Bhotekoshi River. Water levels in rivers downstream rose by between 7 and 9 metres within 30 minutes, according to the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, an intergovernmental scientific institution.Scientists are still examining the precise mechanics of the Himalayan disaster, but manyobserve thatglaciers and permafrost around the world are being weakened by global heating, caused by the burning of gas, oil and coal.View image in fullscreenFlooding in the Bhotekoshi River has affected low-lying areas along the riverbanks and nearby homes in Nuwakot, Nepal.Photograph: Ap Tolang/Nexpher/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockThe detachment of a chunk of the glacier wall came amid unusual heat that was likely to have melted the ice that bound the splintered bedrock together.Two days before the collapse, the ground temperature hit its highest point in the last two years, according to Dr Hamish Pritchard, a glaciologist with the British Antarctic Survey, whose team had sensors 6 miles (10km) away from the site.“These high temperatures would have weakened the snowpack, filled crevasses with water and thawed the bonds between ice and rock that hold these glaciers in place,” he told the Science Media Centre.A series of intense heatwaves has hit the region since early this year and affected countries around the world. Another factor here was the monsoon season, which saturated the soil and swelled rivers.A map showing the timeline of the disaster.Disasters like this were foretold. In 2023 theUN’s top scientific advisory body warnedthat previously ice-bound landmasses – from permafrost tundra to mountain glaciers – would become increasingly unstable as temperatures rose.“Every increment of warming will multiply and intensify future hazards from cryosphere regions,” observed the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change in its sixth synthesis report. “Floods, landslides and freshwater shortages from glacier retreat and snow loss pose a serious threat to mountain regions across the world.”Average global temperatures are nudging closer to 1.5C above preindustrial levels.Even faster warmingis occurring in alpine and polar regions because the loss of snow and ice is removing the thermal insulation of the land.Dr Richard Waller, a senior lecturer in physical geography at Keele University, said: “The progressive loss of snow and glacier ice results in the surface being less reflective, so it absorbs more solar energy and heats up. In combination with atmospheric warming, this is leading to the melting of mountain permafrost.“Think of the high mountains like this as shattered bedrock glued together by ice-filled joints. As the permafrost and the ice-filled joints melt, then there’s the potential for these types of catastrophic failure.”View image in fullscreenA destroyed building in Devighat, Nuwakot.Photograph: Niranjan Shrestha/APThe thaw is altering the shape, colour and solidity of the landscape, creating or expanding glacial meltwater lakes and, in the long term, threatening the origin of many rivers and the drinking supplies of populations downstream. In many parts of Asia, hundreds of millions of people depend on the rivers such as the Ganges and the Brahmaputra that descend from the glaciers.Scientists have high confidence that glacier retreat is caused by human-driven global heating. This has caused glacier collapses from the Alps to the Andes. In the Langtang catchment area in Nepal, glacier loss rates have increased more than fourfold since 1964, astudy has shown.TImeline of how deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – explainerThis has contributed to a loss of life on multiple occasions. A smaller floodhit the Bhotekoshi River in July 2025and in 2015, the Langtang Lirung mountain was hit by an earthquake-induced avalanche that destroyed Langtang village.As emergency services look for bodies and humanitarian relief groups mobilise for survivors, others are asking where next. Waller said any high mountain areas with glaciers and permafrost could be vulnerable, including the European Alps, Caucasus, Himalayas, Andes and beyond.As glacier weakening accelerates, Pritchard called for greater disaster preparedness. “More avalanches and more floods are inevitable, particularly as lakes grow in front of the retreating glaciers,” he said. “Early warning systems are urgently needed to protect the people living in these valleys.”Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalTibetChinaSouth and central AsiaClimate crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: El Niño climate patterns supercharged by burning of fossil fuels, study finds | El Niño southern oscillation | The Guardian
description: ‘Godzilla’ event currently brewing could push 50 million people into acute hunger before the end of next year
Author: Oliver Milman
Headline: ‘Godzilla’ event currently brewing could push 50 million people into acute hunger before the end of next year
Content: Heavy rain in San Francisco, California, on 12 April 2026.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHeavy rain in San Francisco, California, on 12 April 2026.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesEl Niño southern oscillationEl Niño climate patterns supercharged by burning of fossil fuels, study finds‘Godzilla’ event currently brewing could push 50 million people into acute hunger before the end of next yearOliver MilmanThu 27 Aug 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 00.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA series of strong El Niño climatic patterns in recent decades, such as the “Godzilla” event currently brewing that is set to warp weather around the world, have been supercharged by the broader overheating of the planet caused by the burning of fossil fuels, a major new study has found.El Niño is a naturally occurring phenomenon, taking place every two to seven years, when the waters of the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean heat up, causing a cascade of impacts around the world. The latest developing El Niño, set to peak later this year, is set to be thestrongestin living memory and has been informallydubbeda “Godzilla” event.It’s well understood that El Niño, which typically brings a surge of global heat, further amplifies theescalatingclimate crisis, with next year almost certain to be the hottest on record globally. But the new research has established that the reverse is also the case: human-caused global heating is making El Niño itself more intense when it does arrive.“Our findings suggest El Niño can supercharge global warming but also global warming can supercharge El Niño – that is what we are seeing,” said Julia Cole, a climate researcher at the University of Michigan, who led the new study,published in Science.‘Super El Niño’ could bring wet winter and flooding to western US, climate scientists warnRead more“We are seeing a trend of stronger El Niños and the one we have now is consistent with that trend – it’s not a fluke. We are seeing a shift where El Niño doesn’t look like what it did prior to industrial times. That is bad news for climate hazards and for people, particularly those who are badly impacted and yet have done little to cause climate change.”As the world has heated up due to the use of fossil fuels, a string of recent “super” El Niño events has provided extra acceleration, with intense events causing the global temperature record to fall in1998, then2016and then further in2024.Such strong El Niño episodes have become far more common as overall global temperatures have risen, scientists found in the new research, which painstakingly analyzed the composition of large boulder-like deposits of coral fossils found on the Galápagos Islands.These old corals, which date to 1,000 years ago, contain chemical compositions that indicate what the sea surface temperature was like when they were alive. The Galápagos, situated off the coast of mainland Ecuador, is “right in the heart of El Niño country”, Cole said, where surrounding waters heat up during such an event.While El Niños remained fairly stable for most of this long period, things started to change around the time the world started to mass industrialize in the late 19th century. This process has become even more extreme in the past 40 years, with El Niños’ variability now around 37% higher than during preindustrial times.“After the El Niño in 1982, we start seeing much more variability; it’s a lot more extreme and looks like nothing in the previous 1,000 years,” said Cole, whose team managed to rule out any random or naturally occurring reason for this switch.“What surprised me was how consistent it was. There is just such a large, distinct difference between what has been happening in the last 40 years compared to preindustrial times.”The findings could help provide an answer to one of the more vexing questions in climate science, which has until now been unclear, on whether the climate crisis is significantly changing the strength of El Niño events.“This is a strong indication that climate change may already be amplifying El Niño events,” said Samantha Stevenson-Karl, a University of California, Santa Barbara scientist and study co-author. “If that’s true, then really large events like the one that seems to be brewing in the tropical Pacific right now might become more common in the future.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSuch a scenario is set to have profoundimpactsupon countries already dealing with growing incidences of heatwaves, wildfires and flooding worsened by the climate crisis. As El Niño gathers strength, caused by the weakening of trade winds that usually push surface heat to the western Pacific, parts of South America and the southern US often face heavier rainfall and floods.In India, meanwhile, the monsoon season is typically reduced by El Niño, while countries such as Indonesia and Australia face drier conditions, triggering droughts. The huge El Niño event that is currently growing could push about 50 million people worldwide into acute hunger before the end of next year due to the impact upon food production,a recent forecast found.The understanding that the climate crisis is also making El Niño more severe should prompt countries to ramp up their adaption ahead of such events, such as the food stockpiling that India iscurrently undertaking, Cole said.“We can prepare and try to adapt,” she added. “But we also need to look at the root cause, which is the fossil fuels we are burning every day. We need to get away from greenhouse gas-producing technologies as quickly as possible.”Andrew Dessler, a climate scientist at Texas A&M University, who was not involved in the research, said the paper was an “important validation” of model predictions that El Niño events would strengthen with global heating.“It underscores that a substantial share of the damage from the upcoming El Niño should be linked to our fossil-fuel-driven economy,” he said. “The findings reinforce the urgent need to transition away from fossil fuels to climate-safe renewable energy.”Explore more on these topicsEl Niño southern oscillationExtreme weatherExtreme heatWildfiresFloodingClimate crisisFossil fuelsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Forever chemicals’ surge during pilot of Thames Water plan to combat drought | Water | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: utility company wants to draw off tens of millions of litres of water a day from Thames and replace it with treated effluent
Author: Sandra Laville
Headline: Exclusive: utility company wants to draw off tens of millions of litres of water a day from Thames and replace it with treated effluent
Content: Rocks exposed on the River Thames by Teddington Lock, London, on 8 August as drought conditions continue.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersView image in fullscreenRocks exposed on the River Thames by Teddington Lock, London, on 8 August as drought conditions continue.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersWater‘Forever chemicals’ surge during pilot of Thames Water plan to combat droughtExclusive: utility company wants to draw off tens of millions of litres of water a day from Thames and replace it with treated effluentSandra LavilleEnvironment correspondentThu 27 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 03.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLevels of a toxic “forever chemical” rose to 13 times the legal limit duringThames Waterpilots for a controversial multimillion pound water recycling scheme that will pump millions of litres of treated sewage into the River Thames during drought.The data from the pilots is in stark contrast to public comments from ThamesWaterthat their water recycling project in south-west London will not harm the riverine environment.In technical notes in the company’s files for the project, seen by the Guardian, the results from two pilots reveal the recycling system rapidly and significantly increased levels of a particularly toxic type of Pfas chemical perfluorooctane sulfonate (Pfos), a suspected carcinogen – breaching the legal limits by as much as 13 times.As standard wastewater treatment plants are not designed to filter or destroy them, treated and untreated sewage contains Pfas chemicals (short for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances). They are known as “forever chemicals” because they do not break down in the environment, and the detrimental impact on rivers has beenfoundto be widespread.New figuresshow every English water body is polluted with toxic chemicals. They are alsoconsidered a threatto human health.Thames Water’srecycling systemis intended to provide more water to cope with shortages resulting from both a rising population, and predicted droughts caused by climate breakdown, over the coming decades.It involvesabstracting up to 75m litresof water a day from the Thames at Teddington, south-west London, when the river is in low flow at times of drought, and replacing it with the same amount of treated sewage from the Mogden treatment plant via a new tunnel into the river. The 75m litres a day is a fraction of the 571m litres of water the company leaks each day.The results of the company’s tests, however, reveal the scale of the treated sewage input would make it very difficult for the water to meet current standards for forever chemicals and pesticides.Thames Water, which is seeking a development consent order for the scheme, has insisted publicly that the water recycling system – which will cost at least £350m – would not harm the river, its habitats or be a threat to the public.But the technical note on the pilots shows levels of Pfos rose to 6.3 nanograms per litre in test one and 8.7 nanograms per litre in test two of the recycling technology. The UK legal limit for surface waters is 0.65 nanograms per litre.The documents show there was a “rapid breakthrough of Pfos” above the legal threshold in less than one month of operation. The company said keeping within legal limits would be “operationally challenging”, requiring carbon filters to be frequently regenerated, reactivated and replaced, and would require “significant additional operational expense”.In addition to the forever chemical, the pilots also showed the treated water contained very high levels of iron, which the document states would have a “significant detrimental impact” on the river.View image in fullscreenSwimmers at Teddington Lock on the River Thames, 9 July 2026.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesIan McNuff, of the campaign groupSolar, which opposes the project because of what they say will be irreversible environmental damage to the river, said: “Thames Water described the results for the pilot as ‘operationally’ challenging.“In essence, they can’t make it work properly. Test failures were rapid, and the idea that they can switch this on and off as a completely reliable asset during drought is unrealistic against current standards, let alone the higher ones expected around Pfas and pesticides.”Costs for the water recycling scheme are already rising for Thames, which isstruggling under debtsof £20bn and teetering on the brink of a government-handled administration.The original cost of £350m is now expected to rise to more than £500m, as Thames Water has discovered it needs to install more mechanical pumps within a nature reserve near Teddington to pump the water, according to sources close to the project.TheEnvironment Agencyhas been given the results of the two pilots carried out by Thames Water. The agency rejected an earlier scheme in 2019 because of the unacceptable impact on the environment of releasing millions of litres of treated effluent into the river.The project is opposed by the local council and local MPs, including the Liberal Democrat MP Munira Wilson. But as a strategic infrastructure project, it can be pushed through without local consent.An Environment Agency spokesperson said:“We have strict legal requirements in place to protect our rivers, groundwater and drinking water catchments from toxic chemicals and the Teddington site will continue to undergo rigorous environmental assessments to ensure these conditions are met before any development work can begin.“Environmental protection and sustainable development must go hand-in-hand and water recycling projects, combined with new reservoirs, will be critical to securing future water supplies effectivity.”A Thames Water spokesperson said: “The Teddington Direct River Abstraction (TDRA) project will not be allowed to operate without securing an environmental permit from the Environment Agency.“The pilot plant study was set up to test a range of technologies to help inform and refine the final design of the tertiary treatment plant. The data from the pilot plant study is not indicative of what would be released back into the river when the project is operational.”The spokesperson added: “We want to see Pfas banned and the development of a national plan to remove it from the environment, which should be paid for by manufacturers as opposed to water bill payers.”Explore more on these topicsWaterThames WaterPollutionDroughtEnvironment AgencyWater industryRiversnewsShareReuse this content

title: Homes damaged as storms follow heatwaves in England and Wales | UK weather | The Guardian
description: Environment Agency issues 40 flood alerts across Midlands, Yorkshire and south-east of England
Author: Neha Gohil
Headline: Environment Agency issues 40 flood alerts across Midlands, Yorkshire and south-east of England
Content: People walk through heavy rain in Liverpool today. Met Office warnings for thunderstorms are in place across much of England and Wales as warm, humid conditions bring an increased chance of heavy rain.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAView image in fullscreenPeople walk through heavy rain in Liverpool today. Met Office warnings for thunderstorms are in place across much of England and Wales as warm, humid conditions bring an increased chance of heavy rain.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAUK weatherHomes damaged as storms follow heatwaves in England and WalesEnvironment Agency issues 40 flood alerts across Midlands, Yorkshire and south-east of EnglandNeha GohilMidlands correspondentThu 27 Aug 2026 11.41 EDTFirst published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 10.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDozens of homes have been damaged by flooding and the Met Office had issued warnings for thunderstorms and heavy rain at the end of a summer in which most ofEnglandand the whole of Wales was declared in drought.The Met Office said thundery showers in England and Wales could cause 75mm of rain to fall in just 12 hours in some areas.The Environment Agency (EA) issued 40 flood alerts, where flooding is possible, across the Midlands, Yorkshire and the south-east on Thursday morning.
