A flood alert was issued for the River Maun at Edwinstowe and Ollerton in Nottinghamshire.The EA said river levels at Mansfield The Dykes gauging station were rising rapidly due to the nature of the catchment, and Old Rufford Road was most at risk.A yellow thunderstorm warning for parts of the Midlands, east of England, south of England, the north-west, Yorkshire and Humber and Wales is in place until 10pm on Thursday.View image in fullscreenA road in Birmingham becomes flooded after the River Tame, which runs under the road, burst its banks.Photograph: British News and Media/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.A second yellow warning for Lincolnshire, parts of the east of England, parts of Yorkshire, Kent and Medway will be in place from 5pm on Thursday to 7am on Friday.Climate scientists have repeatedly warned that global heating is causing more volatile weather patterns in the UK, with intense heatwaves, droughts, flooding and storms. Five heatwaves have been recorded in the UK this summer.ABirminghamman whose property was damaged in thunderstorms on Wednesday night described seeing a “river coming around the corner” before his home was flooded.Areas of Birmingham saw significant flooding on Wednesday after the EA issued a flood warning for the Perry Barr area. Staffordshire, where a lower-level flood alert is in place, had 60mm of rainfall in 12 hours, according to the Environment Agency.West Midlands fire service was alerted to flooding at 32 properties near the Tame Valley canal on Wednesday evening and sent seven fire engines to the scene.View image in fullscreenCommuters holding umbrellas cross London Bridge.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPARyan Goodwin, who lives on one of the affected streets, said his conservatory was flooded with 3ft (1 metre) of water and his living room was damaged.He said: “About 7.30pm I got home, I was in the car with the kids and I thought I don’t want to get out yet, there’s too many puddles here. Then in a matter of about half an hour it was just a river coming round the corner, all the way down the road.”Describing the damage to his home to the Press Association, he said: “It’s gone under the laminate flooring in the front room. The conservatory got flooded, the electrics went off. The conservatory had about 3ft of water – luckily that is below the house level.“The neighbours’ carpet and sofa and everything got wet as well. Down the road they have two hills running into the corner, it was halfway up their doors, so I think we got a bit lucky here, really.”Goodwin, who lives near the M6, said he was not sure how long it would take to repair his home. “I’m just trying to get everything out that is wet and speak to the insurance at the moment,” he said. “All the water comes off the motorway as well. It has been so dry for so long, all the leaves had blocked the drains and everything. Hopefully it doesn’t happen again.”Goodwin’s father-in-law, Jay Patel, said: “[The water] was really, really fast. I couldn’t believe how fast it was.”View image in fullscreenRain falls on parched ground after a succession of heatwaves in England and Wales.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/ShutterstockThe EA said after a National Drought Group meeting on Thursday morning that 71.3% of England remained in drought. It said only 34% of the rainfall typically expected in August had been received so far.The agency’s chief executive, Philip Duffy, said: “A few days or even weeks of wetter weather cannot reverse the impacts of several months of exceptionally dry conditions. Today’s yellow thunderstorm warnings show it’s possible to experience simultaneous drought and flood as heavy rain falls on compacted soils.”Explore more on these topicsUK weatherWest MidlandsBirminghamEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK expects Meta to match US child safety measures after $18bn settlement | Social media ban | The Guardian
description: Minister calls for Instagram owner to extend sweeping new safeguards for young users to Britain
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Minister calls for Instagram owner to extend sweeping new safeguards for young users to Britain
Content: The UK government expects the Instagram owner, Meta, to roll out the same protections for children in Britain.Photograph: Ekaterina Goncharova; posed by model/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe UK government expects the Instagram owner, Meta, to roll out the same protections for children in Britain.Photograph: Ekaterina Goncharova; posed by model/Getty ImagesSocial media banUK expects Meta to match US child safety measures after $18bn settlementMinister calls for Instagram owner to extend sweeping new safeguards for young users to BritainUK politics live – latest updatesBusiness live – latest updatesRobert BoothUK technology editorThu 27 Aug 2026 06.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK government expects the Instagram owner Meta to roll out the same protections for children in Britain asthose it agreed in the US on Wednesday, as part of a court settlement that could cost the company up to $18bn (£13bn).Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, said on Thursday he did not want young people in the US to have “a higher rate of protection” than those in Britain, after Meta settled a lawsuit brought by dozens of US states accusing the company ofharming children with dangerous products.As well as the payouts, Meta agreed to a default daily time limit of two hours for users under 18 that can be lifted only by a parent – a measure not currently proposed underplans to ban social media for under-16sin the UK – and a default block between midnight and 6am for under-18s, as well as default blocks on user notifications at night and during the school day.Analysts have pointed out the measures largely fall within the bounds of changesMetahas already been required to make elsewhere. But restrictions agreed by Meta in the US that have not been proposed in the UK include bans on under-18s displaying numbers of likes or reactions and on cosmetic procedure image filters.Meta has urged TikTok and YouTube to adopt the same standards “to ensure teens use social media in a healthy and responsible way”.View image in fullscreenCountries around the world are beginning to restrict social media for children children’s access to social media amid rising concern about harms,Photograph: Yui Mok/PAAsked on Sky News whether he expected Meta to roll out the new safety features in the UK, McFadden said: “Yes, we would. We don’t want a situation where young people in America have got a higher rate of protection than young people in the UK.”In June, Keir Starmer’s government announced an Australia-styleban on social media for children under 16would come into force by early 2027. It also said in July thatdefault overnight curfews from midnight to 6am would be switched onfor 16- and 17-year-olds using social media apps, while features designed to keep users scrolling for longer would be switched off by default.McFadden said the social media ban for young people would come into force next year, confirmed the overnight curfews and added: “We’ve got to do something about this endless scrolling, which is so addictive for young people.”Countries around the world are beginning to restrict children’s access to social media amid rising concern about harms. In March, Indonesia began blocking children under 16 from accessing most social media. Malaysia followed suit in June. France passed a law banning social media access for under-15s in July, while Turkey passed a bill with similar restrictions. Bans or limits are beingconsidered by 19 other countries, according to the Tech Policy Press non-profit organisation.The Meta settlement announced on Wednesday cut short a trial in Oakland, California, in which lawyers for 29 US statesaccusedMetaof covering up internal research showing thatInstagramwas addictive for teenagers. Legal experts, including James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell University, described the settlement as “a sign of vulnerability on Meta’s part”. It also prompted calls for the UK government to tighten its grip on social media companies after critics said the2023 Online Safety Act, enforced by Ofcom, had had limited effect.The Molly Rose Foundation, set up by the father of Molly Russell, who took her own life in 2017 after falling into avortex of despair on social media, called on the UK government to “seize this opportunity to deliver a reset to children’s online safety”.“Andy Burnham has now seen that it is possible to take on big tech to address drivers of online harm,” a spokesperson said. “It’s time for the UK government to be brave, bold and decisive in ways it hasn’t been before.”Munira Wilson, who leads on children and families for the Liberal Democrats, said: “If a US court can pressure Meta into making significant changes to its platforms, why is our government still relying on optional curfews, strongly worded statements and unworkable bans?”Meanwhile, experts were sceptical that Meta’s agreed measures would tackle the underlying problems with the compulsive – some say addictive – app design that critics blame for social media harms.Dr Rachael Kent, a senior lecturer in digital economy and society education at King’s College London, said the settlement “does not fundamentally redesign the engagement-driven model. Some of the measures being introduced do not remove many of the underlying engagement mechanisms altogether – infinite scroll, autoplay and algorithmic recommendation remain – but introduce limits and stopping points around them.”Explore more on these topicsSocial media banMetaInternet safetyChildrenSocial mediaDigital mediaLaw (US)newsShareReuse this content

title: Number of asylum seekers living in hotels across UK halves in a year | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Home Office was housing 16,021 asylum seekers across 160 hotels at end of June, while small boat crossings down 23%
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: Home Office was housing 16,021 asylum seekers across 160 hotels at end of June, while small boat crossings down 23%
Content: Police outside the Bell hotel in Epping in July 2025. This summer the Home Office stopped using the hotel to house asylum seekers.Photograph: SOPA Images/LightRocket/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPolice outside the Bell hotel in Epping in July 2025. This summer the Home Office stopped using the hotel to house asylum seekers.Photograph: SOPA Images/LightRocket/Getty ImagesImmigration and asylumNumber of asylum seekers living in hotels across UK halves in a yearHome Office was housing 16,021 asylum seekers across 160 hotels at end of June, while small boat crossings down 23%UK politics live – latest updatesJessica Elgot,Diane TaylorandChris OsuhThu 27 Aug 2026 11.31 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 15.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe number of asylum seekers living in hotels has halved in a year,Home Officefigures show.Sweeping changes to the asylum system have also led to a significant drop in legal arrivals and asylum claims, but the numbers of asylum seekers housed in private accommodation has increased as the government moves people from hotels into privately rented houses in multiple occupation (HMOs).There were 16,021 asylum seekers housed in 160 hotels at the end of June, down from 32,041 at the same point last year and a peak of 56,018 in September 2023.Asylum hotels have been aflashpoint for the far right, especially last summer, and the government has pledged to end their use by the end of the parliament. It said earlier this month another 13 hotels had recently been exited.But tens of thousands of people are still housed in other forms of contingency accommodation, which has also often been highly controversial, both in local communities and because of the conditions of the housing for a vulnerable group of people.The latest figures show 69,038 were housed in temporary accommodation.The shift from asylum hotels to other forms of accommodation has led to an 8% fall in Home Office spending on asylum.The Guardian revealed this month that the government was consideringpaying higher pricesfor housing asylum seekers in private rental properties as part of Andy Burnham’s plan to spread accommodation more evenly across the country.The home secretary,Shabana Mahmood, said figures showed the government was “restoring control at our border and fairness to the migration system”.She said: “A little over two years into office and the asylum backlog is down, the number of asylum seekers in hotels is falling, illegal working arrests are at record levels and deportations and returns are up markedly.”Small boat crossings to the UK have fallen by 23% year on year, which Home Office officials said was down to a combination of more trafficking arrests and more interceptions by French police.View image in fullscreenA counter-protest near an anti-immigration rally in Maidstone, Kent earlier this month.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesThe previous prime minister, Keir Starmer, struck a deal with the French government to deport some would-be migrants back to France in exchange for providing others with a safe and legal route to the UK, known as theone in, one outpolicy.However, Home Office figures show the introduction of the scheme has led to a rise in incidents of use of force against deportees to a record 210, including 181 occasions where restraint equipment was used, a figure that has doubled since the start of the French scheme.Charities say they have documented injuries sustained by asylum seekers as they are removed back to France.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMahmood said there was still more to do to deter small boat Channel crossings. “Small boats numbers are now falling but we are not complacent and there is more we must do,” she said. “That is why I have boosted enforcement on the French beaches and overseas and introduced new legislation to tackle the pull factors that draw people here through unsafe and illegal routes.”From welfare to prisons: the challenges for Burnham when MPs return to CommonsRead moreNuni Jorgensen, of the University of Oxford’s Migration Observatory, told PA the government had been able to close hotels largely because asylum decisions were being made more quickly, but there was now an asylum appeals backlog in the courts.Figures also show that the number of businesses being stripped of the right to sponsor migrant workers has surged to the highest since the post-Brexit scheme was introduced.Analysis of quarterly migration statistics and a freedom of information request by the workplace justice charity the Work Rights Centre found the number of revocations of licences to sponsor migrant workers surged to 4,403 in the 12 months to June 2026, from 1,828 in 2025.The skilled worker visa sponsorship scheme was introduced to fill post-Brexit skills shortages in sectors such as care. Unions and charities have warned that the scheme facilitates exploitation.In some cases, workers have complained of employers using the fact that their migration status is tied to their job to underpay them and force them to work long hours. Other arrivals, such asShabin Shaji, whose case the Guardian reported on earlier this year, paid cash to recruiters to secure a role in the UK but have been left destitute after their employer “ghosted” them.Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumHome OfficeShabana MahmoodnewsShareReuse this content

title: BBC chief proposes ‘public service algorithm’ with YouTube-style user-generated content | BBC | The Guardian
description: Speaking at Edinburgh TV festival, Matt Brittin says BBC platform would be free from interests of US tech giants
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Speaking at Edinburgh TV festival, Matt Brittin says BBC platform would be free from interests of US tech giants
Content: Matt Brittin said the idea would mean creators could access ‘the expertise and … reach and the trust in the BBC’.Photograph: Carl Court/GettyView image in fullscreenMatt Brittin said the idea would mean creators could access ‘the expertise and … reach and the trust in the BBC’.Photograph: Carl Court/GettyBBCBBC chief proposes ‘public service algorithm’ with YouTube-style user-generated contentSpeaking at Edinburgh TV festival, Matt Brittin says BBC platform would be free from interests of US tech giantsMichael SavageMedia editorThu 27 Aug 2026 12.59 EDTFirst published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 12.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe BBC director general has suggested opening up the BBC to YouTube-style user-generated content as he backed the idea of a “public service algorithm” free from the interests of US tech companies.Matt Brittin, who arrived at the BBC after 10 years leading Google in Europe, said the corporation and public service media in Britain had the opportunity to build a platform “unadulterated by commercial interests, by algorithms that have other interests at heart”.Speaking at the Edinburgh TV festival, he said concerns about the influence and impact of social media algorithms were now the “most interesting public debate” in the US.Metaagreed on Wednesday topay out $18bn (£13.2bn) and make big changesto its platforms after claims of addicting and harming children with dangerous products.While stating it was notBBCpolicy, Brittin raised the idea of turning an “iPlayer 2.0” into a YouTube-style site hosting appropriate content from creators. It would be built around an algorithm aimed at “educating, informing and entertaining the public here and ideally around the world”.“I’d like to be an open platform for creativity,” he said. “What if we could say to people, create content about where you live, about the sports teams you follow, about the skills and the businesses that are in the area, and do that in line with our guidelines,” he said. “You don’t have to beLyse Doucet, but there would be some BBC guidelines.“We should have a public service algorithm … [iPlayer] should do it in a way that’s not biased towards the incentives of a US tech company or commercial interests. It should be biased towards what we want public service to be all about.”Brittin said it would allow creators to access “the expertise and the platform and the reach and the trust in the BBC, in return for signing up for some policies that might be different from YouTube”.The idea would be a big departure from the current iPlayer, which Brittin said had “fallen behind”.The proposal may well find favour among some in Downing Street. The concept of the BBC developing a public service algorithm was raised in 2019 byJames Purnell, a former BBC executive who is now Andy Burnham’s chief of staff.Brittin was speaking after the BBC presenterAmol Rajanhad given a speech suggesting the corporation was “screwed” unless it adopted a radically different funding model. Rajan suggested a cooperative model where licence fee owners would own a majority of the broadcaster.Brittin said he “hadn’t understood quite the severity” of the BBC’s financial pressures, stating it had lost about £1.3bn in revenue over the last decade – 60% from government decisions such as freezing the licence fee and 40% from fewer people paying the licence fee.Amol Rajan warns BBC destined to shrink at ‘accelerating rate’Read moreHe conceded that the plan tocut up to 2,000 jobs and save £500mwould be difficult and good programmes would go. “It’s hard and I don’t think there are programmes that nobody’s watching or services that nobody enjoys,” he said. “So anything you do is going to challenge some audience appreciation.“Obviously, to get to that scale of savings, there’s uncertainty hanging over a lot more colleagues than those who will eventually leave the organisation. That’s really hard to deal with. But let’s be clear … 90% of the people in the BBC will remain.”Brittin said Rajan’s fear that the BBC wouldshrink at an accelerating ratewas not inevitable if the corporation reached the right new funding model in ongoing government talks. However, he said reports that Newsnight was under threat were “nonsense”.“We need to create, I think, a sovereign media public space where we can create content that tells stories of who we are, that has our values, that is unadulterated by commercial interests, by algorithms that have other interests at heart,” he said.“So the next generation of creators … can participate in that – and that can reach people around the world.”Explore more on these topicsBBCMatt BrittinTelevisionYouTubeEdinburgh International Television FestivalTelevision industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Senator calls for criminal investigation of RFK Jr after Guardian report | Robert F Kennedy Jr | The Guardian
description: Newly obtained records indicate health secretary lied about Samoa trip during Senate confirmation hearings last year
Author: Michelle R Smith
Headline: Newly obtained records indicate health secretary lied about Samoa trip during Senate confirmation hearings last year
Content: Robert F Kennedy Jr at a press conference on 5 August 2026 in Lexington, Kentucky.Photograph: Michael Swensen/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRobert F Kennedy Jr at a press conference on 5 August 2026 in Lexington, Kentucky.Photograph: Michael Swensen/Getty ImagesRobert F Kennedy JrSenator calls for criminal investigation of RFK Jr after Guardian reportNewly obtained records indicate health secretary lied about Samoa trip during  Senate confirmation hearings last yearMichelle R SmithThu 27 Aug 2026 18.11 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 20.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA senior Democratic senator is calling for a criminal investigation into the US health secretary,Robert F Kennedy Jr, followingreporting by the Guardianthat indicated he lied duringSenateconfirmation hearings last year.Ron Wyden of Oregon said: “RFK’s platform is built on lies and grifts that leave a trail of dead children in their wake. There are consequences for lying to Congress.”The Guardian’s reporting was based on letters that were obtained – by this news outlet and the Associated Press – following a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit.Wyden said in a statement to the Guardian that he would be pressing Republican colleagues, who currently control the Senate, to issue a criminal referral of Kennedy to the Department of Justice for a criminal investigation. “And when Democrats retake the majority in the Senate, RFK will be at the top of the list of Trump officials the finance committee will hold accountable for endangering American families,” he said. Wyden currently serves as the top Democrat on the finance committee.RFK Jr lied in Senate confirmation hearings, newly revealed documents indicateRead moreAlso on Thursday, the government watchdog group American Oversightsent a letterto the justice department requesting that it immediately open an investigation into whether Kennedy violated the law by making false statements to Congress.Other Democratic officials called for Kennedy to be removed or leave office in the wake of the new reporting.Wyden was among the senators who asked Kennedy during two confirmation hearings last year about a 2019 trip he took toSamoa, at a time when Kennedy was leading an anti-vaccine group. Months later, a measles outbreak sickened thousands and killed 83 people, mostly children under five.When asked about the trip by Wyden and Ed Markey, the senator from Massachusetts, Kennedy testified that his visit had “nothing to do with vaccines”. The newly obtained letters contradict that testimony. In one,Kennedy explicitly told the Samoan prime ministerhe wanted to study the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine in the Pacific island nation and used the words “vaccine” or “vaccination” eight times.“Lying to Congress is a crime, whether or not the witness is under oath,” Josh Chafetz, a professor of law and politics at Georgetown University Law Center, said. “But this would require the executive branch to prosecute, and Trump’s [justice department] is unlikely to do so.”Still, attorneys with expertise in Senate procedure said that if Democrats win control of the House or Senate in November’s elections, they could use Kennedy’s statements as grounds for hearings or an impeachment inquiry, or to create other obstacles for theTrump administration.Markey also weighed in on the new reporting, saying the records show it was false when Kennedy said his trip had “nothing to do with vaccines”.“This is a pattern, not a slip. RFK Jr has lied to the Senate, lied to the American people and jeopardized the health of children to advance his anti-vaccine agenda,” Markey said. “He should never have been confirmed, and he cannot be trusted to run [the Department ofHealthand Human Services] for even one more day.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAngela Alsobrooks of Maryland, a member of the Senate health, education, labor and pensions committee, which oversees Kennedy’s department, repeated her call that the health secretary resign or be fired.And Hawaii’s governor, Josh Green, a medical doctor who traveled to Samoa to help in the measles response in 2019,again called for him to step down.“It is clear that Kennedy misled Congress about his intentions in Samoa and his stance on vaccinations during his confirmation hearings two years ago. It is time for him to immediately resign,” Green said. “He must do this for the safety and health of our country.”The federal statute of limitations for lying to Congress is five years, meaning a new justice department under the next president in 2029 could theoretically investigate the case.The Guardian sought comment from the Department of Health and Human Services about the Democratic officials’ calls for investigation or removal, but it did not immediately respond. In a previously issued statement it said Kennedy’s visit to Samoa “was unrelated to vaccines. Any claim or insinuation based on these letters that Secretary Kennedy lied under oath or to Congress is not only false but outright defamatory.”Kennedy was not under oath during the two confirmation hearings. Wyden’s staff said whether he was under oath is not relevant since it is a crime to lie during a confirmation hearing either way.Explore more on these topicsRobert F Kennedy JrTrump administrationUS SenateVaccines and immunisationMMRInfectious diseasesSamoanewsShareReuse this content

title: Bots and bargains: Zara owner launches cut-price Lefties in UK to rival Primark | Retail industry | The Guardian
description: First robot-assisted outlet opens in Liverpool to take on Shein and supermarkets in clothing, shoes and homewares
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: First robot-assisted outlet opens in Liverpool to take on Shein and supermarkets in clothing, shoes and homewares
Content: Lefties in Liverpool. Stores will also open at the Lakeside shopping centre in Essex and at the Metrocentre near Newcastle.Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/ReutersView image in fullscreenLefties in Liverpool. Stores will also open at the Lakeside shopping centre in Essex and at the Metrocentre near Newcastle.Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/ReutersRetail industryBots and bargains: Zara owner launches cut-price Lefties in UK to rival PrimarkFirst robot-assisted outlet opens in Liverpool to take on Shein and supermarkets in clothing, shoes and homewaresBusiness live – latest updatesSarah ButlerThu 27 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 15.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe owner of Zara is taking onPrimark, Shein and the supermarkets with the launch of its cut-price chain Lefties in Britain, backed by an army of robots.The Spanish fashion brand opened its first UK store inLiverpoolon Thursday, a few weeks after quietly launching its UK website.The store has embraced robotics to reduce staffing costs, with self-checkouts that scan a whole basket in one go and a clothes hanger sorter. Shoppers put their hangers in a slot as they pay and they are taken on a hidden conveyor belt to two robots behind a screen that sort them into boxes for different sizes.The outlet at the Liverpool One city centre development also has fitting rooms equipped with a hatch through which unwanted items go to be sorted behind the scenes, again by robots.View image in fullscreenClothes-sorting by robot.Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/ReutersThe garment-sorting system splits clothes into rails for each department ready to be taken away to the shop floor or packed into the stockroom.The Liverpool store is the first of three Lefties planned in the UK this year. The other two will be in the Lakeside shopping centre in Essex and the Metrocentre near Newcastle. More are expected next year.Just before the official opening, as more than 100 customers queued up to be the first British shoppers, the chain’s general director said the group was “not thinking about a specific number” of UK stores and would look at how the first few went before taking next steps.Xavier Ruz Riera said Liverpool had been chosen as the first outlet as it was a city with a vibrant young population that as a port was “open to the world” and “has a great personality”.The Lefties name comes from the fact its owner, Inditex, launched it in 1999 as an outlet for unsold, or leftover, items fromZara. However, it stopped selling its bigger sister brand’s clothing about a decade ago, instead stocking its own range of men’s, women’s and children’s clothing, shoes, and homewares from bedding to vases.View image in fullscreenRobotic arms sort out the clothes hangers on the opening day of Lefties’ first store in Britain.Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/ReutersAs Zara has moved slightly upmarket, Lefties has stepped in as a more cost-conscious option. Its products are a touch above Primark but below Shein on price, with dresses an average of £18, compared with £16 at the British chain and £18.50 at theChinese-founded marketplace, according to analysis by the trade journal Retail Week.In a nod to the UK’s winter weather, the Liverpool store is the first Lefties to stock thermal clothing, presenting a new competitor to Marks & Spencer and Uniqlo on basic underwear, with bras from £7.99.Riera said the store would flex to meet local demands, taking feedback from its sales figures and shop staff.View image in fullscreenMickey and Minnie Mouse-themed children’s clothing in the new store.Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/ReutersIts clothing and stores have more focus on design than Primark and it offers a nationwide online delivery service, unlike its British rival which only offers click and collect from its website. However, Lefties does not offer frequent discounts in the same way as Shein or other rivals such as Tesco’s F&F or Matalan.Its garment-sorting machine is also in use at five UK Zaras, but the clothes hanger sorting system is a first for the group in Britain.The chain operates in 20 countries including Italy, Turkey and Romania, with 225 stores globally. The brand, now Inditex’s fastest-expanding chain, opened its first French and Italian stores last year and is set to go into Germany in the spring.Riera said: “The UK is a natural next step offering an exciting destination for our brand. We believe there is a strong opportunity to bring our proposition to UK customers, offering quality fashion and home collections for the whole family at accessible prices through a seamless in-store and online shopping experience.”Lefties’ online store offers its full collection, with free delivery on orders over £49 and the ability to order or return items for free in store.View image in fullscreenShoes on sale in Liverpool’s Lefties.Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/ReutersIt is likely to add to pressure on cheaper clothing chains such as Primark, New Look and Matalan as well as online specialists including Asos, Shein and Boohoo. However, it faces a market crowded with competitors, including successful supermarket own labels such as Tesco’s F&F, George at Asda and Sainsbury’s Tu.Lefties’ parent group’s decision to prioritise other markets over the UK is likely to reflect apprehension about the level of competition itcould face here.Richard Lim, the chief executive of the industry analyst Retail Economics, said: “Lefties’ arrival in the UK reflects successive waves of disruption across the apparel market. Competition has intensified from Chinese commerce players such as Shein, while the huge momentum behind pre-loved platforms such as Vinted has further fragmented consumer spending.”He added: “This is a direct challenge to Primark’s heartland. Lefties gives Inditex a stronger foothold in value fashion as the fight for the value-conscious fashion shopper is only getting more intense.”Explore more on these topicsRetail industryZaraPrimarkLiverpoolnewsShareReuse this content

title: Greek Orthodox priest and cult musician clarifies views on homosexuality | Experimental music | The Guardian
description: Father Dionysios Tabakis says his views are those of Orthodox church, ‘nothing more, nothing less’
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: Father Dionysios Tabakis says his views are those of Orthodox church, ‘nothing more, nothing less’
Content: Father Dionysios Tabakis also clarified that he performed a sanctification of a neo-Nazi party office at the request of a superior authority.Photograph: Panagiotis Moschandreou/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFather Dionysios Tabakis also clarified that he performed a sanctification of a neo-Nazi party office at the request of a superior authority.Photograph: Panagiotis Moschandreou/The GuardianExperimental musicGreek Orthodox priest and cult musician clarifies views on homosexualityFather Dionysios Tabakis says his views are those of Orthodox church, ‘nothing more, nothing less’Philip OltermannEuropean culture editorThu 27 Aug 2026 13.11 EDTFirst published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 12.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Greek Orthodox priest whose home-recorded album of drone metal and religious dubstep has made him acult figure in experimental musiccircles has issued a statement in which he has clarified his stance on homosexuality and the Greek radical right.“As can be seen from my musical expression, I am in favour of unity, love, empathy and help for every needy, wronged and suffering person in life,” Father Dionysios Tabakis said in a public statement shared with the Guardian. “Whoever they are, whatever they believe, whether they are a saint or a sinner.”The musician-priest’s political views have come under scrutiny over two blogposts he wrote in 2024, around the time thatGreecebecame the first Christian Orthodox-majority country to legalise same-sex marriage.The posts on the Orthodox Christian WordPress blog The Doors The Doors referred to gay people as “Sodomites”, gay marriage as aσοδομικὸ τερατούργημα(“sodomitic monstrosity”) and the same-sex marriage bill as “blasphemous”.‘Techno in a monastery – are you ready?’ The Greek priest whose doom metal album is the year’s hippest recordRead moreIn a statement released on Tuesday, Tabakis said: “My view on homosexuality is the same as that of the Orthodox church for 2,000 years, nothing more, nothing less.“We owe homosexual people love and acceptance because many have at times experienced great rejection from their environment, especially from their families. Over the years, homosexual people have also come to me for confession, and I have always received them with acceptance and love.”In his statement, Tabakis still appears to refer to homosexuality as a sin: “I also always respect the freedom of my fellow man. After all, with freedom we sin, and with freedom we repent. It is better to sin with freedom than to be virtuous with oppression.”The Orthodox priest’s debut albumParadise Metalearned a critics’ score of 7.6 from the experimental music bible Pitchfork, and Tabakis was profiled in international media including theGuardianand the New York Times.In a separate controversy, a 2013 YouTube video that recently resurfaced on Greek social media showed Tabakis performing a sanctification at the opening of an office building for Golden Dawn, the neo-Nazi party that held seats in Greece’s parliament between 2015 and 2019.The group wascriminalised in 2020, and its leadership handed prison sentences for murder, assault and weapons possession.In his statement, Tabakis said he performed the consecration in an official duty and at the request of his superior authority, and that he also attended other consecration ceremonies connected with other political and municipal groups.Heat Crimes, the Greek record label that issued Tabakis’s debut album,told Pitchfork: “In Greek Orthodox practice, priests routinely performagiasmos, blessing ceremonies for homes, shops, businesses, schools, public institutions, military facilities and other premises. A politician or political organisation inviting a local priest to bless new premises therefore does not, by itself, establish that either the priest or the church endorses that organisation. The important distinction is between performing a religious blessing and giving a political endorsement.”In his statement, Tabakis said he was against nationalism “because it has only brought blood and wars to humanity”.“The only ones who have interests in nationalism and borders are the weapons factories that spread death. Besides, my grandparents from Crete fought Hitler and nazism, so I follow their spirit. In fact, one reason I have removed the frets from my guitar is my mental need not to be confined to borders.”Explore more on these topicsExperimental musicGreecePop and rockMetalReligionEuropeLGBTQ+ rightsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ex-Barclays boss denies having sex with woman dressed as Snow White after Epstein emails | Jes Staley | The Guardian
description: Jes Staley made comments to US lawmakers investigating his links to the convicted sex offender
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Jes Staley made comments to US lawmakers investigating his links to the convicted sex offender
Content: Jes Staley was questioned last month about his infamous email exchange with Jeffrey Epstein.Photograph: Tayfun Salcı/Zuma/RexView image in fullscreenJes Staley was questioned last month about his infamous email exchange with Jeffrey Epstein.Photograph: Tayfun Salcı/Zuma/RexJes StaleyEx-Barclays boss denies having sex with woman dressed as Snow White after Epstein emailsJes Staley made comments to US lawmakers investigating his links to the convicted sex offenderKalyeena MakortoffBanking correspondentThu 27 Aug 2026 13.21 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 15.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe former Barclays boss Jes Staley has denied having sex with a woman dressed as Snow White, after being questioned about an infamous email exchange about Disney princesses withJeffrey Epstein.The comments were detailed innewly released transcriptsfrom a closed-door interview last month with US lawmakers as part of their investigation into Epstein, whodied in prisonin August 2019 while awaiting trial on child sex-trafficking charges.In the emailexchangeon 9 and 10 July 2010 Staley and Epstein referred to Disney princesses. In those messages, the details of which have been circulating in the media since 2021, Staley tells Epstein: “That was fun. Say hi to Snow White.”Epstein then asks: “What character would you like next?” to which Staley replied: “Beauty and the Beast.” Epstein responded: “Well one side is availble [sic].”During his congressional testimony, Staley, who spent more than three decades at JPMorgan Chase before joiningBarclaysin 2015, was asked: “Did you ever have sex with a young woman in a Snow White costume?“No, I did not,” Staley said.Lawmakers then questioned Staley about another email,sent to Epsteinby an unnamed individual on 10 July 2010 and which said: “the snow white was f..ed twice as soon as she put her costume))”. Epstein appears to have asked an unnamed individual to buy a Snow White costume weeks before those exchanges, on 20 June 2010.“Why would this young woman have sent this email to Mr. Epstein if the two of you had not had sex while she was wearing a Snow White costume and if Mr. Epstein had not instructed her to do so?” a congressional representative, whose name has been redacted from the transcript, asked.“I have no idea who else she was with. I – it has nothing to do with me, though,” Staley said. When pressed further, he said: “I may have seen her in apartment [sic] and prompted that email. But I was not with a person dressed as Snow White outside of potentially crossing at his apartment.”The representative asked: “So you may have seen her in his apartment, later emailed Mr. Epstein and said, ‘That was fun,’ but it was not because you had sex with her?”“That’s correct,” Staley said.In the transcript, Staley is then asked: “Would you agree that’s a pretty incredible coincidence, that you email him on July 9th, saying, ‘That was fun, say hi to Snow White,’ and then [the unnamed individual] emails him the next day, reporting back on something that just didn’t have anything to do with you?”“Sure. Why not?” Staley said.“That’s pretty hard to believe,” the representative said.The former banker was also asked whether he and Epstein used “Disney princesses as code names for selecting women for sexual encounters”, to which Staley replied, “No.”Staley’s reputation has been tarnished as a result of his well-documented friendship with the child sex offender.Staley originally met Epstein in 2000 after he became head of JP Morgan’s private bank, where Epstein was a client. Staley later took over as chief executive of Barclays, one of the UK’s largest banks, in 2015 but was forced to step down in 2021 after City regulators opened an investigation into his relationship with Epstein.Staley was eventually banned from taking any job in the UK’s financial sector for playing down those ties. He tried andfailed to overturn that banking banlast year in a court battle that revealed intimate details of the pair’s friendship.Explore more on these topicsJes StaleyBarclaysCorporate governanceJeffrey EpsteinJP MorganFinancial sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: AI can detect heart disease in women using mammograms, study suggests | Women's health | The Guardian
description: Experts say findings mean breast screenings for cancer could also flag cardiovascular problems in women
Author: Andrew Gregory
Headline: Experts say findings mean breast screenings for cancer could also flag cardiovascular problems in women
Content: The study examined 97,364 breast scans from 29,921 women who had an average age of 54.Photograph: andresr/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe study examined 97,364 breast scans from 29,921 women who had an average age of 54.Photograph: andresr/Getty ImagesWomen's healthAI can detect heart disease in women using mammograms, study suggestsExperts say findings mean breast screenings for cancer could also flag cardiovascular problems in womenAndrew GregoryHealth editor in MunichThu 27 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 15.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDoctors have discovered a way to use routine mammograms that screen for breast cancer to spot heart disease, the world’s leading – and frequently underdiagnosed – cause of death in women.Researchers analysed the scans using artificial intelligence and were able to successfully identify women with coronary heart disease, high blood pressure or who had suffered a stroke.Experts said it meant breast screening for cancer could become dual-purpose, helping to flag women with heart disease, and other cardiovascular issues, as well as spotting breast cancer early.Millions of women are living with undetected heart disease. For decades, it has often been misdiagnosed or not picked up until the late stages of the disease.Details of the breakthrough were presented in Munich at the European Society of Cardiology’s annual congress, the world’s largest heart conference. The implications are significant because hundreds of millions of women undergo mammograms every year.Doctors in Israel examined 97,364 scans from 29,921 women who had an average age of 54. By cross-referencing medical records, they found 16% of the women had high blood pressure, 2.5% had coronary heart disease, and 2.5% had experienced a stroke.A machine-learning model was trained to identify women with these conditions and was able to reliably identify women who had suffered a stroke, based upon their mammogram alone, 86% of the time.I work in a hospital – and didn’t know I was having a heart attack. Here’s what more women should knowRead moreFor high blood pressure and coronary heart disease, it was 79% and 78% reliable at distinguishing between the women with the condition and those without. The results were also consistent regardless of age, or whether or not a woman also had cancer.Dr Viana Copeland from Tel Aviv University, Israel, presented the findings to delegates in Munich. “Despite being the leading cause of death in women worldwide, CVD [cardiovascular disease] is consistently underdiagnosed and undertreated,” she said.“A common finding in our medical centre, and around the world, is that when women do seek medical help, their CVD is already advanced. On the other hand, many women do attend routine breast cancer screening, even when they haven’t sought care for cardiovascular symptoms.”Because mammography is already widely used, analysing breast scans for information about a woman’s heart health “could potentially offer a scalable approach without requiring an additional imaging examination,” Copeland added.“Mammography also reaches many women in midlife, an important period for recognising and addressing cardiovascular risk.”A team of doctors and medical researchers are working to improve the accuracy of the AI model and reduce false results, while increasing the number of heart conditions it can detect.Elena Arbelo, an expert member of the European Society of Cardiology communication committee, said the findings were “compelling”.“A mammogram may one day do more than look for breast cancer – it may also offer a window on to cardiovascular health. That matters because CVD in women is still too often recognised late.”She added: “The challenge now is to establish accuracy and reliability – to move from experimentation to clinical implementation.”Dr Sonya Babu-Narayan, a consultant cardiologist and clinical director of the British Heart Foundation, a charity, also welcomed the breakthrough.She said: “Heart disease is the world’s biggest killer of not only men, but also women. Despite this, the myth persists that it’s only a ‘man’s disease’, meaning that when it comes to the heart, women are disproportionally unaware, unheard, underdiagnosed, undertreated and typically underrepresented in clinical research.“It is exciting to think that if the approach used in this large study from Israel is further proven, it could lead to better and earlier cardiovascular disease detection and prevention for women. AI could one day allow breast cancer screening programmes to become dual-purpose, helping to flag women with the highest risk of dangerous cardiovascular disease, as well as spotting breast cancer early.”Explore more on these topicsWomen's healthHeart diseaseBreast cancerAI (artificial intelligence)High blood pressureStrokeHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK’s small power plants face higher cyber risk into 2030s despite Iran-linked hack | Energy industry | The Guardian
description: Decision not to improve resilience sooner described as ‘unacceptable gamble with our national security’
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: Decision not to improve resilience sooner described as ‘unacceptable gamble with our national security’
Content: Britain has hundreds of smaller plants which are connected to the wider grid, experts say they may be targeted if they appear vulnerable.Photograph: Kamila OConnell/GettyView image in fullscreenBritain has hundreds of smaller plants which are connected to the wider grid, experts say they may be targeted if they appear vulnerable.Photograph: Kamila OConnell/GettyEnergy industryUK’s small power plants face higher cyber risk into 2030s despite Iran-linked hackDecision not to improve resilience sooner described as ‘unacceptable gamble with our national security’Jillian AmbroseThu 27 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 06.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHundreds of Britain’s smallest power plants could remain at a higher risk to state-sponsored cyber-attacks until the 2030s despite a successful Iran-linked hack last month, it has emerged.Officials this week briefed energy bosses on the breach, which is understood to have shut an unnamed small gas power plant for four days last month, and put the industry on alert over the growing cyber threat facing energy infrastructure.However, the government’s own plan to toughen the baseline cybersecurity standards for Britain’s smallest power generators will not be required until the end of 2030, raising concerns over “an unacceptable gamble with our national security”.Official government documents, published this month, call for the industry regulator, Ofgem, to lay out proposals for new baseline cyber resilience requirements for gas and electricity infrastructure by the end of 2027, ahead of implementing new standards by the end of 2030. The Guardian understands that the hack has not altered this timeline.The new requirements would cover the type of small-scale gas plant which is understood to have been successfullyattacked by the Iran-linked hackersin the weeks before the government set out its timeline for bolstering the sector’s cybersecurity standards.Reports of the unprecedented cyber hack emerged as the Cabinet Office prepares to urge UK citizensto stock up on tinned food and bottled waterto prepare for extreme weather events and potential attacks from hostile states.Calum Miller, the Lib Dems’ foreign affairs spokesperson, said: “Leaving hundreds of small power generators exposed to cyber threats until the 2030s is simply an unacceptable gamble with our national security.”Britain has hundreds of small-scale, unmanned gas plants connected to local power grids which are typically idle for most of the year but can be used to ramp up generation when electricity supplies are squeezed.Although the outage had no impact on the electricity system, the attack has raised concerns about vulnerabilities in locally connected power infrastructure which is not required to meet the same security standards as large-scale power plants and transmission assets.“The government should not have to wait for the lights to go out before taking the security of our energy infrastructure seriously,” Miller said. “They must immediately fast-track these regulations, not leave them until the 2030s. We mustn’t leave an open goal to hostile states at a time of heightened global threats.”The government opened a consultation into the cyber resilience of power generators in March, after it introduced the cyber security and resilience bill to parliament late last year, with a warning that the UK now faces four nationally significant cyber-attacks every week.Michael Shanks, the energy minister, said in the consultation that the UK “needs to keep pace with the current threat landscape”.An industry source familiar with the post-attack industry briefing confirmed reports, which first appeared in the Sunday Telegraph, that the plant was shut down for about four days in one the most successful cyber-attacks on UK energy infrastructure.“We should use it as a warning rather than wait for an incident,” according to Rafael Narezzi, chief executive of Centrii, an energy cybersecurity specialist.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Across the UK energy system we have small, medium and large generation assets, increasingly connected through digital systems, remote access, third parties and operational technology. This particular incident may not have had consequences for the wider grid, but the next one could be different.”“What concerns me about this incident is not necessarily the size of the power generator that was affected, but how many others may be out there,” Narezzi added. “Attackers do not necessarily select their targets according to how many megawatts they generate. They look for vulnerabilities, trusted access and opportunities.“The UK has thousands of distributed assets increasingly contributing to how our energy system operates. Individually, many may appear insignificant. Collectively, their resilience matters enormously.”A government spokesperson said: “The UK has a highly resilient energy system. We work closely with the energy sector to protect infrastructure and ensure the highest security standards.“We are alive to growing cybersecurity threats, which is why we also committed to reviewing the cyber resilience requirement for the downstream gas and electricity sector and are driving this work forward through parliament,” they added.Ofgem was also contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsEnergy industryCybercrimeHackingCyberwarIranGasnewsShareReuse this content

title: City firms race to prepare for FCA crackdown on bullying and harassment | Financial Conduct Authority | The Guardian
description: Hedge funds, insurers and pension firms will have to report all non-financial wrongdoing as watchdog expands focus
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Hedge funds, insurers and pension firms will have to report all non-financial wrongdoing as watchdog expands focus
Content: From next month companies must report bad behaviour – including racism, sexual harassment and violence – to any possible future employer.Photograph: Jason Alden/Bloomberg/GettyView image in fullscreenFrom next month companies must report bad behaviour – including racism, sexual harassment and violence – to any possible future employer.Photograph: Jason Alden/Bloomberg/GettyFinancial Conduct AuthorityCity firms race to prepare for FCA crackdown on bullying and harassmentRules will require hedge funds, insurers and pension firms to report all non-financial wrongdoingKalyeena MakortoffBanking correspondentThu 27 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 00.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe City’s largest hedge funds, insurers and pension funds are racing to prepare for sweeping rules that will stop nearly 40,000 companies from hiding bullying and harassment cases from the financial watchdog.From the start of next month, theFinancial Conduct Authority(FCA) will expand a crackdown on bad behaviour in the banking industry to a wider group of City investment firms and brokers.Under the rules, companies will be expected to report any serious cases of non-financial misconduct to the regulator. The firms will also be required to pass on reports of bad behaviour – including racism, sexual harassment, violence and intimidation – to a manager’s prospective future employer. It is hoped that the rules will prevent cases of “rolling bad apples”, where rogue bosses move to new firms without facing consequences.The FCA’s expanding crackdown beyond financial crime has so far focused on the banking sector. However, with new rules looming for thousands of additional firms, experts say hedge funds, investment managers, insurers and brokers are racing to train their staff and to wrap up any internal investigations before the rules come into force.“The countdown is now on for regulated firms to be ready for the new rules taking effect in September,” said Jill Lorimer, a partner at the law firm Kingsley Napley, who focuses on financial regulation. “We are aware of firms brushing up their policies and procedures in this area and ensuring training has been thoroughly refreshed and completed.“Firms dealing with allegations against their people now may want to ensure that these processes are wrapped up before the new regime takes effect. The FCA will no doubt be looking for cases in this area to show it is willing to flex its muscles.“The City should take these changes very seriously indeed, as no firm will want to be the target of high-profile regulatory attention,” she added.The new rules will apply to any company bound by the FCA’s senior managers and certification regime, which holds top bosses accountable for wrongdoing.It comes despite a regulatory pushback by City firms and some politicians who complain red tape in the finance industry is holding back investment, jobs and growth in Britain.However, a recent spate of misconduct cases have strengthened the argument that cleaning up the financial sector could create a competitive advantage, particularly for an industry long-criticised for operating a boys’ club culture.That includes the case at Lloyd’s of London, which recently revealed that its former boss John Nealfailed to disclose a “close relationship”with a female colleague. The insurance market operator also said that whistleblower reports dating back to 2023 had been mishandled, in a breach of its own governance rules.A recent court battle against the former Barclays chief executive Jes Staley also appears to have strengthened the FCA’s resolve. Last year, judges upheld a decision by the City watchdog to ban Staley from holding a senior finance industry role in future,after he was found to have misled the regulatorover the nature of his relationship with the convicted child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe FCA is now hoping for similar success ina court battle with the hedge fund boss Crispin Odey. The Brexit-backing investor is trying to overturn a ban on him holding senior roles in the UK finance industry, after the FCA said he deliberately tried to frustrate an investigation into allegations of sexual harassment against him at his hedge fund.Those allegations have been extensive, with a Financial Times investigation reporting allegations of sexual assault and harassment against Odey from 20 women.Odey has denied those allegations. He also said in a witness statement that he had not tried to prevent an investigation, and had been treated unfairly by the FCA.Commenting on the expansion of its non-financial misconduct rules, an FCA spokesperson said: “When bullying, harassment or violence goes unchallenged, it raises wider questions about a firm’s culture, and ultimately harms confidence in financial services.“Our rules and guidance will help industry take a more consistent approach. But the primary responsibility for preventing and dealing with this behaviour remains with firms.”Explore more on these topicsFinancial Conduct AuthorityCorporate governanceFinancial sectorRegulatorsBankingBullyingSexual harassmentnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ain’t nobody better: Chaka Khan’s 20 best songs – ranked!  | Chaka Khan | The Guardian
description: Ahead of the release of her 13th solo album, the fantastically titled Chakzilla, we rank the best of a sublime catalogue of funk, slow jams and tears-on-the-dancefloor disco
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: Ahead of the release of her 13th solo album, the fantastically titled Chakzilla, we rank the best of a sublime catalogue of funk, slow jams and tears-on-the-dancefloor disco
Content: Chaka Khan lets loose at the Royal Albert Hall, 1990.Photograph: Michael Putland/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChaka Khan lets loose at the Royal Albert Hall, 1990.Photograph: Michael Putland/Getty ImagesRankedChaka KhanAin’t nobody better: Chaka Khan’s 20 best songs – ranked!Ahead of the release of her 13th solo album, the fantastically titled Chakzilla, we rank the best of a sublime catalogue of funk, slow jams and tears-on-the-dancefloor discoAlexis PetridisThu 27 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 23.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google20. Love You All My Lifetime (1992)Chaka Khan had harsh words for the “assholes” at her then record company, Warner Bros, who she felt under-promoted 1992’s The Woman I Am, her first album in four years. Listening to Love You All My Lifetime’s cocktail of funk and contemporary R&B, you wonder if she didn’t have a point. There’s no obvious reason why it wasn’t huge hit.19. Hello Happiness (2019)Dissatisfied with her treatment by various record labels and managers, Khan released albums with less frequency in the 21st century – which made 2019’s Hello Happiness (and its title track) feel like a comeback. Producer Switch clearly knew what to do, the songwriting was strong, Khan’s voice still sizzles.18. Any Old Sunday (1981)A deep cut nestled in the middle of her best solo album, What ’Cha Gonna Do for Me, Any Old Sunday is easily overlooked amid the bigger hitters, but offers three-and- a-half minutes of instant sunshine: carefree mid-tempo disco funk – a hint of Chic about the guitars – with a vocal that adds heft to the poppy melody.View image in fullscreenKhan in Hollywood, c1978.Photograph: Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images17. Through the Fire (1984)I Feel for You was the smash, but the biggest streaming song from the album of the same name is, by some distance, Through the Fire. Perhaps because Kanye West sampled it on Through the Wire; perhaps because Khan brings an earthy power to a glossy, but classy, adult contemporary ballad.16. Spoon (1998)The most unfairly overlooked album in Khan’s catalogue is Come 2 My House, a collaboration with Prince that had the misfortune to be released when his commercial standing was in the doldrums, despite the fact that he could still turn out funk as sensual and weird as Spoon. But it’s not on streaming; someone rerelease it!View image in fullscreenRufus and Chaka Khan perform on US TV show Midnight Special, in 1975.Photograph: Gilles Petard/Redferns15. Rufus – At Midnight (My Love Will Lift You Up) (ft Chaka Khan) (1977)The sessions for Ask Rufus were turbulent – drummer Andre Fischer and Khan’s then husband, Richard Holland, had a punch-up in the studio – but you’d never guess from the Chicago band’s fifth album. At Midnight is its solitary dancefloor-focused track, but its understated funk is the perfect setting for Khan’s compelling switches from softness to raunch.14. Rufus – You Got the Love (ft Chaka Khan) (1974)Rufus’s debut album was promising, but unfocussed, not least in the fact that it kept allowing Khan to cede the microphone. But on its follow-up, Rags to Rufus, everything snapped into place. Opener You Got the Love offers thrillingly gritty funk – the perfect counterpoint to lush Philly soul – and Chaka in full effect.13. Rufus & Chaka – Any Love (1979)Khan might have been contractually obliged to keep recording with Rufus, despite her solo success, but 1979’s Masterjam doesn’t feel like an album made under duress. Any Love is tough, disco-paced, subtly orchestrated and entirely fantastic, Khan telling a predatory ladies’ man how pathetic she thinks he is in no uncertain terms.12. Chaka Khan and Rufus – Stay (1978)For all the endless turmoil in their ranks – the band’s lineup seemed to change constantly – Rufus and Khan made music that sounded absolutely effortless. The Khan-co-written big hit from their sixth album, Street Player, is a case in point. It’s an extremely cool breeze, which just makes Khan’s vaulting raw vocal seem all the more potent.View image in fullscreenKhan at the Blue Note club in NYC, 2000.Photograph: David Corio/Getty Images11. Rufus – Once You Get Started (ft Chaka Khan) (1974)Boosted by the platinum-selling success of Rags to Rufus, 1974’s Rufusized was a supremely confident album. With one eye on the burgeoning disco scene, opener Once You Get Started sands down some of its predecessor’s rough edges, but its chattering, synth-laden call to the dancefloor is impossible to resist.10. Rufus & Chaka – Do You Love What You Feel (1979)Fresh from collaborating with Khan on his superb 1978 single Stuff Like That, Quincy Jones brought a dose of production sophistication to Rufus’s Masterjam album. His sleek touch is all over the joy-bringing Do You Love What You Feel, a perfect platform for Khan’s exuberant vocal: “I wanna dance all night!”9. Papillon (AKA Hot Butterfly) (1980)Mid-tempo disco so wistful and sad it could cause an outbreak of ugly crying on the dancefloor: Khan sounds fantastic, especially backed by Luther Vandross. The original version, by writer Gregg Diamond’s Bionic Boogie, with a lead vocal from Vandross himself and a 12in mix by Jim Burgess, might be even better.View image in fullscreenKhan giving it some with a gospel choir.Photograph: Echoes/Redferns8. Fate (1981)These days, Fate is hard to listen to without automatically thinking of the more famous track that sampled it: Stardust’s Music Sounds Better With You. But temporarily banish the thought of French touch house from your brain and luxuriate instead in the original’s glorious update of disco for the 80s. It’s a treat.7. Rufus – Tell Me Something Good (1974)You didn’t need to read the credits to work out that Rufus’s breakthough hit was the handiwork of Stevie Wonder: its reggae-influenced groove and vocodered backing vocals could have stepped straight off Innervisions or Talking Book. But, barely into her 20s, Khan sounds entirely in charge, her voice totally commanding.6. Clouds (1980)A Paradise Garage classic, Ashford and Simpson’s Clouds is a disco monster, shifting from a dramatic opening verse that never quite goes where you expect to a headily euphoric chorus, complete with sound effects and a wild guitar solo. Pub quiz fact: it also features a 16-year-old Whitney Houston on backing vocals.5. I Know You, I Live You (1981)The highlight of What Cha’ Gonna Do for Me, co-penned by producer Arif Mardin and Khan, with the latter presumably responsible for the slightly odd, I-will-manifest-a-relationship lyrics. It is beautifully executed post-disco boogie – check Average White Band drummer Steve Ferrone’s superb rhythm track – with a wonderful melody and a frankly awesome performance from Khan herself.4. Rufus – Sweet Thing (ft Chaka Khan) (1975)A Top 5 US hit, Sweet Thing isthego-to Rufus slow jam, its distinctive guitar riff later borrowed by Nile Rodgers for David Bowie’s hit version of China Girl (you can definitely hear the similarity). Worth a mention is Mary J Blige’s superb, subtly updated 1992 cover, best heard in its scuffed-up remix version.View image in fullscreenKhan performing at the Apollo theatre, Harlem, NYC, 1992.Photograph: David Corio/Redferns3. I Feel for You (1984)Previously recorded by its author, Prince, and by the Pointer Sisters (and subsequently by Mickey Mouse Club-era Britney Spears and Justin Timberlake), Khan’s version is the definitive reading. An ultra-catchy song in any version, her vocal cuts through the none-more-mid-80s production to create a slice of electronic funk that’s genuinely timeless.2. I’m Every Woman (1978)The song for which Khan is most likely to be remembered has been variously rendered as reggae, house music, bossa nova and smooth jazz – sampled umpteen times and covered by Aretha Franklin and Whitney Houston. But look beyond its ubiquity, and marvel at the climactic key changes and Khan’s ferocious vocal performance.1. Rufus and Chaka Khan – Ain’t Nobody (1983)One of the greatest singles of the 80s began life on a contract-fulfilling slate of studio tracks, appended to the live Stompin’ at the Savoy record. Khan had already left Rufus and had to be coaxed back for one last album. But Ain’t Nobody was a synth-funk masterpiece that transcended its unpromising beginnings. An eagle-eared Quincy Jones suggested Michael Jackson might want the song for Thriller, but Rufus and producer David “Hawk” Wolinski rebuffed him. It’s hard to see how even Jackson could have improved on the group’s version, with its impossibly infectious synth line, air of nocturnal anticipation and Khan’s vocal, which really doesn’t sound like the work of a woman heading for the door.Explore more on these topicsChaka KhanRankedSoulfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘We’re going to have to groove!’ The cello, horn and sax prodigies jazzing up the Proms | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The finalists from the BBC young musician of 2016 have teamed up with a Mercury-nominated composer to craft a Proms premiere that’s uplifting, lyrical and goes out with an almighty bang
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: The finalists from the BBC young musician of 2016 have teamed up with a Mercury-nominated composer to craft a Proms premiere that’s uplifting, lyrical and goes out with an almighty bang
Content: The magic number … Ben Goldscheider, Sheku Kanneh-Mason and Jess Gillam outside the Royal Albert Hall, London.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe magic number … Ben Goldscheider, Sheku Kanneh-Mason and Jess Gillam outside the Royal Albert Hall, London.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianClassical music‘We’re going to have to groove!’ The cello, horn and sax prodigies jazzing up the PromsThe finalists from the BBC young musician of 2016 have teamed up with a Mercury-nominated composer to craft a Proms premiere that’s uplifting, lyrical and goes out with an almighty bangErica JealThu 27 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 13.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAcellist, a horn player and a soprano saxophonist walk into the Royal Albert Hall … it could be the setup for an exceptionally nerdy joke, but instead it’s a new triple concerto, with three soloists rather than the usual one, to be premiered on the final weekend of the Proms. The concerto – byGwilym Simcock, the Mercury-shortlisted composer, jazz pianist and horn player who in 2006 was the BBC’s firstNew Generationjazz artist – reunites the three finalists from the2016 BBC young musician of the yearcompetition, hence the unusual lineup. “This is a unique combination of instruments,” says the saxophonistJess Gillam. “I’m fascinated by the colours that we’re going to find. I hope we’ll be able to make a sound where people will think: what instrument is that?”BBC young musician has launched many careers, but 2016 was exceptional: all three finalists have become major names. “It’s not like you win the competition and all these things fall from the sky, but it does give you a bit of public exposure,” says the horn playerBen Goldscheider, the 2016 brass section winner. “Then it’s up to you and the people around you what you make of that.”Talking to a friend in the music business a few years later, Goldscheider realised that it wasn’t only the finalists who had found the competition special that year. So he wrote to Gillam and to the cellistSheku Kanneh-Mason, the overall winner in 2016: “I said we should do something to celebrate, 10 years on, maybe a chamber music tour.” That turned into a full-scale BBC co-commission and a Proms premiere, with performances scheduled in Birmingham, Antwerp and Sofia – and now here they are at the Royal Albert Hall, animatedly comparing notes on what Simcock has written for them.View image in fullscreen‘It’s going to be a really interesting challenge’ … Gillam, Goldscheider and Kanneh-Mason.Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian“It’s a very celebratory piece,” says Goldscheider. “It begins with this incredible, uplifting fanfare. There are a lot of jazz harmony influences. The second movement is extremely lyrical” – it is dedicated to Simcock’s father, who died while Simcock was writing the concerto – “and then the third movement is a ‘traditional’ finale, full of fireworks. There’s a nice big cadenza section where the three of us play together for ages.”Simcock will be at the piano, in among the BBC Symphony Orchestra. He has also included a solo improvisation for himself. Do the soloists have to improvise? No, says Gillam, but “there are these moments of jazz-influenced solos in a kind of trad sense, especially in the saxophone part”. More widely, she says: “We’re going to have to groove! I think, together with the orchestra, we’re going to have so many conversations about where the beat actually is, because I imagine how we feel the beat is going to be very different to if we were playing anything typically classical.”There aren’t many triple concertos in the repertoire; the only one that springs to mindis Beethoven’s. It isn’t often regarded as one of his greatest works. Is that fair? “I strongly disagree – I love it!” says Kanneh-Mason, who recorded it two years ago with two alumni of the 2004 BBC young musician competition, the violinistNicola Benedettiand the pianistBenjamin Grosvenor. “It’s usually put together with three characters who come together just for that project, so the complexity comes from three people plus the conductor plus the orchestra agreeing on something. But that doesn’t mean that the music itself doesn’t work.”‘Music is never fixed in me’ … cellist Sheku Kanneh-Mason on surviving a ‘volcano of racism’Read moreHaving three soloists who know each other – and have chemistry – is a different proposition, as is the triple-soloist format. “There are so many options for different kinds of conversations,” says Kanneh-Mason, referring to how the soloists can interact with each other or with individual orchestral musicians. Gillam adds: “It’s going to be a really interesting challenge: my articulation versus your articulation, a bow versus a reed. How are we going to find the sound that’s in the middle? I think I’m going to learn a lot about how to play the saxophone better. Not just by being inspired hearing you two, but by thinking about the way that the instruments operate.”Apart from this concerto, all three soloists are expanding the repertoire in their own directions. In October, Kanneh-Mason will give the UK premiere of the cello concerto written for him byEdmund Finnis. Goldscheider – who has already commissioned more than 70 horn pieces – has a site-specific project at theHayward Gallery’s Anish Kapoor exhibition, plus four concertos in the pipeline from composers includingAnna ClyneandCheryl Frances-Hoad.As for Gillam, she will be back at the Albert Hall next year for a headline show, premiering five commissions. “When I was a very little girl, I dreamed of playing here. And still, every time I walk into the building, I think there’s something it does so beautifully: it gives you the sense that everyone can feel at ease, but also a sense of occasion. ThePromsis an amazing example of that.”Concerto for Soprano Sax, Horn and Cellois at the Proms in London on 6 September, then touringExplore more on these topicsClassical musicProms 2026Gwilym SimcockPromsSheku Kanneh-MasonRoyal Albert HallFestivalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Idiots review – throwback bro comedy is an entertaining summer seat-filler | Movies | The Guardian
description: Dave Franco and O’Shea Jackson Jr lead a goofy roadtrip comedy that is just sharp enough to keep you strapped in
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: Dave Franco and O’Shea Jackson Jr lead a goofy roadtrip comedy that is just sharp enough to keep you strapped in
Content: O'Shea Jackson Jr and Dave Franco in Idiots.Photograph: Courtesy of IFCView image in fullscreenO'Shea Jackson Jr and Dave Franco in Idiots.Photograph: Courtesy of IFCMoviesReviewIdiots review – throwback bro comedy is an entertaining summer seat-fillerDave Franco and O’Shea Jackson Jr lead a goofy roadtrip comedy that is just sharp enough to keep you strapped inOwen MyersThu 27 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 13.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIdiots is billed as a return to the raunchy bro comedies of the 2000s like Pineapple Express and The Hangover and about halfway through there is a visual gag involving bodily functions that is so revolting, so unexpected and so genius that it comes close to them. For a moment, I was transported back to the mix of delight and disgust I felt upon watching a 90s Farrelly Brothers movie when I was far too young:How is this allowed?The Dog Stars review – Ridley Scott’s lethargic postapocalyptic drama is a misfireRead moreDescribed as an “earnest-dipshits-on-the-road screwball comedy” by director Macon Blair (I Don’t Feel at Home in This World Anymore, The Toxic Avenger), this R-rated indie comedy can’t entirely deliver on that enticingly deranged promise, but it has enough testosterone-fueled transgression to make its runtime breeze by. Dave Franco plays Mark, a doofus with a neck tattoo who expresses affection for his fellow man by slapping them on the jowls. When he is invited to vacate his job at a call center – which he has been coasting through by playing gory video games and sneaking shots of whiskey at his desk – he teams up with Davis (O’Shea Jackson Jr) for a dodgy under-the-table job involving transporting wayward teens to rehab. Their first charge is Sheridan (Mason Thames), a moody influencer who has made a name for himself by playing cruel stunts on members of the public like an off-brand Jake Paul. Like Harold & Kumar before it, the road trip is an obvious but effective ruse for Idiots’s freeform, THC-addled approach to storytelling which finds the trio jumping from country diner to crummy motel to a Slavic granny’s living room as Sheridan attempts to derail his passage to rehab.The film has been over a decade in development but it’s hard to resist the leads’ natural-feeling, infectious chemistry. That’s perhaps due to the fact that they have worked together before in various configurations: Jackson and Franco in the short-lived Quibi TV show The Now; Franco and Thames in 2025 weepie Regretting You. Jackson is particularly memorable as a version of the kind of softhearted hustler he played inIngrid Goes West, and Kiernan Shipka steals most of her scenes as a badass eastern European stripper who teams up with the gang after they partake of her … services. I am of course referring to a lapdance set to a heavy metal soundtrack where Shipka stares at Franco like she is burning a hole into his soul.The cast’s strength lets Macon’s film get away with some winning stupidity, such as when Davis is reprimanded by his pastor, played by Killer Mike, for taking a church group of kids to see a movie with full frontal shots of “dongs”. (The film turns out to be Lars Von Trier’sAntichrist.) Sheridan has some great lines that parody the broken-brained slang of lookmaxxing forums: the character is essentially a Clavicular proxy, sneering “you are beta cuck trash” at one adversary. There’s space for a little more insight about the psychology of internet clout-chasing than Idiots provides: it has far less to say on this than dark comedies like Quentin Dupieux’sThe Piano Accident, or indeed Ingrid Goes West. All the same, it is satisfying to see Sheridan face the consequences of his chosen path to fame as the film turns into an all-out brawl thanks to a run-in with a crustpunk gang led by Peter Dinklage as Karl “Koko” Sandoz and Nicholas Braun playing a wannabe rapper with a face tattoo and gold grills.As the stakes intensify, the film grows increasingly muddled, and Idiots begins to feel like it is going round in circles.
