I am sure that director Blair didn’t intend a micro distributor like IFC to pick this up – surely it was picturing a wider release comparable to Franco’s Neighbors given its relatively big-name actors, puerile humor (complimentary) and the fact that it changed its original title of Shitheads to something more commercially viable – though it should be said, far less memorable. There isn’t much space for laughs at the end as the film struggles to tie up its loose ends. You don’t remember the classic bro comedies for the “I love you man” bear hugs, you remember them for their zany set pieces and whipsmart dialogue set to become immortalized as broski memes for evermore.Idiots is out in the US on 28 August and in the UK on 2 October with an Australian release to be announcedExplore more on these topicsFilmComedy filmsPeter DinklageComedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Colony review – zombies return to the mall with a fresh and frenzied range of scares | Horror films | The Guardian
description: This time the ranks of the undead have acquired a hive mind, making them even more formidable adversaries. Can a maverick academic save the day?
Author: Laurence Phelan
Headline: This time the ranks of the undead have acquired a hive mind, making them even more formidable adversaries. Can a maverick academic save the day?
Content: Unhappy shopper … Jun Ji-hyun in Colony.Photograph: Everett/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenUnhappy shopper … Jun Ji-hyun in Colony.Photograph: Everett/ShutterstockHorror filmsReviewColony review – zombies return to the mall with a fresh and frenzied range of scaresThis time the ranks of the undead have acquired a hive mind, making them even more formidable adversaries. Can a maverick academic save the day?Laurence PhelanThu 27 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 11.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is another frenzied K-zombie action-horror from Yeon Sang-ho,the director ofTrain to BusanandPeninsula. Colony is frontloaded with 10 minutes of sciencey exposition and setup during which a biotech CEO mentions maze-solving slime mould and the pioneering work of the entomologist William Wheeler onthe hive mindsof ant colonies. Then the CEO is injected with a disgruntled former employee’s bright green liquid tech – it always needs to be bright green in such circumstances – and becomes the first victim of a bio-terror attack that traps a small cross-section of South Korean society in a tower block with hordes of fast-moving rabid flesh-munchers. An hour and three quarters of goopy, bloody mayhem ensue.An upscale shopping mall occupies the lower floors of the tower, and it takes some nerve to give your zombie film much the same setting as Dawn of the Dead, the masterwork of the godfather of the genreGeorge A Romero. Thankfully Colony can boast an innovation: these zombies have a hive mind, an emergent collective intelligence that makes them more formidable adversaries than your average braindead stumbler. The moment that one of the infected notices you and screams, as in Invasion of the Bodysnatchers, they all turn and attack.And as they do, spasmodically jerking in unison, all angular limbs and unnatural angles, or while they writhe and entwine as they pile upon and devour their latest victim, the importance of movement choreographer Jeon Young is clearer than ever. A collaborator on each of Sang-ho’s zombie films, but this time working with a company of South Korea’s top contemporary dancers, Young makes many of the action and gore scenes resemble something you might see on stage at Sadler’s Wells. Michael Jackson’s Thriller video might have done it first but Colony does it better, more scarily and on an epic scale.As in every zombie movie, the non-infected must collaborate to have any chance of survival. Thankfully a couple of them were attendees of the biotech conference at the start of the film, so Professor Se-jeong (Jun Ji-hyun) becomes the de facto leader of the group and may just be able to outsmart even these massed ranks of collectively non-stupid zombies. She isn’t set up as the most likable character: honest to a fault, possibly somewhere on the spectrum and without much time for social niceties. But then conformism, bureaucratic groupthink and mindless techno-consumerism are the villains here; the heroes are the outcasts and free-thinkers.Colony is in UK and Irish cinemas from 28 AugustExplore more on these topicsHorror filmsSouth KoreaZombiesAction and adventure filmsScience fiction and fantasy filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Billy Strings: So Much for Goodbyes review – staggering, stirring songs of grief draw the blues out of bluegrass | Music | The Guardian
description: The crossover star’s introspective sixth album is full of memories of his mother, who died in 2025, bringing his dextrous guitar to songs rooted in tradition and yearning
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: The crossover star’s introspective sixth album is full of memories of his mother, who died in 2025, bringing his dextrous guitar to songs rooted in tradition and yearning
Content: Astonishingly dextrous … Billy Strings.Photograph: Dana TrippeView image in fullscreenAstonishingly dextrous … Billy Strings.Photograph: Dana TrippeAlexis Petridis's album of the weekMusicReviewBilly Strings: So Much for Goodbyes review – staggering, stirring songs of grief draw the blues out of bluegrass(Reprise)The crossover star’s introspective sixth album is full of memories of his mother, who died in 2025, bringing his dextrous guitar to songs rooted in tradition and yearningAlexis PetridisThu 27 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 12.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the face of it, 2025 was a landmark year for Billy Strings. His fifth album,Highway Prayers, won him his third Grammy. The first bluegrass album in more than 22 years to debut at the top of the US album sales chart, it confirmed him as the genre’s biggest crossover star in decades. He was feted by everyone from Bob Dylan to Post Malone to Willie Nelson, the latter describing him as “the John Coltrane of bluegrass”, a pretty impressive soubriquet in anyone’s book. As theNew York Times noted, he was now capable of filling the arena-sized venues that his idols – Doc Watson, Clarence White, Tony Rice, Béla Fleck – could never have dreamed of performing in, packing them out with an audience that look less like traditional bluegrass aficionados than Deadheads: a vast, mobile, hippy-ish army that call themselves Goats. They’re presumably drawn by the ease with which Strings occupies the no man’s land between country and expansive, psychedelically informed improvisation, his willingness to put acoustic guitar through umpteen effects pedals and stretch out songs for 20 minutes on stage.View image in fullscreenBilly Strings: So Much for Goodbyes album coverIt’s a side of Strings’ music that’s only hinted at on Highway Prayers’ follow-up: as Burn the Other End and Lucid Daydream draw to an end, they briefly unravel into a kind of abstraction that you can imagine as a jumping-off point for heady, out-there exploration live. But So Much for Goodbyes is an album more concerned with introspection, and understandably so. In the midst of 2025’s successes, Strings’ mother died of an overdose. His chaotic upbringing is a matter of record. His father died of a heroin overdose when he was two, both his mother and his stepfather were addicted to meth and he left home at 14 on the grounds that “there was no food in the house and my parents were strung out”. But Strings said he had “no idea” she had relapsed, and her death seeps into every corner of the album: its title and cover art – based on a collage his mother was working on the night she died; the concluding instrumental that bears her name, Debra’s Waltz; the songs that, on the surface, appear to have nothing to do with her passing.Under normal circumstances, Lay Me Down might be read as an exercise in standard-issue granite-faced country posturing – “leave no roses on my headstone / leave no footprints in the clay / lay me down on the hillside / turn away your face” – but in context, it feels more like a song about generational trauma, a plea for a family’s pain to be passed down no further. Similarly, opener I’m One of Those warps another country trope – the rootless ramblin’ man wont to leave ladies crying when he skips town in the dead of night – into something darker: he’s attempted to return home, but found nothing but distress, and the song exists to “warn the ghost that wandered back across this road”.Billy Strings: Burn the Other End – videoInitially at least, this seems to be how the album deals with its overriding theme, via glancing references and lyrics open to interpretation, sprinkled through songs that offer a striking resume of Strings’ skills. His guitar picking is every bit asastonishingly dextrous as his tie-dyed devoteesclaim; his equally impressive backing quartet are particularly talented at working up a ferociously propulsive head of steam, given that their ranks don’t include a drummer. Strings is equally capable of writing songs so perfectly rooted in tradition that you might be forgiven for assuming Light the Way or Lay Me Down were covers dating back to the 1940s or 50s, and of throwing his listeners a curveball that indicates the breadth of his musical tastes: if his penchant for jam band improv is only lightly sketched here, his love of heavy metal is underlined by the way he skilfully works a devil’s horn-provoking riff into the ominous atmosphere of Burn the Other End, while a devotion to heartlands rock is reflected in the Springsteen-ish narrative of Mill Town Flood.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘I was running away from poverty’: the remarkable rise of bluegrass virtuoso Billy StringsRead moreBut long after you feel as if you’ve settled into the album, it sharply detours. There is nothing allusive or open to interpretation about Still I Crash: the guitar melody is stunning, but it’s starkly recorded; the lyrical wail of confusion and despair is addressed directly to his mother. Appearing when it does, it effectively punches the listener in the stomach and casts a long shadow over the remaining tracks, lending a darker hue to I Wish I Wanted To’s saga of indolence and the biblical references in Wrestling an Angel. The album ends on a distinctly overcast note that the beautiful ensemble playing on Debra’s Waltz doesn’t entirely lift. What does cut through the gloom is the lingering thought of how rich and powerful the album you’ve just heard is.This week Alexis listened toCleo Sol – Force of LoveThere’s no dip in the high standards set by Cleo Sol’s previous work on her fifth album, Gentlewoman: Force of Love gently remodels her exquisite soul sound via a hint of dancehall in the rhythm.Explore more on these topicsMusicAlexis Petridis's album of the weekCountryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout audiobook review – brilliant portrait of an existential crisis | Books | The Guardian
description: A teacher’s private anxieties are subtly combined with political events in this Booker-listed tale set in coastal Massachusetts
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: A teacher’s private anxieties are subtly combined with political events in this Booker-listed tale set in coastal Massachusetts
Content: Dread and ennui … Elizabeth Strout.Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDread and ennui … Elizabeth Strout.Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty ImagesAudiobook of the weekBooksReviewThe Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout audiobook review – brilliant portrait of an existential crisisA teacher’s private anxieties are subtly combined with political events in this Booker-listed tale set in coastal MassachusettsFiona SturgesThu 27 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 10.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArtie Dam is a much-loved history teacher from coastal Massachusetts famed for his white socks and old sneakers and who sees a growing hopelessness in his young students. Not only are they dispirited by the state of the world, but they also believe they won’t be able to achieve their professional dreams. Their feelings of dread and ennui are shared by Artie who is aghast at the imminent re-election of a cruel and divisive leader (who remains nameless).Artie is also lonely in the company of his wife, Evie, a therapist who comes from a wealthy family and is dismissive of her “soft” spouse. Artie realises he doesn’t truly know Evie, and she doesn’t care to know him. He traces their loss of connection to their son Rob’s car accident a decade ago in which Rob survived but his girlfriend Heather was killed. Such is Artie’s desolation that he contemplates suicide, if only he can find a way of doing it discreetly. But something happens while he is sailing in his boat that changes his mind. Later, a revelation from his son further shifts his perspective on his relationships.The Things We Never Say is the latest book from Elizabeth Strout which has been longlisted for this year’s Booker prize and which subtly binds together political events and private anxiety to portray a decent man in existential crisis. The reader is the actor Robert Petkoff who conveys Artie’s innate kindness and quiet despair. With that despair comes a realisation that “every single person [holds] within themselves a vast, unknowable universe”.Available via Penguin Audio, 6hr 35minFurther listeningLady Gregory’s ToothbrushColm Tóibín, Picador, 3hr 3minDerbhle Crotty reads the Brooklyn author’s 2003 essay on Augusta Gregory, the Irish playwright and folk historian who famously observed how ownership of a toothbrush separated the gentry from the peasant classes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: Song & Dance album review – Jacques Forestier’s impressive debut has persuasive rhythmic poise | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The Canadian violinist’s album definitely does what it says on the tin: from Bartók to Ernst, there is a quiet and beguiling eloquence to his playing
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: The Canadian violinist’s album definitely does what it says on the tin: from Bartók to Ernst, there is a quiet and beguiling eloquence to his playing
Content: Promising … Jacques Forestier.Photograph: Ryan ParkerView image in fullscreenPromising … Jacques Forestier.Photograph: Ryan ParkerClassical musicReviewSong & Dance album review – Jacques Forestier’s impressive debut has persuasive rhythmic poiseJacques Forestier/Boris Kusnezow(Warner Classics)The Canadian violinist’s album definitely does what it says on the tin: from Bartók to Ernst, there is a quiet and beguiling eloquence to his playingErica JealThu 27 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 11.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePerhaps the most promising thing about this impressive debut album fromJacques Forestier, the young Canadian violinist who tied in first place at the 2024 Joseph Joachim Competition, is the way it lives up to its title.View image in fullscreenJacques Forestier and Boris Kusnezow: Song & Dance album cover.Photograph: Warner ClassicsThere’s a swing to the way he and the pianistBoris Kusnezowplay Bartók’s six Romanian Folk Dances that extends even into the quiet movements, which sound distant and beguiling. Wieniawski’s Polonaise de Concert comes across as a dance rather than just a flashy showpiece. Bach’s D minor Sarabande is framed by movements from Ysaÿe’s solo Sonatas. All have persuasive rhythmic poise.As for the songs, he shapes long-breathed lines in three numbers from Gershwin’s Porgy and Bess – arranged by Jascha Heifetz, seemingly less as showpieces, more because Heifetz wished he were able to sing them himself. Brahms reused his own song melodies in his Sonata No 1; there’s the occasional corner that is arbitrarily turned as played by Forestier, but otherwise it’s a quietly eloquent, lyrical performance. Perhaps the most impressive track is for Forestier alone: Heinrich Ernst’s Grand Caprice, basically an arrangement of Schubert’s song Erlkönig. Forestier, keeping the interweaving threads untangled and the pace urgent, voices its drama beautifully.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com. title: Met Orchestra/Nézet-Séguin review – messy bonbons and a hero’s triumph in a classy all-Strauss lineup | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: Yannick Nézet-Séguin polished up the Rosenkavalier suite then gave a exceptional reading of the composer’s self-congratulatory tone poem, while Elza van den Heever delivered a visceral account of Salome’s final scene
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Yannick Nézet-Séguin polished up the Rosenkavalier suite then gave a exceptional reading of the composer’s self-congratulatory tone poem, while Elza van den Heever delivered a visceral account of Salome’s final scene
Content: A magisterial fury in fuchsia … soprano Elza van den Heever with the Met Orchestra conducted by Yannick Nézet-Séguin.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouView image in fullscreenA magisterial fury in fuchsia … soprano Elza van den Heever with the Met Orchestra conducted by Yannick Nézet-Séguin.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouProms 2026ReviewMet Orchestra/Nézet-Séguin review – messy bonbons and a hero’s triumph in a classy all-Strauss lineupRoyal Albert Hall, LondonYannick Nézet-Séguin polished up the Rosenkavalier suite then gave an exceptional reading of the composer’s self-congratulatory tone poem, while Elza van den Heever delivered a visceral account of Salome’s final sceneClive PagetThu 27 Aug 2026 06.42 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 06.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArtistically ambitious and with an ego the size of a small planet,Richard Strausswas rarely backwards in coming forwards. When quizzed about the wisdom of depicting his 34-year-old self in music he brushed the matter aside, declaring himself no less interesting than Napoleon. The work in question, the self-congratulatory yet brilliantly conceived tone poem Ein Heldenleben, formed the second half of this all-Strauss programme. Before that, the Met Orchestra, here making their Proms debut, stayed on home turf with music from the operas.The Rosenkavalier suite, compiled by hand unknown, is frankly a mess, lurching from one bonbon to the next with never a thought for musical logic (the overblown ending is truly crass). Yannick Nézet-Séguin did a decent job of papering over the cracks, letting the music unfold naturally rather than forcing its ham-fisted transitions. The love scenes were the highlight here, the orchestra spacious and shapely. If the heart didn’t leap as it might, it was likely due to the absence of the human voice.South African soprano Elza van den Heever righted the balance. A magisterial fury in fuchsia, she delivered a visceral account of the final scene from Salome, running the gamut from implacable vengeance to unhinged lust. The voice was refulgent, her diction impressive, even if Nézet-Séguin allowed the orchestra to overwhelm her here and there.Ein Heldenleben, 50 minutes of one man’s triumph over artistic adversity, is symphonic music on a grand scale and the kind of late-romantic meat-and-potatoes Nézet-Séguin cut his teeth on before he took the opera job in New York. This was an exceptional reading, expansive yet resolute and with a welcome determination to embrace the score’s more tender moments. Persnickety woodwind and a duo of baleful tubas conjured up the composer’s carping critics while Benjamin Bowman’s sinuous solo violin invoked the hero’s capricious companion. Martial offstage brass and a tour de force orchestral battle preceded a glowing account of the hero’s works of peace and a perfectly judged ending.The playful exchange surrounding Van den Heever’s memory lapse in an otherwise radiant account of Strauss’s Zueignung only added to the impression of an undeniably class act.Available onBBC Sounds until 12 October. title: Kolkhoz by Emmanuel Carrère review – intricate portrait of an elite French family | Autobiography and memoir | The Guardian
description: The author of The Adversary and Yoga unearths a history that includes the Nazis, Russia, and the Académie Française
Author: Blake Morrison
Headline: The author of The Adversary and Yoga unearths a history that includes the Nazis, Russia, and the Académie Française
Content: Hélène Carrère d’Encausse in 1983.Photograph: Micheline PELLETIER/Gamma-Rapho/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHélène Carrère d’Encausse in 1983.Photograph: Micheline PELLETIER/Gamma-Rapho/Getty ImagesBook of the dayAutobiography and memoirReviewKolkhoz by Emmanuel Carrère review – intricate portrait of an elite French familyThe author of The Adversary and Yoga unearths a history that includes the Nazis, Russia, and the Académie FrançaiseBlake MorrisonThu 27 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 09.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Emmanuel Carrère’s mother, Hélène, died in 2023, at the age of 94, President Macron spoke at her memorial. She had been “perpetual secretary” of the Académie Française, in effect its head, and 200 people gathered at Les Invalides in Paris to pay tribute. Emmanuel’s father, Louis, was there too, in a wheelchair, only half aware of what was going on. This 400-page memoir, translated into English by John Lambert, is a homage to both parents and the unlikely history that brought them together. It’s also an act of reparation towards Hélène, whom Emmanuel worshipped as a child but upset as an adult by publishing a book that she’d forbidden him to write.Hélène grew up in stateless poverty in Paris, the daughter of Georges Zourabichvili, whose parents had fled Georgia in 1921, and Nathalie von Pelken, who as a child had six governesses, one for each day excluding Sunday. Though “the magical world of the fallen Russian aristocracy” was the backdrop, conditions were tough, not least after Georges disappeared in 1944, murdered by partisans for alleged Nazi collaboration. Hélène was 15 at the time and unsuccessfully tried to hide the truth about George’s death from her younger brother, Nicolas.double quotation markCarrère’s mother wouldn’t have slept well if she’d known this book was comingShe was determined and highly ambitious. What she couldn’t excel at, she didn’t do. For a time she considered an acting career but found her metier as a Russian historian. It helped that she was charming and attractive, so much so that an Afghan pilot, on a flight from Tashkent to Paris via Tehran, first invited her to the cockpit, then landed the plane in Kabul in order to kidnap her. He kept her there for four days before a couple of US aid workers sneaked her away on a private plane.By then she was married to Louis, who worked for an insurance company and was often away on business trips. At home Hélène ruled the roost and let Emmanuel and his two sisters sleep around her bed, a setup she called “kolkhoz”, the name for collective farms in the USSR. There was no television or radio; the children were made to read. Her son’s reading was strenuous: from Jules Verne and Alexander Dumas, he moved on to Dostoevsky at 13. His mother brought out his softer side – whenever she went away he’d write long letters saying how “horribly” he missed her.He felt abandoned when she began receiving phone calls from a “Mr N” and had long furtive conversations with him. No less distraught, her husband threatened to kill himself. Hélène ended the affair to spare Louis but he “lost her love for ever” and moved from the marriage bed to a tiny room. Worse, she more or less stopped speaking to him, a habit that lasted to the end. When diagnosed with cancer and admitted to a palliative care home, she merely told him she’d be away at a conference.The mother-son relationship remained close until Emmanuel published A Russian Novel, which explored the story of her father, Georges, which she had asked him not to tell (“It’s my story, not yours. Leave him where he is”). Publication was “a family cataclysm”; she blamed her brother Nicolas for helping with it. Though she did eventually forgive Emmanuel, her loyalty to Russia divided them. A week before the invasion of Ukraine she described Putin as “a rational man”, committed to good relations with Europe. Dismayed, Emmanuel visited Georgia, where his cousin Salome Zourabichvili had become president. A trip to Ukraine followed. He remains violently opposed to Putin.What’s attractive about the book is its intimacy. If Hélène is a grand dame, her son enjoys the role of bon vivant, disclosing his drinking bouts, journalistic forays, failed relationships and blissful third marriage as well as his bipolar disorder. He’d like to write with “filial piety” and both his father’s genealogical research and his uncle Nicolas’s memoirs help him fill out the family story. But he also lets us in on his uncertainties as he proceeds: “what I’m hoping for is the unhoped for. We’ll see.”His mother loved order and completeness. And at her memorial Macron praised her for finishing the latest Académie dictionary – a 40-year task – with the wordzygomatique(an anatomical term). In reality, as she frustratedly told her son, they’d only reached zoo, with 62 more words to come, the last of them zz, onomatopoeia for sleep. She wouldn’t have slept well if she’d known this book was coming, but it’s an epic achievement and an honest, heartfelt account.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories.
