title: Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy review – picture-postcard retelling of haunting Minoan myth | Games | The Guardian
description: The medieval franchise is transplanted to Crete, conjuring action-adventure magic from familiar ingredients
Author: Lewis Gordon
Headline: The medieval franchise is transplanted to Crete, conjuring action-adventure magic from familiar ingredients
Content: A swashbuckling hero … Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy.Illustration: Asobo StudioView image in fullscreenA swashbuckling hero … Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy.Illustration: Asobo StudioGamesReviewResonance: A Plague Tale Legacy review – picture-postcard retelling of haunting Minoan mythPlayStation 5, Xbox Series S/X, PC; Asobo StudioThe medieval franchise is transplanted to Crete, conjuring action-adventure magic from familiar ingredientsLewis GordonThu 27 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 12.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe path in Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy is a familiar one. Amid ancient ruins and sun-dappled gorges, a young woman, Sophia, dutifully treads the same footsteps as a Minoan warrior from millennia ago, one with whom she seems to share a visionary connection. The “resonance” between these two characters is made clear by their echoing actions – a crank pushed in the bronze age that still works in the medieval present, for example. Through these spliced timelines, it becomes clear that Sophia, compelled by her supernatural gift, possesses little agency. Destiny beckons her forwards.This is a smart meta concept for a game that, at its most basic level, boils down to keeping your left thumb planted firmly on the analogue stick, always pushing Sophia onwards in linear fashion. You jostle her through ornate corridors rendered as higgledy-piggledy pirate camps and cobbled Venetian streets. For the greater part of the game, you propel her through the Minoan remains of Crete, which harbour a dark and terrible secret. It is classic third-person action-adventure fare, building on the template laid down by the likes ofTomb Raiderand then refined and complicated by titles such asThe Last of Us. Little, from an interactive perspective, surprises: you dash, vault and swing between teetering podiums, squeeze through tiny gaps in rock and crouch behind conveniently placed walls to avoid enemies.View image in fullscreenImmersed in the bronze age … Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy.Illustration: Asobo StudioYet the Bordeaux-based studio Asobo conjures magic from the familiar. Sophia, a supporting character from the second game in the A Plague Tale series, carries this swashbuckling adventure with aplomb. She is spiky and confident, the daughter of a wealthy mother and a smuggler father. The game starts with her as a young child, recently escaped from abuse in a nunnery, before cutting to roughly a decade in the future. Now in her 20s, Sophia is a capable, cut-throat fighter, on the hunt for the treasure that lurks deep inside the extensive cave network of Crete – the home, according to Greek mythology, of the bull-headed Minotaur.In tone, Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy is a long way off the dour machismo ofChristopher Nolan’s recent Odyssey adaptation. Rather than brooding, greyscale landscapes, Asobo delivers a Crete that, at least initially, seems lifted directly from holiday brochures: soft sandstone cliffs, swallows dancing in the evening light, vivid green vegetation tangling around crumbling statues. Some of the most striking sights arrive via the Minoan frescoes: their deep oranges and eye-popping yellows have not faded but remain ebulliently bright.View image in fullscreenWorthy of a holiday brochure … Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy.Illustration: Asobo StudioIt is always a treat when the game pivots to this classical time period, briefly putting us in control of the warrior and letting us soak up the vibrant atmosphere through their eyes: crowds baying for blood; stands draped in textile finery; magenta-coloured flowers strewn across mosaic floors.A Plague Tale: Requiem review – rat-infested sequel raises stakes and spectacleRead moreBut, slowly, the world and story darken, though Asobo’s fascination with light – a means of warding off hordes of rats in prior A Plague Tale games – remains. Sophia carries a sphere that can reflect and refract light, crucial for solving environmental puzzles that often involve rotating supersized lenses to redirect beams. But these puzzles, like the platforming, are somewhat rudimentary, causing you to only briefly pause and ponder without ever yielding oh-so-satisfying “aha” moments. Rarely is there more than one solution or the opportunity to get creative: rather, you must follow the logic clearly signposted by the designers.Although stealth is sometimes an option, often our champion must engage in hand-to-hand combat. The most memorable fights occur towards the game’s conclusion, in which swirling light causes calcified, zombie-like figures to disintegrate into dust, Sophia teeing up their demise with lethal slashes of her sword. These are some of the most dynamic melee encounters in the game’s roughly 12-hour run time: a balletic, show-stopping dance of light and movement.Sophia may traipse a path similar to that of countless treasure-hunting, action-adventure video game classics – but for all the overfamiliar design choices, there is enough verve in the beguiling presentation and lively, compellingly drawn characters to elevate this beyond mere retread. Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy succeeds, in large part, because of Sophia, a heroine who confronts history head on, before finally breaking free of it in apocalyptically spectacular style.Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy is released 27 AugustExplore more on these topicsGamesPCXbox series S/XAction gamesAdventure gamesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Trainwatch – alone with your thoughts on a railway line to nowhere | Games | The Guardian
description: The flat routines of a dead end railway job screen out an approaching menace in a quietly intriguing game from the indie developer of Cat Lady and Lorelai
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: The flat routines of a dead end railway job screen out an approaching menace in a quietly intriguing game from the indie developer of Cat Lady and Lorelai
Content: Crossing to bear … Trainwatch.Photograph: Harvester GamesView image in fullscreenCrossing to bear … Trainwatch.Photograph: Harvester GamesSummer games previewsGamesTrainwatch – alone with your thoughts on a railway line to nowhereThe flat routines of a dead end railway job screen out an approaching menace in a quietly intriguing game from the indie developer of  Cat Lady and LorelaiKeith StuartThu 27 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 13.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLonely jobs have provided excellent material for independent video games over the years. FromPapers, PleasetoFirewatchtoThe Stanley Parable, players have been happy to spend hours dwelling in depressing cubicles or rural hideaways, usually because there is an intriguingly hidden point to it all.In Trainwatch, a character named Troy has taken a seemingly godforsaken job as a railway worker in an unnamed desolate backwater. His main task over the course of a single month is to manage a level crossing, closing the gate whenever a train comes, while also carrying out daily chores such as cooking and washing. It sounds serene, but Troy is also running away from something. The other stipulations are that he stays sober and calls his wife every night. And there is something lurking in the fog at the edges of the fields – one day he must face it.View image in fullscreenDesolate … Trainwatch.Photograph: Harvester GamesTrainwatch is the sixth game from solo developer Remigiusz “Rem” Michalski (AKA Harvester Games), and was inspired by a childhood memory. “We used to live near the railway tracks,” he says. “Every night, I’d hear that thundering hum of trains in the distance and see their lights moving slowly in the darkness outside my window. I found that oddly comforting. The world seemed dead and empty, and that train rolling through the night was the only sign of life happening out there.”Michalski describes the game as a time-management mystery adventure, which sounds cosy, but the game’s muted colours and uneasy sense of dread suggest otherwise. Previous games, such as Cat Lady and Lorelai, have explored mental anguish and isolation, and it seems that Trainwatch will continue this theme. “I think most of us are lonely, guilty, or isolated in one way or another,” says Michalski. “We all have our demons living deep inside, and we rarely show them to anyone. Most of the time we don’t even want to acknowledge their existence ourselves.”While you’re running the signal room and carrying out daily tasks of self-care, there are also chances to explore nearby buildings and meet the inhabitants of this strange wasteland, some of whom you’ll have the chance to help. So is there a redemptive arc beneath the rather bleak overtones of Trainwatch? Michalski suggests there is: “It’s a game about trying to dig ourselves out of a hole, re-evaluating what our priorities are, fixing our lives while having a million things on our shoulders all at the same time. And while it touches on many difficult topics, it does so with a sprinkle of dark humour. ”When asked if there were movies or novels that inspired the game’s look, setting and themes, Michalski makes his own personal discovery. “Now that I think about it … I guess being an indie game developer is a little like being a Gatekeeper in Trainwatch. Sure, there’s my wife, pottering about in the flat, the kids getting home from school, talking with excitement … but I spend most of my time here, in my little studio, alone, pushing buttons. So really, the main influence for Trainwatch comes from my secluded life in a tiny Polish town. Thanks for making me realise that!”Trainwatch is coming toPCin 2027Explore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsPCfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Freddie Meredith: Need a Light? review – one hilarious hour of cringe | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Watching a man labouring to strike up conversations in the smoking area of a nightclub proves not just funny but also touching and uplifting
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: Watching a man labouring to strike up conversations in the smoking area of a nightclub proves not just funny but also touching and uplifting
Content: A beta man than you … Freddie Meredith: Need a Light?Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA beta man than you … Freddie Meredith: Need a Light?Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewFreddie Meredith: Need a Light? review – one hilarious hour of cringePleasance Courtyard, EdinburghWatching a man labouring to strike up conversations in the smoking area of a nightclub proves not just funny but also touching and upliftingBrian LoganThu 27 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEver pretended to use your phone to avoid the shame of being Norman No-Mates at a party? Freddie Meredith’s new show is a 60-minute channelling of that experience, an hour-long cringe at a man labouring to strike up conversations in the smoking area of a nightclub.Meredith, a familiar face to viewers of Big Boys, Such Brave Girls and other TV series, has alighted on a familiar social type here, albeit one rarely so brilliantly depicted. His alter ego is a shy and insecure beta male desperately trying to look – well, alpha is out of his reach, but even basic social functioning would be an upgrade.He sounds like a dork, right? And so he is, in his wannabe hip dad-wear, with his fantasies about being in the audience on Top Gear and his furtive Amazon purchasing of “cool T-shirts for men”. But beyond the David Brent stylings is someone much more sympathetic, for whom we’re rooting by the show’s uplifting end.View image in fullscreenDrab tenderness … Freddie Meredith.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianMeredith performs the hour, all awkward grooviness, nervous laughter and duff small talk with the crowd (starring as his fellow clubbers), with a face that looks perpetually like it could burst into tears. But there’s something heroic in the effort. Social outcast he may be, but he’s doing his best to learn the route – all those codes and behaviours that come so easily to other people – back in.Kemah Bob: Love Child review – Miss Fortunate’s follow-up is a superbly playful origin storyRead more“Planning any house parties?” to one other raver, doesn’t quite cut it – but it prompts a wonderfully needy monologue on Meredith’s part, pledging to be the best house guest imaginable. “Can you come to the toilet with me?” Again, it’s not quite how things are done. But it leads to a choice routine involving urinals, men’s fragrances and (in due course) a Lady Gaga karaoke duet engineered to ensnare Meredith a new chum.Occasionally, there are sketches that stretch the conceit almost to breaking point. Always, we indulge them – because we’re so seduced by the drab tenderness with which Meredith constructs his world, a round-the-back-of-the-building refuge where a loner fails and fails again to learn social skills – and makes devoted friends of his audience while doing so.AtPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Owl at Home review – this Edinburgh fringe hoot is a wise choice for children | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Songs, physical comedy and clever design come together in Theatr Iolo’s adaptation of Arnold Lobel’s offbeat story, aimed at over-fives
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Songs, physical comedy and clever design come together in Theatr Iolo’s adaptation of Arnold Lobel’s offbeat story, aimed at over-fives
Content: A creature of habit … George Williams in Owl at Home.Photograph: Gilded BalloonView image in fullscreenA creature of habit … George Williams in Owl at Home.Photograph: Gilded BalloonEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewOwl at Home review – this Edinburgh fringe hoot is a wise choice for childrenGilded Balloon Teviot, EdinburghSongs, physical comedy and clever design come together in Theatr Iolo’s adaptation of Arnold Lobel’s offbeat story, aimed at over-fivesChris WiegandThu 27 Aug 2026 10.53 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 10.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArnold Lobel was a writer with a keen sense of the seasons.Frog and Toad Are Friends, one of my favourite books since childhood, has a wonderful story where the excitable Frog wakes up his grumpy friend Toad and tricks him into enjoying the dawn of spring with him. Those stories celebrate togetherness but Lobel’s collection Owl at Home is about aloneness and being at one with your surroundings – even when the arrival of winter brings a snowstorm blowing through your roost.With his hair gelled into tufts, George Williams plays Owl in this adaptation by Rina Vergano andTheatr Iolo, directed by Lee Lyford. We find Williams dozing in an armchair on Anisha Fields’ accomplished set, which retains the cosy essence of Lobel’s illustrations but is less twee. The roost functions as an equally eccentric character in itself, filled with contraptions, dark wooden furniture and a periscope to nervously keep an eye on the world outside.View image in fullscreenCosy essence of the original illustrations … Owl at Home, designed by Anisha Fields.Photograph: Kirsten McternanThe collection’s stories are supplemented with songs and physical comedy including a tail feather-shaking exercise routine and a tussle with a dust buster. There are many delightful details: Owl sleeps with an eye mask, over his horn-rimmed glasses, and swivels it around to become a sporty headband. Not bothered to chase his prey, he catches chocolate mice in traps and hangs them out to ripen; Williams is alarmingly good at producing the postprandial pellet. Children will recognise the trick of turning a half-eaten pancake into a smile or a crescent moon.Robot helpers and flying houses: Edinburgh fringe tips for familiesRead moreAimed at over-fives, the production is as offbeat and sweet as the book, the new material never jarring amid Lobel’s stories of the wind’s visit, the strange bumps in the blanket and filling a kettle with tears. The show captures his owlish wisdom about opening up to the world around you and the perils of being a creature of habit – young or old, feathered or not.AtGilded Balloon Teviot, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreChildren's theatreEdinburgh festivalChildren's books: 7 and underChildren and teenagersreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Penelope review – Odysseus’s other half sings of her own twists and turns | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Grace McLean brings vocal and emotional range in the central role of Alex Bechtel’s Homeric song cycle
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Grace McLean brings vocal and emotional range in the central role of Alex Bechtel’s Homeric song cycle
Content: Defiant and elegant … Grace McLean in Penelope.Photograph: PRView image in fullscreenDefiant and elegant … Grace McLean in Penelope.Photograph: PREdinburgh festival 2026ReviewPenelope review – Odysseus’s other half sings of her own twists and turnsUnderbelly, Cowgate, EdinburghGrace McLean brings vocal and emotional range in the central role of Alex Bechtel’s Homeric song cycleMark FisherThu 27 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 02.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShe is the one played by Anne Hathaway in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, the central figure in Margaret Atwood’sThe Penelopiadand the inspiration behind a 2010 play byEnda Walsh. And here she is again, this time alone with her thoughts, a longsuffering woman in white, in a seductive song cycle by Alex Bechtel.Penelope is played by Broadway actor Grace McLean who brings both vocal and emotional range to the part. Drily witty, defiant and elegant, she is the wife of Odysseus, doggedly hanging on for her husband’s return long after the end of the Trojan war. Much to her annoyance – and occasional temptation – a load of suitors are camping out in her house, ready to take his place.A dramatic challenge presents itself here: there can be little action with a character whose principal function is to wait. But, with a book credited to Bechtel, McLean and director Eva Steinmetz, things keep ticking along for most of the hour-long production for Rigor + Ruckus. Only a reflective song towards the end, in which Penelope looks back to her early romance with Odysseus, seems to tread water.Courtney Büchner: One of the Girls review – all aboard for a rollercoaster relationshipRead moreFor the most part, it is a lively retelling of Homer’s tale, including Penelope’s scheme to string along the suitors by unstitching her knitting every night, although skipping over the archery contest. Bechtel’s songs nod to soul, blues and show tunes, his piano arrangements ranging from the strident to the pretty and filled out by Anna MacLean’s colourful cello patterns and Jonnie Grant’s rolling drums.“This is why people don’t follow politics,” quips McLean, having explained the ins and outs of the Trojan war. The sassy facade slips as she rages at all the waiting, before revealing a tender side in a song of prayer and sacrifice. It is a striking performance not only of vocal control but also physical presence.AtUnderbelly, Cowgate, Edinburgh, until 30 August. Then atUnderbelly Boulevard Soho, London, on 4 September.All our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreHomerEdinburgh festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: A Slow Fire review – hope flickers in Simon Stephens’ postapocalyptic bunker drama | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Two men shelter from catastrophe in this Beckettian tale of memory, companionship and survival, which is intelligently performed but light on tension
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Two men shelter from catastrophe in this Beckettian tale of memory, companionship and survival, which is intelligently performed but light on tension
Content: Hope in the dark … Ross Gaynor (left) and Ian Toner in A Slow Fire at Jermyn Street theatre, London.Photograph: Alex BrennerView image in fullscreenHope in the dark … Ross Gaynor (left) and Ian Toner in A Slow Fire at Jermyn Street theatre, London.Photograph: Alex BrennerTheatreReviewA Slow Fire review – hope flickers in Simon Stephens’ postapocalyptic bunker dramaJermyn Street theatre, LondonTwo men shelter from catastrophe in this Beckettian tale of memory, companionship and survival, which is intelligently performed but light on tensionArifa AkbarThu 27 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 06.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJermyn Street’s basement theatre provides the perfect space for Simon Stephens’ postapocalyptic play about two men hiding in a bunker after an unnamed global catastrophe. Several of Beckett’s plays have been performed on this stage in recent years and these characters are distinctly Beckettian. Ashton (Ross Gaynor) and Reece (Ian Toner) may be the last men on Earth; they spend their time rehearsing the same stories, sometimes singing and, ultimately, waiting. But for what?The difference between Beckett’s men and Stephens’ is the emphasis of hope over despair, although the two converge at times. Ashton and Reece play memory games, it seems, enacting scenes from their former lives. These are filled with optimism and promise: a declaration of love, a moment between father and son, the announcement of a pregnancy. One man is a porter, the other a professor. In ordinary life, they might have little in common but here they become receptacles for each other’s most precious memories.There is no sight of the post-diluvial landscape. Instead, there is a mattress, a camping stove and a record player, the high winds and ominous churn of machinery suggesting the threats above ground (great sound design). Occasional reports come from the outside: they worry about the theft of a nearby track. Does it mean they are literally coming to the end of the road?View image in fullscreenEnd of the road … Ian Toner in A Slow Fire at Jermyn Street theatre, London.Photograph: Alex BrennerThe production, which premiered at Glass Mask theatre in Dublin earlier this year and is again directed by Rex Ryan,is in no rush to reveal its world and the games played within it, making you work to imagine your own apocalypse outside.There are some arresting moments and both actors give strong performances. Sometimes, their role-play turns desolate; at others, they tenderly savour a past memory with gentle humour (that occasionally lacks bite). A third man, Presley (Fionn Ó Loingsigh), and a surprise character, Mary (Holly Demaine), enter this space, the latter bringing a powerful monologue full of shock and horror at what has happened outside, spoken almost in a single breath.Ultimately, these interlopers bring real (as opposed to re-enacted) hope alongside a sense of threat as Presley arrives with a gun. But their intrigues do not contain enough of a story arc or offer sufficient dramatic tension. Too many meaningful silences slow the pace and get in the way of building momentum. Sometimes, messages are spelled out (“humans never heed warnings”, says one character, reflecting on natural disasters, climate catastrophe and human-made destruction). But there are reflective and lyrical moments too and a strongly resonant overarching idea, with intelligence in both the performances and the script.AtJermyn Street theatre, London, until 26 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreSimon StephensJermyn Street TheatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Tim Curry obituary | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Actor and singer best known for his roles in The Rocky Horror Show and the 1990 Stephen King TV miniseries It
Author: Michael Coveney
Headline: Actor and singer best known for his roles in The Rocky Horror Show and the 1990 Stephen King TV miniseries It
Content: Tim Curry as Frank-N-Furter in the The Rocky Horror Picture Show, 1975.Photograph: 20th Century Fox/AllstarView image in fullscreenTim Curry as Frank-N-Furter in the The Rocky Horror Picture Show, 1975.Photograph: 20th Century Fox/AllstarTheatreObituaryTim Curry obituaryActor and singer best known for his roles in The Rocky Horror Show and the 1990 Stephen King TV miniseries ItMichael CoveneyThu 27 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 13.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn June 1973, I went to the Royal Court to see one ofEdward Bond’s best plays, The Sea. On my way out, I met a colleague who said he had a spare ticket for something called The Rocky Horror Show in the Court’s studio space, the Theatre Upstairs, starting at around 10.30pm.We had no idea what this was going to be about. There was a gantry rigged above us and, astonishingly, suddenly, crawling along it was a frizzy haired chap in fishnet stockings, suspender belt and lurid makeup. This was Tim Curry, as the deranged scientist and debauched sex magnet Dr Frank-N-Furter, introducing himself in song as “just a sweet transvestite from Transsexual, Transylvania”.Thus was launched Richard O’Brien’s hilarious, addictive glam rock musical that went on to become a cult classic, after moving, with Curry, along the King’s Road to a former cinema, then crossing toBroadwayin 1975, and later being performed in productions all around the world.It was adapted for the screen in 1975 as The Rocky Horror Picture Show, directed by Jim Sharman, with Curry reprising his role, and O’Brien appearing as Riff Raff, the scientist’s butler, along with Susan Sarandon and Barry Bostwick as the young couple who seek shelter in Dr Frank-N-Furter’s castle after their car breaks down.The film arguably lacked the stage show’s element of subversive innovation and unbridled glee, but it became a huge cult hit with audiences, with both movie and theatre-goers dressing up in glam costumes, and joining in with the dance moves of Time Warp, the show-stopping song led by O’Brien.Curry, who has died aged 80, became a big star on both sides of the Atlantic in film and on stage. He went on to prove himself a class act in stylish comedy and hit musicals, including a rocked-up version of The Pirates of Penzance in 1982 at the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane, and Stephen Fry’s smart version of Me and My Girl, doing the Lambeth Walk as Bill Snibson on a 1987 US national tour, and as King Arthur in Monty Python’s Spamalot (2005-07), directed byMike Nicholson Broadway and in London.View image in fullscreenTim Curry as the Pirate King with Pamela Stephenson as Mabel in The Pirates of Penzance at Drury Lane theatre, London, in 1982.Photograph: James Gray/ANL/ShutterstockHis celebrity was certainly matched by his talent, and his innate charm was equally matched by his louche lifestyle which, for a period, involved party-going withDavid Bowie– a huge fan of his – and cocaine-fuelled benders with Truman Capote.Cruelly, he was struck down by a severe stroke in 2012 and was a wheelchair-user for the rest of his life. He summarised that life in a beautifully written and generously expressed, almost self-deprecating, memoir,Vagabond, in 2025.Curry was born in Grappenhall, on the outskirts of Warrington, the second child of Jim Curry, a Methodist chaplain who had served in the Royal Navy, and his wife, Maura (nee Langmead), a school secretary. He was educated as a boarder at Kingswood school in Bath – after the family had relocated to Plymouth – and took a degree in English and drama at Birmingham University.View image in fullscreenTim Curry as Frank-N-Furter at the Royal Court theatre, Sloane Square, London, in 1973.Photograph: Rocky Horror ShowHis first professional engagement was in the tribal rock musical Hair at the Shaftesbury theatre in 1968 – where he first met O’Brien. That cast included Elaine Page, Paul Nicholas and Marsha Hunt. Between Hair and Rocky Horror, he appeared in David Mercer’s After Haggerty (1969) with the Royal Shakespeare Company at the Aldwych, and as Puck in A Midsummer Night’s Dream in Regent’s Park in 1972.After the Rocky Horror film took off, he spent three years in New York recording and touring as a rock singer. This culminated in his Broadway role, from late 1980, as Mozart inPeter Shaffer’s Amadeus, losing out on the Tony best actor nomination to Ian McKellen as Salieri. His theatrical appetite re-boosted, he returned to London.Back in the capital he brought vim and vigour to his notable stage role asthe Pirate Kingin the production by Michael White – the commercial producer behind the Rocky Horror Show – of Gilbert and Sullivan’s The Pirates of Penzance. He was nominated for an Olivier award for his performance.In 1983, Curry appeared at the National Theatre as Bob Acres inPeter Wood’s sumptuous, elegant production of Sheridan’s The Rivals, which placed the Royal Crescent of Bath on the Olivier stage and co-starred Michael Hordern as Sir Anthony andGeraldine McEwanas Mrs Malaprop (“All men are Bavarians” – instead of barbarians). This show also marked the professional debut of Fiona Shaw. Less successful was the NT’s revival of Brecht/Weill’s The Threepenny Opera in 1986, in which he played Mack the Knife.Other films included Annie (1982), in which he played the con-artist Rooster, Richard Eyre’s The Ploughman’s Lunch (1983), written by Ian McEwan, the black comedy mystery Clue (1985), and The Three Musketeers (1993), in the role of Cardinal Richelieu.He was the clown Pennywise in the 1990 TV mini-series adaptation of Stephen King’s novel It, and also appeared in the films Home Alone 2: Lost inNew York(1992) and Muppet Treasure Island (1996), as Long John Silver. He was a lifelong friend of the art critic Richard Cork with whom he had been to school.His sister, Judy, predeceased him.Timothy James Curry, actor and singer, born 19 April 1946; died 25 August 2026Explore more on these topicsTheatreRocky Horror ShowBroadwayMusicals (Stage)Musicals (Film)New YorkobituariesShareReuse this content

title: Bronze age treasure stolen in four-minute Spanish museum heist | Art theft | The Guardian
description: Gold collection known as Treasure of Villena, worth at least €1.7m, is target of ‘very well planned’ raid
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: Gold collection known as Treasure of Villena, worth at least €1.7m, is target of ‘very well planned’ raid
Content: The Treasure of Villena comprises 29 bracelets, 11 bowls, three bottles and other miscellaneous pieces dating back to 1000BC.Photograph: Museum of Villena/EPAView image in fullscreenThe Treasure of Villena comprises 29 bracelets, 11 bowls, three bottles and other miscellaneous pieces dating back to 1000BC.Photograph: Museum of Villena/EPAArt theftBronze age treasure stolen in four-minute Spanish museum heistGold collection known as Treasure of Villena, worth at least €1.7m, is target of ‘very well planned’ raidPhilip Oltermannand agenciesThu 27 Aug 2026 11.47 EDTFirst published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 07.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThieves in Spain have raided the Treasure of Villena – a stunning collection of bronze age gold artefacts that has been described as the most important prehistoric trove inEurope– in the latest high-profile smash-and-grab heist on the continent.The raid on Thursday morning of the 66 mostly gold objects in the Spanish town of Villena lasted just minutes, officials said.“The alarm at the Villena Museum went off around 5.20am [4.20am BST],” a spokesperson for the town council said, adding that the thieves had left the building by 5.24am. The operation was “super-fast and super-professional”, the spokesperson said.“They’ve taken most of the treasure,” the mayor of Villena, Fulgencio Cerdán, told journalists, his voice breaking.View image in fullscreenThe collection has been held in a specially designated room in the Museum of Villena since May 2024.Photograph: Pablo Miranzo/EPALocal media said the few items the thieves had left behind included three silver vessels, a bracelet and some of the ornamentation of the bastón del reyezuelo, the “Kingfisher staff”, a prehistoric ceremonial scepter.Cerdán said: “We are absolutely devastated, I’m even trembling. The truth is that for those of us from Villena, this destroys us. It’s part of our heritage, of our wealth.”The treasure, which was discovered in 1963 by the archaeologist José María Soler in a vessel sunk in a dried-out riverbed in Villena, included 29 bracelets, 11 bowls, three bottles and other miscellaneous pieces dating back to about 1000BC. It immediately became the main attraction of a small architectural museum in the province of Alicante.Since May 2024, the hoard has been on display in a specially designated room in the newly opened, municipally owned Villena Museum.The unusual material of some of the items has long intrigued researchers. Though mainly gold, some pieces are also made of silver, iron, amber and a dark leaden material covered in a ferrous-looking oxide. A recent study published in the journalTrabajos de Prehistoriaclaimed that these items were probably forged from rare meteoritic iron.While the treasure’s value is incalculable, the gold alone is worth about €1.7m (£1.45m), according to the mayor.The thieves arrived in several vehicles and apparently entered the museum through a window, according to the Spanish government’s deputy representative in Alicante, Manuel Pineda.“All security systems were activated,” according to the Villena spokesperson, who insisted there had been “no failure” by the museum.Shortly before the robbery, another alarm went off at the city’s sports centre, and authorities were now investigating whether that was a diversion created by the thieves, the spokesperson added.Mauro Hernández, a professor of archaeology at the University of Alicante and an expert on the treasure, told the broadcaster Cadena SER that the operation showed signs of prior planning. “They had it very well planned,” Hernández said. “They knew how to do it, how to act and how to escape.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGuns, axes, explosives: violent museum heists are on the rise, says EuropolRead moreLast October, thieves broke into the Louvre Museum in Paris in broad daylight,escaping in less than eight minuteswith jewellery worth €88m. There have since been a series of brazen raids in institutions across Europe.Four works “of extraordinary value” by the Renaissance artist Antonello da Messinawere stolenfrom a museum in Sicily, Italy’s culture ministry said last Sunday.Two days earlier, Italian police said they hadrecovered paintingsby Renoir, Cézanne and Matisse worth more than $10.4m which were stolen from the Magnani-Rocca Foundation Museum near Parma.In a report published at the start of the week, the EU’s police agency Europol said that member states had detected a recent shift “towards violent and forceful methods” that could point to the involvement of new criminal networks focused on specific cultural artefacts.“Some thieves apprehended in recent cases appear to coordinate their efforts on an ad hoc basis, often recruited locally through social media and instant communication channels, without prior connections to each other,” the report said. “This differs from the usual structure of criminal networks involved in cultural goods trafficking, which typically operate in a core group organised around a leader.”Agence France-Presse contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsArt theftMuseumsSpainOrganised crimeEuropeHeritagenewsShareReuse this content

title: BBC to bring back Top Gear amid speculation about show’s next presenters | Top Gear | The Guardian
description: Motoring series to return four years after Andrew ‘Freddie’ Flintoff suffered serious injuries in crash during filming
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Motoring series to return four years after Andrew ‘Freddie’ Flintoff suffered serious injuries in crash during filming
Content: But will the Stig come back too? The BBC has refused to comment yet on who will host the show upon its return.Photograph: Ben A Pruchnie/GettyView image in fullscreenBut will the Stig come back too? The BBC has refused to comment yet on who will host the show upon its return.Photograph: Ben A Pruchnie/GettyTop GearBBC to bring back Top Gear amid speculation about show’s next presentersMotoring series to return four years after Andrew ‘Freddie’ Flintoff suffered serious injuries in crash during filmingCaroline DaviesThu 27 Aug 2026 10.32 EDTFirst published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 07.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTop Gear,the long-running motoring show that has been off air since its co-hostAndrew “Freddie” Flintoffwas seriously injured in a crash during filming almost four years ago, is to return to the BBC, the broadcaster has confirmed.AfterFlintoff’s accidentat Dunsfold aerodrome in Surrey, the BBC said the series would be “rested” for the foreseeable future.The BBC’s director of entertainment, Ed Havard, confirmed the news of its return at a panel event at the Edinburgh TV festival on Thursday. “There has been a lot of speculation about this and we can confirm thatTop Gearis coming back,” he said.Havard refused to be drawn on who would host the show amid reports that the comedian and presenter – and a known car enthusiast –Jimmy Carrwas in the frame. “I’m not going to talk about talent today,” he replied to questions. “Jimmy would be a great host but I won’t be discussing that today.“We will have more information on Top Gear shortly,” Havard added.Carr was a guest on Top Gear in 2004, and has said: “It’s one of the biggest shows in the world. It’s a global phenomenon.”The former England rugby player and Celebrity Traitors starJoe Marleris also reportedly being considered to host.View image in fullscreenThe former England rugby player Joe Marler’s name has been mooted as a possible presenter.Photograph: Ian West/PAThe model Jodie Kidd is another rumoured contender. Kidd has appeared on Top Gear in the past, and after qualifying for a racing licence, began racing in Italy. She has also hosted various automotive shows including Channel 5’s The Classic Car Show, Chubb Insurance’s classic car podcast, and her own YouTube channel, Kidd in a Sweet Shop.View image in fullscreenJodie Kidd taking part in a rally in Brescia, Italy, in 2014.Photograph: Olycom SPA/RexOthers who have featured in speculation include the celebrity chef Gordon Ramsay, who has appeared on Top Gear several times and owns an extensive collection of cars, and the actor Rowan Atkinson, another car enthusiast who appeared during series 17, where he set a lap time of 1min 42.2sec, making him the fastest celebrity on the leaderboard at the time.Top Gear began in 1977 and became one of the BBC’s biggest hits in the hands of Jeremy Clarkson, Richard Hammond and James May in the 2000s.Clarkson’s contract was not renewed at the end of the 22nd season, after he punched a producer.He later issued a formal apology. Clarkson’s co-hosts also left after his departure, with the trio then signing up for another motoring show, The Grand Tour, on Amazon Prime Video.They were replaced by the broadcaster Chris Evans and the Friends star Matt LeBlanc. Evans left after just six episodes. The show also received criticism after LeBlanc and a rally driverperformed “doughnuts” near the Cenotaph war memorialin London’s Whitehall.View image in fullscreenPaddy McGuinness, Chris Harris and Andrew ‘Freddie’ Flintoff.Photograph: Lee Brimble/PAFlintoff, Paddy McGuinness and Chris Harris took over in 2018.Flintoff was taken to hospital with facial and rib injuries when the Morgan Super 3 he was driving – an open-topped three-wheeled car – flipped upside down and skidded on the tarmac before coming to a stop. The BBC later reached a financial settlement with the England cricket captain, an agreementreportedly worth about £9m. He has revealed he wasdeeply affected by the crashand did not leave his house for six months other than to attend medical appointments.View image in fullscreenFlintoff has said he suffers from PTSD as a result of the Top Gear crash.Photograph: Gareth Copley/GettyIn the Disney+ documentary Flintoff, released last year, the presenter admitted that after the accident, he did not think he had it in him to “get through”. Flintoff said his then three-and-a-half-year-old son Preston “wouldn’t come near me”. “I think it frightened him, my face; it frightened me. That was heartbreaking,” he said in the documentary.“I’ve got PTSD [post-traumatic stress disorder] and I get anxious, for periods of time. I just find myself crying for no particular reason.”Flintoff also said he relived the crash every night when he went to bed and described the experience as a “vivid” movie.Explore more on these topicsTop GearBBCEdinburgh International Television FestivalJimmy CarrFactual TVTelevisionAndrew FlintoffnewsShareReuse this content

title: I don’t get along with my sister-in-law. Should I try to address the dynamic?  | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
description: There are two things to consider, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith. Are you hurt by the way she treats you or the way she sees you?
Author: Eleanor Gordon-Smith
Headline: There are two things to consider, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith. Are you hurt by the way she treats you or the way she sees you?
Content: ‘One is about changing her behaviour. The other is about changing her mind. I think your strategy going forward will depend on which you care most about,’ writes Eleanor Gordon-Smith. Painting: Bless, O God, These Thy Gifts to Our Use by Albert Chevallier Tayler  (1887).Illustration: Artepics/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘One is about changing her behaviour. The other is about changing her mind. I think your strategy going forward will depend on which you care most about,’ writes Eleanor Gordon-Smith. Painting: Bless, O God, These Thy Gifts to Our Use by Albert Chevallier Tayler  (1887).Illustration: Artepics/AlamyLeading questionsAustralian lifestyleI don’t get along with my sister-in-law. Should I try to address the dynamic?There are two things to consider, writes advice columnistEleanor Gordon-Smith. Are you hurt by the way she treatsyou or the way she sees you?Read moreLeading questionsEleanor Gordon-SmithThu 27 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 19.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’m struggling with a dynamic with my sister-in-law. We’re not a natural fit personality-wise, and I’ve tried to be mindful of that. At times I wonder whether she might be jealous of the life I have with her brother and our children. I often encourage my husband to spend time with her without me, because she doesn’t seem to particularly enjoy me being there. As a result, we now mostly see each other at family gatherings, which happen about once a month.There’s a recurring pattern where she corrects me quite sharply, with an impatience that often feels disproportionate or plain mean. She might snap while I am talking to her parents (with whom I have a good relationship), laugh at how I pronounce a placename, or dismiss a question as though it’s too stupid to answer. These interactions are quick and barely noticeable to anyone else, although my daughter and husband have both observed and agreed it was pretty mean.I’m unsure how to interpret this behaviour. More importantly, I don’t know what I owe – to myself, to her, and to the wider family in terms of responding.Is this best addressed directly, even at the risk of creating awkwardness? At what point does tolerating this kind of interaction become a failure to stand up for myself? And might there be a cost in not trying to improve a relationship that could otherwise be supportive as we navigate the more ordinary trials of family life – ageing parents, illness and difficult decisions?My friend’s negative self-talk is straining our relationship. What can I do? | Leading questionsRead moreEleanor says:The in-law relationship can be such an unstable combination: you’re simultaneously meant to be part of a family and yet also a guest outside it. There can be all the expectation that you’ll be close – spend holidays together, get on well, share major celebrations and traumas – without the things that tend to make that closeness possible. You probably didn’t grow up together, you don’t spend enough time together to really gain an accurate knowledge of what a person is like and you’re too polite to argue in ways that can lead to honest understanding.So when conflict appears, you can wind up in the bind you’re in now: am I supposed to approach this the way I would with close family? Or the way I would as a polite guest?As you say, the exact diagnosis for why she does this probably matters less than what to do about it. You might be right that she’s jealous. Or perhaps she feels insecure. People who are a bit afraid of failing are often gifted at painting those failings on to others. Maybe ostentatiously finding ways to point out that you don’t “get it” (whateveritis) is her way of anxiously insisting that she does get it. Or she could just plain not like you. You could have trodden on her toes accidentally, who knows.I think your question about what to do depends on how far upstream you want your solution to be. Are you mainly hurt by the way shetreatsyou? Or are you mainly hurt by the way sheseesyou?You might primarily care about how she behaves: “She can believe what she wants about me, I just don’t know whether to keep allowing these barbs.” Alternatively, you might primarily care about what these barbs reveal of how she sees you: “She shouldn’t think I’m foolish and small.”One is about changing her behaviour. The other is about changing her mind. I think your strategy going forward will depend on which you care most about.If what you want most is the behaviour to change, you can get that by making it too socially expensive to treat you like this, or by having an awkward conversation asking her to stop. The catch is, those ways of changing her behaviour might only cement her view of you. If she resents your presence in the family or has an imaginary, disagreeable version of you, a social sanction or confronting conversation might seem to confirm things for her – even if she does pull her head in at the dinner table.This is the annoying trade-off at the heart of all kinds of conflicts: you can very effectively produce certain behavioural changes in others, if you don’t mind paying a cost in how they see you.If instead you most want to improve the way she seems to think of you, that might have to happen one-on-one. Corrections and snaps like this are often for the benefit of an audience, such that when the audience goes away so too does the snapping. A dynamic between the two of you might be quite different from the things she tries to prove in front of your husband or your kids.Your way forward depends on what you most want this relationship to be. Do you want it to feel like family – sometimes awkward, sometimes intense, but aimed at really knowing each other? Or would you be content if you could at least get the treatment you’d expect for any other guest?Ask Eleanor a questionShare your questionTell us hereYour responses, which can be anonymous, are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions. We will only use the data you provide us for the purpose of the feature and we will delete any personal data when we no longer require it for this purpose. For alternative ways to get in touch securely please see ourtips guide.NameWhat is your question for Eleanor?Email addressYour contact details are helpful so we can contact you for more information. They will only be seen by the Guardian.By submitting your response, you are agreeing to share your details with us for this feature.SubmitShow moreExplore more on these topicsAustralian lifestyleLeading questionsFamilyHealth & wellbeingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Suri Pro 2.0 electric toothbrush review: does this sustainable brush live up to the hype? | Health & wellbeing | The Guardian
description: Suri’s eco-friendly brush fixes several flaws in the first-generation model – here’s what it does better (and what still needs work)
Author: Alan Martin
Headline: Suri’s eco-friendly brush fixes several flaws in the first-generation model – here’s what it does better (and what still needs work)
Content: It may lack some of the power of other electric toothbrushes, but the Suri 2.0 is a huge improvement on the original.Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIt may lack some of the power of other electric toothbrushes, but the Suri 2.0 is a huge improvement on the original.Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterHealth & wellbeingReviewSuri Pro 2.0 electric toothbrush review: does this sustainable brush live up to the hype?Suri’s eco-friendly brush fixes several flaws in the first-generation model – here’s what it does better (and what still needs work)The best electric toothbrushes, testedAlan MartinThu 27 Aug 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen I wrote the Filter’s guide to thebest electric toothbrushes, one brand I didn’t need a sample from was Suri. I already owned one of its brushes, drawn in by its impressive commitment to sustainability in a sector that seemed blissfully unbothered by theclimate crisisunfolding around us.Unfortunately, a few things held it back from taking the top spot, and I’m pleased to say that these have mostly been addressed with the Suri Pro 2.0. Is it the best you can buy? Still not quite, but the gap has significantly closed, and there are fewer caveats than ever when giving it a recommendation.If you care about sustainability in any way, it’s the best choice. And now there are fewer drawbacks to doing the right thing.View at SuriView at AmazonHow I testedView image in fullscreenThe Suri Pro 2.0 toothbrush was tested over a month of daily brushing.Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianIt doesn’t take a great deal of imagination to figure out how you test a toothbrush: brush, brush and brush again. Fortunately, Suri was decent enough to give early reviewers a month-long loan, rather than expecting us to burn through several tubes of toothpaste in a matter of hours.Equally fortunate was the fact that, although I’d donated most of the toothbrushes from the group test to Causeway (asexplained here), I held on to our current favourite, theSpotlight Sonic Pro, as a point of reference. Plus, I already had my personal Suri toothbrush, so I could see where the improvements existed.Suri Pro 2.0 electric toothbrush: what you need to knowView image in fullscreenThe first-generation Suri and Suri 2.0 are virtually indistinguishable.Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianView at SuriView at AmazonMy beef with the original Suri toothbrush was essentially twofold. First, it didn’t feel as powerful as its rivals, offering 30,000 brush strokes per minute (BPM), compared with others that went as high as 62,000.The second was a deeper problem: the spring pin chargers felt temperamental, and I personally got through three over the years, deeply damaging the sustainability of the product as a whole. This was likely partly my fault (from not adequately drying brushes before charging, causing them to rust), but I wasn’t the only one with the problem.Suri has addressed both of these weaknesses, and some others that hadn’t bothered me. While the first is a relatively minor tweak – it still vibrates at 30,000 BPM, but with what I’m told is a “more powerful sweeping motion, delivering 25% higher intensity”, whatever that means – Suri Pro 2.0 now charges via wireless induction, both on the charging stand and in the optional carry case. No more spring pins to rust or snap.Other improvements include the introduction of a pressure sensor, a quieter motor (50dB rather than 54), a bundled plant-based brush head cover if you want to ditch the travel case, and a travel lock to stop it turning on by mistake. As someone whose luggage was once delayed by an electric toothbrush prompting a bomb threat, I can’t believe “not being mistaken for a terrorist” wasn’t on my wishlist of upgrades, but there we go.Finally, the optional travel case has been upgraded to include a battery. This isn’t for charging the brush, but to power a built-in UV-C light Suri claims kills bacteria on the go. The UV light was a feature on the original brush, too, but it required a USB-C cable to work, making it a little-used extra for me.All of this comes in the form of a brush that looks virtually indistinguishable from the original, as you’ll see in the photos. This feels like an odd choice from a marketing perspective, but it does have the advantage of meaning therecyclable plant-based headsare interchangeable between the first-generation Suri and the 2.0, as well as the newerCore 1.0.SpecificationsType:sonicModes:two (clean and polish)Power:30,000 BPMPressure sensor:yesBattery life:1+ monthApp:noWarranty:one year (extended to two years with registration)What we loveView image in fullscreenThe wireless charging system is a huge improvement over the first-gen model.Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianThe main thing we love about Suri Pro 2.0 is the same thing we loved in the first-gen brush – the heads are plant based, made from cornstarch with castor oil bristles. Suri will recycle these free of charge, and provide a self-addressed compostable bag to put your used heads in when you’ve collected four. Apack of three costs £14.99, but if you subscribe, you’ll get two sent out every six months for £8.98. Cheaper than some of the big brands, but more expensive than some third-party heads.As a brush, it’s light and easy to use. One press of the button turns it on, with a friendly buzz every 30 seconds reminding you to move on to the next quarter of your mouth before it shuts itself down after two minutes. There are two modes, one gentle and one slightly firmer for a stronger clean.As for those refinements, the pressure sensor is a very good addition indeed. If you push too hard, the brush will buzz three times and then fall asleep. As soon as you reduce the pressure, it’ll stop playing possum, with the timer continuing from where you left off. (Note that you can inadvertently turn this off – something that wasn’t in the review unit’s manual, causing me to think the device might be broken. If your pressure sensor stops working, try pressing and holding the power button for five seconds with the brush switched on. When a light flashes, turn the brush off and back on, and the pressure sensor should be restored.)The wireless charging system is a huge improvement, too. Just pop Suri Pro 2.0 on to the USB-C charging stand or into the case (connected to a USB-C cable), and charging starts immediately. Despite losing the unreliable spring pins, the new stand is still magnetic, so the brush handle won’t topple without a push.Speaking of magnets, one of my favourite design elements of the original is present here too. Each Suri comes with a magnetic wall mount to prevent cabinet clutter. No screws required: just remove the tab and stick it to a wall or mirror with the pre-applied adhesive.While the brush looks nearly identical to the first generation, the case is far nicer to hold and carry, with smoother edges, rather than the first generation’s sharp angles. The built-in battery makes it easier to get into the habit of using the UV-C light, even if it’s not what I’d call an essential feature.There’s also now a plant-based head cover in the box. To prevent accidental activation, a travel lock mode has been added, requiring a five-second press to switch on and off. This is handy if luggage is at a premium and even the slimline case is too bulky, letting you keep your toothbrush head free from fluff and other detritus.What we don’t loveView image in fullscreenThe Suri Pro 2.0 is still a touch underpowered compared with other electric toothbrushes.Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianI generally agree with Suri that toothbrush features such as Bluetooth and connected apps are gimmicks. However, having tested a host of sonic toothbrushes, I do think that 30,000 BPM is still underpowered, even with the supposed higher intensity.To put that into perspective, on the Spotlight Sonic Pro, the 30,000 BPM setting is called “gentle”, and it has four settings that go all the way up to 50,000 BPM. Whether it’s down to the speed or less planet-friendly bristles, all I can say is that after a cider-heavy night at the pub, Spotlight remains notably more effective at eliminating that disgusting furry tooth feel than Suri. (This is not one of my regular toothbrush tests, but it’s an effective one.)Using both the original Suri and the Suri Pro 2.0 side by side, I couldn’t feel much of a difference, though it’s possible that things are happening on a level only visible to dentists. Initially, the Pro 2.0 was only available with the battery-powered travel case at £105, but the company now sensibly allows you to buy the brush on its own for £85. This not only brings the price down significantly, but also avoids creating more e-waste in the long run.Finally, it’s a pity that there’s currently no way to trade in the first-generation Suri brush for its successor. I would be surprised if this remained the case for ever, given its commitment to minimising e-waste.SustainabilityView image in fullscreenSuri works to offset its manufacturing emissions.Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianOn that note, Suri’s sustainability credentials remain second to none in the world of toothbrushes. Admittedly, this isn’t especially high praise, but nonetheless, the company’s visible positive environmental choices should be applauded.The plant-based heads can be recycled free of charge, as previously mentioned. The body is built from aluminium, the packaging is moulded paper, and the Suri works withClimatePartner to measureand offset its manufacturing emissions.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere are limitations to this. There is still a lithium-ion battery on the inside, and some plastic involved, as well as a battery in the optional travel case (something Suri previously avoided on environmental grounds). Suri says there are practical reasons for these ecological compromises, and the company holds itself to account by tracking emissions and publishing annual sustainability reports. You canread the 2025 document here, which states that Suri recycled two tonnes of returned brush heads last year, among other things.Suri Pro 2.0 electric toothbrush:should I buy it?All in all, Suri Pro 2.0 is a huge improvement over the first generation. The enhancements are thoughtful and address real gripes I had, while not feeling the need to lean into gimmicks such as Bluetooth connectivity. A toothbrush I could previously only endorse with a “but” is now an easy recommendation, even if it’s still not the most powerful brush around.Ironically, I’ll now add a “but” – albeit one I imagine Suri will be happy to read. As the company itself points out, almost every toothbrush that has ever been built still exists, whether it’s in a cabinet or a landfill, broken or working.With that in mind, if you need an electric toothbrush, then Suri Pro 2.0 should definitely be on your radar. If you already have one that works well enough, make a mental note and consider picking one up when the time comes(and when it does, you canfind out where to recycle your old electric toothbrush locally here).View at SuriView at AmazonSuri Pro 2.0 vs …Suri Core 1.0 electric toothbrushView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Martin/The Guardian£65 at Suri£65 at AmazonIn August 2026, Suri released a new brush: the Core 1.0. Despite launching at £65, the entry-level addition kept many of the features new to the Suri Pro 2.0, including a pressure sensor, the improved charging mechanic, the travel lock and the plant-based caps for on-the-go use.The latter two are especially important, as Suri Core 1.0 doesn’t come with a travel case, nor will it work with the existing one (it fits, but rattles around and won’t charge). That, for me, is a minor inconvenience, and the other compromises Suri has made don’t feel like compromises at all. The battery lasts up to a month rather than over one, and the body is made from bio-circular plastic made from food-waste materials including used cooking oil and other waste feedstocks instead of aluminium.Yes, the power drops to 28,000 BPM, but as outlined in the review above, it’s not like Suri Pro 2.0 was a high-power option anyway. And with the removal of the case meaning less future e-waste and lower transit emissions thanks to a substantial weight reduction, it’s now my number-one choice for sustainable shoppers.Readour fullSuri Core 1.0 reviewOdonta PowerPlus electric toothbrushView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Martin/The Guardian£29.99 at AmazonEven without the case, the Suri Pro 2.0 isn’t the cheapest option at £85. The current budget champion is the Odonta PowerPlus, which does nothing wrong for its svelte £29.99 price.You get a maximum of 42,000 BPM across five brushing modes, a pressure sensor, three-week battery life and IPX7 water resistance. While it can’t match Suri for sustainability, the bristles are bio-based polyamide nylon 1010, which is made from castor oil rather than the fossil fuels used in most toothbrush heads.Alternatively, the company makes a brush called thePowerLitefor the same price. This is smaller and lighter, but makes some sacrifices along the way. Battery life is doubled for worry-free travel, but it loses 2,000 BPM of power, the pressure sensor and the wireless charging cradle (instead relying on USB-C).Laifen Wave Pro electric toothbrushView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Martin/The Guardian£84.99 at AmazonIf you’re looking for pure performance, our current top electric toothbrush champion is the Laifen Wave Pro. Its secret weapon is that it oscillates and vibrates at the same time, unlike rival toothbrushes that make you pick one or the other.This led to the freshest-feeling mouth I’ve experienced in my time testing brushes (and I’ve now tested 31 for the Filter). There are three modes on the brush, each of which can be customised in the accompanying app, letting you get up to 66,000 BPM of sonic power and/or up to 60 degrees of oscillation. In all, there are around 1,000 possible combinations (and you can delete the app once it’s set up, if you like).Add in a sleek design, 70 days of battery life and a device that seems to charge on any wireless charger, and you’ve got a product that should impress you and your dental hygienist.For more, read our guide to thebest electric toothbrushesAlan Martin is awriter who has been putting products – including phones, gaming devices and wearables – through their paces for more than a decade. Although he wouldn’t call teeth brushing a hobby, it’s something he’s been doing for decades with a degree of aptitude that has largely satisfied dentistsThis article was amended on 27 August 2026.
