title: Why we’re all hooked on tinned fish  | Food | The Guardian
description: Sardines, mackerel, herring, pilchards, sprats and anchovies ... canning only makes the umami flavour better. They’re my top choice for pasta
Author: Rachel Roddy
Headline: Sardines, mackerel, herring, pilchards, sprats and anchovies ... canning only makes the umami flavour better. They’re my top choice for pasta
Content: Good in a crisis … Rachel Roddy's spaghetti with tinned sardines, anchovy, capers, chilli and lemon.Photograph: Rita Platts/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGood in a crisis … Rachel Roddy's spaghetti with tinned sardines, anchovy, capers, chilli and lemon.Photograph: Rita Platts/The GuardianFeastFoodWhy we’re all hooked on tinned fishSardines, mackerel, herring, pilchards, sprats and anchovies ... canning only makes the umami flavour better. They’re my top choice for pastaSign up here for our weekly food newsletter, FeastRachel RoddyThu 27 Aug 2026 08.10 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 08.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIcan’t find it, despite having spent the past 35 minutes looking, but somewhere in the house isThe Crisis Cook Book. It’s a standard paperback, postbox-red with white writing on the cover, and full of recipes from chefs includingRowley Leigh,Heston BlumenthalandJeremy Lee. Not having found it, I needed Amazon to tell me it was published in 2007 and compiled by Nick Lander, at the time the Financial Times’ restaurant correspondent. He asked 28 chefs to donate three recipes – their favourite starter, main course and dessert – and proceeds from the book went to the national homelessness charity Crisis.The reason I needed (and still need – it is now a mission) to find the book is because inside it is Rowley’s recipe for pasta with tinned sardines, fennel, chilli and lemon zest. It’s a recipe that I have made so many times, and for so many years, that I don’t need to look at the book; but, equally, because I’ve made it so many times and so much time has passed, I have no idea how far I have drifted from the original, and want to check. I’ve even written aboutthis recipein my weekly Guardian column, without referring to the book or even mentioning Rowley! Not that a store-cupboard version of the Sicilianpasta con le sarde(pasta with sardines and wild fennel) is owned by anyone, although Rowley did teach me.So here I am, setting the record straight, Rowley taught me to – and this is approximate – soften thinly sliced red onion, fennel and red chilli in lots of olive oil, add a tin of sardines (mashed), then toss the lot with al dente pasta, minced parsley and enough lemon zest to scent the pasta and the kitchen. It’s a meal that is not only deeply delicious but also thrifty, because a small amount of fish goes a long way.In short, tinned fish rules. It gives a product with a notoriously short life an extremely long one, thus drastically reducing the risk of food waste. Sardines, mackerel, herring, pilchards, sprats and anchovies are my tinned fish of choice – tasty, rich in essential omega 3 fatty acids and, if watchfully sourced, sustainable. That sourcing is very important, though (sardine stocksin some parts of the world are struggling), so I’d recommend keeping an eye onthe Marine Conservation Society’s Good Fish Guide. The other thing about tinned fish is the deep umami flavour that can develop during the curing and canning process, especially when the fish is preserved in a good-tasting brine or oil.View image in fullscreenFlexible and thrifty … Rachel’s potato and tinned fish cakes.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianAnd now, more than ever, it’s easier to find fish preserved in these delicious brines and oils thanks to enterprises such as Mitch Tonks’sRockfishin the West Country andSea Sistersin Dorset, both of which take great care with their canning, and to exceptional producers such asGiribizziandLa Belle-Iloise. Not to mention The Tinned Fish Market, which has stalls in Old Spitalfields and Borough markets in London (andan online shop) dedicated to excellent tinned fish. All of which is encouraging supermarkets to keep up.Back to recipes. Yotam Ottolenghi also has a play on the classic Sicilian sardine pasta, usingmackerel fillets, za’atar and lime, served with linguine; another Yotam recipe forconchiglie with tinned smoked oystersis a template that can be adapted to just about any tinned fish you happen to have in the cupboard. Anna Berrill, meanwhile, uses tinned sardines instead of anchovies for hertomato, caper and olive puttanesca, which she serves with polenta, as well as in a great-sounding sardine, caper, chive and celery salad.I generally use sardines in my recipe forpotato and tinned fishcakes, but mackerel, herring, pilchards and sprats all work. Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall’stinned mackerel patéis equally flexible, and yes to his quick-pickled onions, too! Hugh, a tinned fish champion, also suggests a sardine omelette (his daughter’s recipe) and mixing sardines with canned white beans and thinly sliced red onionfor a store-cupboard salad, as well as reminding us they’re tasty just piled on toast. I agree – it is always a good idea to have a tin or two of sardines in the cupboard. Now where is that bloody book?My week in foodView image in fullscreenAn alternative taste test … Marcus Ansell, AKA Tinned Fish Reviews, with his trusty sidekick, King Arthur.Photograph: Lucy Ansell/SWNSCan do|In keeping with the tinned fish theme, Marcus Ansell – known to his millions of Instagram, YouTube and TikTok followers asTinned Fish Reviewsand usually found wearing a fez – opens, decants and taste tests cans of fish. Calm to the extreme, even when appalled or ecstatic about the contents of the tin, he is a joy to watch and learn from. As is his dog, King Arthur.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFeastRecipes from all our star cooks, seasonal eating ideas and restaurant reviews. Get our best food writing every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDear diaries|This week, I have been cooking fromThom Eagle’s Allotment Diaries, which isn’t a cookbook, nor does it contain recipes. Rather, it is a record of a year on an allotment and his thoughts on growing, which are inseparable from those about family, grief, the seasons, and how he might slice, cook and flavour whatever he has picked. In turn, he has sent me into the kitchen with a reminder that a short phrase about courgette “stewed as filling for an omelette” can often be more helpful and inspiring than a long recipe. A stunning book.Wrap up warm|My son this week reminded me how great chickpea flourpancakesare. I’d recommend a batter made from 250g chickpea flour, 450ml cold water and a big pinch of salt, so it’s the consistency of smooth single cream. Leave it to rest, then fried as you would pancakes, they should be firm but floppy, and frilly at the edges. The flavour is like a pancake crossed with hummus and they’re fantastic with some stir-fried greens and a big blob of ricotta.If you want to read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive Feast in your inbox every Thursday.Explore more on these topicsFoodFeastFishSeafoodMain courseSnacksnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Honey, I shrunk the wine: why miniature bottles are big again | Wine | The Guardian
description: Whether they’re consumed as a considered glass for one or something to sip on a short trip, miniature wine bottles are back with a bang
Author: Mina Holland
Headline: Whether they’re consumed as a considered glass for one or something to sip on a short trip, miniature wine bottles are back with a bang
Content: Wine miniatures: instant, easy drinking with a focus on fun.Photograph: Laithwaites/PRView image in fullscreenWine miniatures: instant, easy drinking with a focus on fun.Photograph: Laithwaites/PRGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.WineHoney, I shrunk the wine: why miniature bottles are big againWhether they’re consumed as a considered glass for one or something to sip on a short trip, miniature wine bottles are back with a bangMina HollandThu 27 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the 1920s, the London wine merchant Berry Bros & Rudd was asked to create a wine cellar for adoll’s house, commissioned by Queen Mary, to showcase the best of British craftsmanship. Designed by Edwin Lutyens, it had running water, electricity, a library of tiny books and, naturally, a wine cellar stocked with 1,200 miniature bottles, including vintage ports, an 1889 Montrachet and top-tier bordeaux. These days, the doll’s house resides in Windsor Castle, but Berry Bros has a replica of that cellar in its own Mayfair cellar, complete with 5ml bottles of those same wines.It is fair to say that this is not representative of the calibre of wine one generally finds in miniature bottles, a format associated with air travel and what I once called “journey juice” – ie, a drop that would last me the six stops from home to London Victoria on a Friday night. Google “miniature bottles of wine” and you’ll overwhelmingly be served examples from the very biggest wine brands in the world. This is also true ofcanned wines, although I’d argue there’s more interesting wine going into cans than small bottles.However! There are times when a mini bottle, which is usually somewhere between 200ml and 250ml, is just the ticket; when you’re the only one drinking and want just a glass, say, or maybe you’re sipping fizz and don’t want a larger bottle to lose its bubbles. For both reasons, champagne is ideal in miniature. What’s not to love about a cold, dry, biscuity and very sparkly solo glass of Lanson Le Black Création or Pommery Pink Pop? It’s cute, it’s camp and it’ll cost you a third of the price of a full bottle for those evenings when one (generous) glass is enough.They mostly come in plastic bottles, so minis are also good for a picnic. It’s no coincidence, then, that Marks & Spencer – summer’s temple to the picnic – should have a good selection. Also unsurprising is the disproportionate presence of rosé in mini bottles – the standouts being M&S’s Finca Miguel Cava Rosado, a sprightly, red fruit-forward friend to any fizz-loving prosecco sceptics, and Côteaux Varois en Provence, which is simple but unfailingly delicious. I also think the same store’s Rosso di Puglia is a winner fresh out of a cooler: juicy and food-versatile. Laithwaites, too, has a good selection of minis, including its very popular Cabalié wines from Languedoc-Roussillon. The white, in particular, is a peachy viognier blend, at once rich and fresh.None of these is wine to challenge you, but if you want instant, easy drinking with a focus on fun, stock up your fridge, or even your doll’s house.Four mini marvelsLanson Le Black Création£13.15 (200ml) Sainsbury’s, 12.5%. A classic non-vintage champagne that always hits the spot. Drink straight from the bottle for extra loucheness.M&S Côteaux Varois en Provence£4 (250ml) Ocado, 12.5%. Everything you want from Provençal rosé – a dry, strawberries and cream delight in a voluptuous mini bouteille.Cabalié Blanc 2024£3.99 (187ml) Laithwaites, 12%. Viognier, muscat and colombard have a party so you can, too.M&S Finca Miguel Cava Rosado Brut£3.50 (200ml) Ocado, 11.5%. An impressive, bubbly blend of Catalonian grape trepat with pinot noir – it cries out for picnic tapas.Explore more on these topicsWineFoodPicnicsFrench food and drinkSpanish food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: High in cocoa, high on nostalgia: the chocolate I love most now | Chocolate | The Guardian
description: Including, to my surprise, a 100% cacao bar
Author: Annalisa Barbieri
Headline: Including, to my surprise, a 100% cacao bar
Content: M&S retro chocolate bars from the 1980s: calledNow!,Jet,SparksandCoconut Grove.Photograph: Karen Thomas/M&SView image in fullscreenM&S retro chocolate bars from the 1980s: calledNow!,Jet,SparksandCoconut Grove.Photograph: Karen Thomas/M&SGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The chocolate diariesChocolateHigh in cocoa, high on nostalgia: the chocolate I love most nowIncluding, to my surprise, a 100% cacao bar …Annalisa BarbieriThu 27 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlthough I’mun peu fatiguéeof chocolates in bonbon shape with coloured cocoa-butter splashes atop, I appreciate this is the way many chocolates truffles are made. Overcoming that prejudice, I tucked into a box ofScoffchocolates. They were beautifully fresh tasting – they are made in batches throughout the year and the latest batch has just been let loose. I liked every one of the nine flavours I tested, from lemon to malted milk. But the ingredient list is long and a bit mainstream; a cleaner, more artisan approach and this would be a winning brand.View image in fullscreenScoff chocolates: truffles for the truffle-weary.Photograph: Gem Clack/PRMarks & Spencer has brought out some 1980s classics in original packaging for those wanting to go full Rivals: look out forNow!,Jet,SparksandCoconut Groveand see which chocolate classics they remind you of. My testers loved them.View image in fullscreenM&S Now! bar.My more everyday chocolate, as I am a high cocoa-content woman, has beenWillie’s 100% Cacaowith pistachio and date or raisin and hazelnut. I am not generally a fan of 100% cacao (it can only be called chocolate if sugar is also an ingredient) and I once described the bulk of the hundred percenters as tasting like you’ve woken up after a night out with your face in the ashtray (Firetree 100% is the exception). But these, from Willie’s Cacao, very much make the cut. An absolute joy of a dark chocolate and, boy, do you appreciate the sweetness of the raisins when you come across them.Date for your dairy: 26 and 27 September sees one of my favourite festivals – theAldeburgh Food and Drink Fairin my glorious Suffolk. Various wonderful chocolate makers will be there, as well as lots of other food and drink. The atmosphere is always jolly and you may spot me walking around in my chocolate cord flares.Explore more on these topicsChocolateThe chocolate diariesFoodShareReuse this content

title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for Richard Olney’s saffron and tomato rice | Food | The Guardian
description: Laborious to harvest and extortionately priced, the sunset-coloured stigmas of the saffron crocus have an extraordinarily warm, pungent taste. Fortunately, however, a little goes a very long way …
Author: Rachel Roddy
Headline: Laborious to harvest and extortionately priced, the sunset-coloured stigmas of the saffron crocus have an extraordinarily warm, pungent taste. Fortunately, however, a little goes a very long way …
Content: Rachel Roddy's take on Richard Olney’s saffron and tomato rice.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The Guardian.View image in fullscreenRachel Roddy's take on Richard Olney’s saffron and tomato rice.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The Guardian.A kitchen in RomeFoodRachel Roddy’s recipe for Richard Olney’s saffron and tomato riceLaborious to harvest and extortionately priced, the sunset-coloured stigmas of the saffron crocus have an extraordinarily warm, pungent taste. Fortunately, however, a little goes a very long way …Rachel RoddyThu 27 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe saffron crocus has six lilac-purple flowers, three yellow stamens and three orange-red stigmas that extend beyond the petals like the wiry antennae of an insect. The thread-like stigmas have to be picked only by hand when the flowers are fully open, a laborious, finickety job that hasn’t changed much since ancient times. Then, to avoid the colour and flavour fading, the stigmas need to be dried very quickly, a process that reduces their weight by about 80%. Tens of thousands of fiery-looking filaments are required to produce half a kilogram of the dried threads, which make the “hay” or powder we know as saffron and explains the exorbitant cost. Fortunately, just a few threads of this precious spice go a long way.Native to Crete, Iran and south-west Asia, the saffron crocus has been cultivated since the dawn of civilisation for its medicinal properties, as well as for use in cosmetics, perfume, food and as a dye. According to Alan Davidson inThe Oxford Companion to Food, the Moguls brought the use of saffron from Persia to India, in particular Kashmir; meanwhile, in the westward direction, the Arabs were cultivating saffron in Spain by AD960, although it was not until the 13th century that cultivation spread to Italy, France, Germany and England, particularly Essex. In his bookThe Last Food of England, Marwood Yeatman describes the “orderly strips of purple flowers inches apart in beds of up to 10ft wide” growing in a field outside the prosperous, half-timbered Essex wool town of Chipping Walden. “The women (‘crokers’) stooped to lift the crop on damp and dewy September mornings.” By the early 1500s, Chipping Walden had been renamed Saffron Walden.To preserve the colour and flavour, the stigma must be dried immediately without damage. In hotter, drier countries, this was – and still is – done outside in the shade. An alternative method is to use mesh trays over charcoal, while in England kilns were used, and the resulting threads or “chives”were sold either as hay saffron or pressed between weighted boards. In a year-long project by the University of Cambridge, researchers found documents from as late as 1871 recording thefts of saffron from warehouses and druggists. But, just a few decades later, while a few individuals continued to grow saffron for their own use, commercial cultivation in Britain had ceased.These days,growers such as David Smale, a geophysicist by training, are cultivating English saffron commercially, and it is Smale’s advice I followed this week when I madeRichard Olney’s recipe for buttered saffron rice and slivers of ripe, carefully peeled tomatoes: a delicate, delicious dish that can be served with poached chicken, fish or hard-boiled eggs.Remember, to release their sunset colour and extraordinarily warm, pungent, slightly metallic taste and hay-like fragrance, the saffron threads need to be soaked and infused. Smale notes that, “after infusing, the strands should be very pale and the colour should have leached into the liquid”, adding that “it takes just 10 or so saffron strands” for an exquisite effect.Saffron rice with tomatoServes450g butter3 tbsp olive oil1 medium onion, peeled and finely dicedSalt300g long-grainrice6-10 saffron strands, soaked in 2 tsp just-warm water500mllight vegetable stock, or water500g fresh tomatoes– ripe, flavoursome ones, ideallyIn a heavy-based casserole or saute pan with a lid, melt the butter and oil over a medium-low heat, add the onion and a pinch of salt, then cook, stirring regularly, for about 10 minutes, until the onion softens but remains pale.Add the rice and the saffron with its soaking water and stir for a minute until all the grains glisten. Add the water or stock, stir a few times, then turn down the heat to the gentlest simmer, cover and cook for 18-20 minutes, until the rice is tender.While the rice is cooking, peel the tomatoes by immersing them in boiling water for five minutes, then draining and dunking them in cold water, at which point the skins should pull away easily. Quarter the tomatoes, brush away the seeds and cut the flesh into thin strips or small cubes.When the rice is cooked, pull it off the heat and leave to sit for 10 minutes, during which time it will dry and swell. Finally, stir in the tomatoes and season with salt to taste.Explore more on these topicsFoodA kitchen in RomeItalian food and drinkRiceTomatoesMain courseStarterVegetablesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: You be the judge: should my partner stop eating off other people’s plates? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Helen says grabbing friends’ leftovers is a no-no. Bill thinks wasting food is wrong. You decide who should eat their words
Author: Georgina Lawton
Headline: Helen says grabbing friends’ leftovers is a no-no. Bill thinks wasting food is wrong. You decide who should eat their words
Content: Illustration: Igor Bastidas/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Igor Bastidas/The GuardianYou be the judgeLife and styleYou be the judge: should my partner stop eating off other people’s plates?Helen says grabbing friends’ leftovers is a no-no. Bill thinks wasting food is wrong. You decide who should eat their wordsFind out how to get a disagreement settled or become a jurorInterviews byGeorgina LawtonThu 27 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 12.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheprosecution: Helendouble quotation markI know Billhates waste, but pouncing on people’s leftovers is embarrassing, unhygienic and rudeMy partner, Bill, hates food waste and is passionate about sustainability and the environment. He says: “Thank you, chicken,” or “Thank you, duck,” before he eats, which I think is quite sweet.But Bill’s ethos means he also takes food off other people’s plates, which is an issue for me, particularly in public. I don’t like the way he does it. He’ll wait until everyone’s finished and the waiter is clearing the plates. Then, at the last minute, he’ll grab something.We live in Lisbon, and were recently having dinner with friends we hadn’t seen in a long time. The place was busy and the waitress was rushed off her feet. She came to clear our plates and Bill reached across to finish the duck breast our friends had ordered. He didn’t even say: “Have you finished with your duck?” I think that’s rude.The waitress was trying to clear the table while Bill fished around eating the scraps. It felt inconsiderate to keep everyone waiting. If we’d been with his mum, I’d have made less of an issue of it, but with friends we rarely see I found it embarrassing.double quotation markOnce, I threw away a melon rind and he took it out of the bin to eat the tiny bits of fruit left on itThis isn’t a one-off. At home, if friends are over, he’ll never let something go to waste. I’ve watched him remove mould off leftovers in our fridge and eat them, and he scrapes leftover rice off other people’s plates.I care about the environment too. I don’t throw food away without thinking, but if something has gone off, I will. Bill is militant about what goes in the bin. Once, I threw away a melon rind and he took it out of the bin to eat the tiny bits of watermelon on it.In Lisbon, people often share food when eating out. In a tapas situation, it’s fine to pick at leftovers as everyone is helping themselves. But to me it feels rude and unhygienic to take leftovers off someone else’s plate. Bill often eats far more than he actually wants, then complains about how full he is.I know his intentions come from a good place. I’m not asking him to waste food. But if he’s going to ask for somebody’s leftovers, I wish he’d do it earlier rather than waiting until somebody is clearing the plates.You be the judge – send us your domestic disputesRead moreThedefence: Billdouble quotation markI worked in renewablesand believewasting food, especially meat, is wrong – why throw it away?Some of Helen’s points have been taken out of context. It wasn’t really our friends’ duck dish, because it was a tapas-style meal. I was thinking: “We’re kind of sharing that.”Normally, I’ll wait until everyone’s stopped eating and then ask: “Are you finished?” I just forgot. I was waiting for the moment to pounce on it. I can see it was more embarrassing for Helen because the whole table witnessed it. I don’t think the waitress was waiting long, certainly not more than a minute, but I appreciate that it was awkward.I hate food waste. A few grains of rice or a bit of salad isn’t an issue, but I struggle with seeing meat wasted. I’m concerned about animal welfare and the fact that an animal has died. You could say that makes me hypocritical, because I eat meat, but when I see this piece of beautiful pan-fried duck, I don’t think it should go in the bin. It’s about respect for the animal and not letting it go to waste.Sometimes I probably come across as self-righteous. I used to work in renewables and I feel strongly about how much food we waste globally. I like educating people.double quotation markI realise my behaviour was a bit odd but the bin bag I picked the melon out of was newI don’t think there’s anything wrong with asking to eat people’s leftovers to reduce food waste. There are limits, of course. If it was a business meeting or dinner with my boss, I wouldn’t do it. If I knew it would jeopardise things for Helen socially, I’d be on my best behaviour. Around family and close friends, though, I don’t see it as a bad thing.As for the watermelon, the bin bag I picked it out of was brand new. The melon rind was right on top with barely anything else in there. I realise my behaviour was a bit odd. I don’t want to make myself ill, and if food has genuinely gone off, I’ll throw it away. Equally, if anyone at the table was ill, I wouldn’t pick at food and spread germs by eating from their plate.I know I can get carried away. But it always comes back to one thing: I don’t think good food, especially meat, should go to waste if it could be eaten.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNames have been changedThe jury of Guardian readersIf this was a one-off occurrence and Bill just forgot to ask the others before tucking in, then he can be forgiven. But if he makes a habit of “pouncing” on his neighbours’ food without warning, they won’t stick around for long.Christian, 50Eliminating food waste in your own home is responsible and aligned with Bill’s morals, but time and place should be considered. Ultimately, he should acknowledge Helen’s embarrassment and adjust his behaviour in public accordingly.Tracey, 33While I sympathise with Bill’s wish to reduce food waste, especially meat, taking food from others’ plates is rude and embarrassing. He and Helen should establish clear boundaries they both agree on, maybe keeping it to family meals. Also, if animal welfare matters so much, why not become vegetarian?Alicja, 33There’s no problem with finishing leftovers if you ask politely. But Bill using the environment as an excuse, instead of just apologising, suggests that he’ll keep forgetting his manners. He should at least stop eating meat if he’s going to lecture others on food waste.Sinead, 25I think it’s fine to swoop on other people’s food, but I may be biased because I do it myself. A lot. These are Bill’s friends – and what is a bit of spit between friends? His heart is in the right place.Kitty, 34Now you be the judgeIn our online poll, tell us: should Bill bin his leftovers habit?The poll closes on Wednesday 2 September at 9am BSTLast week’s resultsWe asked if Dave shouldstop hogging his partner’s preferred side of the bed88%of you said yes –Dave is guilty12%of you said no –Dave is not guiltyExplore more on these topicsLife and styleYou be the judgeRelationshipsHygienefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Architourism in France: the retro futurist seaside town near Montpellier that’s out of this world | France holidays | The Guardian
description: With buildings inspired by Mayan pyramids and featuring ‘intergalactic curves’, La Grande-Motte is a great alternative beach resort for fans of modern architecture
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: With buildings inspired by Mayan pyramids and featuring ‘intergalactic curves’, La Grande-Motte is a great alternative beach resort for fans of modern architecture
Content: The sport harbour in the futuristic seaside town of La Grande-Motte.Photograph: Michael Runkel/Robert Harding/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe sport harbour in the futuristic seaside town of La Grande-Motte.Photograph: Michael Runkel/Robert Harding/Getty ImagesFrance holidaysArchitourism in France: the retro futurist seaside town near Montpellier that’s out of this worldBuilt in the 60s and 70s to curb a holiday exodus to Spain, with apartments inspired by Mayan pyramids and featuring ‘intergalactic curves’, La Grande-Motte is having another moment in the sun with fans of modern architectureMark C O’FlahertyThu 27 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 02.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy dream holiday is a trip back in time. Not to see the results of seismic Pompeii or 15th-century Machu Picchu – although I love both – but somewhere created specifically between the mid 1950s and 1970s, when cities were getting weird. I love postwar architourism, exploring urban planning at its most frenzied and optimistic. I have relished trips to Niemeyer’s Brasília and Le Corbusier’s Chandigarh in India, where the monumental and visionary modernist architecture and interiors are at odds with the minimal population. So La Grande-Motte, the retro futurist folly of a resort town on the southern coast of France, a 30-minute drive from Montpellier, had long been on my “must visit” list.The tourist board of this Occitanie seaside town likes to flag up some superficial parallels between it and the aforementioned cities, but this isn’t a high-concept capital city or administrative hub. It was built in the late 1960s and early 1970s purely to persuade the French to stop going south to the Costa Brava in Spain. As part of an initiative by the French government, a stretch of windswept mosquito-infested coast between Montpellier and Perpignan, including Gruissan and Port Leucate, was reimagined as an alternative to the Côte d’Azur with several new-build beach towns. La Grande-Motte would be the weirdest project. It was made for fun. It’s also well positioned to visit the nearby salt marshes and 13th-century walled-in town of Aigues-Mortes, for when you want to feel as if you’ve ticked a few more holiday boxes.The mastermind behind the town’s architecture, Jean Balladur, took inspiration from temples and Mesoamerican pyramids from the first century, imagining what the 21st century would look like in the 1970s. Why shouldn’t modernist apartments be arranged in the shape of a Maya pyramid, or an intergalactic curve? I rented a tiny studio with my husband in the Incas building for part of my trip, and while there was nothing in the way of high design about the interior, being on that terrace immersed us in a timewarp.View image in fullscreenShops and apartments facing the main port.Photograph: Mark C O’FlahertyWalking around Point Zéro (named for being the site of the earliest construction), home to La Grande-Motte’s main beach, all looks fairly standard: families playing on the sand, couples drinking cocktails outside cafes. The beach gained a Blue Flag award for environmental management and water quality in 2025. But the place is unique: the ferris wheel is solar powered and the buildings suggest you’re on another planet entirely – there are no rectangular blocks and few right angles to be seen. The urban planning has been driven by pedestrian pathways and cycle routes, punctuated by thousands of trees.double quotation markIt seems a renaissance is under way, as the grandchildren of people who first bought apartments here are discovering itOn the beach there are concrete sculptures by artistJoséphine Chevry, which look like the tips of the wartime sound mirrors in Dungeness, Kent. Chevry created them to help shape the dunes (AKA “the big mound”) but also to serve as functional wind breakers and shade when Point Zéro was created. They’re now mostly buried in the sand. Time has moved on but they will for ever be core to the town’s concept.View image in fullscreenThe beach at Le Couchant seen through one of the town’s many sculptures.Photograph: Hemis/AlamyThe place has had cyclical fortunes. As with many seaside towns, it fell from grace in the 1980s. It was gauche. In 2014 the fashion designer Simon Porte Jacquemus created a nostalgic collection and book in homage to the town and talked to AnOther Magazineof its “trashy reputation”, but he also said he found it “inspiring and exciting” and remembered his holidays there as a child. And it seems a renaissance is under way as the grandchildren of people who first bought apartments here are discovering it.double quotation markThe balconies jut out like theatre boxes and create an optical illusion of the building being slantedI’d recommend the fabulously vintage three-starHotel Le Quetzal(doubles from €114 room-only) as an interesting base. It feels brilliantly 1970s, being part of the original wave of development in the town, but was refurbished a few years ago so the essentials are fresh and modern. Its design is as interesting as anywhere in town: the balconies jut out like theatre boxes and create an optical illusion of the building being slanted. There’s no restaurant but people microwave meals in the lobby or bring back a margherita from nearbyL’Atelier de la Pizzato have on their balcony.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA couple of days by the pool here are great, fending off seagulls from your pain au chocolate at breakfast and watching stray cats wander around the loungers; the same families have been coming for years. Nearby,L’innatenduis a better restaurant than anything on the seafront (I particularly recommend the squid with black rice), although the most enjoyable meal I had was a bunch of simple marinated skewers atLa Guinguette des Alizés, opposite the seafront carousel on Avenue du Couchant that looks like a piece of pop art.View image in fullscreenBalladur’s architecture seems to anticipate the 21st century from the 1970s viewpoint.Photograph: Remi A/Getty ImagesStrolling around La Grande-Motte’s apartment blocks was as fascinating to me as a visit to the Colosseum. I walked through the open-air theatre that looks like a derelict World’s Fair site but is used for shows regularly, around the elegant white bow shape of Saint-Augustin’s church, down to the water and the Big Pyramid apartment complex facing the yachts on the dock, and to the low and curved buildings of Le Couchant. I spent hours photographing stairwells and walkways, and the hundreds of balconies that make the town the sum of its geometric parts – graphic beauty reminiscent of the Bauhaus, Saul Bass posters and Verner Panton furniture. La Grande-Motte is a sunny, gleaming white vision of a future that we could never live up to. Or perhaps deserve.Explore more on these topicsFrance holidaysCultural tripsCity breaksEurope holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to spot a psychopath: ‘It’s like the difference between a domestic cat and a wild cat’ | Psychology | The Guardian
description: People with persistent predatory personalities cause an inordinate amount of pain. Recently, our shared understanding of them has grown – and it could help protect us
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: People with persistent predatory personalities cause an inordinate amount of pain. Recently, our shared understanding of them has grown – and it could help protect us
Content: Malignant narcissist, psychopath, Machiavellian, toxic leader – all part of the same phenomenon, the Dark Personality.Composite: Guardian Design/Westend61/Getty Images/posed by modelsView image in fullscreenMalignant narcissist, psychopath, Machiavellian, toxic leader – all part of the same phenomenon, the Dark Personality.Composite: Guardian Design/Westend61/Getty Images/posed by modelsPsychologyHow to spot a psychopath: ‘It’s like the difference between a domestic cat and a wild cat’People with persistent predatory personalities cause an inordinate amount of pain. Recently, our shared understanding of them has grown – and it could help protect usZoe WilliamsThu 27 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 04.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe classic checklist for psychopathy was developed in 1980 by Prof Robert Hare, who is still the recognised giant of the territory. The 20 traits, which ranged from pathological lying to a lack of empathy, were based entirely on prison populations. This worked because not only did Hare have the benefit of a large sample, with pronounced psychopathic behaviours, but he was able to compare interviews and self-reporting with data collected about the individuals – so inconsistencies could be identified.However, Hare knew this approach was limited. In 1976, he said that he simply didn’t know to what extent his results could be generalised to non-incarcerated psychopaths, including female ones. “Research into the socially successful psychopath is badly needed,” he concluded. Even decades later in the early 2000s, when Hare wanted to look into psychopaths in politics, he still needed to go to prison to find them (Pinochet’s henchmen in Chilean jails). Research into the higher-functioning psychopath – who doesn’t get caught, or maybe doesn’t even resort to crime – has proved elusive, not least because self-reporting questionnaires don’t work. Psychopaths lie; arguably, that’s their main thing.View image in fullscreenHare studied Pinochet’s henchmen.Photograph: APIt wasn’t from a forensic psychology but a business studies background that Dr Karen Mitchell arrived in the territory of high-functioning psychopathy. By the late 2010s, she’d spent 30 years working as a consultant on large-scale change in corporate culture. Her work tended to be with organisations in crisis: “So it might be market alignment, or deaths or suicides in companies,” she tells me from her home in Australia. Observing the sheer number of problems at work that stemmed from specific individuals with predatory traits, she started to research those same “dark personality” behaviours in other precincts. “Child sex abuse in religion, coercive control in human trafficking and domestic violence and terrorism,” she says. “When you look at all our global knowledge on human predators, there are so many fields and none of them interact.”This matters because predatory personalities cause an astronomical amount of harm. We’re bad at recognising them interpersonally, for reasons to be discussed, but we’re also bad at pattern finding in aggregate – mainly because different disciplines have so many different names for these kinds of people. Mitchell lists some of the terms: “Malignant narcissist, dark triad, psychopath, coercive controller, primary psychopath, grandiose narcissist, corporate psychopath, Machiavellian, dark tetrad, covert narcissist, toxic leader.” These are all traits that she argues are part of the same phenomenon, the Dark Personality, or the Persistent Predatory Personality.View image in fullscreenPredatory personalities are hard to recognise, but they can cause an astronomical amount of harm.Photograph: Victor Dyomin/Getty ImagesMitchell embarked on a PhD, published in 2024, in which she interviewed people who had met persistent predatory personalities professionally – some clinical, but others not, from fields as wide as HR, social work, family courts, the FBI and other law enforcement agencies, church leaders, and academics from different fields.Her method, she says, was unorthodox, being qualitative, not quantitative. And some of her conclusions directly contradict clinical definitions of psychopathy, which rely heavily on impulsivity. Mitchell says this is because other definitions such as Hare’s are derived from the prison population, which is the low-functioning end of the scale. “People try and put Hare’s stuff into workplaces and domestic violence spheres, but there’s no way you can overlay something so blunt, built from criminal offenders, on to sophisticated CEO-type behaviours.”Mitchell’s interviews are remarkable. People from very different fields say alarmingly similar things: there’s one question about whether the interviewee had themselves ever been frightened of a persistent predatory personality (bear in mind that these weren’t victims, they were seasoned professionals) and the answers came back: “I constantly worry that he will ruin my career” (from an HR person); “I worry that they will … want to seek revenge” (from a social worker); “I am pretty sure there are no lengths to which this man would not go to, to see that I am destroyed” (expert practitioner from the charity sector). These and arguably every statement from the interviews are so extreme that you can’t imagine saying them socially because you would sound mad – which some testimonies explicitly address. “People can’t get it. People who don’t work in our fields … often don’t hear about or see the kind of evilness perpetrated on others, and just can’t believe it. Whereas, unfortunately, it’s commonplace in my work.” (That’s from one forensic expert practitioner).From this research, which took her five years, Mitchell built a template of 20 attributes, divided into four clusters, and 25 tactics that would identify a high-functioning persistent predatory personality type. Cluster one includes a need for control; a grandiose sense of self; pathological inner response to challenge; vengefulness; refusal to compromise. Cluster two includes being predatory or exploitative; sadistic and cruel; having a low regard for laws, agreements, social and moral codes; no boundaries in sexual relationships; unreasonable expectations of others. Cluster three relates to the truth: Dark Personalities cultivate a façade of normality; they are chameleon-like; dishonest; devious and manipulative; and unwilling to accept responsibility for the negative impacts they cause. Finally, cluster four is around the Dark Personality’s own interior life: their emotions are acted and they do not experience affinity or the joy that comes with it; they are callous and devoid of empathy; unremorseful; self-interested; and brazen.View image in fullscreen‘Across the ages, we’ve had people who exploit other peoples’s altruism.’ … Essi VidingPhotograph: John MoloneyEssi Viding, a professor of developmental psychopathology at UCL, is a leading figure from the classic research sphere, co-director of the Developmental Risk and Resilience Unit and Hare’s natural successor in many ways. “I often think of these individuals as having an in-group of one,” she says. “In social psychology, we talk about people that we care about, and most of us, because we’re group-living animals, collaborate, do altruistic acts, we’ll behave in ways that across the ages have increased our survival. But across the ages, we’ve had people who exploit other people’s altruism, and when the chips come down, only care about themselves.”Viding fixes on the traits that leave society extremely bad at protecting itself against predatory behaviour. We all know that people lie, but think instinctively that we know when we’re being lied to. “These individuals almost short-circuit us in our ability to detect the danger signals until it’s too late,” Viding says. “The majority of us, if we get caught lying, look deeply uncomfortable. It’s not nice to get caught lying, we worry about our reputation, it’s embarrassing. But these individuals are not embarrassed when they’re caught lying. This has not been formally tested, but one might hypothesise that they take people in much more readily, precisely because they display these characteristics of extreme confidence and do not seem nervous.” She cites a2019 paperin the Journal of Personality Disorders which developed the idea that behaviours which don’t normally go together in the human population – for example, absolute confidence and total untruth – tend to go together in Dark Personalities. This, Viding says, is why these people “can often do a lot of damage before anyone catches them”.This causes much more havoc outside prisons than it does in them. While Mitchell says she stays out of politics, her tactics, once you see them assembled, are strikingly visible on the world stage. Indeed, the first time I read the phrase “dark triad” was when Donald Trump got elected the first time around.The idea of a “pathocracy”, a democracy of normal people taken over by psychopaths, was conceived by an obscure Polish psychologist, Andrew Lobaczewski, who had lived under both the Nazis and then Soviet-era communists. His ideas never landed, because “the psychology publishers thought it was too political, and the political publishers thought it was too psychological,” according to editor and bloggerHarrison Koehli. It’s unfashionable to the point of being taboo in psychiatry and psychology now to ascribe personality disorders to public figures. “One of the perils of bringing psychology into politics is that it’s very easy for anyone with any given political perspective to look at their political enemies or rivals and say: ‘OK, well, they’re all psychopaths,’” says Koehli. There’s also the Goldwater Rule, which established as a psychiatric principle that professionals are not allowed to diagnose public figures they haven’t had clinical contact with or met (this was after 1,189 psychiatrists declared Barry Goldwater unfit to be president in the 1964 election). Viding, however, finds the fixation with diagnosis perhaps irrelevant in this context. “I always find the obsession with diagnosing these people interesting. You don’t need to diagnose them, there are a set of personality traits, and you can recognise individuals with those traits. If someone’s in political power, you can see those exemplified in behaviour, and most people are perfectly capable of making an assessment of what that signifies.”View image in fullscreenA ‘pathocracy’ is when a democracy is taken over by psychopaths.Photograph: Connect Images/Getty ImagesBrazen lying in public life is a tactic Lobaczewski recognised – he called it the “reversive blockade”. Koehli describes it as: “When you tell a lie convincingly and it’s such an absurd lie, most people’s automatic reaction is that they can’t comprehend a lie told on that scale, so they try to find the ‘golden mean’ between the statement and the reality. But that, Lobaczewski says, is the intention of the big lie. They know it will sow confusion.” The impact on the population over which a dark personality presides is huge: some will try and find that golden mean; others will remain steadfast in calling it a lie and fall out with the first lot; others will try to adjust their own reality to make the lie true; while others will become inured to the new normal – that we just all lie now.On an interpersonal level, this brazenness is even more head-spinning. Often both predator and victim know it’s a lie, or the predator is accusing the victim of exactly the thing he or she just did, or the lie has been expressed using the victim’s own language. Reverse attribution is so familiar in the domestic-abuse sphere that it has its own acronym – Darvo, for deny, attack, reverse victim and offender – yet it still absolutely fogs the victims, who feel their credibility is permanently in doubt. In the workplace, the effects are also devastating, because there tend to be spectators who themselves have a decisive impact on the outcome. As Mitchell says about one of her interviewees who worked in HR: “People were genuinely convinced the dark personality was the victim and the victim was the dark personality. It destroyed the life of the victim, even though they had an excellent professional track record.”The reality is that the higher the levels of these traits, the wider the harm caused. Mitchell describes one of her research participants, “The head of a large Catholic diocese, in charge of child sex abuse. She had a horrible job, right? Incredible, impeccable credentials, CEO of several children’s organisations. She’d go to the Holy See and say, ‘Look, this person has been abusing children’ and they’d go: ‘Really? But he’s such a nice guy.’”In the non-criminal, non-violent space of endless persecution – as might happen in a workplace – there are layers of disbelief. People can’t fathom that the Dark Personalityisdark, they can’t believe that anyone would want to be deliberately harmful, they can’t process that harm was caused at all. It was bracing to hear Mitchell describe workplace suicides as an issue that partly spurred her research, since it is completely forbidden, in the mental health world, to ascribe a person’s suicide to anyone else’s behaviour. Yet alandmark ruling in Francedid exactly that in 2019, and found “torment” in the workplace, linked to a number of executives, had created the culture at France Télécom in which 19 employees took their own lives, 12 attempted suicide, and eight suffered from serious depression, between 2006 and 2009. Jane Monckton-Smith, professor of public protection at the University of Gloucestershire, hassaid in the pastthat, if we included provoked suicides, domestic homicide statistics could be multiplied “five, six or seven times”.In Hare’s study of Pinochet’s lieutenants, which spanned 20 years and was written up in 2022, “when they looked at individuals who were commanding officers, this top brass had really high levels of psychopathic features, particularly the lack of empathy for others,” says Viding.Mitchell delivers her conclusion with businesslike bluntness: “These are completely boundary-less, dangerous people with very different brains – it’s like the difference between a domestic cat and a wild cat. Millions and millions of people have been hurt because we haven’t known the red flags, so we have to put them out there and then teach people to be discerning.” Viding, in different terms, and by a different route, has the same conclusion. “As I’ve done this research for 20-plus years now, I have increasingly started to think we really need to understand more about how we can inoculate people against being victimised. Because based on the literature, and what little I know about evolutionary and cross-cultural psychology, we are very unlikely to weed these traits out.”Explore more on these topicsPsychologyPsychiatryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: What caused the catastrophic flood in Nepal and Tibet – and how does a glacier collapse? | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: A glacial collapse registering as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event occurred near the border on Wednesday morning
Author: Donna Lu
Headline: A glacial collapse registering as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event occurred near the border on Wednesday morning
Content: What happened in Nepal? Scientists are starting to piece together the possible causes of the devastating Nepal-Tibet flash floods, which have killed hundreds.Photograph: Safal Prakash Shrestha/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenWhat happened in Nepal? Scientists are starting to piece together the possible causes of the devastating Nepal-Tibet flash floods, which have killed hundreds.Photograph: Safal Prakash Shrestha/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockNepal-Tibet flood disasterExplainerWhat caused the catastrophic flood in Nepal and Tibet – and how does a glacier collapse?A glacial collapse registering as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event occurred near the border on Wednesday morningDonna LuThu 27 Aug 2026 10.53 EDTFirst published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 01.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHundreds of people have died in catastrophic flash floods inNepal. Here’s what we know so far about what caused the disaster.What happened and when?On Wednesday morning local time, a landslide of ice and rock resulted in a torrent of mud, water and debris bursting the banks of the Trishuli River, also known as the Bhotekoshi, which runs between China and Nepal. Homes, roads, bridges and power plants were swept away.Experts at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development said water levels on the Trishuli River rose by as much as nine metres in half an hour. The Lhende Khola River, a tributary of the Trishuli, was most affected, they said.Map of where the glacial collapse occurredWhat caused the flooding in Nepal?Nepal’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, told the country’s parliament on Wednesday that initial reports suggested the floods could have been caused by an earthquake in the ⁠area that triggered a landslide.However, theUS Geological Survey(USGS) subsequently said that a glacial collapse was responsible for the seismic event and for the flooding itself.The USGS noted that the glacial collapse had registered as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event, occurring near the border between Nepal and China at 8.37am local time on Wednesday.According to Daniel Shugar, a geomorphologist and associate professor at the University of Calgary in Canada, initial satellite analysis showed a 0.2 sq km chunk of ice had “collapsed about 1.2km vertically”.“What I can see in … satellite imagery from Planet Labs, the lower part of a glacier broke off at about 5,200 metres and crashed on to the valley floor about 1,200 metres below,” he ​said.Before and after images showing the glacier’s collapseBefore and after images showing the glacier’s collapseThe imagery seemed to show that a large ‌amount of snow had melted in the 24 hours prior to the disaster, he said. “Some of the glaciers in the valley were covered in snow yesterday and today they are mostly bare ice. So in other words (and I haven’t seen any weather station data yet), it was probably warm.”Shugar said construction could also be a factor.Prof Andrew Mackintosh, a glaciologist at Monash University in Melbourne, said it was unclear whether the collapse was isolated to the glacier, or was the “whole mountainside collapsing that included part of the glacier”.“When a glacier of that scale collapses, it generates a lot of water, and then there’s a cascading sequence of events … where the water and the sediment combine and bulks up and creates the flood.”How often do glaciers collapse – and is the climate crisis a factor?“These sorts of large glacier collapses are really shocking,” Mackintosh said. “It’s hard as a glaciologist not be alarmed by these events that seem different to what we’ve observed previously.”However, he said there had been “so few of these documented that we’re not really able to make very clear statements about the specific relationship between glacier collapse and climate change yet”. Scientists do, however, “have very high confidence in the relationship between glacier retreat and climate change”.“We also know that mountain permafrost is degrading under a warming climate,” Mackintosh added. He describedpermafrost, ground that is frozen year round, as being akin to a “glue that holds the rock and sometimes adjacent glaciers … together on very steep slopes”.The Himalayas – spanning Nepal, India, China, Bhutan and Pakistan – are warmingtwice as fastas the global average, putting the region at increased risk ofavalanches,landslidesand floods.The UN said in 2023 that Nepal’s mountains had lost close to one-third of their ice in just over 30 years due to global heating. Anassessmentpublished that year found that the Hindu Kush Himalayan glaciers had disappeared 65% faster between 2011 and 2020 than in the previous decade.In 2021, aHimalayan glacier broke offand caused flash flooding in the Indian state of Uttarakhand, leaving 200 peopledead or missing. Subsequentresearchsuggested that a 27m-cubic-metre avalanche of rock and glacier ice had transformed into “an extraordinarily large and mobile debris flow”.Though not thought to be a cause of the August 2026 event, mountain areas are also at risk of “glacial lake outburst floods”.Glacial lakes form behind natural dams as a result of glacier melt, and can cause catastrophic outburst floods if their natural dam walls are breached.Adrian McCallum, a glaciologist, polar engineer and associate professor at the University of the Sunshine Coast in Australia, said: “With a warming climate, glaciers recede, ice becomes water, that water gets trapped.”More than12,000 deathshave already been attributed to such floods globally.According to the UN, Nepal has more than 2,000 glacial lakes, of which 21 are considered potentially dangerous.With Reuters and Associated Press9:21‘Tsunami from the sky:’ floods leave trail of devastation in Nepal and Tibet - The LatestExplore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterClimate crisisFloodingTibetChinaNepalexplainersShareReuse this content

title: Drugs in pastries, months on the run: the double-life of Lebanese influencer Dr Food | Lebanon | The Guardian
description: Georges Dib, who had 8.7m TikTok followers, was arrested on Sunday after being sentenced in absentia to life in prison
Author: William Christou
Headline: Georges Dib, who had 8.7m TikTok followers, was arrested on Sunday after being sentenced in absentia to life in prison
Content: Georges Dib, AKA Dr Food, whom security forces finally managed to track down after months of surveillance.Photograph: Georges Dib/InstagramView image in fullscreenGeorges Dib, AKA Dr Food, whom security forces finally managed to track down after months of surveillance.Photograph: Georges Dib/InstagramLebanonDrugs in pastries, months on the run: the double-life of Lebanese influencer Dr FoodGeorges Dib, who had 8.7m TikTok followers, was arrested on Sunday after being sentenced in absentia to life in prisonWilliam Christouin BeirutThu 27 Aug 2026 05.58 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 13.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKnown to his 8.7mTikTokfollowers as Dr Food, Georges Dib was a popular Lebanese food influencer who would hold giveaways, post behind-the-scenes tours of his food production facilities and wax philosophical about the ingredients of success.But Lebanese authorities allege that when the camera was off, the chef was living a double life. For months they sought his arrest on charges of international drug trafficking and production, accusing him of hiding narcotics in his pastries.On Sunday, security forces finally managed to track him down to a house in Akkar, northLebanon, after months of surveillance.Dib had been sentenced in absentia last month to life imprisonment with hard labour for drug trafficking. Investigators alleged they had found drugs hidden in his branded chocolates and biscuits, intended to be shipped abroad.View image in fullscreenDib’s videos on social media helped Lebanese authorities to track him down.Photograph: Georges Dib/InstagramThe accusation was tied to a 2024 drug bust in which 820kg (1,800lb) of hashish was found hidden in cakes. A warrant had already been issued for his arrest, though it had previously been suspected he was outside the country.Despite the charges and warrant, Dr Food evaded authorities for a year and a half, continuing to post videos on his TikTok page without addressing the allegations against him. In one video, he filmed himself on Beirut’s Corniche asking any of his followers who had been displaced by the Israel-Hezbollah war what food they missed, so that he could deliver it to them.Less than two weeks ago, Dr Food filmed himself in what appeared to be one of his food production facilities, showing his followers how he made cheese.“He would broadcast live [videos] and directly after … he would change his car and mobile and his house,” said a Lebanese security source. Ultimately, the source said, his videos helped authorities to track him down and carry out the arrest.Shortly after his detention, Dr Food’s Instagram page shared a food giveaway sweepstake that followers could enter.Lebanese authorities have tried to crack down onthe country’s reputation as a drug-smuggling hubin recent months, tightening controls at Beirut international airport and the port.Lebanon has faced pressure from the Arab Gulf, the main market for drugs in the Middle East, and the US, which wanted tighter checks to stop goods travelling to Hezbollah. The country has a long history with drug smuggling, as narco-gangs exploited its porous borders, plethora of militias and weak government to move drugs.During Syria’s civil war, hashish andcaptagon, a catch-all name for an amphetamine cocktail, would transit into Lebanon’s Bekaa valley and through the country’s port.Saudi Arabia halted the trade of fruit and vegetables with Lebanon in 2021, cutting off access for Lebanese produce to much of the Gulf market, after repeated shipments were found to be a front to smuggle captagon. Fake vegetables were being used as containers for the pills.Border wars: Syria’s new authorities grapple with Lebanese smugglersRead moreSince the fall of Bashar al-Assad, the former Syrian president, in December 2024, captagon production has shifted more towards Lebanon, with drugs flowing from there into Syria rather than the reverse. The ultimate destination for these narcotic shipments is Jordan and the Gulf.Dr Food is not Lebanon’s first TikTok star alleged by authorities to be leading a double life.In May 2024, Lebanese authorities uncovered an alleged child trafficking ring run through TikTok. They said a group of 30 traffickers would lure children through private messages, then sell compromising photos of them being sexually abused on the dark web.One of the most public figures alleged to be involved with the paedophile ring was a Lebanese barber with thousands of followers on TikTok, who would often post videos of himself giving haircuts to children. Authorities alleged he had used his viral fame to exploit children.On 31 July Lebanese courtsfoundsix men and one woman guilty of taking part in the child sexual abuse ring. Sentences ranged from four years to life in prison.Explore more on these topicsLebanonDrugsDrugs tradeTikTokMiddle East and north AfricaSocial mediafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: UK urged to help free British-Egyptian ‘arrested in Cairo over sister’s activism’ | Egypt | The Guardian
description: Lawyers claim Eman el-Shazly, from Birmingham, was detained in effort to silence her sister, a critic of Sisi regime
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Lawyers claim Eman el-Shazly, from Birmingham, was detained in effort to silence her sister, a critic of Sisi regime
Content: Eman el-Shazly, 45, was arrested on 16 August while visiting Egypt.Composite: suppliedView image in fullscreenEman el-Shazly, 45, was arrested on 16 August while visiting Egypt.Composite: suppliedEgyptUK urged to help free British-Egyptian ‘arrested in Cairo over sister’s activism’Lawyers claim Eman el-Shazly, from Birmingham, was detained in effort to silence her sister, a critic of Sisi regimePatrick WintourDiplomatic editorThu 27 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK Foreign Office has been asked to intervene to secure the release of a British-Egyptian woman who it is claimed has been arrested in Cairo because of her sister’s political activism.Eman el-Shazly, a 45-year-old based in Birmingham, was arrested on 16 August while visiting Egypt. Her lawyers say she has been detained in an attempt to silence her sister Mona, a relentless and harsh critic of the Egyptian government on her UK-based YouTube channel.Her two brothers have already spent three years in jail and, in May, were rearrested. They were previously held in pre-trial detention, facing charges of “promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation on social media, as well as broadcasting false news harmful to state security”.The UK Foreign Office has confirmed to the husband of Eman that she is being held in the Ramadan rehabilitation centre and her case has been given the same file number as that of her two brothers, Hassan and Eid.The government of PresidentAbdel Fatah al-Sisihas faced allegations that it frequently arrests relatives of political critics to put indirect pressure on the dissidents to end their overseas criticism of his rule or of state corruption. Much of Mona’s activism focuses on alleged cases of corruption inside the security services or public utilities, a highly sensitive subject in Egypt.Arfan Rashid, the lawyer acting for Eman’s husband with whom she has four children, says that unlike Mona his wife has never been involved in politics, and had gone to Cairo two months ago to look after her ill mother after the arrest of her two brothers.“There is ample evidence that Eman has been arrested to silence Mona,” Rashid said. He added that Eman had told the security officials she was no longer in contact with her sister, and that many family members had repeatedly asked her to stop her political activism in the UK, but to no effect.Mona confirmed to the Guardian that she had been asked to halt her activism by other family members, including to take down her YouTube videos.But she added: “I have done nothing wrong nor broken any law … I am a very strong woman, but it is very traumatic for me since 11 or 12 children are without their parents. It is a horrible situation, but the Egyptian government will not stop if I appear weak. The government is close to collapsing.”Rashid said the UK government had recognised the practice of “punishment by proxy” in Egypt in its country profile policy and information note published in March 2026. Human Rights Watch and the House of Commons library warned in 2021 of an escalating pattern in which Egyptian family members of critics living abroad were being targeted.Mona runs a YouTube channel in the UK that has 130,000 subscribers. She is also active on X, making specific and controversial claims about government officials.The UK’s Foreign Office representation in Cairo has asked for access to see Eman but has not yet received a positive reply.Eman’s husband, Zeesharn Moustapha, has said Egyptian police and security officers attended the family home where she was staying a few days before the arrest, and demanded that Eman tell Mona to stop publishing material against the Egyptian government.On X, Mona has claimed as many as five members of her family have been detained or harassed by the Egyptian authorities. She wrote: “Kinship is something beyond my family’s will, and I invite them to disown me to save themselves from this despicable, illegitimate dictator. I am the one opposing Sisi, not five individuals from my family. This is a crime against humanity that does not lapse with time.” She has lived in the UK for 18 years.Eman became a British citizen through marriage. Her lawyer has asked whether Alistair Burt, the UK’s new envoy on complex consular cases, should be asked to intervene by the Foreign Office. Burt was appointed a month ago and has been tasked with working to secure the release of British citizens held abroad.Burt has already met Gurpreet Singh Johal, the brother of Jagtar Singh Johal, who has been detained by the Indian authorities for nearly nine years without a conviction.The Foreign Office has been approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsEgyptAbdel Fatah al-SisiForeign policyAfricaMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump signs executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Mark Carney rejects attempt to rename lake as did several US governors, with Tony Evers mocking the move
Author: George Chidi
Headline: Mark Carney rejects attempt to rename lake as did several US governors, with Tony Evers mocking the move
Content: Donald Trump signs the executive order in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington DC on Thursday.Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump signs the executive order in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington DC on Thursday.Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty ImagesDonald TrumpTrump signs executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake AmericaMark Carney rejects attempt to rename lake as did several US governors, with Tony Evers mocking the moveUS politics live – latest updatesGeorge ChidiThu 27 Aug 2026 18.55 EDTFirst published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 13.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump signed an executive order on Thursday directing the federal government to rename Lake Ontario, making it Lake America, amid his escalating trade war with Canada.The order directs federal agencies to adopt the name-change on US maps, documents and databases. But Trump has no authority to rename Canada’s portion of the lake, nor to compelCanada, international legal bodies, international mapmakers, or the rest of the world to adopt a new name.The move follows a similar action the president took on the first day of his second term in office, when hesigned an orderrenaming the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America”.“We have a gulf and we have a lake – now all we need is an ocean. Maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific,” he told reporters, sitting at the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office. “Maybe we’ll change them both.”Propped behind the US president was a large map of the Great Lakes region, with “Lake America” printed in red lettering above Lake Ontario.Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister, rejected the US’s attempt to rename the body of water, explaining in a post on social media that its name comes from the language of the Indigenous Wendat people and predates both the Canadian Confederation and the US Declaration of Independence.“We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms,” hewroteon X. “Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always.”Tim Houston, the premier of Nova Scotia, responded: “We’re into some real foolishness now. It’s Lake Ontario, buddy.”Several US governors in the Great Lakes region also dismissed the name change.“New York won’t be calling it that,” the state’s governor, Democrat Kathy Hochulreplied. New York shares a border with the lake.Michigan governor Gretchen Whitmer, a Democrat,recalledthat school children learn the acronym H-O-M-E-S for the names of the five great lakes: Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie, Superior. And the Wisconsin governor, Democrat Tony Evers,mockedthe move by sharing a video of himself changing the name of Lake Michigan to Lake Wisconsin, signed on a restaurant napkin.The latest tweak of Canada’s nose by the US president comes as tensions fray between the US and its northern neighbor. Over the weekend, trade talks between Washington and Ottawa collapsed and the US imposed a 50% tariff on several Canadian imports, with Trump threatening another round of 50% duties on Canadian steel, trucks, cars and auto parts to take effect in the new year. Carney hit back with 25-50% tariffs on hundreds of US goods.“They want to be treated like a state, but they’re not a state,” Trump said, a nod to his previous suggestions that Canada should become the “51st state” in the union, a prospect that has enraged Canadians. “But they want to be treated like they’re a state, and so we just can’t do that any more.”Trump complained about a $60bn US trade deficit with Canada, which economists note is attributable almost entirely to US imports of oil; without that exchange, the US runs a sizable trade surplus. Trump claimed that American farmers were being charged a 400% tariff; about 97% of US agricultural exports to Canada enter duty-free under the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement, though over-quota eggs, milk and dairy have Canadian tariffs of up to 300%.“As you know, Canada has been ripping us off for a long time on trade. Sad,” Trump said after signing the executive order updating the Department of Interior’s naming conventions. “Even the military: we defend Canada for nothing. We don’t get anything. They don’t pay us to defend Canada. But we defend Canada.”Both Canada and the United States are Nato members and have treaty obligations of mutual defense under the North Atlantic Treaty, the Ogdensburg Agreement and numerous other treaties.Trump claimed the name change was something he had been considering for “a long time”.“We’ve notified all the various people we have to notify,” he said after signing the order … This is official effective immediately.”An administration official noted that the lake bordering Canada and the state of New York has most of its volume in the United States and that the deepest part of the lake is in US territory.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpCanadaAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: USS Abraham Lincoln to visit port in Thailand after more than 250 days at sea | US military | The Guardian
description: Thai navy says ‘routine’ visit’ will allow personnel to rest and recuperate amid reports of poor conditions onboard
Author: Anna Betts
Headline: Thai navy says ‘routine’ visit’ will allow personnel to rest and recuperate amid reports of poor conditions onboard
Content: In a photo supplied by the US navy, the USS Abraham Lincoln is seen in the Indian Ocean on 22 August.Photograph: Zoe Simpson/US Navy/Handout Via ReutersView image in fullscreenIn a photo supplied by the US navy, the USS Abraham Lincoln is seen in the Indian Ocean on 22 August.Photograph: Zoe Simpson/US Navy/Handout Via ReutersUS militaryUSS Abraham Lincoln to visit port in Thailand after more than 250 days at seaThai navy says ‘routine’ visit’ will allow personnel to rest and recuperate amid reports of poor conditions onboardAnna BettsThu 27 Aug 2026 11.05 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 12.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier is set to make a temporary stop inThailandnext week as it heads back to the United States, Thai navy officials said, after spendingmore than 250consecutive days at sea supportingUS operationsagainstIranamid recentreportsof poor living conditions and low morale onboard the vessel.The Lincoln left the Middle East several days ago after being relieved by theUSS George Washington, and is now headinghometo San Diego. A Thai navy official toldReutersthis week that the carrier was expected to make a brief port visit in Thailand next week for the crew to rest and recuperate before continuing their journey home.“The stop is ‌a ⁠routine port visit intended to allow personnel to rest and recuperate … as well as to receive logistical support,” the spokesperson for the Thai navy said.Earlier this week, the Thai navysaidthat three ships from a US navy carrier strike group would be making a brief port call in eastern Thailand to allow personnel to rest. No military exercises would take place during the visit, the statement added. The Thai navy did not identify ​the vessels or provide a date.Families of US sailors denounce Trump and Hegseth for ‘dismissing their experiences and calling them liars’Read moreThe planned stop comes as the Lincoln’s deployment has faced scrutiny in recent weeksamid reportsof poor living conditions onboard among its crew. Family members of sailors have described shortages of supplies and water, plumbing problems, low morale, andworsening mental healthamong the roughly5,000 personnelon the carrier. TheNavy Timesalso reported that there had been several attempts by sailors to jump overboard.On Wednesday, the wife of a sailor who jumped overboard toldMS Nowthat her husband, who she said had since returned to the US, was now facing disciplinary action from the navy.Charging documents viewed by MS Now reportedly accuse the sailor of violating Article 83 for “malingering”, which isdefined assomeone who, “with the intent to avoid work, duty, or service”, fakes “illness, physical disablement, mental lapse, or mental derangement” or “intentionally inflicts self-injury”.The document also reportedly accuses the sailor of violating Article 86 for “absence without leave” whichis whenthe service member, without authority, “fails to go to his appointed place of duty at the time prescribed”, “goes from that place” or “absents himself or remains absent from his unit, organization, or place of duty at which he is required to be at the time prescribed”.The couple, both 19, have a three-year-old son and welcomed a daughter in February while he was deployed. His wife told the outlet that he had requested paternity leave but was denied.The sailor is now reportedly facing non-judicial punishment, which MS Now notes is typically used by commanding officers to address minor rule-breaking without a court martial.The navy did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the Guardian. In a statement to MS Now about the decision to pursue a non-judicial punishment for the sailor, a navy official said that “the Navy is fully committed to the health and wellbeing of every Sailor”.“We strive to foster environments that support mental health by removing barriers to seeking help, increasing awareness of resources, and taking appropriate action when someone is in need,” they added. “Mental health resources are available to our Sailors 24/7, and asking for help is a sign of strength.”The Lincoln left San Diego on 21 Novemberbound for the Pacific, but was redirected to the Middle East. It has since spent more than250 consecutivedays without a significant port visit.Reports about the conditions onboard havepromptedseveral Democratic lawmakersto demandanswers from the Pentagon.Explore more on these topicsUS militaryThailandAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nearly 1,400 missing, mostly tourists, after Nepal-Tibet flash flood kills at least 356 | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Entire villages swept away after glacial collapse triggers flood in mountainous region popular with trekkers and pilgrims
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Entire villages swept away after glacial collapse triggers flood in mountainous region popular with trekkers and pilgrims
Content: A drone view shows mud covering properties after the flash flood in Trishuli, Nepal.Photograph: Navesh Chitrakar/ReutersView image in fullscreenA drone view shows mud covering properties after the flash flood in Trishuli, Nepal.Photograph: Navesh Chitrakar/ReutersNepal-Tibet flood disasterNearly 1,400 missing, mostly tourists, after Nepal-Tibet flash flood kills at least 356Entire villages swept away after glacial collapse triggers flood in mountainous region popular with trekkers and pilgrimsNepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updatesHave you been affected by the flash floods?Hannah Ellis-Petersenin Delhi,Sam Jones,Kate Lamband agenciesThu 27 Aug 2026 08.41 EDTFirst published on Wed 26 Aug 2026 23.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRescuers are searching for nearly 1,400 people, most of them tourists, who are missing after a catastrophic flash flood hit Nepal andTibet, thundering down valleys, obliterating entire villages and killing at least 356 people.Efforts to locate those missing – including hundreds of people from India, the US, UK, Australia and Canada – have been complicated by the destruction of dozens of bridges and almost 25 miles (40km) of roads in the mountainous region popular with trekkers and pilgrims.Videos from Wednesday’s disaster showeda massive wall of water crashing down on the borderas people tried to flee. Trucks were upended and houses, roads ⁠and power plants swept away in Nepal, while ​officials in Tibet said they feared “major casualties” after a mudslide hit a border crossing.Deadly flash flood hit Nepal and China - cinemagraphRescue teams have found bodies hundreds of miles downstream from the disaster zone in the Chitwan district ofNepal, near the Tibetan border.
