Dozens of injured people have been transported to Kathmandu for advanced medical care. By Thursday morning, the Nepali army had rescued more than 100 people from flood-affected areas by helicopter.David Fisher, the head of the Nepal delegation of the International Federation of the Red Cross, said entire villages and market areas had been wiped out.In the affected areas, houses, trees and vehicles were submerged or buried in mudslides. Helicopters hovered overhead all day, helping to rescue survivors.The power, volume and speed of the surging waters gave little time for anyone to flee.9:21‘Tsunami from the sky:’ floods leave trail of devastation in Nepal and Tibet - The LatestPeople from the hard-hit areas of Nuwakot and Dhading were seen gathering outside a Nepali army training centre – the base for helicopter rescue operations – seeking information about missing family members.Police were recording the names of the missing just outside the barracks gate. Mobile phone torches were their only source of light as the area remained without electricity due to damaged hydroelectric infrastructure.The village of Soley, in Nuwakot, which had about 25 homes, was virtually wiped out, according to Nirajan Paudyal, a Kathmandu-based journalist whose parents and other relatives live there. Desperate for information, he travelled to the area on Thursday for news of his family.Tell us: have you been affected by the flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border?Read more“There is no update till now,” he said. “I fear there won’t be any update.”Almost 600 foreigners were among 826 people missing in Nepal, police and tourism ⁠officials said. Among those unaccounted were 177 from India, 63 from the US, 34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 25 from Canada.Chinese state media said at least 558 were missing on the Tibet side of the border, of whom at least 260 were foreign nationals.Before and after images showing the glacier’s collapseBefore and after images showing the glacier’s collapsePolice in Nepal said 353 ⁠bodies had been recovered by Thursday afternoon local time, while Chinese state media reported three dead on the Tibet side of the border.Many of the victims were on a pilgrimage to Kailash Mansarovar, a high-altitude site in ‌Tibet revered by Hindus and Buddhists among others.Early reports from Nepali ​officials suggested an earthquake could have caused the lower part of a glacier to collapse and trigger ‌the floods. But the US Geological Survey later said what was initially reported ‌as a 4.4-magnitude earthquake was a seismic shock generated by glacial rock and ice collapsing and the flow of debris. “No earthquake had occurred,” it said.View image in fullscreenDamaged section of highway in Nepal after the flash flood.Photograph: Subaas Shrestha/NurPhoto/ShutterstockAn initial study of Planet Labs satellite imagery indicated a landslide of ice and rock triggered the debris-laden flood in the Lhende River, about 12 miles (20km) north-east of the Nepal-China Rasuwagadhi border crossing, Nepal’s national disaster authority said. Experts say the risk of such events is compounded by the extreme topography of the Himalayas.People shared harrowing stories of how they managed to survive. “I started running. Then a wall of water came thundering down as if it was an earthquake,” said Bibek Kumal, a labourer who was working downstream from the worst-hit Rasuwa district, near Nepal’s Himalayan border with China’s Tibet.From his hospital bed, Kumal said the torrent swept him downstream amid mud and debris but he survived by clinging to a mango tree. “Had there been no mango tree, I would ‌have been washed away to death,” he said.Keshav Prasad Baral, a 68-year-old survivor who was being treated at a small hospital, said: “It was a huge gush of mud coming straight towards us. As it got closer, it kept rising higher and higher.“I tried to grab my wife’s hand and take ⁠her to the terrace. But she was swept away by the mud. Four or five hours later, a helicopter came to rescue me. My wife is still somewhere beneath the mud. She’s gone.”View image in fullscreenNepali soldiers carrying a survivor of the flash flood.Photograph: Nepal Army/EPAThe United Nations secretary general, António Guterres, said UN teams and partners were mobilising supplies and personnel to support communities affected by the disaster. The US government said it would provide $500,000 in emergency assistance.Tibet government officials deployed nearly 800 emergency workers and 150 vehicles as well as sniffer dogs and speedboats to help the rescue efforts, China’s official Xinhua news agency said.The Chinese premier, Li Qiang, travelled to the affected area on the China-Nepal border on Thursday to oversee search efforts there.Map showing the flooding-affected locations in Nepal and ChinaThe tour company Himalayan Glacier said 47 people, including two children, were missing from one of its groups in Nepal. Among them were 15 Australians, 10 Canadians, nine Nepalis, eight Americans, two Britons, two Singaporeans and one Russian-American dual citizen, its managing director, Sanket Pandey, said.The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said his thoughts were with those concerned about their loved ones, and that getting information about the status of missing people remained difficult.Reuters and Agence France-Presse contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalTibetChinaFloodingSouth and central AsiaAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Yayoi Kusama, Japanese artist who became a global superstar, dies aged 97 | Yayoi Kusama | The Guardian
description: From the 1950s to the 2020s, Kusama produced vivid paintings, sculptures and vast installations that often drew on her experience of hallucinations
Author: Tim Jonze
Headline: From the 1950s to the 2020s, Kusama produced vivid paintings, sculptures and vast installations that often drew on her experience of hallucinations
Content: Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama poses inside her Infinity Mirrored Room installation in 2013. She has died aged 97.Photograph: Mike Segar/ReutersView image in fullscreenJapanese artist Yayoi Kusama poses inside her Infinity Mirrored Room installation in 2013. She has died aged 97.Photograph: Mike Segar/ReutersYayoi KusamaYayoi Kusama, Japanese artist who became a global superstar, dies aged 97From the 1950s to the 2020s, Kusama produced vivid paintings, sculptures and vast installations that often drew on her experience of hallucinationsKusama – a life in picturesWas Kusama the world’s favourite artist?Tim JonzeandSian CainWed 26 Aug 2026 22.17 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 00.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYayoi Kusama, the Japanese outsider artist who reached superstar status after decades living in a psychiatric hospital, has died aged 97.Kusama died in a Tokyo hospital on 14 August, her company Yayoi Kusama Inc announcedin a statementon Thursday.Yayoi Kusama: the world’s favourite artist?Read more“Throughout an extraordinary lifetime devoted entirely to artistic creation, Kusama pursued an internationally acclaimed career as a pioneering avant garde artist whose creative practice encompassed visual art, performance, fiction, and poetry,” the statement read. “She continued to paint until her final days, never setting aside her brush, and continued exploration of forever love and eternal soul.”“We will carry forward Kusama’s wishes and, through art, continue to bring hope and strength for the future to people around the world.”Instantly recognisable by her bright red bobbed wig, Kusama became known for herpsychedelic colour schemesand “infinity mirror room” installations, which helped her find a huge audience in the age of the social media selfie:her 2024 show in Australiawas the most popular exhibition in the country’s history. Yet she had pioneered many of her enduring themes as a young artist in the 1960s, before fading into temporary obscurity.View image in fullscreenKusama’s work The Hope of the Polka Dots Buried in Infinity Will Eternally Cover the Universe, at the Museum Ludwig in Cologne, Germany in 2026.Photograph: Ina Fassbender/AFP/Getty ImagesAs well as being a sculptor and painter, Kusama put on numerous performance pieces throughout the hippy era that saw her name attached to scandal. She staged “body festivals” with naked performers painted in polka dots and once wrote to US president Richard Nixon offering to sleep with him in return for an end to the Vietnam war. News of such events appalled her conservative family back home.Kusama was born in Matsumoto,Japan, in 1929, enduring an unhappy childhood at the hands of an abusive mother and philandering father. Her wealthy family managed plant nurseries and Kusama would sit and draw the flowers despite her mother’s frequent attempts to stop her. As a child, Kusama began experiencing hallucinations, in which the flowers would swarm around and talk to her. Her coping mechanism was to draw what she saw.During the second world war, 13-year-old Kusama was conscripted to produce fabric for Japanese army parachutes. She later studiednihonga, a traditional Japanese style of painting, in Kyoto, but grew frustrated with its limitations. Rejecting her planned future of an arranged marriage and children, Kusama left Japan for New York in 1958. There, she fell in with the artist and theoristDonald Juddand made a breakthrough with her “infinity net” paintings – vast fields of impastoed polka dots that stretched across the canvas. In 1962, she sold her first of these to the artists Frank Stella and Judd for $75. In 2014, her White No 28 sold for $7.1m (£5.7m) at auction, a record at the time for a living female artist.View image in fullscreenKusama next to her Dot Car (1965) in Scheveningen, the Netherlands.Photograph: Harrie VerstappenIn 1963, Kusama started making “soft sculptures” – pieces of furniture and other objects, such as ladders, covered with white, fabric-stuffed phallic shapes. They were, she said, her attempt to healher disgust around sex, which she had been brought up to believe was dirty and shameful.Despite working loosely within the spheres of pop art and minimalism, Kusama was not embraced by the art world. She always maintained that many of her ideas from this period were appropriated by white male artists, including Andy Warhol, while she was written out of art history.Kusama’s work was often centred around the infinite and the idea of “self-obliteration”, a concept inspired by the hallucinations that would engulf her. Talking about her 1954 painting Flower (DSPS), she once said: “I was looking at the red flower patterns of the tablecloth on a table, and when I looked up I saw the same pattern covering the ceiling, the windows and the walls, and finally all over the room, my body and the universe. I felt as if I had begun to self-obliterate, to revolve in the infinity of endless time and the absoluteness of space, and be reduced to nothingness.”View image in fullscreenKusama’s work Narcissus Garden, which she presented at the Venice Biennale in 1966 without being invited. The work was eventually shut down by the biennale.Photograph: Yayoi KusamaAt the 1966 Venice Biennale she continued these studies, presenting her infamous Narcissus Garden, a “lake” of 1,500 reflective balls that strived for a sense of mirrored infinity. When Kusama began selling the balls for $2 each under the banner “Your narcissism for sale”, the biennale moved to close the operation down.Kusama developed a flair for controversy. Her artistic “happenings” were often criticised for being mere shock material, yet their political statements now seem ahead of their time. In 1968, she staged New York’s first “homosexual wedding” in Tribeca and washed a “dirty” Soviet flag outside the United Nations building in protest over the invasion of Czechoslovakia.By this time Kusama was engaged in a platonic yet obsessive relationship with theoutsider artist Joseph Cornell, which continued even after she had left the US to return to Japan. She had been frequently admitted to hospital during her time in New York and when Cornell died in 1972, her mental health deteriorated further, with hallucinations, panic attacks and suicide attempts. In 1977, she checked herself into a psychiatric hospital in Tokyo that offered art therapy courses and provided Kusama with the stability needed to pursue her projects without distraction. She made the decision to live there permanently, working each day from morning until night in her nearby studio.View image in fullscreenKusama at work in her studio in Tokyo, Japan in 2017.Photograph: Toru Hanai/ReutersAlthough she published several novels during the 1980s, interest in Kusama appeared to have waned almost completely by the start of the 90s. But the recognition that eluded her during her early artistic career finally arrived later in life. In 1993 she created a mirrored room filled with small pumpkin sculptures for the Venice Biennale’s Japanese pavilion and won plaudits for the work. She had first seen a pumpkin with her grandfather when she was 11. When she tried to pick it, it had appeared to start speaking to her, and now it became a recurring motif in works such as All the Eternal Love I Have for the Pumpkins, from 2016.Kusama’s focus shifted towards installations that built on her 1965 work Infinity Mirror Room: Phalli’s Field. In that piece, hundreds of soft, pink phallic forms were arranged within a mirrored room. Half a century later, such immersive experiences connected with audiences on a global scale, with the coloured lights and brightly painted pumpkins providing perfect Instagram content. It was not without irony that an exhibition of hers at the Hirshhorn Museum in Washington DC in 2017 was temporarily closed after someone damaged an artwork while attempting to take a selfie.View image in fullscreenVisitors inside one of Kusama’s ‘infinity rooms’ at her exhibition at Tate Modern, London in 2012.Photograph: Guy Bell/REX/ShutterstockKusama received retrospectives at the New York’s Museum of Modern Art in 1998,Tate Modern in London in 2012and Washington DC’s Hirshhorn Museum in 2017. Tickets for her shows sold out swiftly around the world and fans would queue for hours just to be allowed a 30-second experience within her installations.Despite some critics wondering if she had become the world’smost popular artist, Kusamaalways believed that her place in history would not be decided by the art establishment.“I cannot imagine how I will be classified after my death,” she once said. “It feels good to be an outsider.”Explore more on these topicsYayoi KusamaJapanAsia PacificNew YorknewsShareReuse this content

title: Russia says UK ‘playing with fire’ amid reports CIA chief has warned Kremlin not to attack Nato | Russia | The Guardian
description: Moscow threatens retaliation after Andy Burnham says UK will help Ukraine start producing long-range missiles
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: Moscow threatens retaliation after Andy Burnham says UK will help Ukraine start producing long-range missiles
Content: Vladimir Putin in Moscow this week. Russia has made frequent threats against Ukraine’s western allies.Photograph: Mikhail Metzel/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenVladimir Putin in Moscow this week. Russia has made frequent threats against Ukraine’s western allies.Photograph: Mikhail Metzel/AFP/Getty ImagesRussiaRussia says UK ‘playing with fire’ amid reports CIA chief has warned Kremlin not to attack NatoMoscow threatens retaliation after Andy Burnham says UK will help Ukraine start producing long-range missilesPeter BeaumontandJessica ElgotThu 27 Aug 2026 15.26 EDTFirst published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 07.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussia has said it could retaliate against the UK for its support of Kyiv by striking military targets inside and outsideUkraine, amid reports that the director of the CIA warned the Kremlin against attacking Nato during a secretive visit this week.Andy Burnham, Britain’s prime minister, said on Monday the UK wouldallow Kyiv access to classified technologyto start ⁠its own production of Storm Shadow ​long-range ​cruise missiles. France has also agreed to supply missile technology. Maria ⁠Zakharova, Russia’s foreign ministry spokesperson, said on Thursday Britain and France were “playing ⁠with ​fire”.Responding to the latest Russian threats, a Ministry of Defence official reiterated UK support for Ukraine. “Britain stands shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine and we are committed to providing the equipment Ukraine needs to defend itself against Putin’s illegal invasion.Russiashould be in no doubt about the resolve of this government to stand against Russian aggression, in Ukraine and against the UK and our allies,” they said.The Wall Street Journal reported thata visit by John Ratcliffe, the CIA chief, to Moscowon Tuesday had followed a US intelligence assessment that Russia could be planning to test Nato with a limited assault on an allied country. This could range from a cyber-attack to a small-scale incursion, probably in a Baltic nation.Russia has made frequent threats against Ukraine’s western allies during the war, including thinly veiled nuclear threats and others apparently aimed at diplomatic missions in Kyiv.View image in fullscreenK2 Black Panther main battle tanks will be deployed by Poland near the border with Russia’s Kaliningrad region as Nato countries neighbouring Russia move to increase their military readiness.Photograph: Roman Koziel/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockAsked ‌to comment ‌on the reports of Ratcliffe’s visit – and despite Thursday morning’s threat against UK targets – Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin spokesperson, said: “A lot of this kind of scare-story material is being published right now. Of course, it has ‌nothing to do with reality and nothing to do ​with the intentions of the Russian Federation.”The intense scrutiny around the Ratcliffe trip and Russia’s intentions comes amid a new report over shortfalls of missile interceptors available inEurope.A report by the Associated Press says the US military is experiencing a “beyond critical” shortage of advanced missile interceptors in Europe largely driven by Donald Trump’s war with Iran, according to a US defence official in Europe and aNatoofficial, raising concerns about vulnerabilities in Nato countries to a potential Russian attack.The US defence official said the most concerning shortfall involved Patriot missile interceptors, which can shoot down Russia’s high-speed ballistic missiles. The Nato official confirmed the low inventories of Patriots among American and Nato forces in Europe. Both spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military matters.Russia is believed to be contemplating a further escalation of its war with Ukraine after months ofescalating Ukrainian attackson Russia’s oil refining infrastructure and other sites, which are imposing an increasing economic toll.View image in fullscreenA Japanese government sign in Tokyo says ‘the Northern Territories are an inherent part of Japan’s territory’, referring to the Russian-controlled Southern Kuril Islands. Russia has invoked its nuclear threat against Japan over the claim.Photograph: Yuichi Yamazaki/AFP/Getty ImagesThe Kremlin has adopted ever more bellicose rhetoric, much of it aimed at a domestic audience, as the war in Ukraine has been brought to its doorstep.In the space of a few days Russia has invoked the threat of its nuclear arsenal against Japan over its territorial claim to the disputed Kuril Islands. It has described relations with the US as a “crisis” and at a historic low point.Ratcliffe’s reported warning mirrored onemade by his predecessor, William Burns, in 2021before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine – which Moscow also denied it was contemplating.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionConcerns over Moscow’s intentions have been increasing amid a rise in incidents of Russian hybrid warfare attributed to Moscow across Europe, from cyber-attacks and drones to arson, at facilities associated with supporting Ukraine’s war efforts.Russia and the US have tried to play down Ratcliffe’s meeting with his Russian counterparts: Trump on Wednesday described the visit as “semi routine”. However, the unusual nature of the encounter has caused intense speculation in the west and Russia.The US president continued to play down the encounter on Thursday, telling Axios that Ratcliffe had arrived in Moscow with “no message” and claiming there was “nothing unusual” about the meeting.Asked later by reporters about reports about the CIA director Ratcliffe had delivered a warning to Russia, Trump replied: “I don’t want to comment on that, but they’re not going to attack.”Nato countries neighbouring Russia have moved quickly to increase their military readiness.Polandthis week announced it had taken delivery of its first shipment of South Korean Black Panther main battle tanks, which will be deployed near the border with Russia’s Kaliningrad region.Cezary Tomczyk, Poland’s deputy defence minister, said this month Warsaw was preparing for the possibility of a full-scale conflict.Tomczyk toldSuper Express media: “We are preparing for war, hoping it never happens.”Explore more on these topicsRussiaUkraineNatoPolandEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Greek Orthodox priest and cult musician clarifies views on homosexuality | Experimental music | The Guardian
description: Father Dionysios Tabakis says his views are those of Orthodox church, ‘nothing more, nothing less’
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: Father Dionysios Tabakis says his views are those of Orthodox church, ‘nothing more, nothing less’
Content: Father Dionysios Tabakis also clarified that he performed a sanctification of a neo-Nazi party office at the request of a superior authority.Photograph: Panagiotis Moschandreou/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFather Dionysios Tabakis also clarified that he performed a sanctification of a neo-Nazi party office at the request of a superior authority.Photograph: Panagiotis Moschandreou/The GuardianExperimental musicGreek Orthodox priest and cult musician clarifies views on homosexualityFather Dionysios Tabakis says his views are those of Orthodox church, ‘nothing more, nothing less’Philip OltermannEuropean culture editorThu 27 Aug 2026 13.11 EDTFirst published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 12.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Greek Orthodox priest whose home-recorded album of drone metal and religious dubstep has made him acult figure in experimental musiccircles has issued a statement in which he has clarified his stance on homosexuality and the Greek radical right.“As can be seen from my musical expression, I am in favour of unity, love, empathy and help for every needy, wronged and suffering person in life,” Father Dionysios Tabakis said in a public statement shared with the Guardian. “Whoever they are, whatever they believe, whether they are a saint or a sinner.”The musician-priest’s political views have come under scrutiny over two blogposts he wrote in 2024, around the time thatGreecebecame the first Christian Orthodox-majority country to legalise same-sex marriage.The posts on the Orthodox Christian WordPress blog The Doors The Doors referred to gay people as “Sodomites”, gay marriage as aσοδομικὸ τερατούργημα(“sodomitic monstrosity”) and the same-sex marriage bill as “blasphemous”.‘Techno in a monastery – are you ready?’ The Greek priest whose doom metal album is the year’s hippest recordRead moreIn a statement released on Tuesday, Tabakis said: “My view on homosexuality is the same as that of the Orthodox church for 2,000 years, nothing more, nothing less.“We owe homosexual people love and acceptance because many have at times experienced great rejection from their environment, especially from their families. Over the years, homosexual people have also come to me for confession, and I have always received them with acceptance and love.”In his statement, Tabakis still appears to refer to homosexuality as a sin: “I also always respect the freedom of my fellow man. After all, with freedom we sin, and with freedom we repent. It is better to sin with freedom than to be virtuous with oppression.”The Orthodox priest’s debut albumParadise Metalearned a critics’ score of 7.6 from the experimental music bible Pitchfork, and Tabakis was profiled in international media including theGuardianand the New York Times.In a separate controversy, a 2013 YouTube video that recently resurfaced on Greek social media showed Tabakis performing a sanctification at the opening of an office building for Golden Dawn, the neo-Nazi party that held seats in Greece’s parliament between 2015 and 2019.The group wascriminalised in 2020, and its leadership handed prison sentences for murder, assault and weapons possession.In his statement, Tabakis said he performed the consecration in an official duty and at the request of his superior authority, and that he also attended other consecration ceremonies connected with other political and municipal groups.Heat Crimes, the Greek record label that issued Tabakis’s debut album,told Pitchfork: “In Greek Orthodox practice, priests routinely performagiasmos, blessing ceremonies for homes, shops, businesses, schools, public institutions, military facilities and other premises. A politician or political organisation inviting a local priest to bless new premises therefore does not, by itself, establish that either the priest or the church endorses that organisation. The important distinction is between performing a religious blessing and giving a political endorsement.”In his statement, Tabakis said he was against nationalism “because it has only brought blood and wars to humanity”.“The only ones who have interests in nationalism and borders are the weapons factories that spread death. Besides, my grandparents from Crete fought Hitler and nazism, so I follow their spirit. In fact, one reason I have removed the frets from my guitar is my mental need not to be confined to borders.”Explore more on these topicsExperimental musicGreecePop and rockMetalReligionEuropeLGBTQ+ rightsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ratko Mladić, the ‘Butcher of Bosnia’, dies in The Hague | Ratko Mladić | The Guardian
description: Bosnian Serb commander responsible for Srebrenica massacre dies in prison while serving life sentence for genocide
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: Bosnian Serb commander responsible for Srebrenica massacre dies in prison while serving life sentence for genocide
Content: Bosnian Serb army commander Gen Ratko Mladić  addresses his troops in the eastern Bosnian town of Vlasenica in December 1995.Photograph: Oleg Stjepanovic/APView image in fullscreenBosnian Serb army commander Gen Ratko Mladić  addresses his troops in the eastern Bosnian town of Vlasenica in December 1995.Photograph: Oleg Stjepanovic/APRatko MladićRatko Mladić, the ‘Butcher of Bosnia’, dies in The HagueBosnian Serb commander responsible for Srebrenica massacre dies in prison while serving life sentence for genocideFrom the archive:Fourteen years a fugitive: the hunt for the Butcher of BosniaRatko Mladić will die in jail. But go to Bosnia: you’ll see that he wonPeter BeaumontSenior international correspondentThu 27 Aug 2026 12.12 EDTFirst published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 10.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRatko Mladić, the infamous Serbian general who was serving a life sentence for genocide committed during the Bosnian war, has died in prison in The Hague.Mladić had been one of the main architects of the policy of ethnic cleansing during the Bosnian war. He wasconvicted of genocidefor orchestrating the 1995killing of at least 8,000 Muslims in the UN-designated “safe area” Srebrenica, the worst massacre in Europe since the second world war.Mladić, who was nicknamed the “Butcher of Bosnia”, had been in ill health after having a series of strokes.A UN international tribunal confirmed Mladić’s death, saying he had died in hospital in The Hague earlier in the day.“Mladić passed away today while hospitalised in The Hague,” the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals said in a statement, adding that judge Graciela Gatti Santana had ordered “a full inquiry into the circumstances” of his death.Described by the former UN rights chief Zeid Ra’ad al-Hussein as “the epitome of evil” after his conviction,Mladić was one of the most notorious figuresof the war that killed more than 100,000 people and left more than 1 million homeless.View image in fullscreenThe Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadžić (right) with Mladić in 1995. Karadžić was also sentenced to life imprisonment for genocide and war crimes.Photograph: Ranko Cukovic/ReutersHe commanded his troops to “scorch the brains” of Bosnian Muslim people and had boasted of being a “Serbian god”.The news of Mladić’s death was first broken on Serbian state television after his son, Darko, had spoken earlier about his father’s declining health.‘The voices of our dead have not faded away’: the fight for the memory of genocide in SrebrenicaRead moreMladić was sentenced by a UN tribunal to life imprisonment in 2017 over genocide and war crimes committed during Bosnia’s 1990s war. He was arrested in Serbia in 2011 after 16 years on the run.The slaughter in Srebrenica was the culmination of a brutal war that had lasted more than three ⁠years, during which Mladić oversaw the siege of Bosnia’s capital, Sarajevo, which was pounded daily by artillery, tank and sniper fire, killing 10,000 people.The goal of the Serbian leadership, which Mladić was tasked with implementing – as determined ⁠by the UN’s international criminal tribunal for ⁠the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) – was the forcible expulsion of ​Bosnian Muslims, Croats and other non-Serbs to clear Bosnian land for the creation of a greater Serbia.The tribunal found that Mladić, together with the late Serbian president Slobodan Milošević and the Bosnian Serb political leader Radovan Karadžić, were part of a criminal conspiracy to implement the plan.View image in fullscreenSlobodan Milošević.Photograph: Srdjan Ilic/AP“I do not recognise this court,” Mladić said at an ⁠ICTY hearing on his case in 2014. When he was sentenced, he shouted: “This is all lies, you are all liars!”The Serbian campaign culminated in the horror of Srebrenica when, after the withdrawal of Dutch UN peacekeeping forces, thousands of Bosnian men and boys were rounded up, killed and their bodies bulldozed into mass graves.View image in fullscreenMladić (front left) entering Srebrenica in 1995.Photograph: Sipa Press/Rex ShutterstockMladić had the siege filmed to show him praising his “lads” and haranguing the UN peacekeepers who misguidedly accepted his solemn word that the inhabitants would be safe in his hands.“We give this town to the Serb people as a gift,” Mladić said to the camera, claiming the victory as revenge against Muslim Turks, who had once held the area as part ‌of the Ottoman empire.The next day, Mladić’s forces were filmed handing out sweets to children, promising their safe passage. Meanwhile, thousands of men and boys were being readied for slaughter.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA screengrab from 12 July 1995 shows Mladić speaking to a young Muslim boy after he had assured residents of Srebrenica they would be safe.Photograph: APWhen Nato tried in 1995 to rein in his forces with the threat of limited airstrikes, his troops seized UN peacekeepers as human shields, chaining them to likely targets.14 years a fugitive: the hunt for Ratko Mladic, the Butcher of Bosnia | Julian BorgerRead moreThe son of a second world war partisan fighter killed in 1945, Mladić was, according to his family, born in March 1943 in the tiny Bosnian village of Bozinovici, putting his age at death at 83 (though official documents recorded his date of birth a year earlier, in 1942).Mladić was an officer in the communist Yugoslav People’s Army (JNA) when Yugoslavia’s disintegration began in 1991.When Bosnian Serbs rose in 1992 against Bosnia’s Muslim-led secession, Mladić was chosen to command the new Bosnian Serb army that swiftly overran 70% of the country.Dozens of towns were besieged with heavy weapons that once belonged to the JNA and villages were burned down, as 22,000 troops with the UN Protection Force stood by, more or less helplessly, under orders not to take sides.View image in fullscreenEdiba Salihović raises her hands as she reacts with other Bosnian women upon hearing the sentence at the end of Mladić’s trial in Potočari, near Srebrenica, in November 2017.Photograph: Amel Emrić/APA combination of western pressure, Nato strikes and covert US arms and training for Croats and ⁠Muslims gradually turned the tide against Mladić’s army. After the war, Mladić went into hiding, with the reformists ruling post-conflict Serbia not daring ​to move against a man who was a hero to a core of nationalist Serbs.Mladić continued to insist he was “a simple man” chosen to protect his people. When he was finally arrested in 2011, he put up no resistance. He had a heart ​attack in 2013 and seemed older than his years. By his own account, he felt like a frail old man.This month, a UN doctor said Mladić’s death “may occur at any time”, possibly within weeks, but his application for release was again rejected.View image in fullscreenMunira Subašić (pictured in 2019), from the Mothers of Srebrenica group, said she deplored that Mladić’s crimes were still being denied by many Bosnian Serbs.Photograph: Anadolu Agency/GettyMunira Subašić, from the Mothers of Srebrenica group, said she deplored that Mladić’s crimes were still being denied by many Bosnian Serbs. “Today, a major war criminal died, the criminal of the Balkans,” Subašić said. But while 31 years later mothers of victims were “still carrying the pain in our souls … we are still listening to denials, we are still listening to how Ratko Mladić was a hero for the Serbs”.Elizabeth Evenson, the international justice director at Human Rights Watch, said: “The death of Ratko Mladić, the former Bosnian Serb army commander found guilty of genocide, including the massacre of up to 8,000 Bosnian men and boys after the fall of Srebrenica, Bosnia, in July 1995, is a reminder of the ongoing need for justice, truth, and reparations in the western Balkans.“Full accountability for such terrible crimes, in Bosnia and elsewhere, demands commitment by governments to justice, even decades after the events themselves.”Explore more on these topicsRatko MladićSerbiaBosnia and HerzegovinaEuropeSrebrenica massacreRadovan KaradzicnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bronze age treasure stolen in four-minute Spanish museum heist | Art theft | The Guardian
description: Gold collection known as Treasure of Villena, worth at least €1.7m, is target of ‘very well planned’ raid
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: Gold collection known as Treasure of Villena, worth at least €1.7m, is target of ‘very well planned’ raid
Content: The Treasure of Villena comprises 29 bracelets, 11 bowls, three bottles and other miscellaneous pieces dating back to 1000BC.Photograph: Museum of Villena/EPAView image in fullscreenThe Treasure of Villena comprises 29 bracelets, 11 bowls, three bottles and other miscellaneous pieces dating back to 1000BC.Photograph: Museum of Villena/EPAArt theftBronze age treasure stolen in four-minute Spanish museum heistGold collection known as Treasure of Villena, worth at least €1.7m, is target of ‘very well planned’ raidPhilip Oltermannand agenciesThu 27 Aug 2026 11.47 EDTFirst published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 07.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThieves in Spain have raided the Treasure of Villena – a stunning collection of bronze age gold artefacts that has been described as the most important prehistoric trove inEurope– in the latest high-profile smash-and-grab heist on the continent.The raid on Thursday morning of the 66 mostly gold objects in the Spanish town of Villena lasted just minutes, officials said.“The alarm at the Villena Museum went off around 5.20am [4.20am BST],” a spokesperson for the town council said, adding that the thieves had left the building by 5.24am. The operation was “super-fast and super-professional”, the spokesperson said.“They’ve taken most of the treasure,” the mayor of Villena, Fulgencio Cerdán, told journalists, his voice breaking.View image in fullscreenThe collection has been held in a specially designated room in the Museum of Villena since May 2024.Photograph: Pablo Miranzo/EPALocal media said the few items the thieves had left behind included three silver vessels, a bracelet and some of the ornamentation of the bastón del reyezuelo, the “Kingfisher staff”, a prehistoric ceremonial scepter.Cerdán said: “We are absolutely devastated, I’m even trembling. The truth is that for those of us from Villena, this destroys us. It’s part of our heritage, of our wealth.”The treasure, which was discovered in 1963 by the archaeologist José María Soler in a vessel sunk in a dried-out riverbed in Villena, included 29 bracelets, 11 bowls, three bottles and other miscellaneous pieces dating back to about 1000BC. It immediately became the main attraction of a small architectural museum in the province of Alicante.Since May 2024, the hoard has been on display in a specially designated room in the newly opened, municipally owned Villena Museum.The unusual material of some of the items has long intrigued researchers. Though mainly gold, some pieces are also made of silver, iron, amber and a dark leaden material covered in a ferrous-looking oxide. A recent study published in the journalTrabajos de Prehistoriaclaimed that these items were probably forged from rare meteoritic iron.While the treasure’s value is incalculable, the gold alone is worth about €1.7m (£1.45m), according to the mayor.The thieves arrived in several vehicles and apparently entered the museum through a window, according to the Spanish government’s deputy representative in Alicante, Manuel Pineda.“All security systems were activated,” according to the Villena spokesperson, who insisted there had been “no failure” by the museum.Shortly before the robbery, another alarm went off at the city’s sports centre, and authorities were now investigating whether that was a diversion created by the thieves, the spokesperson added.Mauro Hernández, a professor of archaeology at the University of Alicante and an expert on the treasure, told the broadcaster Cadena SER that the operation showed signs of prior planning. “They had it very well planned,” Hernández said. “They knew how to do it, how to act and how to escape.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGuns, axes, explosives: violent museum heists are on the rise, says EuropolRead moreLast October, thieves broke into the Louvre Museum in Paris in broad daylight,escaping in less than eight minuteswith jewellery worth €88m. There have since been a series of brazen raids in institutions across Europe.Four works “of extraordinary value” by the Renaissance artist Antonello da Messinawere stolenfrom a museum in Sicily, Italy’s culture ministry said last Sunday.Two days earlier, Italian police said they hadrecovered paintingsby Renoir, Cézanne and Matisse worth more than $10.4m which were stolen from the Magnani-Rocca Foundation Museum near Parma.In a report published at the start of the week, the EU’s police agency Europol said that member states had detected a recent shift “towards violent and forceful methods” that could point to the involvement of new criminal networks focused on specific cultural artefacts.“Some thieves apprehended in recent cases appear to coordinate their efforts on an ad hoc basis, often recruited locally through social media and instant communication channels, without prior connections to each other,” the report said. “This differs from the usual structure of criminal networks involved in cultural goods trafficking, which typically operate in a core group organised around a leader.”Agence France-Presse contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsArt theftMuseumsSpainOrganised crimeEuropeHeritagenewsShareReuse this content

title: Officials urge calm after malaria outbreak kills two staff at Frankfurt airport | Germany | The Guardian
description: Mosquito traps are set up at Germany’s biggest airport and doctors are asked to look out for symptoms of disease
Author: Kate Connolly
Headline: Mosquito traps are set up at Germany’s biggest airport and doctors are asked to look out for symptoms of disease
Content: A plane at Frankfurt airport where six workers have contracted malaria, two of them fatally.Photograph: Michael Probst/APView image in fullscreenA plane at Frankfurt airport where six workers have contracted malaria, two of them fatally.Photograph: Michael Probst/APGermanyOfficials urge calm after malaria outbreak kills two staff at Frankfurt airportMosquito traps are set up at Germany’s biggest airport and doctors are asked to look out for symptoms of diseaseKate Connollyin BerlinThu 27 Aug 2026 11.23 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 15.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGerman health officials are seeking to reassure the public after two workers at the country’s biggest airport died of malaria.Mosquito traps have been set up at Frankfurt airport and a mosquito monitoring process is under way. A detailed investigation is being conducted to clarify how the workers contracted the disease.Since last month, six people are known to have caught malaria tropica – the most dangerous form of the disease – in connection with their work at the airport.Of the two that have died, one began getting sick at the start of July and the other in mid-August. The four other people who were infected have been treated in hospital and are now out of danger, according to Frankfurt’s public health department.Letters have been sent to all airport workers to raise awareness about symptoms and urge vigilance. Doctors are being asked to watch out for patients with unexplained fever who work in and around the airport.In astatementon its website, the health department acknowledged the existence of “airport malaria”, where mosquitoes from malaria-endemic areas are transported in flight cabins or in baggage holds.View image in fullscreenA femaleAnopheles stephensimosquito. The species has been linked to the Frankfurt malaria outbreak.Photograph: CDC/Phanie/Rex FeaturesIt said that because this was “a very rare occurrence”, malaria could easily be overlooked and diagnosis delayed, increasing the chance of death. It said human-to-human transmission was not possible.The Robert Koch Institute, which is responsible for disease control and prevention inGermany, believes the Frankfurt infection was transmitted by anAnopheles stephensimosquito imported by plane.A spokesperson for Fraport, which operates the airport, confirmed that mosquito traps had been set up in and around the site and that mosquitoes had been caught. These are being examined in a tropical medicine laboratory in Antwerp, Belgium.Can you stop malaria crossing borders? One nation’s bid to wipe out the diseaseRead morePeter Tinnemann, the head of Frankfurt’s health department, told the broadcaster Hessische Rundfunk: “The mosquito is probably already dead.”He said higher temperatures in Germany increased the likelihood of mosquitoes surviving for extended periods but the risk to the population of Frankfurt was low.“Not everyone should assume that just because they have a headache, fever and nonspecific symptoms they are now infected with malaria because of the case at the airport,” he added.But he said the rise in malaria cases made it necessary to check whether existing measures, including the disinfection of aircraft and removing breeding grounds for mosquitoes, were being correctly followed.A study that set out to record all cases of airport and baggage malaria inEuropefrom 1969 to 2024 found 145 instances, nine of them in Germany.The Robert Koch Institute said Germany’s last outbreak of airport malaria was also at Frankfurt, in 2023, when a single documented infection was successfully treated.About 90% of all malaria cases occur in sub-Saharan Africa. Countries from this region with direct flight connections to Frankfurt include Ethiopia, Kenya, Nigeria and Tanzania, all of which have a high to widespread malaria risk. Namibia and South Africa also have direct flights but are considered to be moderate to low risk.Explore more on these topicsGermanyMalariaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Climate crisis could be destabilising mountain areas like Nepal, experts warn | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Unusual heat this year may have melted ice and thawed bonds that hold glaciers in place – leading to catastrophe
Author: Jonathan Watts
Headline: Unusual heat this year may have melted ice and thawed bonds that hold glaciers in place – leading to catastrophe
Content: Nuwakot in Nepal. The UN’s scientific advisory body warned in 2023 that ice-bound landmasses would become more unstable.Photograph: Sanjit Pariyar/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenNuwakot in Nepal. The UN’s scientific advisory body warned in 2023 that ice-bound landmasses would become more unstable.Photograph: Sanjit Pariyar/NurPhoto/ShutterstockNepal-Tibet flood disasterClimate crisis could be destabilising mountain areas like Nepal, experts warnUnusual heat this year may have melted ice and thawed bonds that hold glaciers in place – leading to catastropheNepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updatesWhat caused the flash flood in Nepal and Tibet?Jonathan WattsThu 27 Aug 2026 14.25 EDTFirst published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 14.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe devastating flash flood that has ripped through the border communities of Nepal andTibethas heightened fears that the climate crisis is destabilising the geology of mountain and polar regions, threatening millions of people.Satellite imagery suggests a glacier collapse high in the Himalayas was the primary cause of the deadly torrent of mud, water and ice that tore along the Bhotekoshi River on Wednesday. It swept away buildings and roads and left at least 360 dead and 1,400 missing.A magnitude 4.4 earthquake was initially blamed for the collapse. However, it is now thought to have been caused by the huge wall of ice that crashed down on to the north slope of Langtang Lirung, a 7,000-metre (23,000ft) mountain, the impact of which registered a magnitude of 5.2.“Additional analysis of long-period seismic waves indicates that the seismic energy was instead generated by a glacial collapse and debris flow,”the US Geological Survey said.A map showing the area where the flash flood hit.The ice-rock avalanche pushed boulders and other debris into the Lhende Khola River, a tributary of the Bhotekoshi River. Water levels in rivers downstream rose by between 7 and 9 metres within 30 minutes, according to the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, an intergovernmental scientific institution.Scientists are still examining the precise mechanics of the Himalayan disaster, but manyobserve thatglaciers and permafrost around the world are being weakened by global heating, caused by the burning of gas, oil and coal.View image in fullscreenFlooding in the Bhotekoshi River has affected low-lying areas along the riverbanks and nearby homes in Nuwakot, Nepal.Photograph: Ap Tolang/Nexpher/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockThe detachment of a chunk of the glacier wall came amid unusual heat that was likely to have melted the ice that bound the splintered bedrock together.Two days before the collapse, the ground temperature hit its highest point in the last two years, according to Dr Hamish Pritchard, a glaciologist with the British Antarctic Survey, whose team had sensors 6 miles (10km) away from the site.“These high temperatures would have weakened the snowpack, filled crevasses with water and thawed the bonds between ice and rock that hold these glaciers in place,” he told the Science Media Centre.A series of intense heatwaves has hit the region since early this year and affected countries around the world. Another factor here was the monsoon season, which saturated the soil and swelled rivers.A map showing the timeline of the disaster.Disasters like this were foretold. In 2023 theUN’s top scientific advisory body warnedthat previously ice-bound landmasses – from permafrost tundra to mountain glaciers – would become increasingly unstable as temperatures rose.“Every increment of warming will multiply and intensify future hazards from cryosphere regions,” observed the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change in its sixth synthesis report. “Floods, landslides and freshwater shortages from glacier retreat and snow loss pose a serious threat to mountain regions across the world.”Average global temperatures are nudging closer to 1.5C above preindustrial levels.Even faster warmingis occurring in alpine and polar regions because the loss of snow and ice is removing the thermal insulation of the land.Dr Richard Waller, a senior lecturer in physical geography at Keele University, said: “The progressive loss of snow and glacier ice results in the surface being less reflective, so it absorbs more solar energy and heats up. In combination with atmospheric warming, this is leading to the melting of mountain permafrost.“Think of the high mountains like this as shattered bedrock glued together by ice-filled joints. As the permafrost and the ice-filled joints melt, then there’s the potential for these types of catastrophic failure.”View image in fullscreenA destroyed building in Devighat, Nuwakot.Photograph: Niranjan Shrestha/APThe thaw is altering the shape, colour and solidity of the landscape, creating or expanding glacial meltwater lakes and, in the long term, threatening the origin of many rivers and the drinking supplies of populations downstream. In many parts of Asia, hundreds of millions of people depend on the rivers such as the Ganges and the Brahmaputra that descend from the glaciers.Scientists have high confidence that glacier retreat is caused by human-driven global heating. This has caused glacier collapses from the Alps to the Andes. In the Langtang catchment area in Nepal, glacier loss rates have increased more than fourfold since 1964, astudy has shown.TImeline of how deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – explainerThis has contributed to a loss of life on multiple occasions. A smaller floodhit the Bhotekoshi River in July 2025and in 2015, the Langtang Lirung mountain was hit by an earthquake-induced avalanche that destroyed Langtang village.As emergency services look for bodies and humanitarian relief groups mobilise for survivors, others are asking where next. Waller said any high mountain areas with glaciers and permafrost could be vulnerable, including the European Alps, Caucasus, Himalayas, Andes and beyond.As glacier weakening accelerates, Pritchard called for greater disaster preparedness. “More avalanches and more floods are inevitable, particularly as lakes grow in front of the retreating glaciers,” he said. “Early warning systems are urgently needed to protect the people living in these valleys.”Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalTibetChinaSouth and central AsiaClimate crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Race to get aid into Nepal and Tibet amid warnings flood lake could burst | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Flash floods have killed at least 469 people while homes and infrastructure have been swept away
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Flash floods have killed at least 469 people while homes and infrastructure have been swept away
Content: The aftermath of the floods in Nuwakot, Nepal. More than 1,300 people are missing.Photograph: Skanda Gautam/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe aftermath of the floods in Nuwakot, Nepal. More than 1,300 people are missing.Photograph: Skanda Gautam/SOPA Images/ShutterstockNepal-Tibet flood disasterRace to get aid into Nepal and Tibet amid warnings flood lake could burstFlash floods have killed at least 469 people while homes and infrastructure have been swept awayNepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updatesWhat caused the flash flood in Nepal and Tibet?Hannah Ellis-PetersenandGaurav Pokharelin Kathmandu,Sam JonesandAmy HawkinsThu 27 Aug 2026 14.03 EDTFirst published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 12.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe international community was scrambling to get aid into flood-stricken parts of Nepal andTibeton Thursday as authorities warned that a lake ⁠formed at the ⁠site ⁠where the ​deadly torrents occurred ⁠was rising and ⁠at risk ​of ‌bursting.The catastrophic flash floods that hitNepaland Tibet on Wednesday, thundering down valleys and obliterating entire villages, killed at least 469 people and left more than 1,300 missing.Efforts to locate those unaccounted for – including hundreds of tourists from India, the US, Britain, Australia and Canada – have been complicated by the destruction of dozens of bridges and 25 miles (40km) of roads in the mountainous region, which is popular with trekkers and pilgrims.Satellite images showing before and after collapseRescue teams reported finding bodies hundreds of miles downstream from the disaster zone in the Chitwan district of Nepal, near the Tibetan border. Dozens of injured people were transported to Kathmandu for advanced medical care and more than 100 people were rescued by Nepali army personnel in helicopters.Videos from Wednesday’s disaster showed amassive wall of water crashing down on the borderas people tried to flee. The power, volume and speed of the floods gave little time for escape.Trucks were overturned and houses, roads ⁠and power plants were swept away in Nepal, while ​officials in Tibet said they feared “major casualties” after a mudslide hit a border crossing.How the deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – a visual guideRead moreTom Fletcher, the UN’s humanitarian chief, described the flood as “horrifying”. He said emergency teams had been mobilised and an initial $2m (£1.5m) of disaster funds allocated to cover emergency medical care, shelter and water.9:21‘Tsunami from the sky:’ floods leave trail of devastation in Nepal and Tibet - The LatestNepal’s disaster authority warned of continuing danger on Thursday, appealing to residents and rescuers to stay away from a swelling lake that had formed at the flood site. Chinese authorities said a barrier lake at the confluence of the Tsogyal and Purupqiangzangbu rivers was overflowing and could burst.Girilal Budhathoki, 36, who lives in the Rasuwa district of Nepal’s Bagmati province, said the flood waters swept away his wife and four children while he was away from the family home.“A huge surge of water came,” he said. “Everything turned completely black, and I couldn’t understand what was happening. Suddenly, something heavy crushed me and I fell down.”Budhathoki realised what had happened only when he returned to the place where his house had stood. “I searched desperately for my wife and children but I couldn’t find them,” he said. “They didn’t make it out. My wife was swept away too. I am all alone now.”Map showing location of the disasterKamal Kharel, who works at a hydropower plant in Chilime, also in Rasuwa district, was in the office when the floods hit. “The whole place shook as if there had been a huge earthquake,” he said. “But when I went outside, I saw everything a storm and raging water.”Kharel and some of his colleagues managed to climb a hill, where they stayed until they were rescued by the army on Thursday morning. He said: “I had never seen waves crashing that high. You only see waves like that in the sea.”People from the hard-hit districts of Nuwakot and Dhading, in Bagmati province, were seen gathering outside an army training centre – the base for helicopter rescue operations – seeking information about missing family members.Police were recording the names of the missing outside the barracks gate. Mobile phone torches were their only source of light as the area remained without electricity because of damaged hydroelectric infrastructure.View image in fullscreenFlooding has caused widespread damage to homes, roads, bridges and other infrastructure in Nuwakot, Nepal.Photograph: Ap Tolang/Nexpher/Zuma Press/ShutterstockThe village of Soley, in Nuwakot, which had about 25 homes, was almost wiped out, according to Nirajan Paudyal, a Kathmandu-based journalist whose parents and other relatives lived there. Desperate for information, he had travelled to the area on Thursday for news of his family. “There is no update till now,” he said. “I fear there won’t be any update.”More than 500 foreigners were among 826 people missing in Nepal, police and tourism ⁠officials said. Among those unaccounted for were 177 from India, 90 from the US, 34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 25 from Canada.Chinese state media said at least 558 were missing on the Tibet side of the border, of whom at least 260 were foreign nationals.Many of the victims were on a pilgrimage to Kailash Mansarovar, a high-altitude site in ‌Tibet revered by Hindus and Buddhists among others.Early reports from Nepali ​officials suggested an earthquake could have caused the lower part of a glacier to collapse and trigger ‌the floods. But the US Geological Survey later said what was initially reported ‌as a 4.4-magnitude earthquake was a seismic shock generated by glacial rock and ice collapsing, and the flow of debris. “No earthquake had occurred,” it said.A graphic showing how the situation unfolded.Srijana Gurung, the acting Nepal director for the international NGO Plan International, said communities across the Himalayan country were facing “climate shock after shock” with hardly any time to recover.“Floods and landslides have always happened in Nepal but the climate crisis is making them far more frequent and intense,” she said. “The priority now must be reaching those affected, supporting families searching for loved ones and ensuring vulnerable communities have the assistance they need.”Gurung said children and families who had lost their homes and livelihoods would be in urgent need of medical help, food, shelter and hygiene kits. “There is also a risk of waterborne disease as access to clean water and sanitation is likely to have been damaged,” she said.View image in fullscreenPeople look at the devastation left by flash flooding in Nepal’s Nuwakot district.Photograph: Rajesh Kumar Singh/APScant information has emerged from the Chinese authorities about the scale of the destruction. Tibet is the most tightly controlled part ofChinaeven under normal circumstances. Foreign journalists cannot visit the region unless they are part of a government-controlled tour and the authorities have cracked down harshly on calls for greater autonomy from the Tibetan people. Tibetans have almost no contact with the international media because of fears of retribution.Only brief, state-controlled media reports about the floods have been allowed to circulate in China and the authorities have confirmed only three deaths. Chinese reports have focused on rescue efforts.Locator map for the wider regionMaya Wang, the deputy Asia director at Human Rights Watch, wrote on X: “The floods raise questions about whether Chinese authorities could’ve done more to reduce disaster risks, given longstanding concerns from Tibetan diaspora groups & experts about rapid, state-led development in areas where Tibetans have little say.”She called on Beijing to “allow Tibetans access to information and international researchers and journalists unfettered access to the region, and conduct a rigorous investigation into the disaster”.Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalTibetChinaSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Search is on for at least 33 Britons missing after flash floods in Nepal and Tibet | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Rescue teams try to locate nearly 1,400 missing people, mostly tourists, while police report recovery of 389 bodies
Author: Rachel Hall
Headline: Rescue teams try to locate nearly 1,400 missing people, mostly tourists, while police report recovery of 389 bodies
Content: Rescuers search for survivors in Devghat, in Nepal's Nuwakot district, on Wednesday.Photograph: Prakash Mathema/AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenRescuers search for survivors in Devghat, in Nepal's Nuwakot district, on Wednesday.Photograph: Prakash Mathema/AFP/GettyNepal-Tibet flood disasterSearch is on for at least 33 Britons missing after flash floods in Nepal and TibetRescue teams try to locate nearly 1,400 missing people, mostly tourists, while police report recovery of 389 bodiesNepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updatesRachel HallandNadeem BadshahThu 27 Aug 2026 14.02 EDTFirst published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 05.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRescue teams in Nepal are searching for at least 33 British nationals who are among those missing after flash floods ravaged its border withTibet, killing more than 380 people.Nearly 1,400 people are missing, most of them tourists, authorities have said, after a glacier collapse triggered floods thatroared down valleys and razed entire villages.Nepal police said 389 bodies had been recovered and the number of injured and rescued people had reached 466.Nepal’s national disaster risk reduction and management authority said the number of out-of-contact foreign nationals had increased to 517.The tour company Kailash Journeys confirmed it had not been able to account for seven UK nationals – five women and two men aged between 18 and 55 – travelling with the operator.Another tour company, the Trekkers’ Society, said among the British citizens who had been completing one of its tours to the sacred Hindu site of Mount Kailash were four males aged 14, 50, 50 and 54, and five women aged 40, 46, 50, 50 and 53.9:21‘Tsunami from the sky:’ floods leave trail of devastation in Nepal and Tibet - The LatestNearly 1,400 missing, mostly tourists, after Nepal-Tibet flash flood kills at least 270Read moreThe tour operator Alpine Eco Trek said a 13-year-old girl was among the missing British nationals and two Irish citizens were also missing. They were on a nine-day tour to Mount Kailash and crossing into Tibet from Nepal when they became trapped at the border as the flash floods struck.Other missing British nationals with Alpine Eco Trek are three men aged 65, 64 and 52, and seven women aged 44, 47, 51, 60, 63, 63 and 65, according to travel logs.The tour company Himalayan Glacier US told the BBC it had lost contact with a group of 47 guests, including two British citizens, who were en route to Mount Kailash. Fishtail Tours, a Nepali travel agency, said one British person was missing.View image in fullscreenA damaged bridge in Galchhi, Nepal.Photograph: Francis Mascarenhas/ReutersAmong those missing with links to the UK are Sarada Simkhada, a senior nurse at Darent Valley Hospital in Kent, who was making a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash.Her brother Shambhu wrote on social media: “My dear sister, wherever you are, please stay strong. We are praying for your safety every moment and waiting desperately for you to return home.”Leena Bector, a director of a care agency from Slough, west London, is among 27 travellers associated with the Fishtail Tours and Travels group currently unaccounted for.Hema Amin, from Croydon in south London, started a pilgrimage to Gosainkunda lake on Monday that was supposed to last until 4 September.Her husband, Sunil Amin, told Sky News: “I keep trying to call her. I’ve been trying, trying, trying.”Nabhi Nandan Das, 64, a Hindu priest from south London, was leading a group on a tour to Mount Kailash and Lake Mansarovar.Mala and Bipin Patel, from Coventry, went missing after travelling to Nepal and Tibet on a pilgrimage. Their son, Anant Patel, told Sky News he was “shocked” at the lack of information about their whereabouts.Pramod Poudel, from Uckfield, East Sussex, told the BBC that his wife, Sumitra Sapkota, as well as his parents, brother and uncle, had been caught in flash flooding. He said he would fly to Nepal on Thursday night to try to make contact with them.View image in fullscreenPramod Poudel said his wife, Sumitra Sapkota, had been caught in the flash flooding along with his parents, brother and uncle.Photograph: Family HandoutPoudel said: “I guess there is no power so they can’t charge their phones – to be honest, it’s a very hard and difficult time at the moment.”In an emotional interview, he said: “I have seen pictures of where my home town used to be … and there is nothing there now.”Andy Burnham has pledged an initial £5m in UK government support and offered to send emergency responders and rescue support to assist Nepal’s disaster response efforts. Speaking to journalists during a visit to south Wales, he said: “It’s a devastating picture that is emerging from what has happened in Nepal. Scenes that we’ve never seen the like before, I don’t think, certainly the scale of the devastation.“So there is immediate action being taken. We are deploying consular support staff to the region so that British nationals will be able to access support 24/7. Obviously there are a number of British nationals who currently are thought to be missing and we’ll be providing all the support we can to their families in what is a very distressing and devastating situation.”He added in a statement: “In the past, Nepal has been there for Britain in our hour of need, and we will be there for Nepal in its hour of need right now.”King Charles said he and Queen Camilla were heartbroken and sent their “most profound sympathy” to those affected. “Many in the United Kingdom have strong, deep and personal ties to this part of the world,” he said.location mapThe Prince and Princess of Wales also expressed their shock. “We are thinking of everyone caught up in this terrible disaster,” they said.The president of the Nepal Centre for Disaster Management, Bishal Nath Upreti, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that the flash floods were like a “tsunami from the sky”. He said: “It’s a huge debris, and in fact, after the 2015 earthquake, this is one of the largest disasters that we have [had] in Nepal.”He added: “It was such a huge amount of water. You can imagine it is 20m cubic metres excess water on the river … Villages and villages along the almost 40 to 50 kilometres were completely wiped out.”The Nepal tourism board said on Wednesday that 33 UK citizens were among the foreign nationals unaccounted for. At least three people had died in Tibet, according to China’s state broadcaster CCTV, while the Xinhua news agency said 558 people were unaccounted for in the region.before and after glacier collapseRescuers are racing to locate people missing in the mountainous Rasuwa region, which borders China’s autonomous region of Tibet and is popular with trekkers and pilgrims.The UK ministerPat McFaddentold Times Radio the picture was “not completely clear yet”, with “many, many more” people understood to be missing than those reported by the Nepalese authorities, and no clear figures from China yet.Mudslide submerges China-Nepal crossing point – videoHe said: “In terms of missing Britons, my colleague the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has posted on social media phone numbers that people can call for further information.“But it’s a fast-moving picture. We don’t have a full picture yet of the numbers missing.”The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office said it was “deeply saddened by the loss of life and devastation caused by the floods in Nepal”. It added: “British nationals in Nepal should follow local authority advice and exercise caution while travelling. For consular assistance call (+44) (0)207 008 5000 or (+977) (0)14237100.”Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalTibetChinaSouth and central AsiaPat McFaddenAndy BurnhamnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham announces crackdown on rogue bailiffs and ‘cowboy builders’ | Borrowing & debt | The Guardian
description: New rules are aimed at protecting people in debt in England and Wales and stopping homeowners being ripped off
Author: Rupert Jones
Headline: New rules are aimed at protecting people in debt in England and Wales and stopping homeowners being ripped off
Content: More than 7m cases are sent to bailiff enforcement each year and the industry collects more than £1bn annually.Photograph: Ian Francis/AlamyView image in fullscreenMore than 7m cases are sent to bailiff enforcement each year and the industry collects more than £1bn annually.Photograph: Ian Francis/AlamyBorrowing & debtBurnham announces crackdown on rogue bailiffs and ‘cowboy builders’New rules are aimed at protecting people in debt in England and Wales and stopping homeowners being ripped offRupert JonesThu 27 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 17.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA clampdown on “rogue bailiffs” has been launched byAndy Burnhamamid concerns that vulnerable people are being overcharged and face aggressive behaviour.In the latest in a series of “everyday fixes” to ease the cost of living and “make Britain fairer”, the prime minister said he was strengthening the rules that apply to bailiffs inEnglandand Wales to better protect people in debt.He also announced measures to target “cowboy” tradespeople, including builders who rip off homeowners.The crackdown on bailiffs comes two months after the Guardian revealed that the government had beenaccused of dragging its feeton the issue.In June 2025, the Ministry of Justice announced it wouldlegislate to make independent regulation of bailiffs mandatory. But a year later, with no clear plan in sight, the body that oversees the industry in England and Wales criticised the lack of progress.More than 7m cases are sent to bailiff enforcement each year and the industry collects more than £1bn annually, most of which relates to unpaid parking and traffic fines and council tax arrears.It is not a requirement for enforcement companies to be authorised by the Enforcement Conduct Board (ECB) and some companies have refused to sign up.In June, Martin Lewis, the founder of MoneySavingExpert.com, said it was“outrageous that we still don’t have a proper independent regulator [of bailiffs]”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWater firms sent bailiffs to tens of thousands of homes for debts under £1,000Read moreIn its announcement, the government said private bailiffs in England andWaleswould need to be accredited by the ECB, or work for an enforcement company that is, in order to obtain or renew the certificates they are required to hold.It added: “Private bailiffs will be held to consistent professional standards, and those facing enforcement action will have access to an independent complaints process – strengthening the rights of the most vulnerable.”It is thought the new regime will not fully take effect until next year.Poor practices highlighted by consumer groups range from aggressive behaviour on the doorstep and overcharging, to clamping vehicles used by disabled people and threatening to remove “exempt” possessions.Sarah Sackman, the minister for courts and legal services, said that when someone was already struggling with debt “the last thing they should face is intimidating behaviour, unfair treatment or being pushed into excessive repayment arrangements they cannot afford”.Burnham said that after taking on subscription traps and fake discounts, “we’re coming for the cowboy builders” and other unscrupulous traders. From next month, a government-backed scheme will help people identify and hire trusted builders and other traders “with confidence”.Businesses who sign up to the “Approved Code” scheme for the home improvement sector – developed by the furniture and home improvement ombudsman – will be able to show they meet higher standards, said a spokesperson. This will go live with the first businesses by the end of September and be fully implemented by December.A separate app-based service called Trusted Payments, due to go live next week, will allow consumers to better protect their money during a building project by ensuring it is held safely – similar to deposit protection schemes for tenants. It will allow them to release cash to pay their builder bit by bit, linked to key project milestones.Explore more on these topicsBorrowing & debtConsumer rightsRegulatorsAndy BurnhamEnglandWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham accused of U-turn after initially backing political donations cap to fall below £500k | Party funding | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Campaigner says PM wrote in email he believed £500k cap should be reduced over time to guard against undue influences
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Exclusive: Campaigner says PM wrote in email he believed £500k cap should be reduced over time to guard against undue influences
Content: Other campaigners, including the broadcaster Carol Vorderman, are urging Andy Burnham not to back down over a donations cap in the face of opposition from trade unions.Photograph: WPA/GettyView image in fullscreenOther campaigners, including the broadcaster Carol Vorderman, are urging Andy Burnham not to back down over a donations cap in the face of opposition from trade unions.Photograph: WPA/GettyParty fundingBurnham accused of U-turn after initially backing political donations cap to fall below £500kExclusive: Campaigner says PM wrote in email he believed £500k cap should be reduced over time to guard against undue influencesKiran StaceyPolicy editorThu 27 Aug 2026 14.51 EDTFirst published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 14.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham recently supported an even lower donations cap than previously reported, according to correspondence seen by the Guardian, as the row over next week’s elections bill escalates.The prime minister wrote to a campaigner in May outlining his support for a £500,000 individual donations cap, which he said would “guard against the perception of any one party being unduly influenced or swayed by one person or organisation”.In a follow-up email seen by the Guardian, Burnham went on to say he believed the cap should gradually be reduced – a proposal now being put forward by the Labour MPStella Creasy.Campaigners are accusing Burnham of a U-turn afterthe Guardian reportedthe prime minister had decided not to back the attempts by Creasy and others to introduce a donations cap in next week’s elections bill.In his first message to Shaun Bowler, who runs the websitewakeupgb.co.uk, Burnham wrote: “I do think there should be a cap on political donations. This would guard against the perception of any one party being unduly influenced or swayed by one person or organisation.“As to the level, I think that would have to be subject to wider review of political funding but my gut feeling would suggest somewhere in the region of £500k.”In a second message, the then would-be MP for Makerfield said: “[I] would definitely want to see that reduced over time. I am in complete agreement that there needs to be wholesale culture change in Westminster.”Bowler has now written to the prime minister accusing him of abandoning his previous commitments. He wrote: “It appears you are going to break your promise to me – and the nation …. Weeks after being elected, you have made your first major U-turn.”Burnham drops support for political funding cap aimed at curbing mega-donorsRead moreHe added: “This is your chance to actually deliver the start of that cleanup. Show us that politics can be clean and trustworthy. Don’t surrender to the mess.”Other campaigners, including the broadcaster Carol Vorderman, are also urging the prime minister not to back down in the face of opposition from trade unions, who havewarned that a donations cap could undermine their ability to contributeto the Labour party.Senior figures at groups including Transparency International, Spotlight on Corruption and Greenpeace have also written to Burnham. In an open letter, they call for a “low and hard cap on all political donations”, adding: “We know you agree that politics should not be for sale. Please take action now to ensure it will not be under your leadership.”The issue will come to a head next week when MPs debate the next stage of the elections bill. The bill will lower the voting age to 16 and cap donations by Britons based abroad, but not on domestic donations.Creasy had put forward an amendment to cap domestic donations at £100,000, while her colleague put forward an amendment to cap them at £1m.Creasy has now changed her amendment to set the cap at £500,000, reducing in the second year to £100,000 unless ministers intervene to set it at a different level. The proposal, which has cross-party backing, mirrors what Burnham told Bowler he would support in May.The prime minister’s aides say that while he is not backing a donations cap next week, he is not ruling one out in the future. ALaboursource said: “This bill was designed to deliver our manifesto commitments on votes at 16 and to strengthen political donation rules to guard against foreign interference and that’s what the government is prioritising. But we’re not ruling out taking further steps to protect our democracy in the future.”Officials also said the government would not support an attempt by the Labour MP Anneliese Dodds to reduce the amount political parties can spend during an election campaign after the limit was raised by the previous Conservative government.Explore more on these topicsParty fundingLabourAndy BurnhamElectoral reformStella CreasyTrade unionsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Three journalists sue Pentagon after being fired from military news outlet | US military | The Guardian
description: Three employees of Stars and Stripes, a government-funded news service, allege they were fired after reporting on USS Abraham Lincoln
Author: Robert Mackey
Headline: Three employees of Stars and Stripes, a government-funded news service, allege they were fired after reporting on USS Abraham Lincoln
