breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPhD candidate Hai Nhan Le said accurate positioning of the paraborgs was one of the key engineering challenges.“The cyborg insect has to navigate to the target, position itself accurately and remain stable enough to perform the injection,” Le said.“A lot of people might not like the sight of a giant cockroach scurrying towards them, but if you’re trapped in rubble or stuck in a cave and need help, it could make a real difference between life and death.”The cockroaches, like the team’s previous cyborg insect models, are anaesthetised during electrode and microchip fitting and live for as long as other cockroaches once the harnesses are removed.Fire and Rescue NSWSupt Tim Hassiotis said the technology could extend the reach of rescue teams.“If cyborg insects can safely enter spaces we can’t, locate casualties and ultimately help deliver emergency care, they could become another valuable tool in the future of urban search and rescue,” he said.Vo-Doan said the longer-term vision was to deploy swarms of specialised cyborg insects, with individuals performing complementary roles.“Hopefully, within the next five to 10 years, we could see cyborg insect rescue teams deployed to help people in real emergencies,” he said.Explore more on these topicsRobotsQueenslandnewsShareReuse this content

title: An $18bn settlement is a drop in the ocean for Meta – but the tide will still come for it | Chris Stokel-Walker | The Guardian
description: This week’s settlement without liability was pragmatic, but it doesn’t change the inevitability of further lawsuits around the world, says technology writer Chris Stokel-Walker
Author: Chris Stokel-Walker
Headline: This week’s settlement without liability was pragmatic, but it doesn’t change the inevitability of further lawsuits around the world, says technology writer Chris Stokel-Walker
Content: Mark Zuckerberg arrives at a court in LA for a trial over whether social media platforms deliberately addict and harm children, 18 February 2026.Photograph: Ryan Sun/APView image in fullscreenMark Zuckerberg arrives at a court in LA for a trial over whether social media platforms deliberately addict and harm children, 18 February 2026.Photograph: Ryan Sun/APOpinionMetaAn $18bn settlement is a drop in the ocean for Meta – but the tide will still come for itChris Stokel-WalkerThis week’s settlement without liability was pragmatic, but it doesn’t change the inevitability of further lawsuits around the worldThu 27 Aug 2026 09.11 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 13.59 EDTShareNot many people would count paying $18bn they didn’t expect to when they woke up that morning as a victory. Yet for Meta, the owners of Facebook and Instagram, the agreementwith 52 US attorneys generalto settle claims that it designed its products to be addictive to children, and misled people about their safety, could be described as a win of sorts.Meta denies wrongdoing, and the amount it plans to pay will be spread over a decade. Some of it is contingent on other big tech firms not named in its case coughing up too. The cash is chump change forMeta, which made around $60bn in profit last year. More damaging to the tech giant in the long run could be the agreement to unwind some of the mechanics it has spent two decades perfecting to keep us on its platforms.Under-18s in the US will face a default two-hour daily limit on Facebook andInstagram, with access blocked overnight – unless a parent changes the setting. Teachers will be glad to hear notifications will be muted during school hours, while teenagers will be nagged as much by the platform itself as their parents about exactly how long they have spent staring at their screens.All of these are significant changes that materially change how the company’s products work – and all of them should be welcomed. But in lots of ways, Meta has got off lightly with this agreement, both in what it’s been asked to do and the fine it must pay.What the decision shows, just months after Meta chose to fight its corner in court, and lost significantly, is how the economics of fighting social media litigation have changed. This settlement signifies an important and deliberate shift in strategy. In August, Meta went to court in New Mexico – a decision that cost it dearly. The judge thereordered the firm to pay $942m and overhaul some protections for children– a decision it is appealing. The fact that Meta lost that case, and was found to have done wrong, was far more damaging than this week’s settlement without liability, even if the amounts involved were smaller. Still,thousands more cases involving social media addiction claims are still wending their way through US courts.And chastened by a couple of losses, it looks – at least in this instance – like Meta has taken the approach that a pyrrhic victory is better than the risk of another real loss. Settlements without admission of fault avoid judgments and a legal situation that could quickly spiral out of control for Meta’s product offering.While Meta has had to make significant changes to its platforms as a result of this week’s settlement, it still ultimately has control over what changes are made, and has sought to limit them to the bare minimum. Settling, however expensive, is a way of protecting its core business proposition.Meta now faces a Hobson’s choice when it comes to litigation. It can gamble on a jury and risk vast damages, damaging internal disclosures and a judge deciding which parts of Instagram orFacebookmust change. Or it can pay an eye-watering but manageable sum to settle, negotiate the product changes on its own terms and staunch the bleeding.That $18bn is certainly more than most companies could pay, but it pales in comparison with the $1.5tn Meta’s own PR team warned the case could cost it had it gone through the courts – and the more realistic $200bn the prosecuting lawyers sought to squeeze from the firm. And even more than that, Meta has managed to make some of the bill somebody else’s problem. About a third of the settlement it has agreed to pay is conditional on TikTok and YouTube introducing similar restrictions and each making matching payments. Meta ispublicly calling on both companiesto sign up.As this is a negotiated settlement–and one in which no one wins, but Meta certainly doesn’t lose–not everyone has been won over. While attorneys general from 48 US states agreed to Meta’s proposition, Florida’s representative has publicly rejected the deal and intends to continue pursuing Meta. James Uthmeierdismissed the settlementas “peanuts” and said “We’ll see them at trial.”Nor is this necessarily just an American story. The settlement formally applies only to the participating US states and territories. A Meta spokesperson told me it already offers strong protections for teenagers elsewhere. It will watch how the new measures work before deciding what comes next internationally.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut running substantially different versions of Facebook and Instagram around the world is hardly attractive. And Meta has now demonstrated putting these restrictions in place is possible. Given the drive towards child safety online in the UK and Australia, it seems likely that politicians will soon ask why American teenagers get them and children in their own countries don’t. The UK’s own Online Safety Act is a useful stick for the government to wield in this instance, adding extra leverage to bring those changes here, too.And it’s that which may prove the settlement’s biggest consequence. Meta has paid billions to manage to duck liability in one court case. But in doing so, it may have opened up the possibility of change in a raft of other countries.Chris Stokel-Walker is the author of TikTok Boom: The Inside Story of the World’s Favourite AppDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsMetaOpinionFacebookInternet safetyChildren's healthSocial mediaInstagramChildren's techcommentShareReuse this content

title: AI slopper in chief: Trump turns to social media amid tough questions | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: As the US president struggles to end his Iran war, and approval ratings hit new lows, he leans on a familiar gambit
Author: Adam Gabbatt
Headline: As the US president struggles to end his Iran war, and approval ratings hit new lows, he leans on a familiar gambit
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design/@realDonaldTrump/TruthSocialView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/@realDonaldTrump/TruthSocialDonald TrumpAnalysisAI slopper in chief: Trump turns to social media amid tough questionsAdam GabbattAs the US president struggles to end his Iran war, and approval ratings hit new lows, he leans on a familiar gambitThu 27 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 15.14 EDTShareDonald Trump knows the power of an image – of himself, with everyone fromVladimir PutinandKim Jong-untoKim Kardashian. How about George Washington?As the US president struggles to end his war with Iran, and with his approval ratings hittingthe lowestlevels of his second term, he has in recent weeks posted a series of AI-generated images of himself alongside key historical American figures.Facing tough questions over reports ofpoor living conditions and morale aboard the USS Abraham Lincolnfollowing its record-breaking deployment, and his efforts to reach a deal with Tehran, Trump has repeatedly turned to his Truth Social platform to post images apparently designed to bolster his legacy.Earlier this month, he posted an AI image of himself and Washington standing side by side in what appears to be an imagining of Trump’s completed White House ballroom. A minute later, he posted three more AI pictures of himself and Washington in the ballroom. In one image, they’re looking into the middle distance; in another, Trump is holding a piece of paper andpointing at the ceiling.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump in the Rose Garden, next to a statue of George Washington, at the White House in Washington DC on 24 August.Photograph: Win McNamee/Getty ImagesTrump wasn’t done. The next day, he posted an AI image of himself and Washington sitting at a table, holding quills over what appears to be a map. Three minutes later, he posted an image of the pair on horseback – Washington on a white horse, Trump on a black horse. There was no caption on either.Still, it was Sunday’s post that was the most striking:a videothat showed Washington and Trump walking through the ballroom, taking turns to point to the ceiling as if appraising the room’s construction.“I think part of the reason he’s posting it is because it ties in with this deeper sentiment that he has that he is on par with, or even potentially better than, George Washington,” said Angelo Carusone, president and CEO of Media Matters, a non-profit media watchdog organization.“He’s trying to basically be a founder,” added Carusone. “And AI gives him the ability to project his imagination out into the world.”The Guardian asked the White House whether Trump, 80, thought he had actually met with Washington, who died more than 200 years ago. A spokesperson did not directly address the question, but responded: “Truth Social is the most powerful and popular social media platform in the world [sic] because it serves as President Trump’s authentic voice, where he communicates directly with the American people [sic] and the world without the biased media taking him out of context.”“Every day in Washington DC the city changes and gets more Trump-branded,” Carusone said. “That is the analog to Washington: there are all these things named after him, but that happened posthumously. With Trump, it’s almost like he’s building a living mausoleum.”Trump’s ballroom has at times appeared to be among his main interests during his second term. The president has openly admitted he wants the ballroom to serve as a “legacy project”, and when the going gets tough, this seems to be a topic to which he retreats.There is evidence, too, that Trump wants to secure a legacy that sees him not just as an accomplished ballroom builder, but as a successful wartime leader.Trump has also postedan AI imageshowing him wearing a military uniform, flanked by second world war generals George Patton and Douglas MacArthur on a battlefield. In the image, two tanks appear to be on fire in the background, and Trump, who has received a generous AI glow-up, has six rows of medals on his chest – more than Patton and MacArthur are shown with combined.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpSocial mediaAI (artificial intelligence)Digital mediaUS politicsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Three UK airports hit by cyber-attack with data of 8.7m customers accessed | Airline industry | The Guardian
description: Company that runs Manchester, Stansted and East Midlands hubs says passenger safety is unaffected
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Company that runs Manchester, Stansted and East Midlands hubs says passenger safety is unaffected
Content: Manchester airport. Most of the accessed data related to wifi sign-ups in the three airports’ terminals.Photograph: AP S (uk)/AlamyView image in fullscreenManchester airport. Most of the accessed data related to wifi sign-ups in the three airports’ terminals.Photograph: AP S (uk)/AlamyAirline industryThree UK airports hit by cyber-attack with data of 8.7m customers accessedCompany that runs Manchester, Stansted and East Midlands hubs says passenger safety is unaffectedBusiness live – latest updatesLauren AlmeidaThu 27 Aug 2026 10.53 EDTFirst published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 08.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester, London Stansted and East Midlands airports have been hit by a cyber-attack in which hackers accessed the data of about 8.7 million customers.The incident involved data related to “car park, lounge and fast-track bookings and in-airport wifi sign-ups”, and the hackers obtained email addresses, phone numbers, vehicle registration numbers and postcodes, said Manchester Airports Group (MAG), which operates the three hubs.The company said that “at no point has passenger safety or aviation security been compromised” during the incident and operations at the airports were unaffected. The hacked system did not hold customers’ bank or payment details.View image in fullscreenAn email sent to an affected customer from London Stansted airport.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAIn an email to customers, London Stansted said: “We would urge you to be particularly cautious of unexpected emails, calls or text messages claiming to be from us. We will never contact you unexpectedly to ask for payment or banking information. We apologise for any inconvenience or concern this may cause.”The cyber-attack hit the airports during the peak summer travel season. Many families are flying back into the UK this week before the start of the new school year. Fifty-four million passengers flew through Manchester, London Stansted and East Midlands airports combined last year.A MAG spokesperson said the company had “immediately contained the risk” from the incident and was “working with specialist advisers and taking appropriate steps to protect our customers and systems”.“We have informed and are working with the relevant authorities. At no point has passenger safety or aviation security been compromised,” they said. “Airport operations remain unaffected and customer parking services continue to operate normally.“We would like to reassure customers that Manchester Airport Group takes the security of customer information extremely seriously and we apologise for any inconvenience or concern caused.”Lauren Wills-Dixon, a partner at the law firm Gordons, said the scale of the attack was notable.“Airports sell a number of services including lounge access, parking and fast-track bookings. Wi-fi access also requires customers to input their data,” she said. “As a result, operators will hold large amounts of customer data and this, together with the increased use of technology, only increases the threat of a cyber-attack.”The incident comes as pressure grows on suppliers and operators of national infrastructure to improve their cyber-defences.Flights were delayed and cancelled last year at three major European airports – including London’s largest, Heathrow – after thecompany behind the software used for check-in and boarding said it had been hit by a cyber-attack.Hackers linked to Iran were blamed earlier this monthfor a cyber-attack that caused the temporary shutdown of a British power plant. The government said the incident involved a small-scale generator and that at no point was there a risk to the wider energy system.There was a wave of high-profile cyber-attacks against British companies last year, ranging from one thatshut down the operations of Jaguar Land Rover for weeksto others targetingMarks & Spencer,Harrodsand theCo-op food chain.Explore more on these topicsAirline industryCybercrimeHackingStansted airportManchesterDerbyshireTransportnewsShareReuse this content

title: AI can detect heart disease in women using mammograms, study suggests | Women's health | The Guardian
description: Experts say findings mean breast screenings for cancer could also flag cardiovascular problems in women
Author: Andrew Gregory
Headline: Experts say findings mean breast screenings for cancer could also flag cardiovascular problems in women
Content: The study examined 97,364 breast scans from 29,921 women who had an average age of 54.Photograph: andresr/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe study examined 97,364 breast scans from 29,921 women who had an average age of 54.Photograph: andresr/Getty ImagesWomen's healthAI can detect heart disease in women using mammograms, study suggestsExperts say findings mean breast screenings for cancer could also flag cardiovascular problems in womenAndrew GregoryHealth editor in MunichThu 27 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 15.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDoctors have discovered a way to use routine mammograms that screen for breast cancer to spot heart disease, the world’s leading – and frequently underdiagnosed – cause of death in women.Researchers analysed the scans using artificial intelligence and were able to successfully identify women with coronary heart disease, high blood pressure or who had suffered a stroke.Experts said it meant breast screening for cancer could become dual-purpose, helping to flag women with heart disease, and other cardiovascular issues, as well as spotting breast cancer early.Millions of women are living with undetected heart disease. For decades, it has often been misdiagnosed or not picked up until the late stages of the disease.Details of the breakthrough were presented in Munich at the European Society of Cardiology’s annual congress, the world’s largest heart conference. The implications are significant because hundreds of millions of women undergo mammograms every year.Doctors in Israel examined 97,364 scans from 29,921 women who had an average age of 54. By cross-referencing medical records, they found 16% of the women had high blood pressure, 2.5% had coronary heart disease, and 2.5% had experienced a stroke.A machine-learning model was trained to identify women with these conditions and was able to reliably identify women who had suffered a stroke, based upon their mammogram alone, 86% of the time.I work in a hospital – and didn’t know I was having a heart attack. Here’s what more women should knowRead moreFor high blood pressure and coronary heart disease, it was 79% and 78% reliable at distinguishing between the women with the condition and those without. The results were also consistent regardless of age, or whether or not a woman also had cancer.Dr Viana Copeland from Tel Aviv University, Israel, presented the findings to delegates in Munich. “Despite being the leading cause of death in women worldwide, CVD [cardiovascular disease] is consistently underdiagnosed and undertreated,” she said.“A common finding in our medical centre, and around the world, is that when women do seek medical help, their CVD is already advanced. On the other hand, many women do attend routine breast cancer screening, even when they haven’t sought care for cardiovascular symptoms.”Because mammography is already widely used, analysing breast scans for information about a woman’s heart health “could potentially offer a scalable approach without requiring an additional imaging examination,” Copeland added.“Mammography also reaches many women in midlife, an important period for recognising and addressing cardiovascular risk.”A team of doctors and medical researchers are working to improve the accuracy of the AI model and reduce false results, while increasing the number of heart conditions it can detect.Elena Arbelo, an expert member of the European Society of Cardiology communication committee, said the findings were “compelling”.“A mammogram may one day do more than look for breast cancer – it may also offer a window on to cardiovascular health. That matters because CVD in women is still too often recognised late.”She added: “The challenge now is to establish accuracy and reliability – to move from experimentation to clinical implementation.”Dr Sonya Babu-Narayan, a consultant cardiologist and clinical director of the British Heart Foundation, a charity, also welcomed the breakthrough.She said: “Heart disease is the world’s biggest killer of not only men, but also women. Despite this, the myth persists that it’s only a ‘man’s disease’, meaning that when it comes to the heart, women are disproportionally unaware, unheard, underdiagnosed, undertreated and typically underrepresented in clinical research.“It is exciting to think that if the approach used in this large study from Israel is further proven, it could lead to better and earlier cardiovascular disease detection and prevention for women. AI could one day allow breast cancer screening programmes to become dual-purpose, helping to flag women with the highest risk of dangerous cardiovascular disease, as well as spotting breast cancer early.”Explore more on these topicsWomen's healthHeart diseaseBreast cancerAI (artificial intelligence)High blood pressureStrokeHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: AI-proof? Younger workers desert the digital world for traditional crafts | Work & careers | The Guardian
description: In a disrupted job market people are turning to heritage crafts such as bookbinding, metalwork and boatbuilding
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: In a disrupted job market people are turning to heritage crafts such as bookbinding, metalwork and boatbuilding
Content: Eryn Lawley, Imogen Carney and Harriet Bone, apprentices at Ludlow Bookbinders in Shropshire.Photograph: Andrew Fox/The GuardianView image in fullscreenEryn Lawley, Imogen Carney and Harriet Bone, apprentices at Ludlow Bookbinders in Shropshire.Photograph: Andrew Fox/The GuardianWork & careersAI-proof? Younger workers desert the digital world for traditional craftsIn a disrupted job market people are turning to heritage crafts such as bookbinding, metalwork and boatbuildingLauren AlmeidaThu 27 Aug 2026 09.38 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 14.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s a bleak moment for young peopleentering the workforce for the first time. For decades, a university degree seemed to promise a stable career – but entry-level white-collar jobs across almost all sectors arebeing disrupted by AI. Budding accountants, software engineers and junior lawyers increasingly find themselves displaced by cheap automation.Even creative fields are struggling against AI tech that can produce artwork, lengthy prose or complex design briefs in seconds.But many young workers have responded by turning to what they see as “AI-proof” heritage crafts. These are the centuries-old, hands-on jobs, such as boat-making, metalwork or bookbinding, that require specialist knowledge built on creative judgment and dexterity, skills not yet mastered by AI.Eryn Lawley, a 27-year-old politics graduate, said future-proofing her career meant walking away from the digital world. She is now a second-year bookbinder apprentice at Ludlow Bookbinders in Shropshire, learning a trade whose core techniques have not changed for centuries.“Even just staring at a screen too long was bad for me,” she said. “I always wanted to do something more material, and I think there is something more inherently valuable to something when it is made by a person.”The work at Ludlow is slow, detailed and tactile. Thebookbinding processis almost entirely by hand, using Victorian-built presses, foil-blocking machines and glue brushes.“People are discovering that, as everything is already decided for you by a computer or algorithm, being able to make or own something physically is good,”Lawley said. “And it is very satisfying to repeat a task to perfection. It is meditative as a job so it is extremely low-cortisol.”View image in fullscreenLucky Emerson, a Cox London apprentice.Photograph: Inge Clemente/Cox LondonPaul Kidson, Ludlow chief executive and a fourth-generation bookbinder, said an influx of interest from young people represented a lifeline for a rapidly shrinking industry. He estimates there are now fewer than 50 handcraft-operating bookbinders in Britain today.“British bookbinding has a terrific reputation across the world, but like so many things in the 50s, 60s and 70s, the training just started to dry up,” Kidson said. “All the formal apprentice schemes collapsed in the early 1980s, and the industry got no training at all.“We have to train our own people because you can’t recruit at volume because there aren’t any [courses]. Fortunately there is now a desire among a lot of people to want to have the satisfaction of actually making something.”There is no lack of commercial demand. High-end publishers are betting that shoppers will pay a premium for objects that are crafted by human hands. Joanna Reynolds, chief executive of the Folio Society book publisher – which partnered with Ludlow for a limited edition release of a Game of Thrones book – said the company rejected generative AI tools in its creative processes.“We do not use AI in terms of our art,” she said. “We believe in the importance of supporting the creative world, and we know there is huge pressure on them at the moment. Their skills and their abilities need to be supported by as many people as possible.”The number of young people hoping to fill these creative posts is growing rapidly. Cox London, a design house that specialises in artistic metalwork, started its apprenticeship scheme last year. Nicola Cox, a co-founder, said this year the company received more than 160 applications for two apprenticeship places.“People want to make things and work with materials, [to] have that closeness with it,” she said. “There is AI-proofness about art that is made with someone’s hands. There is a real resonance in something that has a mark and the energy of human hands.”For Lucky Emerson, an apprentice at Cox London, there is a “worrying feeling” that AI is taking over the creative world.“The physicality of actually making things is incomparable, especially when people crave originality. Even though technology has advanced, handcrafted art is considered a lot more valuable and will always remain that way.”View image in fullscreenNazifa Tabassum, an apprentice at Cox London.Photograph: Inge Clemente/Cox LondonNazifa Tabassum, also an apprentice at Cox London, said she did not think AI would replace her work, but that it could change it.“For me it isn’t just about making things with my hands,” she said. “It’s about continuously developing my skills, and using technology where it adds value, while still providing the expertise and craftsmanship that people can’t easily automate.“I see AI as a tool that can assist, but not something that replaces, the satisfaction and value of skilled manual, handcrafted work.”At the National Theatre in London, technical apprenticeships span everything from IT to traditional wig-making, costume design, prop-making and metalwork.“Our apprenticeships are partly about the need to create a more representative workforce, both for the National Theatre and for the [wider] creative sector,” said Kath Geraghty, head of technical qualifications.“It is also about plugging the skill gap. These theatre crafts are dying out – our metalworkers are all over 50, wig-making as a skill is really dying. There’s a real need to create our own talent.“And it’s always been about creating a skilled workforce for the wider creative sector beyond theatre, such as film, TV and broadcast.”View image in fullscreenSarah Ray-Dobson, an apprentice prop-maker at the National Theatre.Photograph: Cameron SlaterSarah Ray-Dobson, a 27-year-old apprentice prop-maker at the National Theatre, said she felt her practice had been shielded from AI disruption that affected other creative pursuits.“Everything I’ve been doing for the past two years is very hands-on,” she said. “At my level, it has not been affected by AI.”But Geraghty adds that, like many employers, the National Theatre is struggling with the huge number of AI-generated applications for its apprenticeship programme.“We used to think that 100 applicants was a popular apprenticeship,” she said. “In this most recent round of recruitment, we had 728 applications for one role.“We haven’t yet worked out how to manage it, because it’s not viable for our staff to read 700 applications with care and attention. But the job market that young people are in is difficult, and they are applying for anything they can.”Explore more on these topicsWork & careersCraftEmployabilityAI (artificial intelligence)ApprenticeshipsManufacturing sectorGraduate careersfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy review – picture-postcard retelling of haunting Minoan myth | Games | The Guardian
description: The medieval franchise is transplanted to Crete, conjuring action-adventure magic from familiar ingredients
Author: Lewis Gordon
Headline: The medieval franchise is transplanted to Crete, conjuring action-adventure magic from familiar ingredients
Content: A swashbuckling hero … Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy.Illustration: Asobo StudioView image in fullscreenA swashbuckling hero … Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy.Illustration: Asobo StudioGamesReviewResonance: A Plague Tale Legacy review – picture-postcard retelling of haunting Minoan mythPlayStation 5, Xbox Series S/X, PC; Asobo StudioThe medieval franchise is transplanted to Crete, conjuring action-adventure magic from familiar ingredientsLewis GordonThu 27 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 12.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe path in Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy is a familiar one. Amid ancient ruins and sun-dappled gorges, a young woman, Sophia, dutifully treads the same footsteps as a Minoan warrior from millennia ago, one with whom she seems to share a visionary connection. The “resonance” between these two characters is made clear by their echoing actions – a crank pushed in the bronze age that still works in the medieval present, for example. Through these spliced timelines, it becomes clear that Sophia, compelled by her supernatural gift, possesses little agency. Destiny beckons her forwards.This is a smart meta concept for a game that, at its most basic level, boils down to keeping your left thumb planted firmly on the analogue stick, always pushing Sophia onwards in linear fashion. You jostle her through ornate corridors rendered as higgledy-piggledy pirate camps and cobbled Venetian streets. For the greater part of the game, you propel her through the Minoan remains of Crete, which harbour a dark and terrible secret. It is classic third-person action-adventure fare, building on the template laid down by the likes ofTomb Raiderand then refined and complicated by titles such asThe Last of Us. Little, from an interactive perspective, surprises: you dash, vault and swing between teetering podiums, squeeze through tiny gaps in rock and crouch behind conveniently placed walls to avoid enemies.View image in fullscreenImmersed in the bronze age … Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy.Illustration: Asobo StudioYet the Bordeaux-based studio Asobo conjures magic from the familiar. Sophia, a supporting character from the second game in the A Plague Tale series, carries this swashbuckling adventure with aplomb. She is spiky and confident, the daughter of a wealthy mother and a smuggler father. The game starts with her as a young child, recently escaped from abuse in a nunnery, before cutting to roughly a decade in the future. Now in her 20s, Sophia is a capable, cut-throat fighter, on the hunt for the treasure that lurks deep inside the extensive cave network of Crete – the home, according to Greek mythology, of the bull-headed Minotaur.In tone, Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy is a long way off the dour machismo ofChristopher Nolan’s recent Odyssey adaptation. Rather than brooding, greyscale landscapes, Asobo delivers a Crete that, at least initially, seems lifted directly from holiday brochures: soft sandstone cliffs, swallows dancing in the evening light, vivid green vegetation tangling around crumbling statues. Some of the most striking sights arrive via the Minoan frescoes: their deep oranges and eye-popping yellows have not faded but remain ebulliently bright.View image in fullscreenWorthy of a holiday brochure … Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy.Illustration: Asobo StudioIt is always a treat when the game pivots to this classical time period, briefly putting us in control of the warrior and letting us soak up the vibrant atmosphere through their eyes: crowds baying for blood; stands draped in textile finery; magenta-coloured flowers strewn across mosaic floors.A Plague Tale: Requiem review – rat-infested sequel raises stakes and spectacleRead moreBut, slowly, the world and story darken, though Asobo’s fascination with light – a means of warding off hordes of rats in prior A Plague Tale games – remains. Sophia carries a sphere that can reflect and refract light, crucial for solving environmental puzzles that often involve rotating supersized lenses to redirect beams. But these puzzles, like the platforming, are somewhat rudimentary, causing you to only briefly pause and ponder without ever yielding oh-so-satisfying “aha” moments. Rarely is there more than one solution or the opportunity to get creative: rather, you must follow the logic clearly signposted by the designers.Although stealth is sometimes an option, often our champion must engage in hand-to-hand combat. The most memorable fights occur towards the game’s conclusion, in which swirling light causes calcified, zombie-like figures to disintegrate into dust, Sophia teeing up their demise with lethal slashes of her sword. These are some of the most dynamic melee encounters in the game’s roughly 12-hour run time: a balletic, show-stopping dance of light and movement.Sophia may traipse a path similar to that of countless treasure-hunting, action-adventure video game classics – but for all the overfamiliar design choices, there is enough verve in the beguiling presentation and lively, compellingly drawn characters to elevate this beyond mere retread. Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy succeeds, in large part, because of Sophia, a heroine who confronts history head on, before finally breaking free of it in apocalyptically spectacular style.Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy is released 27 AugustExplore more on these topicsGamesPCXbox series S/XAction gamesAdventure gamesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Trainwatch – alone with your thoughts on a railway line to nowhere | Games | The Guardian
description: The flat routines of a dead end railway job screen out an approaching menace in a quietly intriguing game from the indie developer of Cat Lady and Lorelai
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: The flat routines of a dead end railway job screen out an approaching menace in a quietly intriguing game from the indie developer of Cat Lady and Lorelai
Content: Crossing to bear … Trainwatch.Photograph: Harvester GamesView image in fullscreenCrossing to bear … Trainwatch.Photograph: Harvester GamesSummer games previewsGamesTrainwatch – alone with your thoughts on a railway line to nowhereThe flat routines of a dead end railway job screen out an approaching menace in a quietly intriguing game from the indie developer of  Cat Lady and LorelaiKeith StuartThu 27 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 13.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLonely jobs have provided excellent material for independent video games over the years. FromPapers, PleasetoFirewatchtoThe Stanley Parable, players have been happy to spend hours dwelling in depressing cubicles or rural hideaways, usually because there is an intriguingly hidden point to it all.In Trainwatch, a character named Troy has taken a seemingly godforsaken job as a railway worker in an unnamed desolate backwater. His main task over the course of a single month is to manage a level crossing, closing the gate whenever a train comes, while also carrying out daily chores such as cooking and washing. It sounds serene, but Troy is also running away from something. The other stipulations are that he stays sober and calls his wife every night. And there is something lurking in the fog at the edges of the fields – one day he must face it.View image in fullscreenDesolate … Trainwatch.Photograph: Harvester GamesTrainwatch is the sixth game from solo developer Remigiusz “Rem” Michalski (AKA Harvester Games), and was inspired by a childhood memory. “We used to live near the railway tracks,” he says. “Every night, I’d hear that thundering hum of trains in the distance and see their lights moving slowly in the darkness outside my window. I found that oddly comforting. The world seemed dead and empty, and that train rolling through the night was the only sign of life happening out there.”Michalski describes the game as a time-management mystery adventure, which sounds cosy, but the game’s muted colours and uneasy sense of dread suggest otherwise. Previous games, such as Cat Lady and Lorelai, have explored mental anguish and isolation, and it seems that Trainwatch will continue this theme. “I think most of us are lonely, guilty, or isolated in one way or another,” says Michalski. “We all have our demons living deep inside, and we rarely show them to anyone. Most of the time we don’t even want to acknowledge their existence ourselves.”While you’re running the signal room and carrying out daily tasks of self-care, there are also chances to explore nearby buildings and meet the inhabitants of this strange wasteland, some of whom you’ll have the chance to help. So is there a redemptive arc beneath the rather bleak overtones of Trainwatch? Michalski suggests there is: “It’s a game about trying to dig ourselves out of a hole, re-evaluating what our priorities are, fixing our lives while having a million things on our shoulders all at the same time. And while it touches on many difficult topics, it does so with a sprinkle of dark humour. ”When asked if there were movies or novels that inspired the game’s look, setting and themes, Michalski makes his own personal discovery. “Now that I think about it … I guess being an indie game developer is a little like being a Gatekeeper in Trainwatch. Sure, there’s my wife, pottering about in the flat, the kids getting home from school, talking with excitement … but I spend most of my time here, in my little studio, alone, pushing buttons. So really, the main influence for Trainwatch comes from my secluded life in a tiny Polish town. Thanks for making me realise that!”Trainwatch is coming toPCin 2027Explore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsPCfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Is NBC’s Premier League coverage in the US too English? | Premier League | The Guardian
description: One wonders when, if ever, a US broadcast can win the same plaudits presenting the English league with a more American voice
Author: Leander Schaerlaeckens
Headline: One wonders when, if ever, a US broadcast can win the same plaudits presenting the English league with a more American voice
Content: The new Premier League season kicked off last week.Photograph: Jacques Feeney/Offside/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe new Premier League season kicked off last week.Photograph: Jacques Feeney/Offside/Getty ImagesPremier LeagueIs NBC’s Premier League coverage in the US too English?Leander SchaerlaeckensOne wonders when, if ever, a US broadcast can win the same plaudits presenting the English league with a more American voiceThu 27 Aug 2026 12.36 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 13.47 EDTShareThere they were again, signaling with their unchanging faces and voices and their unchanging studio backdrop that anotherPremier Leagueseason had begun. On Friday afternoon, and again on Saturday and Sunday morning, Rebecca Lowe welcomed American viewers to what is somehow already the 14th season of the world’s most popular sporting circuit to air on NBC.She was flanked, as ever, by her merry band of pundits, her gang of fellow British expats. The Robbies and the other ones. Also, Tim Howard as the token American, albeit one who spent 13 seasons of his goalkeeping career in the Premier League, deemed sufficiently English by osmosis to join the crew.Post-Pep Premier League era begins with blast of hyper-managed shock and awe | Barney RonayRead moreThe games’ announcers would be British, too. And they would all speak of “football” and “pitches” and “away matches.” Teams would be “they,” of course. The ads, too, would sound very English, supremely English, maximally English. For Barclays, among other longtime sponsors leaning hard into the image of the beleaguered American fan, embattled but persevering in his or her niche pursuit of following this plucky little league that airs on one of the nation’s most readily available channels.Taking it all in, I couldn’t help but think back to watching the BBC’s coverage of the final day of the last season for the first time in years with some English expat friends and some VPN trickery. It struck me that somehow, despite originating from the country, it didn’t actually look or sound or feel quite as English-coded as theNBCoffering of the events. Except for the diversity of mellifluous regional accents on offer on the BBC, NBC has out-Englished the English.Other broadcasters have chosen different approaches. Fox leans into its Americanness as hard as NBC does the Englishness in its World Cup presentation. Apple sits somewhere in the middle, on neutral ground, when it airs Major League Soccer.If Major League Baseball’s core product is really nostalgia, and the NFL’s is consumerism and nationalism, then the Premier League’s, going by NBC’s presentation, is anglophilia. It’s all there. The satellite zoom-ins on the league’s quaint stadiums nestled between the brick row houses. The reverence for the club anthems and traditions. The poppies pinned to the on-air talent’s lapels every November to commemorate Britain’s fallen soldiers – a tradition which doesn’t entirely resonate in an American context.NBC’s unsaid sales pitch feels like it should be: Catch a match, and you, too, could look and sound and feel more English, to yourself and to all your friends.For NBC’s part, this has been a perfectly justifiable and coherent business strategy. And it has worked outstandingly well for the broadcaster. In a landscape of shrinking audiences, NBC’s Premier League viewers seem to tick up every year andposted their highest totals ever last season.And in a way, all of this is baked into the recipe. Soccer owes much of its rise in these United States to the worldliness it confers. As the upper middle class discovered soccer – or rediscovered it, to be historically accurate – in the late 1990s and early 2000s, following it signaled that you knew there was more to sports than the NFL, NBA or baseball. That the rest of world mostly followed different sports, and that you were in on its secrets. Bonus points for drinking a Carling in a pub of some American downtown at 7.30 am on a Saturday.But the question that is now imposing itself is how and when the US will develop its own soccer culture, where it no longer has to apologize for its quirks and its lingo. The wildly profitable –almost counterproductively profitable– 2026 World Cup demonstrated anew that the US has been a soccer country for a long time. The sport is mature here now. It is long past needing to establish itself and is now on to the trickier work of consolidating its status and making the smaller gains.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionYet American soccer remains beset by a sense that it doesn’t entirely belong. Its players and teams must still scrap to be taken seriously outside their own borders. There is an unmistakable undercurrent of imposter syndrome running through our soccer scene. And when the sport’s most popular games are presented with an English accent, it stunts the growth of something authentic. How can an organic soccer culture blossom here, after belatedly taking root in the supporter sections of the many MLS and NWSL teams that rushed to brand themselves as “football club”, when NBC’s coverage chooses to stand in the shadow of another?This isn’t to diminish NBC’s Premier League crew or their otherwise excellent work or indeed their career choices. And part of the appeal of the US is that, at its best, it accepts the cultures and norms of the world and finds a place to integrate those things into a kaleidoscopic whole.Lowe even announced that she was a naturalized citizen in 2022.But eventually, American soccer will have to start doing its own things in its own way, rather than just copying what the cool soccer countries are doing. And, among other tasks, that means acknowledging that we speak differently. One wonders what that could do for the growth of the game here.Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: U.S. Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts,which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueUS sports mediaNBCNBC UniversalUS television industrycommentShareReuse this content

title: Unlike needy Keir, trash-talking Andy speaks a language Trump understands | John Crace | The Guardian
description: Burnham has nothing to hide as he prepares to meet president he once called poisonous. It may actually win him more respect
Author: John Crace
Headline: Burnham has nothing to hide as he prepares to meet president he once called poisonous. It may actually win him more respect
Content: ‘He wasn’t going to apologise to The Donald for what he had said. Not least because he had meant every word.’Composite: Kin Cheung/Getty; Tasos KatopodisView image in fullscreen‘He wasn’t going to apologise to The Donald for what he had said. Not least because he had meant every word.’Composite: Kin Cheung/Getty; Tasos KatopodisThe politics sketchAndy BurnhamUnlike needy Keir, trash-talking Andy speaks a language Trump understandsJohn CraceBurnham has nothing to hide as he prepares to meet president he once called poisonous. It may actually win him more respectThu 27 Aug 2026 10.47 EDTFirst published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 10.30 EDTShareIt makes a pleasant change. Not so long ago,Keir Starmerwas falling over himself in his efforts to keep things sweet with Donald Trump. Offering the US president a second state visit within minutes of meeting him. Everyone knows you should never put out on the first date: it only makes the other person think you’re a pushover. Sure enough, The Donald banked the marching bands and the Windsor silver service, made polite conversation for three days and then went back to trash-talking him.Yet still, Starmer just sat there and took it. As if one word of criticism would be too much. Wittering on about the “special relationship” as if Trump gave a moment’s thought to the UK before he did anything. The rest of us wouldn’t have put money on the US president even being able to locate Britain on a map. It was only latterly, when The Donald chose to bomb Iran, that the penny finally dropped for Keir. And even then he looked pained by the apparent betrayal, as he resisted the calls of Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage to join in the war.UK officials prepare for potential Trump talks as Burnham plans New York tripRead moreNo such misgivings forAndy Burnham. This week, the prime minister was reminded that when he had been mayor of Greater Manchester, he had said The Donald wouldn’t be welcome in his city and that he could take his poisonous politics elsewhere. Words that had been loudly cheered at the time by many in Britain who had had enough of all the toadying. After all, it wasn’t as if the Trump-whispering had made any difference. If anything, it had only added to his contempt for us. You’ll never get any thanks from a narcissist.Nor did Andy have any regrets now that he was prime minister and was likely to meet Trump in person for the first time at the UN general assembly in New York at the end of next month. Far from it. “Shit happens” was pretty much his precis of what had gone down. He wasn’t going to apologise to The Donald for what he had said. Not least because he had meant every word.This was the real world. Politicians say stuff. Trump had said all sorts of things about him, too. That he had beenmayor of “some town”. To be fair to Agent Orange, it’s quite likely he had never heard of Manchester before. Neither geography nor an interest in other people have ever been his strongest suits. All he had known about Andy was that he was “extremely liberal”. Which in Maga language is the same as saying he’s a “Commy bastard”.So here was Burnham’s deal. He wasn’t planning to go out of his way to insult the US president, but neither would he be offering unexpurgated sycophancy. Instead, we would be getting a very British type of pragmatism. He would do what was necessary in the UK’s interest but not much more. They would be polite and try not to accentuate their differences, but there would be no pretence of any lasting friendship. Just stick to the matters in hand and get the hell out. After New York, Andy wouldn’t be sending weekly WhatsApps. Out of sight, out of mind.Weirdly, this performative show of an ersatz friendship – the US and UK are meant to be more or less on the same side, after all – is likely to be far more effective than Keir’s more needy approach. Because this is the type of language The Donald understands. Although he craves the fawning, he has no respect for those who offer it. He takes it as a sign of weakness. Equally, no amount of flattery is ever enough. There is a hole in Trump’s psyche that can never be filled.With Burnham, there is going to be more a meeting of equals. Two world leaders who are doing what it takes to get along with each other. It’s as close to respect as a sociopath like Trump can get. Andy hasn’t taken a backward step, or attempted to deny his previous comments. More that that was then and this was now. Just get used to it.View image in fullscreenNo amount of flattery from Keir could ever be enough. There is a hole in Trump’s psyche that can never be filled.Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersYou can say one thing one day and the opposite the next. It’s up to the other person to work out which one was the truth. Or maybe neither, or maybe both. After all, that’s precisely what The Donald does. Contradiction is his modus operandi. And it’s got him to the White House. So if it works for Trump, why not for Burnham? Sincerity can be an overrated virtue for a world leader. You don’t always need a Love, Actually moment to make your feelings known.“So I’m looking forward, actually, to my first meeting [with Trump],” said Andy. And he probably is. His cards are on the table and he has nothing to hide. Plus, he has a sense of humour and self-deprecation, which also might confuse the US president, who has neither.It also feels as if there’s less at stake with this meeting than there was with many of Starmer’s. Back in the early days of Trump’s presidency, it was as if much of the world was holding its breath for what he might do next. Now, not so much. We’ve all learned to adapt to The Donald. Even to his never-ending war with Iran, which has jacked up the cost of living. All his bad habits are now priced in. And suddenly he looks more vulnerable. A man who has found the world doesn’t automatically bend to his will. A man who is under pressure on the domestic front, with many Americans fed up with his foreign wars and angry at the cost of petrol (never get between an American and their car). A president facing tricky midterm elections and in danger of becoming a lame duck.For Burnham, it’s also the home front that is occupying most of his attention. Good vibes are a decent start, but sooner or later he has to do something different to Starmer while boxing himself in with the same fiscal rules. So who knows? The meeting between Andy and The Donald may be less tricky than first imagined. A welcome distraction for both of them.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamThe politics sketchDonald TrumpKeir StarmerForeign policycommentShareReuse this content

title: We surveyed 6,000 Americans. Here is the winning message for Democrats | Dustin Guastella and Erica Etelson | The Guardian
description: It’s about ‘kitchen-table populism’: focusing on Americans’ day-to-day economic struggles
Author: Dustin Guastella
Headline: It’s about ‘kitchen-table populism’: focusing on Americans’ day-to-day economic struggles
Content: ‘Troy Jackson, a fifth-generation logger who built his career fighting corporate landowners, is the Democratic Senate nominee in Maine.’Photograph: Brian Snyder/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Troy Jackson, a fifth-generation logger who built his career fighting corporate landowners, is the Democratic Senate nominee in Maine.’Photograph: Brian Snyder/ReutersOpinionDemocratsWe surveyed 6,000 Americans. Here is the winning message for DemocratsDustin Guastellaand Erica EtelsonIt’s about ‘kitchen-table populism’: focusing on Americans’ day-to-day economic strugglesThu 27 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 13.25 EDTShareThis year’s Democratic primaries look and sound a lot more populist than usual.Brian Poindexter, a union iron worker running on a “workers first” message, won a House primary outside Cleveland.Sherrod Brownis mounting a Senate comeback in Ohio on the same “rigged system” message that has allowed him to outshine other Democrats in Ohio.Troy Jackson, a fifth-generation logger who built his career fighting corporate landowners, is the Democratic Senate nominee in Maine. AndJosh Turek, a self-described “prairie populist”, is on the Senate ballot in Iowa.In fact, according to research we’ve conducted through the Center for Working-Class Politics (CWCP), more than 70% of 2026 Democratic candidates now rely on populist rhetoric in their campaigns, laying the blame for our broken system on rich elites of one kind or another.It seems after decades of bleeding working-class support,Democratsare converging on a solution to win them back: run populists.The real question, then, is not whether Democrats should embrace populism, but rather what kind of populism they should embrace. To settle that argument, CWCP teamed up with the Rural Urban Bridge Initiative (RUBI) toconduct a new survey.This is the question Democrats should ask voters in order to win this November | Robert ReichRead moreIn polling conducted by Verasight between late June and early July, we asked more than 6,000 Americans to rate 13 different kinds of messages commonly deployed by Democratic candidates to see which pitch would draw the strongest support. We also randomly presented each respondent with one of two Republican attack messages modeled on actual Republican campaign rhetoric in order to see how well Democratic messages hold up under attack.The top-performing messages we tested have a simple formula. They focus on Americans’ day-to-day struggles to pay for rent and groceries, and the widespread frustration with prices that rise faster than working-class wages. They insist that working people should be able to give their kids a better shot. They promise to bring costs down, make the biggest corporations pay their fair share, and crack down on the people who game the system. Ultimately, they tell a simple story: hard work should pay off.We call this winning combination “kitchen-table populism”.None of the plausible alternatives to this kind of messaging performed nearly as well. Consider what we call the “divide-and-conquer playbook” messaging popular with certain progressive campaign consultants. One prominent proponent of this style is the Texas senatorial candidate James Talarico. Talarico strikes a populist posture, emphasizing that economic elites keep working people divided over race, immigration, and cultural issues so that no one sees that they’re all getting fleeced. It sounds good, and Talarico is holding his own in red Texas, but this tactic is not the slam dunk against the culture war that some progressives think it is. In fact, in our survey, it was not all that effective, severely underperforming the pure kitchen-table messages we tested.The weakest variant of the divide-and-conquer narrative is the one that tells voters they’ve been tricked into blaming scapegoats. These “race-class narrative” appeals, so popular in progressives circles, finished at the bottom of the field. Why? Because telling people they’ve been duped comes off more like a condescending sermon than an invitation. Unlike kitchen-table populist messages that meet voters where they’re at, the race-class narrative strays from voters’ concrete economic woes to expound a more abstract theory of political gamesmanship. These messages trailed our top kitchen-table populist pitches with every group, including non-white voters and Democrats.Another alternative to populist messaging is a big-tent anti-Trumpism, pushed by some establishment liberals. The argument here is that candidates could unite all those Never-Trump Republicans, anti-Trump independents, and Resistance Democrats with a simple opposition message – one that steers clear of divisions over policy or ideology. Again, the theory makes sense. The trouble is that messaging focused on attacking Trump performed poorly across the board. We fielded the strongest-testing anti-Trump message we know, one that ties his attacks on democratic norms directly to pocketbook pain, and even this steelman version was a net negative with rural voters and Trump waverers.It wasn’t all roses for populism either. We found that anti-elite messages varied in their efficacy. While naming corruption, and promising to end it, was a powerful way to convey anti-elite sentiments – especially with Republicans, where adding an anti-corruption pledge to a plain cost-of-living pitch lifted support by 18 points – messages that leaned too stridently into class war turned off these same voters. Republicans swung 25 pointsagainstmessages that blamed “big corporations” and “the wealthy few”.We also tested a progressive-coded anti-plutocrat message that railed against oligarchs and fascists: it trailed kitchen-table populism by about 14 points among Democrats and by huge margins among working-class, rural and swing voters.The American left is making strides. But can they win in November? | Ben DavisRead moreTo be clear, this shouldn’t be understood as a plea for centrism or moderation. While it may seem like Democratic candidates are forced into a trade-off – either you opt to fire up the progressive base with ultra-liberal anti-Trump bromides or you aim to persuade Trump-voting working-class voters with a more conservative pitch – our results show that this is a false choice. The winning messages do neither; instead, they name a rigged system, call out the people rigging it, and promise to rebalance the economy in favor of those who work for a living. But they also avoid moral high-handedness and the preachy activist rhetoric that turns off many working-class, rural and swing voters. These are the lessons Democrats must internalize if they want to win back the working class, including some of the 59% of working-class white voters who, according to a March poll by Catalist, still plan to vote Republican in 2026.Some of the strongest-performing Democrats have already shown the power of kitchen-table populism in tough districts. Pat Ryan rode what he calls “patriotic populism” to a 14-point win in a Hudson Valley swing district in 2024, naming greedy corporations and corrupt politicians as the villains while casting working people as heroes. And Gabe Vasquez has won one of the country’s toughest seats in rural New Mexico twice with a similar pitch: Vasquez points the finger at corporate landlords, elites in Washington DC, and price-gouging investors who get rich by bending the rules, while praising hard-working blue-collar families that are struggling to stay afloat. That’s the winning formula, one we hope to see more Democrats and independents deploy.Dustin “Dino” Guastella is director of operations for Teamsters Local 623 in Philadelphia and sits on the board of the Center for Working-Class PoliticsErica Etelson is president of the Rural Urban Bridge InitiativeExplore more on these topicsDemocratsOpinionUS politicsUS midterm elections 2026US economyUS CongresscommentShareReuse this content

title: Jon Ossoff went low on Natalie Harp. The plan worked | Moira Donegan | The Guardian
description: The senator’s remarks reflect a turning point in Democrats’ attacks on the president. What should we make of them?
Author: Moira Donegan
Headline: The senator’s remarks reflect a turning point in Democrats’ attacks on the president. What should we make of them?
Content: ‘What is the moral consequence of this kind of sexism, the kind that Ossoff evoked – obliquely, subtly, but definitely – with his remark?’Photograph: American Photo Archive/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘What is the moral consequence of this kind of sexism, the kind that Ossoff evoked – obliquely, subtly, but definitely – with his remark?’Photograph: American Photo Archive/AlamyOpinionTrump administrationJon Ossoff went low on Natalie Harp. The plan workedMoira DoneganThe senator’s remarks reflect a turning point in Democrats’ attacks on the president. What should we make of them?Thu 27 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 13.36 EDTShareApparently, he likes to say her namewith a French accent. “Na-tah-lee!” the president cries out, in that affected tone of faux-formality that one might use with a person they love but do not quite respect, and she comes running, her thin legs teetering on her heels.Natalie Harp, Trump’s 35-year-old “executive assistant”, was an odd recurring character in the latest blockbuster Trump administration book, Regime Change, by the New York Times’ Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan. In the book, Harp features like a silent sentinel, ever present but eerily quiet as Trump rants and raves. It’s not exactly clear what the scope of her responsibilities are; though, asJamelle Bouiepoints out, the fact that she evidently helps run the president’s social media accounts, which can sway markets and influence his foreign counterparts, makes her one of the most powerful people in the federal government.But the dignity of Harp’s character does not often seem to equal the gravity of her influence: once, she wascaught on videosprinting across a golf course on foot, chasing the golf cart that was speeding the president away to the next hole. For a while, she wascalled the “human printer”among Trump aides, in reference to the portable printer that Harp carries around with her: one of the primary ways she spends her time appears to be searching for flattering news stories and social media commentary about the president online, and printing it out to nourish his self-regard. But from Haberman and Swan’s reporting, it was not always clear exactly what Harp was thinking. Though many Trumpworld insiders are clearly identifiable as off-the-record sources in their book, Harp does not seem to be among them.It’s a miracle: Natalie Harp has turned Republicans into feminists | Arwa MahdawiRead moreBut recently, more of Harp’s own words have come to light. The Daily Beast published the full text of two letters from Harp to Trump, whose existence had previously been reported by Haberman and Swan. In the letters, Harp is rapturously worshipful, sycophantic, almost slavish. “You are all that matters to me,”she wroteto Trump. She called him her “Guardian and Protector in this Life”. (The capitalization is in the original.) It’s long been known that Trumpprizes devotionamong his underlings, that he seeks out flattering commentary about himself, and that he is surrounded, particularly in his second term, exclusively by the kind of people who will never tell him anything that he does not want to hear. Still, the spectacle of Harp’s obsequiousness – her willingness to debase herself for an 80-year-old man whose vulgarity, misogyny, racism, narcissism and impulsiveness have damaged her country in ways it will probably never recover from – is disturbing and grotesque.Still, Harp herself might be less unsettling than the near certainty that there are others like her – White House staffers and federal bureaucrats and petty functionaries of the Maga machine – who have made flattery of Trump a large portion, if not the entirety, of their jobs. Probably, few Americans would ever have heard of Harp if it were not for Jon Ossoff, the Democratic Georgia senator running for re-election and widely assumed to be mulling a presidential bid, who mentioned Harp in a pointed barb in a campaign stump speech in Atlanta. Trump,Ossoff said, doesn’t want to do the job of president; he wants, instead, to “build his ballroom and travel with Natalie”.We do not need to be stupid: it strains credulity, and discredits the considerable savvy of Ossoff’s team, to claim that this remark was not meant to arouse salacious suspicion about the nature of Harp’s relationship with the president, and speculation that it might be sexual. Ossoff’s wording retained plausible deniability; still, I think he knew exactly what he was doing. Ossoff, in his campaign, has styled himself as firm-minded, resolute and morally ambitious – aninheritor to Barack Obama. But in this remark, he diverged noticeably from Michelle Obama’s famous mantra “when they go low, we go high,” which has long been a shibboleth for the kind of Democratic politicians who have preferred dignity over effectiveness in the Trump era. Ossoff was going low.It is shocking how well it worked. The evocation of Harp in Ossoff’s speech triggered a slew of news stories about the aide, delivered by White House reporters who seemed almost giddy to be able to cite as newsworthy something that before had been merely creepy. Asked about Harp on television, Habermanreferred toher as Trump’s “binky” and “comfort blanket”, infantilizing him in humiliating terms. Trump surrogates were dispatched todefend Harpwith a ferocity and insistence that couldn’t help but suggest that the president himself was angered. Ossoff, it seemed, had struck a nerve. At the beginning of Trump’s rise to power, many in politics gawked at his seemingly sui generis ability to dictate the news cycle: to say outrageous things, or make bizarre provocations, and send reporters, commentators, surrogates and his opponents into a frenzy trying to respond to them. The effect was that Trump determined the subject of discourse; everyone else responded to him. Ossoff turned the tables, and he made it look easy.Unhinged White House response shows senator’s ‘Natalie’ barb struck a nerveRead moreOne of the allegations that Trump’s aides spewed in their responses to the remark was that in insinuating that something inappropriate was afoot between Trump and Harp, Ossoff was being sexist. Those on the left rushed to discount this: no one, after all, really believes thatDonald Trump, he of “grab ’em by the pussy”, is leading a movement that has serious or sincere concerns for women’s dignity. But to say that Ossoff’s remark contained no misogyny would be naive, if not dishonest: if his suggestion was made deliberately, then he was using Harp’s gender to undermine her professionalism, and to evoke a sex scandal. Of course there is misogyny in this gesture, the suggestion that a young woman is not entirely serious. That Harp’s character and conduct suggest this much more than her sex does need not force us to pretend not to see things that we do.What is the moral consequence of this kind of sexism, the kind that Ossoff evoked – obliquely, subtly, but definitely – with his remark? For my part, I do not see any equivalence between the misogyny imposed on American women by the Trump regime – or, for that matter, the misogyny imposed on American women by Trump personally – and the minor distastefulness of Ossoff. It’s like comparing a dropper of water to the Pacific Ocean. Every woman, every feminist, knows that she has accepted things out of necessity or convenience that the most stringent adherence to principle would require her to reject. And I confess, I am more encouraged by Ossoff’s pugnaciousness than I am put off by the gendered undertones of the remark. After all, it is a grim reality of our gendered world that wherever there is a straight man who esteems himself to be godlike and extraordinary, there will be a straight woman somewhere not far behind who inexplicably believes him. We must work on building a world where this is not true. The first step might be getting this guy out of the White House.Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnistExplore more on these topicsTrump administrationOpinionUS politicsWomenDonald TrumpGenderDemocratsNatalie HarpcommentShareReuse this content

title: Food allergies when flying are no joke. That’s why nuts should be banned on planes | Lucy Pasha-Robinson | The Guardian
description: People with allergies must be able to travel without fear, and a compassionate society should respect that, says Lucy Pasha-Robinson, an assistant Opinion editor at the Guardian
Author: Lucy Pasha-Robinson
Headline: People with allergies must be able to travel without fear, and a compassionate society should respect that, says Lucy Pasha-Robinson, an assistant Opinion editor at the Guardian
Content: ‘Most airlines will make an announcement asking passengers to avoid consuming nuts if you let them know that somebody in your party has a severe nut allergy.’Photograph: Nigel Blake/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Most airlines will make an announcement asking passengers to avoid consuming nuts if you let them know that somebody in your party has a severe nut allergy.’Photograph: Nigel Blake/AlamyOpinionAllergiesFood allergies when flying are no joke. That’s why nuts should be banned on planesLucy Pasha-RobinsonPeople with allergies must be able to travel without fear, and a compassionate society should respect thatThu 27 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 13.59 EDTShareWhat are you most scared of? Perhaps snakes send a chill down your spine. Or heights leave your knees weak. Peanuts may sound like an odd source of phobia, but they have taken on an absurd bogeyman quality for me since my daughter was taken to hospital by ambulance after eating peanut butter when she was six months old. Just the sight of a bowl on a pub bar, or their shells discarded on the pavement, can raise my heart rate – even when I’m not with her.Nowhere is the sight of peanuts more confronting than at 30,000ft, especially now when millions are jetting back from their holidays. Travelling with a severely allergic child can be a nightmare for all sorts of reasons, but the idea you could be sat next to a passenger consuming the very thing that has hospitalised them is its own kind of hell.Most airlines will make an announcement asking passengers to avoid consuming nuts if you let them know that somebody in your party has a severe nut allergy. But I brace for impact when these announcements are piped out. On almost every flight there is at least one passenger who sighs or makes some inane comment, loud enough for everyone to hear, about how annoying it is.Oh, I’m sorry – is not being able to eat nuts for a few hours inconveniencing you? Does one passenger’s desire to consume peanut M&M’s trump someone else’s right to stay alive? I didn’t realise the right to eat nuts was a civil liberties issue. How utterly absurd.And yet, people get disproportionately upset about being told not to eat things. Chloë Dickson, who runs the Instagram accountpeanutfreezone,recently posted a horrifying video of her experience flying with a severe peanut allergy and a man behind her responding, “Really?” to an announcement asking passengers not to eat nuts. He “then proceeded to make comments throughout the entire journey about eating peanuts around me, along with two other people nearby,” the caption reads.I am mystified by this mean-spiritedness. Allergies are not a lifestyle choice but a medical condition. And yet, they seem to inspire a lack of empathy in the public consciousness. Perhaps it’s due to a misunderstanding of what allergy actually is. For people such as Chloe and my daughter, we’re not talking about skin irritation or a dodgy stomach, however unpleasant that might be.Anaphylaxisis a severe, potentially life-threatening allergic reaction that can affect multiple body systems and commonly impacts breathing or consciousness. The primary treatment is adrenaline via an EpiPen and it requires immediate medical attention.But I suspect many people do know what severe allergy can look like, they just think this level of caution is overblown and are frustrated by having to make accommodations. Take a look at some of the comments under Chloë’s post and you’ll see what I mean. They are staggering in their stupidity. “Fly private or DON’T FLY AT ALL. Don’t make other people’s lives miserable just to please yours!” one reads. “I travel with a bag of peanuts for these moments,” says another. There really are people who seem to believe that those with allergies should just not travel at all. Or not go out to eat. Or not be able to participate fully in life outside their own homes. I wonder if they would feel that way if it was their children who were diagnosed.Allergic people can’t be wrapped in cotton wool. Some of the best advice I got when my daughter was small, from an angelic NHS allergy nurse, was that you do your very best to keep her safe and then you carry EpiPens as your insurance policy. That’s given me lots of comfort over the years when gauging risk. But when you’re trapped in a metal tube in the sky with no possibility of medical attention, the stakes feel much higher.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionExperience: I’m allergic to nearly everythingRead moreWhat scares allergic people most is not necessarily the risk of an airborne reaction, which isvanishingly rare, it’s the possibility of cross-contamination. That peanut dust on someone’s fingers could then spread to the tray table, the seat, perhaps the toilet door. That a rogue peanut from a previous flight has fallen between the seats or touched the seatbelt. On quick turnaround budget airlines with minimal cleaning, the risk you may come into contact with the allergen starts to feel frighteningly high. And even tiny amounts of nut protein can trigger a life-threatening reaction for some people.Banning nuts on planes seems like a no-brainer. And I say nuts because of all the common allergens, they are the least likely to beoutgrown in childhoodand have ahigher rate of causing severe reactions. That means telling passengers not to bring nut products on board. But even just stopping the practice of serving them on flights would drastically reduce the risk of cross-contamination when travelling. And it would take the pressure off anxious, allergic passengers to advocate for their safety. Of course, no ban could be watertight, which is why airlines should make a blanket rule that anyone with severe allergy should be offered priority boarding to clean their own seats before takeoff as a precaution.Allergic people shouldn’t have to justify their medical needs to people who don’t understand them. Banning nuts on planes could send an important message to the broader public. That people with allergies should be able to travel without fear. That compassionate societies make accommodations.Lucy Pasha-Robinson is a Guardian assistant Opinion editorDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
