title: It’s time for all of us to get a grip and stop flaking on friends for no good reason | Johanna Cosgrove | The Guardian
description: It has become normal to cancel on one another because we are so desperate to avoid even the most minor discomfort. It must cease immediately
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: It has become normal to cancel on one another because we are so desperate to avoid even the most minor discomfort. It must cease immediately
Content: ‘The insipid emphasis on seclusion is far too normalised. Humans are social,’ writes Johanna Cosgrove.Photograph: klebercordeiro/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreen‘The insipid emphasis on seclusion is far too normalised. Humans are social,’ writes Johanna Cosgrove.Photograph: klebercordeiro/Getty Images/iStockphotoOpinionFriendshipIt’s time for all of us to get a grip and stop flaking on friends for no good reasonJohanna CosgroveIt has become normal to cancel on one another because we are so desperate to avoid even the most minor discomfort. It must cease immediatelyThu 27 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 23.23 EDTShareIt’s a Thursday night. You are sitting on the couch (the TV is on or you could be reading a book but most likely you are doom-scrolling). You know full well that you have plans to meet a dear friend who you’ve been “meaning to catch up with for ages!” at the pub down the road in exactly 45 minutes.Maybe this friend has been going through a rough time? Maybe they’ve got some exciting news about a perfect Hinge date (rare and shocking)? Maybe you’ve simply been “ships in the night” sailing through the capitalist rat race and miss each other’s company.Either way, this hangout is premeditated and has been organised in advance with many exclamations of excitement. However, there is but one tiny problem: you no longer want to go. You are just … comfortable where you are.Community-maxxing: gen Z are done with doomscrolling – and ready to socialiseRead moreYou vaguely start calculating the hours left in the day – you might want to go to the gym in the morning (despite not having gone in weeks) and work was slightly strenuous today (you had to actually do your job).You pick up your phone to text them something along the lines of “Massive day today – can we postpone? Maybe the weekend after next? Don’t wanna have a big one on a school night!” None of this is due to any sort of change of heart towards your pal: you simply can’t be bothered.I think the most alarming thing about this scenario is how real it is. It’s been me. It’s been you. It might even be you right now, reading this article.The swing into prioritising self care over endless hustle has swung too far and now it is completely normal to cancel on one another because we are desperate to avoid even the most minor discomfort, ie going out in public and down the road for a perfect glass of wine. Using the excuse of “it’s a school night” feels particularly sinister coming from a (usually) millennial or gen Z who hasn’t attended school in over a decade.The self-infantilisation must cease immediately!On a personal note, I’ve spent the last year firmly reacquainting with my personal capability. I am extremely capable! And actually … we all are. I now lie in bed at night, grinding my molars to nubs, vowing to stop any and all weak behaviours. Being unable, as a fully functioning adult with the gift of a healthy body and mind, to get up off the couch for no reason other than “cbf” is weak. You will catch me muttering to myself “being uncomfortable is not the same as being unsafe”. Life is precious and living is a verb. Insufferable? Sure! But! I don’t think I’m wrong.We have become addicted to comfort – we can order anything direct to the door, we “connect” with others through our phones, we are entertained by TikTok and Netflix and endless gaming options. We can live our lives in thehikikomoristyle – without ever having to engage with another human person. My feed is clogged with videos of skinny people glamorising “protecting your peace”, “self-dating” and doing expensive morning and evening routines (alone). I’m constantly besieged by muted infographics encouraging me to lean into my “soft girl era” which really feels like … laziness repackaged.The insipid emphasis on seclusion is far too normalised. Humans are social.We need our friends and our communities more than ever. We need to feel real connection and prioritise our actual relationships over a 30-second video from someone we will never meet. “Popping over for a chat” is almost a lost art. In this digital age, with the horrifying tendrils of AI draining our water reservoirs, poised to topple entire creative industries, getting in a room together feels unfortunately more and more radical by the year.So, if you’ve said you’re gonna do something with a mate – do it.News flash: the world is a hot mess right now and no one really wants to do anything. We’ve all got full calendars. Say no upfront! Being with our friends IRL is a joy and a treat not a chore, and energy actually begets more energy (one thing the fitness girls are right about). It’s time to collectively get a grip. Go out and have some fun – I promise it’s always better than staying on the couch.Johanna Cosgrove is an award-winning actor/writer/comedianExplore more on these topicsFriendshipOpinioncommentShareReuse this content

title: A Britain of wildfires and flood risks: be sure, the climate crisis is real, and we will deal with it  | Angela Eagle | The Guardian
description: Reform and the Conservatives are willing to mislead the public, but as environment secretary, I believe we must be honest – and act boldly, says Angela Eagle
Author: Angela Eagle
Headline: Reform and the Conservatives are willing to mislead the public, but as environment secretary, I believe we must be honest – and act boldly, says Angela Eagle
Content: Smoke rising from burning homes in Stourbridge, West Midlands, 13 August 2026.Photograph: WEST MIDLANDS FIRE SERVICE/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSmoke rising from burning homes in Stourbridge, West Midlands, 13 August 2026.Photograph: WEST MIDLANDS FIRE SERVICE/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionExtreme weatherA Britain of wildfires and flood risks: be sure, the climate crisis is real, and we will deal with itAngela EagleReform and the Conservatives are willing to mislead the public, but as environment secretary, I believe we must be honest – and act boldlyThu 27 Aug 2026 08.05 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 13.32 EDTShareThis long, hot summer has brought our third drought in five years and thedriest July in almost two centuries. We’ve seenwildfires burn down homesand now face the risk of flash floods as we move into autumn. It should be a wake-up call for those saying that concerns about the climate crisis are overblown; that we should simply sit back and do nothing; or row back on attempts to restore our natural environment. As the new environment secretary, I won’t let that happen.No one who has experienced this summer in the UK should be in any doubt that our climate is already changing. We know the future holds warmer, wetter winters, hotter, drier summers, and more extreme weather.Honesty about what is required to deal with this changing reality is the least we should expect from our politicians. But last week we saw an astonishing response from Reform UK’s deputy leader,who told peopleto “enjoy” the scorching heatwaves and described this government’s efforts to combat the climate crisis as “arrogant”.This response isn’t just ignorant; it is insulting.From bone-dry to soaked to the bone, welcome to the age of climate whiplash | Aditya ChakraborttyRead moreInsulting to the firefighters risking their lives to fight blazes up and down the country. Insulting to the public whose lives are disrupted by scorching temperatures that were once a rare occurrence. And insulting to our farmers struggling to turn a profit as drought damages their crops.This government’s response is not to throw in the towel and accept the chaos caused by extreme weather. It is to work to build and manage landscapes so they are resilient enough to withstand it and recover.We know that healthy ecosystems retain more water and can help act as natural firebreaks. That resilience does not just protect us from the impacts of wildfire. It guards against flooding and pollution, too.But some, including the Conservatives, have made the argument thatrewilding lowers resilience to fireand that we should reverse restrictions on burning heather on our moors and peatlands. The exact opposite is true.The evidence clearly shows that wetter, healthy peatlands hold more water and are less likely to develop species that are vulnerable to fires. The damage that has been done to these vital habitats by decades of burning has made them more vulnerable to wildfires in the long term, not less.The solution to raging wildfires is not more burning of our countryside. It is to restore and better manage our environment.Where rewilding has been prioritised, as at the National Trust’s Holnicote estate, you can clearly see the stark difference that it makes to the ability to withstand extreme weather. In areas where rivers and wetlands have been restored, the plants are green and blooming. Elsewhere, the ground is brown and dry.As environment secretary, most of what comes across my desk is underpinned by the need to adapt to our changing climate – and this government is taking these challenges head on.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat’s why the prime minister this month convened anemergency Cobra meeting, bringing together senior ministers, firefighters, weather forecasters and other experts to make sure we’re doing all we can to keep the country safe from wildfires. That includes a temporary ban on the sale of disposable barbecues.We arespending almost £100mto strengthen the country’s capacity to respond to wildfires and extreme weather.And we are backing our farmers during the droughtwith a £65m funding boost, rule changes to make building on-site reservoirs easier and the largest nature-friendly budget in history to make our farms more resilient to extreme weather and to protect our food security.Adapting to our changing climate demands sustained attention, effort and investment. Others may simply deny the problem or stick their heads in the sand, but this government will rise to the challenge.Angela Eagle is the secretary of state for environment, food and rural affairsExplore more on these topicsExtreme weatherOpinionClimate crisisWildfiresDroughtLabourcommentShareReuse this content

title: If MPs want to take on Nigel Farage over his dodgy finances, they need to clean up their own act | Frances Ryan | The Guardian
description: It’s hard to beat back charges that MPs are ‘all the same’ when they have accepted £400k in freebies this year, says Guardian columnist Frances Ryan
Author: Frances Ryan
Headline: It’s hard to beat back charges that MPs are ‘all the same’ when they have accepted £400k in freebies this year, says Guardian columnist Frances Ryan
Content: Illustration: Eleanor Shakespeare/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Eleanor Shakespeare/The GuardianOpinionPoliticsIf MPs want to take on Nigel Farage over his dodgy finances, they need to clean up their own actFrances RyanIt’s hard to beat back charges that MPs are ‘all the same’ when they have accepted £400k in freebies this year – £100k up on last yearThu 27 Aug 2026 06.03 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 13.59 EDTShareHow has your summer been? Done anything nice? As MPs prepare to head back to parliament next week, you’ll be relieved to hear that some of the most prominent figures in British politics have been enjoying the season’s cultural highlights – and without paying a penny. MPs throughout the Commons havereceived £400,000 of “freebies”to concerts, sports matches and other events so far this year, according to the most recent disclosures.Over the summer alone, Wes Streeting, now the defence secretary, enjoyed the Chelsea flower show thanks to Lloyds Banking Group covering the £1,839 cost, as did the shadow chancellor, Mel Stride. Lucy Powell, who has since become deputy leader of theLabourparty and education secretary, accepted £858-worth of tickets to a Harry Styles concert at Wembley from the PRS for Music industry group. Meanwhile, the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, nabbed seats at Wimbledon worth £1,360 from the All England Club.Totalled up,MPs have been gifted£100,000 more so far this year than in the whole of 2025, with recipients seemingly learning few lessons from Keir Starmer’s“passes for glasses” scandal, in which a Labour peer gifted the then prime minister designer eyewear and clothes before being spotted in Downing Street with a temporary security pass.Like many of these types of stories, there’s some nuance lurking behind the headlines. MPs quite rightly go to events linked to their constituency or local area. Andy Burnham accepting £3,800 tickets to the Brit awards in Manchester – when he was the regional mayor – to spotlight the city hosting the event for the first time is not the same as Streeting presumably just really wanting to meet Monty Don.The increase can also partly be explained by the fact MPs have become more consistent about declaring hospitality on the parliamentary register after Starmer changed the rules, while ticket prices are well known to have gone up across the board. And yet, wade through the details of gigs and horse racing and it’s hard not to conclude some MPs are simply practising blatant grifting. Call it a treat for a seat, where our elected officials are enjoying must-see shows as a kind of unofficial bonus.That much of this stuff was gifted by big business, including gambling firms and banks, makes the whole thing feel considerably grubbier. Why did the betting company Flutter want to shower then local backbencher and now chief whip, Anneliese Midgley, with high-priced tickets to the Grand National and Cheltenham?Public perception of such luxury perks will be even more unforgiving against a backdrop of an ongoing cost of living crisis. A night at the Ivor Novello awards may not be theduck house-level opulenceof 2009’s expenses scandal,but the optics are little better. While much of the population are struggling to pay their electric and food bills, MPs are getting out the fascinators for Ladies’ Day at Aintree.View image in fullscreenHarry Styles on stage at Wembley this year.Photograph: Anthony Pham/Live Nation/PAPoliticians, of course, are human. Who among us wouldn’t be tempted by Harry Styles? The electorate, for its part, tends to want leaders to connect with everyday life. There’s a reason why Malcolm Tucker in The Thick of It – based on the rumour Alastair Campbell got Tony Blair clips of EastEnders and reality shows – makes a “zeitgeist tape” to help his useless ministers seem “in touch”. But it would be disingenuous to pretend MPs are driven to accept hospitality gifts as a bid to be down to earth,or that balancing such demands from the public is somehow a complex, grey area. Most people like to see their MP letting loose at a concert – they just want them to have paid for their ticket.With the standards watchdogdue to question Nigel Faragewhen parliament reopens – an inquiry he temporarily dodged by calling a byelection – the coming weeks will very likely see a renewed focus on what MPs receive and the transparency around it.On paper, Farage’s gifts are in another league to his colleagues’ freebies: forget a ticket to the tennis, we’re talking£5m from a crypto billionaire and further “financial support” from a convicted fraudster. And yet to a public who have for decades seen front-page stories about politicians’ finances – from expenses and second jobs to tax avoidance – the idea that the Reform UK leader is an outlier worth investigating rather than one of a bad bunch can feel at best a hard sell and, at worst, hypocritical.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRupert Lowe set to be paid as much for divisive posts on Elon Musk’s X as for being MPRead moreIf MPs wish to be able to hold Farage to account with credibility, they will need to show they care about cash and transparency in every form. That means the government looking harder into how some MPs are using their influence to make extra money, not least when it’s linked with the growth of the far right. Just this week it emerged that the Restore leader, Rupert Lowe, is set to earn as much from his –anti-migrant– posts on X as he does from his MP’s salary (which he gives to charity) since Elon Musk took over and financially rewarded some high-reach posts. “Gifts” come in many forms.Winning public trust will also require MPs to be squeaky-clean themselves and stop accepting hospitality unless it’s linked to their constituency – even if that means watching the Chelsea flower show on iPlayer like the rest of us.Because every time an MP goes to an event for free, it comes with a hidden cost: a public with ever-decreasing faith in the political class, who are more likely to greet outright corruption or cronyism with a weary shrug. “They’re all the same” is a dangerous public mood for a democracy and one that, once embedded, can be deeply hard to dislodge.Frances Ryan is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: A 16-year-old girl has died from suspected sexual choking. How do we come to terms with this? | Lucy Clark | The Guardian
description: We can no longer deny that many children get their sex education from online pornography. But the normalisation of violence can lead to tragedy
Author: Lucy Clark
Headline: We can no longer deny that many children get their sex education from online pornography. But the normalisation of violence can lead to tragedy
Content: Proponents of sexual strangulation say that between two consenting adults who have discussed boundaries it’s fine. But when people die, you have to ask: is it worth the risk?Photograph: AlexLinch/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenProponents of sexual strangulation say that between two consenting adults who have discussed boundaries it’s fine. But when people die, you have to ask: is it worth the risk?Photograph: AlexLinch/Getty ImagesOpinionAustralia newsA 16-year-old girl has died from suspected sexual choking. How do we come to terms with this?Lucy ClarkWe can no longer deny that many children get their sex education from online pornography. But the normalisation of violence can lead to tragedyThu 27 Aug 2026 01.59 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 21.29 EDTShareHow can we possibly come to terms with reports a 16-year-old girl may have died as a result of consensual sexual strangulation with her 16-year-old boyfriend? Police are still investigating this case. Meanwhile what do we do, as a society, to contend with children getting their sex education from pornography when this may be what they learn? When this is what they think sex is?Often mistakenly referred to as choking, sexual strangulation in the mainstream is new. It has arrived into the bedrooms of young people via online porn which has become part of life, one of the many addictive services generously provided by tech companies making billions of dollars. Some companies do a good job of cleaning up the urgent issues of child sexual abuse material and trafficking, but still, violent porn proliferates.Police investigate death of teenage girl two days after alleged ‘sexual choking’ act in SydneyRead moreResearch that hasanalysed thousands of randomly chosen videosfrom popular pornographic websites found that physical aggression like strangulation, slapping and hair-pulling was present in 35-45% of scenes, depending on the website.It’s important to be wary of clutching our pearls about porn here – there is no evidence to suggest that watchingethical pornresults in an upswing in violent behaviour, butresearch released last year by the Australian Institute of Criminologydoes indeed show that more frequent intentional viewing of violent pornography is associated with a “small but statistically significant” increase in violence against women by men after they watched violent porn.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailCouple this with the knowledge thatone in three Australian childrenhave seen online porn and that theaverageage of initial consumption of porn is 13 – and we can all feel a desperate kind of sorrow for adolescents navigating this world. Girls thinking this is what boys want, boys thinking that this is what girls want. The confusion, the painful wanting to be wanted, that perennial need to be thought of as cool that comes with teenagehood, all of it is now shadowed by the normalisation of something that is clearly dangerous – as any medical expert will tell you, there is no safe way to lose oxygen to the brain.Some other facts to make you weep: sexual strangulation is now thought to be thesecond most common cause of strokesin women under 40 in the UK. It can lead to seizures, brain damage, memory issues, depression, anxiety. Two years ago anAustralian study found that more than half of 4,700 peopleaged between 18 and 35 had engaged in sexual strangulation. A majority of them, 61%, had seen it depicted in porn. Others had seen it in movies, talked about it with friends.One desperately sad anecdotecomes from the UK children’s commissioner, Dame Rachel de Souza, whose office has researched the harms of online pornography on young people. “I will never forget,” she says, “the girl who told me about her first kiss with her boyfriend, aged 12, who strangled her. He had seen it in pornography and thought it normal.”Proponents of sexual strangulation say it feels euphoric, like a head rush, and that between two consenting adults who have discussed boundaries it’s fine. But when people die, you have to ask: is it worth the risk?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEveryone is very careful not to shame anyone about their sexual practices, trusted consenting adults and all that, but we can’t deny that many children are learning how to have sex by watching porn. And children’s brains are different and developing. They react differently to the dopamine hits that come from watching porn, the addictive nature of it. Adolescence is a vulnerable time when they are forming ideas of themselves and gender stereotypes and power dynamics, all the while dealing with an onslaught of hormones and peer pressure. We can’t definitively and solely lay the blame for the rise in sexual strangulation at the feet of online porn – it’s a complex ecosystem of influence – but when it comes to children, it’s a good place to start. It’s a burden that shouldn’t be shouldered by parents alone.I know from personal experience how hard it is to have the conversation about porn with young children. You look at your sweet prepubescent boy child and think he is definitely the only child on the planet not being exposed too early to things he definitely shouldn’t see. He is. They are. Not talking about it is no longer an option.Explore more on these topicsAustralia newsOpinionYoung peoplePornographySexual consentcommentShareReuse this content

title: Does Nigel Farage know what people really think of him? I do – and he won’t like it | Aditya Chakrabortty | The Guardian
description: An anti-Farage army of voters is there to be galvanised, as exclusive data shows. But getting them out will be tricky, says Guardian columnist Aditya Chakrabortty
Author: Aditya Chakrabortty
Headline: An anti-Farage army of voters is there to be galvanised, as exclusive data shows. But getting them out will be tricky, says Guardian columnist Aditya Chakrabortty
Content: Illustration: Bill Bragg/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Bill Bragg/The GuardianOpinionReform UKDoes Nigel Farage know what people really think of him? I do – and he won’t like itAditya ChakraborttyAn anti-Farage army of voters is there to be galvanised, as exclusive data shows. But getting them out will be trickyThu 27 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 09.52 EDTShareWho can stopNigel Farage? Which voters would actually dig out their ID and schlep down to the polling booth to fight him?Over the past year, these two questions have come to shape British politics. From Runcorn and Helsby to Caerphilly and Aberdeen South, via countless flimsy leaflets claiming “Only X can win here”, parties have jostled for the part of his majesty’s opposition to Reform. Those battles have given us Hannah Spencer and Andy Burnham; they have bulldozed Labour in Wales and forcedKeir Starmerout of No 10.Those questions hang over Britain even now, in what is easily Farage’s summer horribilis. He faces a shiny new prime minister and fronts a team that keeps scrapping with itself, while ahead looms a parliamentary investigation into whether he should have declared a £5m gift from agenerous crypto billionaire from the other side of the world. Look at these turquoise clowns, chortle the Westminster commentators. Check out that Burnham bounce, marvel analysts.And despite it all, Farage’s side are almost neck and neck in the polls with Burnham’s. Constituency-level analysis suggests that, were an election called tomorrow, Reform would leap from eight to somewhere between 100 and 200 seats. Among thoseLabourMPs swept out by a turquoise tide could easily be the party chair, Bridget Phillipson, the chancellor, John Healey, and the justice secretary, who is in charge of the prisoner release programme, Alex Norris.A hard-right organisation thatexerts a mysterious yet reliable pull on former membersof theBritish National partymay have a lower electoral ceiling than many feared; but its floor remains high enough to help deny Burnham an outright majority. A party that wants Trump-style deportation squads on British streets, to curb further the right to protest and to slash social security might still lead the next government, or at least become the official opposition.Anyone worried by that prospect needs to understand who those anti-Farage voters are and what could get them off their sofas at an election. That’s why I was glad to have an exclusive look at the first-ever study of the anti-Reform electorate.Published today by anti-racist campaigners Hope Not Hate, it is based on a large survey by Focaldata of nearly 9,000 Britons. These are people who, if a snap election were called tomorrow, could be persuaded to go out and put their “x” against an opponent to Reform. They are some of the most important voters in the country and they are probably not who you think.If I say “anti-Reform army”, who do you see? Perhaps a bunch of leftwingers who live in cities, haver between Zack Polanski and Andy Burnham and ask their baristas for exotic milks. That’s half of them, and, the study shows, they skew young, minority ethnic and graduate. But the other half aren’t on the left at all. The joint-largest group in the Farage resistance is what Hope Not Hate describe as “rightwing on cultural issues and very rightwing on economics”. Think driveways, tidy lawns, a fondness forLudwig. Their worry isn’t that the turquoise troops will be conservative – it’s that they won’t be conservative enough, instead bringing chaos. One other key demographic fact in the fight against Farage: women just don’t like what he stands for. That weak spot has been known to analysts for years and it’s partly why in Makerfield theReform candidate’s saloon-bar sexismhelped torpedo his chances.Perhaps you too have spotted the curious omission in this little list of black marks against Farage’s name. To any question in Britain today, Reform reliably provides one answer: it’s the immigrants’ fault. Housing? Immigrants. Welfare? Immigrants. Oh, and small boats. Yet many who dislike Reform don’t object to its anti-migrant rhetoric. Those comfortable rightwingers I’ve just mentioned were vital in denying GB News regular Matt Goodwin a victory in Gorton and Denton earlier this year, according to one local campaigner who spent weeks doorknocking there – but not for the reasons lefties might think. “Racism doesn’t offend them; they just think it’s vulgar.”In that one-liner lies a grave fault in mainstream politics and media: they have made racism more socially acceptable than at any point in the past 40-odd years. Keir Starmer and his flags, Yvette Cooper and the British bunting she says she used for home decor, Shabana Mahmood telling“white liberal hecklers” to “fuck right off”: look on your works, ye mighty, and despair.I draw two big conclusions from this important study. The first is that what works against Reform in one seat will almost certainly not work in others. At the time of the Caerphilly showdown, Cardiff University’s Dr Jac Larner was regularly rung up by the London-based media: what lessons should they learn from Plaid Cymru’s success? He doesn’t think there are many. “Plaid can provide an alternative political identity for voters: progressive, working class – and Welsh. In Scotland, the SNP can still do that.” But in England, the nationalist politicians wear red corduroys and are bankrolled by foreign billionaires while bleating on about remigration for brown and black people.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHere’s the other conclusion: opponents of Reform share with its supporters an utter abhorrence of Westminster. By two to one, the pollsters find, they are deeply unhappy with mainstream politicians and media. Writing aboutHope Not Hate’s analysis last yearinto Reform voters, I noted that very few of them were unreachable by other parties – it’s just that most politicians didn’t bother to reach out. In the case of Starmer’s Labour it was a patronising pat on the head, and next to no attempt to tackle urgent problems such as the cost of living.Farage returns to our screens next week, as the Reform party conference kicks off. One imagines there will be the mandatory triumphalism and speeches promising that tomorrow belongs to them. It isn’t true, of course. Voters might back Farage or Burnham, but they are mainly lending their support, not committing it. The kind of compromises that the new prime minister has begun making this week oncouncil housebuildingand needless dithering on nationalising Thames Water will arouse little ire now. The people who will mind are those leftwingers who helped get Burnham into parliament, and for now they may be mollified by a couple of token gestures. But if Labour’s strategy is essentially to do what Starmer did, but with better comms and more social-media dopamine, it will get the same result as he did: a disaster, not just for Labour, but for the rest of us.Aditya Chakrabortty is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsReform UKOpinionNigel FarageAndy BurnhamKeir StarmerLabourcommentShareReuse this content

title: My home state is set to hand a breakthrough to the German far right. It’s a disaster decades in the making | Marcus Böick | The Guardian
description: A sense of abandonment could make Saxony-Anhalt the first state government to be solely led by the AfD. But the party’s hollow promises will only make a dire situation worse, says historian Marcus Böick
Author: Marcus Böick
Headline: A sense of abandonment could make Saxony-Anhalt the first state government to be solely led by the AfD. But the party’s hollow promises will only make a dire situation worse, says historian Marcus Böick
Content: People gather during an Alternative for Germany (AfD) campaign rally ahead of Germany's Saxony-Anhalt state election on 6 SeptemberPhotograph: Fabrizio Bensch/ReutersView image in fullscreenPeople gather during an Alternative for Germany (AfD) campaign rally ahead of Germany's Saxony-Anhalt state election on 6 SeptemberPhotograph: Fabrizio Bensch/ReutersOpinionAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)My home state is set to hand a breakthrough to the German far right. It’s a disaster decades in the makingMarcus BöickA sense of abandonment could make Saxony-Anhalt the first state government to be solely led by the AfD. But the party’s hollow promises will only make a dire situation worseThu 27 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 09.31 EDTShareIt was in the summer of 2004 that I stopped understanding my own people. I was standing on a sweltering market square in Aschersleben, the town where I was born, picturesquely situated on the northern edge of the Harz mountains. A large crowd of angry people had gathered in front of a stage to protest about the welfare reforms (or, as many saw them, welfare cuts) introduced by the Social Democratic-Green coalition government under chancellor Gerhard Schröder. They chanted “We are the people!”, waved handpainted placards and seemed utterly beside themselves.I had gone to secondary school nearby, volunteered at the local hospital and interned at the local newspaper: I knew this place. And yet I found myself bewildered. What, exactly, did these deeply aggrieved people want – standing on a freshly renovated, almost idyllic market square? Weren’t things going reasonably well for them? Where did this burning resentment toward the west come from? Wasn’t the east-west divide supposed to be disappearing by now?More than two decades later, similar questions can once again be asked.Eastern Germany is facing a blue wave – or rather, a blue flood. In thestate electionin Saxony-Anhalt on 6 September, the far rightAlternative für Deutschland (AfD), whose party colour is blue, is almost certain toemerge as the largest party. Opinion polls consistently place theAfD above 40%, while the governing Christian Democrats (CDU) trail on around 23%. The Left party, once dominant in the east, has fallen to just 13%, while the Social Democrats (SPD) are struggling to clear the 5% electoral threshold.Should only three or four parties enter parliament, the way would be open for Germany’s first-ever state government led solely by the AfD. The established parties would find themselves stranded on the other side of the much-invoked political “firewall” against cooperation with the far right – and, for the first time since 1945, a party containing openly extremist factions would hold governmental power in a German federal state.The AfD would exercise considerable authority over policing, the judiciary, education and cultural affairs – areas that the party seeks fundamentally to “re-nationalise”, for example by reducing funding for memorial sites commemorating Nazi crimes and revising school curriculums to place greater emphasis on what it regards as the achievements of German history.For me – and, I suspect, for many East Germans who have left their homeland – the rise of these developments did not come as such a surprise. During my infrequent visits home over the past 10 years, it was palpable that something fundamental was shifting.When we celebrated the milestone birthday of an old school friend in early 2024, a group of longtime friends flew in to spend a cold January weekend together in Hettstedt. Yet while we cheerfully reminisced about old times, the friend’s family, whom I had always remembered as lively and eager to debate, just sat by, saying almost nothing. I was perplexed. Only later was I told that my friend’s mother – the heart of the family – had forbidden any political discussion. She feared that the guests who had come from afar would be deeply unsettled by how openly people now voiced views that had once been considered taboo.Saxony-Anhalt has always been a state with a difficult identity. In spite of an extraordinary cultural heritage – it is the home of Martin Luther, George Frideric Händel, Friedrich Nietzsche and the Bauhaus – it lacks a clearly defined regional character. Assembled from various territories of Prussia after its dissolution in 1947, it was abolished during the socialist German Democratic Republic and then re-established after reunification in 1990.Home to almost 3 million inhabitants at the time, Saxony-Anhalt entered the new era with tremendous optimism – only to suffer a brutal crash landing in the spring of 1991. East Germany’s state-owned industries were to be rapidly privatised by the Treuhand agency in an attempt to make them competitive in a market economy. Yet after decades of central planning and chronic shortages, the socialist combines were scarcely capable of surviving the massive shock produced by the economic and monetary union. Instead of the “flourishing landscapes” that chancellor Helmut Kohl had boldly promised, the whole region entered an unprecedented downward spiral.The metalworking and chemical industries of southern Saxony-Anhalt were hit particularly hard. During the spring of 1991, hundreds of thousands lost their jobs. Over the rest of the decade, many areas outside the main cities experienced industrial dismantling, mass unemployment and large-scale outmigration.Younger people, particularly well qualified women, began leaving the region. For my own generation, graduating around the turn of the millennium, moving away appeared to be the only viable path. At the same time, the state steadily withdrew from shrinking rural areas, closing schools and hospitals, relocating courts and police stations. Even the democratic political parties, always much less firmly rooted in eastern than in western Germany, became increasingly invisible.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe echoes of these immense transformations have grown louder once again over the past 35 years. On average, East Germans remain considerably poorer than their western counterparts. They possess significantly less wealth, inherit much less and often face markedly weaker career prospects. A lingering feeling of being “second-class citizens” has become deeply entrenched, extending even to generations born long after German reunification.I can understand these feelings, and I can understand how the AfD has channelled this pervasive sense of abandonment: throughsocial media, local WhatsApp groups, football clubs and neighbourhood pubs. The anger no longer gathers helplessly on the town square; instead, it has found new energy and vastly greater reach in the digital sphere. And in the polling stations.What I can’t understand is that the people I grew up among are failing to see how hollow the AfD’s promises are. The slogans this party offers are not solutions. Many of the measures it advocates would only make a grim situation worse. How are businesses or hospitals supposed to recruit the skilled workers they urgently need if the main party simultaneously calls for large-scale “remigration”? How can anyone develop a positive vision of the future while at the same time expressing admiration for theNazi reichor the GDR? It seems a case of suicide out of fear of death, asBismarckis supposed to have said.Whether on a sun-drenched market square in the summer of 2004 or at a wintry family celebration in 2024, one thing became unmistakably clear to me: there are neither simple answers nor quick solutions. In Saxony-Anhalt, as elsewhere, the task will be to give people with sometimes very different views and values a genuine sense that they are being included on a shared path toward a common future.Marcus Böick is assistant professor in modern German history at the University of CambridgeExplore more on these topicsAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)OpinionEuropeGermanyThe far rightcommentShareReuse this content

title: The royal commission revealed the breadth of antisemitism in Australia – but key opportunities were missed | Michael Visontay | The Guardian
description: Key gatekeepers, and even the prime minister, should have faced more questions over what can be done to address rising hatred
Author: Michael Visontay
Headline: Key gatekeepers, and even the prime minister, should have faced more questions over what can be done to address rising hatred
Content: ‘The testimony of lived experience highlighted the extent to which intimidation and victimisation of Jews has permeated virtually every corner of life in this country,’ writes Michael Visontay.Photograph: Dean Lewins/AAPView image in fullscreen‘The testimony of lived experience highlighted the extent to which intimidation and victimisation of Jews has permeated virtually every corner of life in this country,’ writes Michael Visontay.Photograph: Dean Lewins/AAPOpinionAntisemitismThe royal commission revealed the breadth of antisemitism in Australia – but key opportunities were missedMichael VisontayKey gatekeepers, and even the prime minister, should have faced more questions over what can be done to address rising hatredWed 26 Aug 2026 20.25 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 02.31 EDTShareFrom the moment the prime minister,Anthony Albanese, belatedly announced the royal commission into antisemitism and social cohesion, he clearly wanted the inquiry to be short and tightly focussed. No detours.By setting Commissioner Virginia Bell a deadline of December 14 – the anniversary of the Bondi massacre – to deliver her report, the PM signalled he had no appetite for surprises or delays.He seems to have got his wish. The public hearings started in May and wrapped up this week, less than four months in total. Given that there were several intertwined agendas – the spread of antisemitism, a probe into the Bondi massacre, and the impact on social cohesion – it always felt like a race against time.Four months of grief, tension and pain: key moments from the antisemitism royal commissionRead moreThe commission’s signal achievement has been to hold a mirror to the broader Australian community about the breadth and intensity of hostility that has been directed at Jews since the Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023 and the following war in Gaza.The testimony of lived experience highlighted the extent to which intimidation and victimisation of Jews has permeated virtually every corner of life in this country, from children’s sporting fields to schools and universities, the public service, union movement, arts and entertainment, politics and even the healthcare system.Much of it grew out of anger at Israel’s conduct of the war in Gaza, which does not excuse a single act. But Australian Jews cannot be held responsible for the actions of another government. The repeated rejection of this twisted logic at the hearings has been a crucial takeaway.Another shocking byproduct was the hatred unleashed towards the witnesses who had been brave enough to step up, identify themselves and give testimony. Just three weeks in,Commissioner Bell said “we have received reportsfrom a number of witnesses concerning a dramatic increase in online hate messages”. This outpouring reinforced the sense that Jews were still fair game.We had already seen a man outside the commission building in Sydney, during the first week,wearing a T-shirt with a swastika around a Star of Davidand the words “Antisemitism. Proud to be accused” written on it. In the lead-up to the commission, Jewish communal leaders asserted that antisemitism was being expressed so openly that it had become normalised. The brazenness of the T-shirt incident made it all too clear.As the hearings moved from individuals to public servants, heads of institutions and civil society organisations, there was a creeping sense that the commission missed a few opportunities to bare its teeth. Yes, the NSW policegot a grillingabout the Opera House demonstration and security stuff-ups ahead of Bondi, and university chiefs felt the blowtorch over their passivity around the student encampments.But some gatekeepers of the arts and cultural sector were not called. I would have liked to hear the Sydney Biennale Board asked aboutthe American DJ who unleashed a rant at the opening night partyagainst the “Zio-Australian-Epstein empire” and declared that “one day we will all be free from the Zionist entity”.Her performance pointed to a toxic conundrum that often went under the commission’s radar: the intertwining of Zionism and coded language – “Zio” for Zionists – to vilify Jews (and their defenders) over their support for Israel. The subject was not thoroughly interrogated, even after theeminent Indigenous activist Marcia Langton told the Commission last weekshe had been labelled a “Zio” for expressing her support for Jewish Australians.Finally, it was also open to Commissioner Bell to call the prime minister to appear. While there are limits to what governments can do to mitigate social bigotry, Albanese, as the leader of this country, had more power than anyone to make a difference.In the wake of the Bondi massacre on December 14,the PM openly admittedthat he could have done more to address rising antisemitism. Was this admission performative or genuine? Either way, it provided the commission with a legitimate reason to call him to spell out exactly what measures and policies he had in mind when he made this admission.I say this not in the name of blaming him for Bondi, as many in the Jewish community have done, but in the hope he may have shared tangible ideas about how to navigate the future. Australian society, from the top down and the ground up, must leave no stone unturned in eradicating the scourge that has taken hold. Even if that means taking a detour off the straight and narrow.Michael Visontay is a senior writer at The Jewish IndependentThis article was amended on 27 August 2026. An earlier version incorrectly stated that the heads of Creative Australia did not appear at the royal commission.Explore more on these topicsAntisemitismOpinionAnthony AlbaneseJudaismReligioncommentShareReuse this content

title: Yayoi Kusama’s psychedelic art was at its best when taken in high doses | Yayoi Kusama | The Guardian
description: With dots that dizzied the viewer, the giddy sensory overload of seeing the grandest installations of her octopuses and giant pumpkins was hard to resist
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: With dots that dizzied the viewer, the giddy sensory overload of seeing the grandest installations of her octopuses and giant pumpkins was hard to resist
Content: Enchanting … Yayoi Kusama: You, Me and the Balloons at Aviva Studios, Manchester, in 2023.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenEnchanting … Yayoi Kusama: You, Me and the Balloons at Aviva Studios, Manchester, in 2023.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianYayoi KusamaYayoi Kusama’s psychedelic art was at its best when taken in high dosesJonathan JonesWith dots that dizzied the viewer, the giddy sensory overload of seeing the grandest installations of her octopuses and giant pumpkins was hard to resistYayoi Kusama, Japanese artist who became a global superstar, dies aged 97A life in picturesThu 27 Aug 2026 07.14 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 00.25 EDTShareIonce had an argument aboutYayoi Kusamawith Peter Gabriel. Not in person – I’ve never met the prog rock hero. But after I recorded some critical comments on her work for the BBC, I watched the segment only to see Gabriel passionately defending her. My onscreen cynicism seemed harsh indeed compared with his soulful appreciation of all those dots.My scepticism about Kusama started the first time I saw her work at the Museum of ModernArtin New York. The context is significant because after a big dose of Jackson Pollock’s looping, tangled forests of colour and line (colour as line), Piet Mondrian’s pulsing Broadway Boogie Woogie and other great abstract art, Kusama’s dots appeared to me static, planned, predictable. I wasn’t excited or moved.View image in fullscreenA woman admires The Hope of the Polka Dots Buried in Infinity Will Eternally Cover the Universe by Yayoi Kusama at Aviva Studios, Manchester.Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty ImagesWell, things grow on you, or perhaps you just give up resisting when something is everywhere. Kusama is truly ubiquitous, not just in galleries but social media, her moving life story adding to the popularity of her art, her cosmic sensibility carrying global audiences along on psychedelic journeys into a natural world supercharged with outsized pixelations.It was hard to resist her vision when I caught up with the Kusama phenomenon at Aviva Studios, Manchester, where vast installations andinflatables of dot-covered octopus tentacles and giant pumpkinsmade an industrial space feel enchanted and sublime.But I can still walk into a Kusama mirror room and see just an infinity of nothing. And when I come across one of her pumpkins at an art fair or biennial, it can be extraordinarily blank, a by-the-numbers exercise in commodified multiple art. The Kusama cult has grown alongside and inside a contemporary art world of slick worldwide galleries, with branches from LA to Hong Kong, and a clientele of one percenters who buy art like jewellery. Her work has an obvious decorative appeal to this modern art market: one of those big spotty fruits would be great by the pool. Yet so meaningful!In truth, there’s little connection between Kusama’s troubled life and anti-war activism and the feelgood vibes of her art. Those lurid greens and oranges punctuated by lines of little black circles cannot really be experienced as marks of trauma or expressive howls. Instead they create a dreamy utopia.There’s nothing wrong with that. Art has a vocation to soothe and delight. But it takes a lot of Kusama to get me in the mood: where one of her works leaves me shrugging, a vast gathering does create enjoyable sensory overload.It all depends your receptiveness and in particular how much of your critical brain you are able to shut down. There is art that’s nice to look at and art that harrows the soul. Kusama is seen by some as soulful but her work is as harrowing as a cupcake. It can be a lot of fun, but I don’t think she was a patch on truly mind-bending abstract artists like Pollock or Bridget Riley.When you look into one of Riley’s abstract vortices your brain is interfered with. You see depths and heights that are not there. It’s an intelligent trip that opens the mind, leading you to imagine infinities of space while also seeing the illusory nature of the everyday assumptions we live by. One work by Kusama, least of allher Infinity Rooms, can’t provide that complexity. You have to overdose on them, drowning out your inner nay-saying voice with so many dots you dizzy yourself.Lots of everything, on infinite screens, filling every moment, crowding out thought. Yayoi Kusama was the mirror of our time. That is undeniable.Explore more on these topicsYayoi KusamaInstallationArtcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘She should have been queen of the world!’ Readers remember Dolly Parton | Dolly Parton | The Guardian
description: From quiet acts of generosity and life-changing gigs to singing for a professional puppeteer, Dolly Parton has had a profound impact on readers’ lives
Author: Nicola Slawson
Headline: From quiet acts of generosity and life-changing gigs to singing for a professional puppeteer, Dolly Parton has had a profound impact on readers’ lives
Content: ‘She made a sound that I could see’… Dolly Parton performing in 1973.Photograph: Alamy/PAView image in fullscreen‘She made a sound that I could see’… Dolly Parton performing in 1973.Photograph: Alamy/PADolly Parton‘She should have been queen of the world!’ Readers remember Dolly PartonFrom quiet acts of generosity and life-changing gigs to singing for a professional puppeteer, Dolly Parton has had a profound impact on readers’ livesPhoto gallery: fans pay tribute to Dolly PartonGuardian readers andNicola SlawsonThu 27 Aug 2026 09.02 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 10.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘She was as genuine as they come’I had the opportunity to meet her when I volunteered to work the Country Music Awards in the late 70s. Me and three other kids had Dolly all to ourselves for about 20 minutes. I remember with disbelief how she took several unhurried minutes with each of us and gave us her undivided attention for that time. She had no reason to do this. She was just as genuine as they come. Her philanthropy was exceptional. Her talent speaks for itself. I miss her already.Larry Lipman, Tennessee‘We were not ready to let her go’I always said Dolly should have been queen of the world. She was a natural unifier, humanist and all-round good egg. She never alienated anyone and, given the chance, could have solved any political problem. She was unique. Her magnificence is reflected in the outpouring of shock and grief at her passing. The world still needed Dolly and we were not ready to let her go yet. You will be sorely missed, Dolly.Ruth, LondonView image in fullscreenDolly Parton performing with Elton John at the 39th Annual Country Music Association Awards at Madison Square Garden in 2005.Photograph: Scott Gries/Getty Images‘I have yet to hear a person make a more beautiful tone’I’m not usually terribly affected when famous people pass away. But this one took the wind out of my sails. I’m a puppeteer and actor and I worked with her for a week in 1987 on her variety TV series. It was the Christmas episode, and they had hired a group of character puppets to fill out the sketches and musical numbers.Normally, when you get to a song in a table read, you just skip over it. But Dolly was in a mood to start singing the song herself, a cappella. When Dolly began to sing, all the other people disappeared. There was just Dolly, me and The Voice in that room. She made a sound that I could see. It was as if the ceiling had vaporised and the room filled with a golden light. I was mesmerised. She sang only the beginning of the song, and though this was almost 40 years ago, I have yet to hear a person make a more beautiful tone.Allan Trautman,CaliforniaView image in fullscreenParton and Katy Perry perform Coat of Many Colors at the 51st annual Academy of Country Music Awards in 2016.Photograph: Matt Sayles/Invision/AP‘I thought about her Coat of Many Colors when I had to wear hand-me-downs to school as a kid’Growing up as another hillbilly, I used to think about Dolly and Loretta Lynn when a few folks made fun of me for my incorrect pronunciations. I thought about her Coat of Many Colors when I had to wear hand-me-downs to school as a kid. But I pursued my dreams, stiffening my spine, as she did. I remember the very first time she appeared with Porter Wagoner and I have loved her music ever since. Her Smoky Mountain Christmas CD was only sold at Cracker Barrel but it is one of my favourites. She had such talent, such grace and goodness. She was so comfortable and authentic in her own skin. There will not be another like her.Anonymous, South Carolina‘More of us could stand to model Dolly’s bravery and kindness’Dolly Parton stood up for women, Black people and LGBTQIA people, and she did so in a region and industry where it was not trendy. On the one hand, I identify as Black and gay, and I appreciate being stood up for. But I think the more important element is the way she modelled speaking up for all her values, including those, in a culturally conservative part of America where doing so requires vastly more grit and risk than it does in regions like the east or west coast. She stood up anyway in the face of a potentially overwhelming backlash to those causes on her own turf.She also supported HIV/Aids treatment access, the development of the Moderna Covid vaccine, and she gave numerous children a chance to develop literacy skills by donating books.In the southern USA, where I am from, Dolly Parton will go into the pantheon of heroes. In this modern day world where cruelty and injustice are far too common, more of us could stand to model Dolly’s bravery and kindness, and I hope to see us do that.Antonio, Hanoi (originally from Kentucky)View image in fullscreenParton during a concert at Théâtre Mogador, Paris, in 1978.Photograph: Christian Rose‘She presented me with a pair of boots after a day spent shopping’I met Dolly in November 1978 when she came to perform in Paris at the Théâtre Mogador. I had just started to work for RCA records as a junior publicist. On the day before the concert, my boss called me at 7am saying she was sick and I had to replace her. I had to pick Dolly up at the George V hotel, with a chauffeur and limousine and take her everywhere she wanted to go.So there was young me, heart beating fast, meeting my first American artist, setting foot in a palace hotel and sitting in a limousine for the first time in my life. Her first request was to go to Christian Dior, which was another first for me. Due to the snobbish attitude of the shop assistants, who did not even bother to speak to her, we quickly retreated. Their mistake, she could have bought the building.When we returned to the George V she presented me with a box containing a pair of boots. I later realised she had carefully planned this as her assistant had asked about my shoe size and what style I liked when we were at the Galeries Lafayette. I was absolutely gobsmacked. Over the years when I would hear about all her good deeds, I was never surprised, having experienced her generosity first-hand.Fabienne Drinkwater, Australia (originally from France)View image in fullscreenDolly Parton in 2022.Photograph: NBC/Katherine Bomboy/Getty Images‘As a singer, I appreciated her incredible range and expressive quality’In the mid-early 1970’s when I was still in high school in Ohio, my brothers and I went to see Merle Haggard at the Akron Civic theatre and were blown away by the warm up act, which was Dolly Parton. We went home and worked out a few of her songs in our basement “studio” and years later one of my brothers formed a Dolly Parton tribute band in San Francisco called Parton Me. When Merle died in 2016 my brother said it felt like a member of our family had passed away. I have that same sense today hearing of Dolly’s passing. As a singer, I appreciated her incredible range, expressive quality, choice of songs in a set, her songwriting, and her interpretation of covers.Kathy Adams, UtahView image in fullscreenDolly Parton reads her book Coat of Many Colors, at the Library of Congress in Washington in 2018.Photograph: Andrew Harnik/AP‘Thanks to her, my son receives one book per month’I didn’t know much about Dolly Parton apart from Jolene. But thanks to herImagination Library, my 18-month-old son receives one book per month. I think it’s an amazing project and I hope it will survive her.Antoine, London‘She made me feel better about myself’As a trans girl growing up in rural Australia in the 1970s and 1980s, Dolly was one of the few celebrities who really made me feel better about being trans. Well before it was the thing to do, she made positive and supportive comments about trans women and LGBT people more generally. Her approach to life was also something that helped me through. In the early 1980s, a friend had one VHS tape and it was 9 to 5. We must have played it a thousand times until we didn’t need the sound any more to act out the movie from end to end.I was also a very freckled redhead, and I was bullied a lot for it. The lines from Jolene: “Your beauty is beyond compare / With flaming locks of auburn hair” also made me feel better about myself. It would have been great if she’d got her wish and died on stage at 120, but the 80 years she did give us were beyond compare.Maya, Australia‘A monumental loss for us all’How is it possible to cry for the loss of someone I’ve never met? Dolly’s kindness and sheer decency just shone from her. A monumental loss for us all but what a legacy she leaves behind.Jackie McDee, ScotlandExplore more on these topicsDolly PartonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ain’t nobody better: Chaka Khan’s 20 best songs – ranked!  | Chaka Khan | The Guardian
description: Ahead of the release of her 13th solo album, the fantastically titled Chakzilla, we rank the best of a sublime catalogue of funk, slow jams and tears-on-the-dancefloor disco
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: Ahead of the release of her 13th solo album, the fantastically titled Chakzilla, we rank the best of a sublime catalogue of funk, slow jams and tears-on-the-dancefloor disco
Content: Chaka Khan lets loose at the Royal Albert Hall, 1990.Photograph: Michael Putland/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChaka Khan lets loose at the Royal Albert Hall, 1990.Photograph: Michael Putland/Getty ImagesRankedChaka KhanAin’t nobody better: Chaka Khan’s 20 best songs – ranked!Ahead of the release of her 13th solo album, the fantastically titled Chakzilla, we rank the best of a sublime catalogue of funk, slow jams and tears-on-the-dancefloor discoAlexis PetridisThu 27 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 23.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google20. Love You All My Lifetime (1992)Chaka Khan had harsh words for the “assholes” at her then record company, Warner Bros, who she felt under-promoted 1992’s The Woman I Am, her first album in four years. Listening to Love You All My Lifetime’s cocktail of funk and contemporary R&B, you wonder if she didn’t have a point. There’s no obvious reason why it wasn’t huge hit.19. Hello Happiness (2019)Dissatisfied with her treatment by various record labels and managers, Khan released albums with less frequency in the 21st century – which made 2019’s Hello Happiness (and its title track) feel like a comeback. Producer Switch clearly knew what to do, the songwriting was strong, Khan’s voice still sizzles.18. Any Old Sunday (1981)A deep cut nestled in the middle of her best solo album, What ’Cha Gonna Do for Me, Any Old Sunday is easily overlooked amid the bigger hitters, but offers three-and- a-half minutes of instant sunshine: carefree mid-tempo disco funk – a hint of Chic about the guitars – with a vocal that adds heft to the poppy melody.View image in fullscreenKhan in Hollywood, c1978.Photograph: Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images17. Through the Fire (1984)I Feel for You was the smash, but the biggest streaming song from the album of the same name is, by some distance, Through the Fire. Perhaps because Kanye West sampled it on Through the Wire; perhaps because Khan brings an earthy power to a glossy, but classy, adult contemporary ballad.16. Spoon (1998)The most unfairly overlooked album in Khan’s catalogue is Come 2 My House, a collaboration with Prince that had the misfortune to be released when his commercial standing was in the doldrums, despite the fact that he could still turn out funk as sensual and weird as Spoon. But it’s not on streaming; someone rerelease it!View image in fullscreenRufus and Chaka Khan perform on US TV show Midnight Special, in 1975.Photograph: Gilles Petard/Redferns15. Rufus – At Midnight (My Love Will Lift You Up) (ft Chaka Khan) (1977)The sessions for Ask Rufus were turbulent – drummer Andre Fischer and Khan’s then husband, Richard Holland, had a punch-up in the studio – but you’d never guess from the Chicago band’s fifth album. At Midnight is its solitary dancefloor-focused track, but its understated funk is the perfect setting for Khan’s compelling switches from softness to raunch.14. Rufus – You Got the Love (ft Chaka Khan) (1974)Rufus’s debut album was promising, but unfocussed, not least in the fact that it kept allowing Khan to cede the microphone. But on its follow-up, Rags to Rufus, everything snapped into place. Opener You Got the Love offers thrillingly gritty funk – the perfect counterpoint to lush Philly soul – and Chaka in full effect.13. Rufus & Chaka – Any Love (1979)Khan might have been contractually obliged to keep recording with Rufus, despite her solo success, but 1979’s Masterjam doesn’t feel like an album made under duress. Any Love is tough, disco-paced, subtly orchestrated and entirely fantastic, Khan telling a predatory ladies’ man how pathetic she thinks he is in no uncertain terms.12. Chaka Khan and Rufus – Stay (1978)For all the endless turmoil in their ranks – the band’s lineup seemed to change constantly – Rufus and Khan made music that sounded absolutely effortless. The Khan-co-written big hit from their sixth album, Street Player, is a case in point. It’s an extremely cool breeze, which just makes Khan’s vaulting raw vocal seem all the more potent.View image in fullscreenKhan at the Blue Note club in NYC, 2000.Photograph: David Corio/Getty Images11. Rufus – Once You Get Started (ft Chaka Khan) (1974)Boosted by the platinum-selling success of Rags to Rufus, 1974’s Rufusized was a supremely confident album. With one eye on the burgeoning disco scene, opener Once You Get Started sands down some of its predecessor’s rough edges, but its chattering, synth-laden call to the dancefloor is impossible to resist.10. Rufus & Chaka – Do You Love What You Feel (1979)Fresh from collaborating with Khan on his superb 1978 single Stuff Like That, Quincy Jones brought a dose of production sophistication to Rufus’s Masterjam album. His sleek touch is all over the joy-bringing Do You Love What You Feel, a perfect platform for Khan’s exuberant vocal: “I wanna dance all night!”9. Papillon (AKA Hot Butterfly) (1980)Mid-tempo disco so wistful and sad it could cause an outbreak of ugly crying on the dancefloor: Khan sounds fantastic, especially backed by Luther Vandross. The original version, by writer Gregg Diamond’s Bionic Boogie, with a lead vocal from Vandross himself and a 12in mix by Jim Burgess, might be even better.View image in fullscreenKhan giving it some with a gospel choir.Photograph: Echoes/Redferns8. Fate (1981)These days, Fate is hard to listen to without automatically thinking of the more famous track that sampled it: Stardust’s Music Sounds Better With You. But temporarily banish the thought of French touch house from your brain and luxuriate instead in the original’s glorious update of disco for the 80s. It’s a treat.7. Rufus – Tell Me Something Good (1974)You didn’t need to read the credits to work out that Rufus’s breakthough hit was the handiwork of Stevie Wonder: its reggae-influenced groove and vocodered backing vocals could have stepped straight off Innervisions or Talking Book. But, barely into her 20s, Khan sounds entirely in charge, her voice totally commanding.6. Clouds (1980)A Paradise Garage classic, Ashford and Simpson’s Clouds is a disco monster, shifting from a dramatic opening verse that never quite goes where you expect to a headily euphoric chorus, complete with sound effects and a wild guitar solo. Pub quiz fact: it also features a 16-year-old Whitney Houston on backing vocals.5. I Know You, I Live You (1981)The highlight of What Cha’ Gonna Do for Me, co-penned by producer Arif Mardin and Khan, with the latter presumably responsible for the slightly odd, I-will-manifest-a-relationship lyrics. It is beautifully executed post-disco boogie – check Average White Band drummer Steve Ferrone’s superb rhythm track – with a wonderful melody and a frankly awesome performance from Khan herself.4. Rufus – Sweet Thing (ft Chaka Khan) (1975)A Top 5 US hit, Sweet Thing isthego-to Rufus slow jam, its distinctive guitar riff later borrowed by Nile Rodgers for David Bowie’s hit version of China Girl (you can definitely hear the similarity). Worth a mention is Mary J Blige’s superb, subtly updated 1992 cover, best heard in its scuffed-up remix version.View image in fullscreenKhan performing at the Apollo theatre, Harlem, NYC, 1992.Photograph: David Corio/Redferns3. I Feel for You (1984)Previously recorded by its author, Prince, and by the Pointer Sisters (and subsequently by Mickey Mouse Club-era Britney Spears and Justin Timberlake), Khan’s version is the definitive reading. An ultra-catchy song in any version, her vocal cuts through the none-more-mid-80s production to create a slice of electronic funk that’s genuinely timeless.2. I’m Every Woman (1978)The song for which Khan is most likely to be remembered has been variously rendered as reggae, house music, bossa nova and smooth jazz – sampled umpteen times and covered by Aretha Franklin and Whitney Houston. But look beyond its ubiquity, and marvel at the climactic key changes and Khan’s ferocious vocal performance.1. Rufus and Chaka Khan – Ain’t Nobody (1983)One of the greatest singles of the 80s began life on a contract-fulfilling slate of studio tracks, appended to the live Stompin’ at the Savoy record. Khan had already left Rufus and had to be coaxed back for one last album. But Ain’t Nobody was a synth-funk masterpiece that transcended its unpromising beginnings. An eagle-eared Quincy Jones suggested Michael Jackson might want the song for Thriller, but Rufus and producer David “Hawk” Wolinski rebuffed him. It’s hard to see how even Jackson could have improved on the group’s version, with its impossibly infectious synth line, air of nocturnal anticipation and Khan’s vocal, which really doesn’t sound like the work of a woman heading for the door.Explore more on these topicsChaka KhanRankedSoulfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Jeers, walkouts, stage invasions: will Catarina and the Beauty of Killing Fascists trigger British audiences too? | Stage | The Guardian
description: It has inspired violent protests from Norway to Rome – and now it’s hitting the UK. Playwright Tiago Rodrigues explains why the far-right speech at the drama’s climax has proved so incendiary
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: It has inspired violent protests from Norway to Rome – and now it’s hitting the UK. Playwright Tiago Rodrigues explains why the far-right speech at the drama’s climax has proved so incendiary
Content: ‘Kill him!’ … a 2023 production at the Teatro Piccolo Arsenale, Venice.Photograph: © Joseph BanderetView image in fullscreen‘Kill him!’ … a 2023 production at the Teatro Piccolo Arsenale, Venice.Photograph: © Joseph BanderetStageJeers, walkouts, stage invasions: will Catarina and the Beauty of Killing Fascists trigger British audiences too?It has inspired violent protests from Norway to Rome – and now it’s hitting the UK. Playwright Tiago Rodrigues explains why the far-right speech at the drama’s climax has proved so incendiaryPhilip OltermannThu 27 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn February, turbulent scenes inside a German theatre madeheadlinesaround the globe. During the final act of a play at Schauspielhaus theatre in Bochum, the audience first jeered and whistled at a performer in the role of a far-right politician. An orange lobbed from the auditorium narrowly missed its target; eventually, two spectators climbed on to the stage and tried to wrestle the actor off. News of the incident travelled around the world: it seemed a bizarre throwback to a world in which people were not able to tell the difference between art and real life, like 19th-century Parisians stampeding out of a cinema after watching a train hurtle towards the camera.For the man who wrote the play, however, it was nothing unusual. “I was not surprised by the reaction,” says Portuguese playwright Tiago Rodrigues. “I was surprised by the fact that it was so surprising for so many people.” He describes the audience’s reaction to his play Catarina and the Beauty of Killing Fascists as “very intense”, but also “typical”.double quotation markIn Portugal, the audience sang an anti-fascist anthem over the speechThe play, which visits London’sNational Theatrenext month, tells the story of a macabre family tradition: once every year, a group of relatives gather over a feast of wild boar and asparagus in the southern Portuguese countryside to kill a fascist they have kidnapped. Their ritual is designed to avenge the real-life murder of Catarina Eufémia, a harvester in revolt who was killed at the hands of the Salazar regime’s police force in 1954. But this year the family member tasked with the execution voices some doubts about the ritual’s righteousness, and things go awry: in the play’s last half hour, the freed fascist gives a victory speech that is uninterrupted by the rest of the cast. Ever since its September 2020 premiere in Guimarães, audiences have stepped in to intervene.In Portugal, spectators chantedGrândola, Vila Morena, José Afonso’s song of the 1974 Carnation revolution, to drown out the actor’s words. In Italy, they sang anti-fascist resistance anthemBella Ciao. In Austria, spectators stood up and walked out. There were attempts to storm the stage and hit the actor impersonating the fascist politician at performances in Lisbon, Paris, Marseille and in Montreal. In other places, it was the far right that expressed its indignation: the Rome premiere of Catarina and the Beauty of Killing Fascists was met with protests from the local branch prime minister Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy party, which asked for the play to be removed from the programme.View image in fullscreen‘Some of the cast were in tears at rehearsals’ ... Romeu Costa delivers the speech in Venice.Photograph: Joseph Banderet“We always get these reactions, whether we’re in Switzerland or in Norway,” Rodrigues says, matter-of-factly. “In around 200 performances, we’ve had perhaps a handful of shows where the audience just listened to the final speech in silence.”What is it about his play that has made it a 21st-century equivalent of Stravinsky’s The Rite of Spring, triggering mini-riots wherever it is shown? One answer may be that Catarina and the Beauty of Killing Fascists is essentially two plays in one, each of which annuls the answers offered by the other: an anti-fascist play that asks difficult questions of both liberal and militant anti-fascists.For the first two hours, Rodrigues’s play is a reflection on what the philosopher Karl Popper called the “paradox of tolerance”: to preserve an open and tolerant society, must we be intolerant towards those who advocate intolerance? Or does our society cease to be a tolerant one when we do so? The second question carries particular weight in Rodrigues’s staging, for the anti-fascist tradition that the family at the heart of the play represents is one that comes across as self-absorbed, self-regarding and, in its own way, reactionary. “Our family killed fascists during the dictatorship, we killed fascists during the democracy and will continue to kill fascists,” says one of the characters, Pedro. “You shouldn’t ask yourself ‘Why?’ or ‘Why also me?’. The real ‘why’ is in the ‘how’. There’s a method, a ritual, a tradition, a beauty.”double quotation markThe people who feel most strongly that the left should not use violence are the loudest to scream: ‘Kill him’It’s hard not to side with Sara, the young woman who has been chosen to kill her first fascist this year but instead of duty feels only doubt. Is killing not like imposing a dictatorship, she asks: “Death, where you don’t think, don’t argue, where you can’t change your mind, is that not the greatest dictatorship of all?” And if the end supposedly justifies the means, why has their ritual not managed to fend off fascism for good (in the play, the extreme right has recently gained power over Portugal again)? “Why don’t we have a revolution, a coup d’état, a guerrilla campaign, a war? Why don’t we kill all the fascists once and for all and get this thing sorted?”Rodrigues, who has been artistic director of the D’Avignon theatre festival since 2022, does not hide his sympathies with Sara’s inner conflict. “My own views are quite simple,” he says. “I consider the far right an enemy that has to be fought, but we should fight them in a democratic way, and if that doesn’t work, you keep on playing it democratic. I think most of the audience usually position themselves in a similar way: they feel Sara is right.View image in fullscreen‘My owns views are quite simple’ … Tiago Rodrigues.Photograph: Sopa Images/LightRocket/Getty Images“Nevertheless, there have been moments in history where violence was considered a legitimate response to fascism. Where I live today, in the south of France, I don’t think it’s controversial to say that armed resistance was a legitimate answer to the Nazi occupation.”With the family of anti-fascists unable to come to a collective decision on how to address their problem, the fascist politician is freed and gives a victory speech straight out of the modern far right’s rulebook, decrying the dictatorship of “minorities” over “the people”, the biased mainstream media, the intolerant liberal left. If you overthink your anti-fascism, Rodrigues seems to be saying in response to the first part of the play, this is what you get.The playwright says he wrote the final monologue during the rehearsals. “We had this problem: how do we finish? If Sara’s side won, it would be very didactic and politically correct. And I realised the victory of the far right would be the most troubling, the most dystopian and also the most thought-provoking.” His own cast’s response to the ending foreshadowed the reactions the play has received around the globe. “Some people felt sick, others were in tears and left the room or thought about quitting the project altogether. There were a lot of debates about whether we have the right to put such a speech on stage today.”He condemns those who have tried to assault members of his cast, but says it’s not for him to judge spectators shouting down a fascist speech: “It’s not something that we find to be a mistake.” Some viewers, he believes, feel the play is inviting them to react in a visceral way: “They feel they have to show emotion because the actor is addressing them, and if they don’t protest they are accomplices of his speech. For them, it’s a kind of game they’ve been invited to play.”View image in fullscreenTrigger warning … a production in Germany.Photograph: Armin SmailovicIn other cases, he suggests, the outrage may also cloak a deeper feeling of helplessness: “The audience have spent two hours following a complex debate and worked out their own position within it, and suddenly that choice is not there any more. That’s very disturbing. Some of the same people who agreed most strongly with Sara that the left should not use violence are the loudest to scream ‘kill him’ at the end of the play.”Rodrigues decided to tackle the question of how societies can protect themselves from fascism after André Ventura, the founder of anti-immigration party Chega, in 2019 became the first far-right politician to be elected as a member of Portugal’s parliament since the end of the Salazar regime. Until that point, the Iberian country had looked immune to the brand of rightwing populism that was rattling most countries in Europe.“I remember when I mentioned in rehearsals that the story would be about a victory for the far right in 2028. Everybody laughed: yeah, that’s never going to happen, eight years is too short. And I agreed with it.
