My defence was that we needed to exaggerate to focus the audience’s mind.” Today, Chega is the second largest party in Portuguese politics; earlier this year, Ventura came second in a rare runoff vote for the presidency.“As a playwright, you are sometimes dystopian because you don’t want to be prophetic,” he adds. “Unfortunately, reality keeps making this piece more relevant.”Catarina and the Beauty of Killing Fascists is at theNational Theatre, London, 19-26 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatreThe far rightNational TheatrefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘He could arch both eyebrows and curl his lips in every direction all at once’: Tim Curry’s five best screen roles | Movies | The Guardian
description: The actor fully embraced his physical talents and outsized personality with a line in theatrical baddies teetering deliciously on the edge of serious and silly
Author: Laurence Phelan
Headline: The actor fully embraced his physical talents and outsized personality with a line in theatrical baddies teetering deliciously on the edge of serious and silly
Content: Terrifying a generation … Tim Curry in Stephen King’s ItPhotograph: Cinematic/AlamyView image in fullscreenTerrifying a generation … Tim Curry in Stephen King’s ItPhotograph: Cinematic/AlamyMovies‘He could arch both eyebrows and curl his lips in every direction all at once’: Tim Curry’s five best screen rolesThe actor fully embraced his physical talents and outsized personality with a line in theatrical baddies teetering deliciously on the edge of serious and sillyTim Curry, star of The Rocky Horror Picture Show and Stephen King’s It, dies aged 80Tim Curry on sexuality, surviving a stroke – and 50 years of stardomClowns, corsets and kings: Tim Curry – a life in picturesLaurence PhelanThu 27 Aug 2026 07.29 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 18.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Rocky Horror Picture Show (1975)As Dr Frank-N-Furter, the gender-nonconforming alien mad scientist who presides over Richard O’Brien’s glam rock musical, admits two innocents to his gothic castle and induces them into all sorts of delicious naughtiness, Curry is so thrillingly liberated as to seem a menace. An irresistibly appealing menace. Apparently able to arch both eyebrows and curl his lips in every direction all at once, Curry wraps his mouth around the double-entendres and belts out the lyrics with lip-smacking relish, and fully fleshes out this avatar of sexual confidence. The film earned one of the original cult fandoms, the stage musical endures and many other actors have pulled on Frank’s corset and high heels – but the role indelibly and for ever belongs to Curry.Legend (1985)A physical actor bursting with personality, Curry was at his best inhabiting outsized roles. He near fills up the entire frame as the prowling Lord of Darkness who kidnaps a princess and torments innocent forest child Tom Cruise in Ridley Scott’s visually sumptuous high fantasy.Clue (1985)The debonair manner and hint of a self-amused smile that were seemingly Curry’s birthright were deployed to delightful effect as Wadsworth, the butler who is just about a half a step ahead of everyone else in this madcap murder-mystery comedy, reputedly worked on by Tom Stoppard, and inspired by the board game that’s called Clue in North America and Cluedo everywhere else.It (1990)Inculcating coulrophobia in an entire generation of kids who stayed up late to watch this TVStephen Kingadaptation, Curry played a shapeshifting child-murdering interdimensional entity – but ever a devotee of the theatrical arts, he did it in clown makeup. Charming baddies were his metier, and Pennywise the Clown was the baddest of the lot.Muppet Treasure Island (1996)It was Curry’s great gift as an actor to always know exactly how seriously to take a role – certainly no more than necessary but never any less either. As the devious West Country buccaneer Long John Silver in a Muppets movie, he was fully on board with the make-believe, fully on board with the silliness.Explore more on these topicsFilmTim CurryThe MuppetsHorror filmsMusicalsScience fiction and fantasy filmsComedy filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Billy Strings: So Much for Goodbyes review – staggering, stirring songs of grief draw the blues out of bluegrass | Music | The Guardian
description: The crossover star’s introspective sixth album is full of memories of his mother, who died in 2025, bringing his dextrous guitar to songs rooted in tradition and yearning
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: The crossover star’s introspective sixth album is full of memories of his mother, who died in 2025, bringing his dextrous guitar to songs rooted in tradition and yearning
Content: Astonishingly dextrous … Billy Strings.Photograph: Dana TrippeView image in fullscreenAstonishingly dextrous … Billy Strings.Photograph: Dana TrippeAlexis Petridis's album of the weekMusicReviewBilly Strings: So Much for Goodbyes review – staggering, stirring songs of grief draw the blues out of bluegrass(Reprise)The crossover star’s introspective sixth album is full of memories of his mother, who died in 2025, bringing his dextrous guitar to songs rooted in tradition and yearningAlexis PetridisThu 27 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 12.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the face of it, 2025 was a landmark year for Billy Strings. His fifth album,Highway Prayers, won him his third Grammy. The first bluegrass album in more than 22 years to debut at the top of the US album sales chart, it confirmed him as the genre’s biggest crossover star in decades. He was feted by everyone from Bob Dylan to Post Malone to Willie Nelson, the latter describing him as “the John Coltrane of bluegrass”, a pretty impressive soubriquet in anyone’s book. As theNew York Times noted, he was now capable of filling the arena-sized venues that his idols – Doc Watson, Clarence White, Tony Rice, Béla Fleck – could never have dreamed of performing in, packing them out with an audience that look less like traditional bluegrass aficionados than Deadheads: a vast, mobile, hippy-ish army that call themselves Goats. They’re presumably drawn by the ease with which Strings occupies the no man’s land between country and expansive, psychedelically informed improvisation, his willingness to put acoustic guitar through umpteen effects pedals and stretch out songs for 20 minutes on stage.View image in fullscreenBilly Strings: So Much for Goodbyes album coverIt’s a side of Strings’ music that’s only hinted at on Highway Prayers’ follow-up: as Burn the Other End and Lucid Daydream draw to an end, they briefly unravel into a kind of abstraction that you can imagine as a jumping-off point for heady, out-there exploration live. But So Much for Goodbyes is an album more concerned with introspection, and understandably so. In the midst of 2025’s successes, Strings’ mother died of an overdose. His chaotic upbringing is a matter of record. His father died of a heroin overdose when he was two, both his mother and his stepfather were addicted to meth and he left home at 14 on the grounds that “there was no food in the house and my parents were strung out”. But Strings said he had “no idea” she had relapsed, and her death seeps into every corner of the album: its title and cover art – based on a collage his mother was working on the night she died; the concluding instrumental that bears her name, Debra’s Waltz; the songs that, on the surface, appear to have nothing to do with her passing.Under normal circumstances, Lay Me Down might be read as an exercise in standard-issue granite-faced country posturing – “leave no roses on my headstone / leave no footprints in the clay / lay me down on the hillside / turn away your face” – but in context, it feels more like a song about generational trauma, a plea for a family’s pain to be passed down no further. Similarly, opener I’m One of Those warps another country trope – the rootless ramblin’ man wont to leave ladies crying when he skips town in the dead of night – into something darker: he’s attempted to return home, but found nothing but distress, and the song exists to “warn the ghost that wandered back across this road”.Billy Strings: Burn the Other End – videoInitially at least, this seems to be how the album deals with its overriding theme, via glancing references and lyrics open to interpretation, sprinkled through songs that offer a striking resume of Strings’ skills. His guitar picking is every bit asastonishingly dextrous as his tie-dyed devoteesclaim; his equally impressive backing quartet are particularly talented at working up a ferociously propulsive head of steam, given that their ranks don’t include a drummer. Strings is equally capable of writing songs so perfectly rooted in tradition that you might be forgiven for assuming Light the Way or Lay Me Down were covers dating back to the 1940s or 50s, and of throwing his listeners a curveball that indicates the breadth of his musical tastes: if his penchant for jam band improv is only lightly sketched here, his love of heavy metal is underlined by the way he skilfully works a devil’s horn-provoking riff into the ominous atmosphere of Burn the Other End, while a devotion to heartlands rock is reflected in the Springsteen-ish narrative of Mill Town Flood.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘I was running away from poverty’: the remarkable rise of bluegrass virtuoso Billy StringsRead moreBut long after you feel as if you’ve settled into the album, it sharply detours. There is nothing allusive or open to interpretation about Still I Crash: the guitar melody is stunning, but it’s starkly recorded; the lyrical wail of confusion and despair is addressed directly to his mother. Appearing when it does, it effectively punches the listener in the stomach and casts a long shadow over the remaining tracks, lending a darker hue to I Wish I Wanted To’s saga of indolence and the biblical references in Wrestling an Angel. The album ends on a distinctly overcast note that the beautiful ensemble playing on Debra’s Waltz doesn’t entirely lift. What does cut through the gloom is the lingering thought of how rich and powerful the album you’ve just heard is.This week Alexis listened toCleo Sol – Force of LoveThere’s no dip in the high standards set by Cleo Sol’s previous work on her fifth album, Gentlewoman: Force of Love gently remodels her exquisite soul sound via a hint of dancehall in the rhythm.Explore more on these topicsMusicAlexis Petridis's album of the weekCountryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We’re at a crisis point’: Chappell Roan, Shirley Manson and Eli on playing Olivia Rodrigo’s women-led festival  | Olivia Rodrigo | The Guardian
description: Ahead of playing Rodrigo’s Daisy Chain Fields, artists explain why female-first festivals are due for a resurgence
Author: Emma Madden
Headline: Ahead of playing Rodrigo’s Daisy Chain Fields, artists explain why female-first festivals are due for a resurgence
Content: Shirley Manson, Chappell Roan, Olivia Rodrigo and Eli.Composite: The Guardian/Getty Images/Charlotte RutherfordView image in fullscreenShirley Manson, Chappell Roan, Olivia Rodrigo and Eli.Composite: The Guardian/Getty Images/Charlotte RutherfordOlivia Rodrigo‘We’re at a crisis point’: Chappell Roan, Shirley Manson and Eli on playing Olivia Rodrigo’s women-led festivalAhead of playing Rodrigo’s Daisy Chain Fields, artists explain why female-first festivals are due for a resurgenceEmma MaddenThu 27 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 17.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen I first saw the poster forOlivia Rodrigo’s inaugural Daisy Chain Fields festival in June, I assumed it was AI. Chappell Roan, Doechii, Mitski, the Breeders, Bikini Kill and Garbage, all arranged in a neat line – and this was before I got to the words “special guests”. Karen O, Sarah McLachlan. And, to top it all off, Stevie Nicks? No.I saw the post confirmed on Rodrigo’s Instagram, and thought: how?Olivia Rodrigo review – crushing riffs and infectious hooks at secret New York showRead moreAccording toShirley Manson, the Garbage singer, Rodrigo called up every act one by one. “I told her it was very unusual for an agent not to be doing that.” Rodrigo isn’t shy about her influences, and has gushed about Garbage’s music as an inspiration for her own. “And unlike many artists, she doesn’t say she’s inventing the wheel; she knows she’s just a spoke within it,” said Manson.Rodrigo has earned the regard of some of the world’s most respected musicians partly for this reason: she had a feature with Robert Smith on her latest album,You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love, and has duetted with the Smashing Pumpkins and Sheryl Crow. Which brings us to the lineup of the summer: a string of major coups assembled for Rodrigo’s intergenerational celebration and first festival, Daisy Chain Fields. The one-day event will take place on 29 August at the Great Park in Irvine, California, bringing together an unusually broad assembly of women spanning Rodrigo’s influences, both new and lifelong.View image in fullscreenShirley Manson of Garbage performs in Manchester in 2024.Photograph: Shirlaine Forrest/WireImageThere is no competitive element or hierarchy among the acts: no two sets will overlap, and on the poster, every name appears in the same typeface and font size, no matter how established or fresh the act. “It creates a necessary and refreshing culture of community, setting up women’s art to be received and valued in a less competitive and capitalist environment,” saidEli, the pop artist whose music answers the question: what if Ashlee Simpson, but camp?Olivia Rodrigo: You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love review – who’s she singing about? Who cares when the songs are this goodRead moreEli is one of the festival’s most obviously new-generation additions, her name listed on the poster between Doechii and Garbage. Daisy Chain Fields is her first festival. Eli had no idea Rodrigo was a fan until Rodrigo called her herself on a video call. She was driving home from a writing session when Rodrigo FaceTimed her, forcing her to pull over.“It was almost like she was pitching it to me, and I was like: ‘Girl, you could’ve asked me to work the concessions for free and I would’ve been there,” she said.On an equally sincere note, Eli said she was “completely blown away by the heart of her efforts and inspired by the depths of her intentions to stand for something: women’s rights and peace on Mother Nature’s globe”.One hundred per cent of Daisy Chain Fields’ net proceeds will be distributed among organizations including Planned Parenthood and the Center for Reproductive Rights, while reproductive-rights education and non-profit activations will be spotted throughout the festival site.View image in fullscreenThe lineup for Daisy Chain Fields.Photograph: Courtesy of Olivia RodrigoDaisy Chain Fields belongs to a lineage of women-led music festivals that have tried to raise money for female-focused causes while correcting a stubborn gender imbalance across festival lineups – one that has always existed, and still does. (A 2025reportfrom Book More Women found that women accounted for just 21.6% of headliners across nine major music festivals.) In 1976, second-wave feminists and lesbian separatists founded the Michigan Womyn’s Music Festival, which combined an all-women lineup with educational workshops and health services.But Rodrigo’s most direct model for Daisy Chain is Sarah McLachlan’sLilith Fair, the hugely successful touring festival McLachlan launched in 1997 as a showcase for women in music. McLachlan was the first person Rodrigo called when she began dreaming up Daisy Chain, and McLachlan is scheduled to perform both her own set and alongside Rodrigo during hers.Garbage, meanwhile, was invited to play Lilith Fair in the 90s and turned it down. Nearly three decades later, Manson sees a different urgency in Rodrigo’s festival. “I might have been naive, but it felt like there was more progress for women then,” she explained of her decision to decline McLachlan’s invitation. “And here we are in 2026, as women’s rights are regressing all over the world. We’re at a crisis point.”View image in fullscreenChappell Roan performing at the 2025 Grammy awards.Photograph: John Shearer/Getty Images for The Recording AcademyChappell Roan, who will perform right before Rodrigo’s headlining set, is pursuing a similar idea from a different angle. In October, she will launch her inaugural two-night charity fundraiser,the Super Graphic Spectacular, with 100% of net proceeds directed to LGBTQ+ community mutual-aid funds. With a slightly different focus, she answers the same question as Rodrigo: what can an artist do with the scale of a major live event besides selling tickets?Roan said she felt “honored” when Rodrigo asked her to play her own festival. “Being able to go see a show right now feels like such a privilege, and it’s more important than ever for those shows to be safe spaces of inclusivity where fans can disconnect, even if only for a few hours, to have fun and just be together and feel joy,” said Roan. She sees the charitable component as far more than an adjunct, but the main reason for doing it. “Being able to give back, especially to the people who have shown me so much support, is at the center of my project and what keeps me going,” she said.Eli, looking at what Rodrigo has assembled, sees something larger in it still. “Olivia gives me hope that we can lead our generation and generations to come to a harmonious earth filled with strange girls and happy hearts.”Daisy Chain Fieldswill take place in the Great Park in Irvine, California, on 29 AugustExplore more on these topicsOlivia RodrigoChappell RoanShirley MansonPop and rockReproductive rightsWomenCaliforniafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The technique was revolutionary’: Ha Chong-Hyun, the 91-year-old South Korean artist who turned painting inside out | Art | The Guardian
description: In his trailblazing work, paint is pushed through the back of hemp to create spare, striking paintings. Abstraction is a form of rebellion, he says – and he has no intention of slowing down
Author: Gabrielle Schwarz
Headline: In his trailblazing work, paint is pushed through the back of hemp to create spare, striking paintings. Abstraction is a form of rebellion, he says – and he has no intention of slowing down
Content: Ha Chong-Hyun’s White Paper on Urban Planning No.5, 1968.Photograph: George Darrell/© Ha Chong-Hyun; Courtesy Lisson GalleryView image in fullscreenHa Chong-Hyun’s White Paper on Urban Planning No.5, 1968.Photograph: George Darrell/© Ha Chong-Hyun; Courtesy Lisson GalleryArt‘The technique was revolutionary’: Ha Chong-Hyun, the 91-year-old South Korean artist who turned painting inside outIn his trailblazing work, paint is pushed through the back of hemp to create spare, striking paintings. Abstraction is a form of rebellion, he says – and he has no intention of slowing downGabrielle SchwarzThu 27 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 11.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the early 1970s, the Korean artist Ha Chong-Hyun had a simple but novel idea: why not apply oil paint to the back of a surface rather than the front? Instead of canvas, he stretched pieces of hemp, a coarse and loosely woven fabric, and pushed the thick oil paint through the holes in the cloth. For each work he used a single colour, in a neutral or muted tone such as white or brown. On the “front” side, he then moved the paint around with various handmade tools to create something akin to brushstrokes.Ha, now 91, has remained dedicated to this technique, known as the “back-pressure method” (bae-ap-bubin Korean), ever since. He titles every piece Conjunction – because for him the work is essentially about the coming together of artist and material – along with numbers denoting the date of its creation. “The technique he developed was really revolutionary. It hadn’t been done before,” says Max Bossier, director at Lisson Gallery in London, where a selection from this decades-spanning body of work, alongside several of Ha’s earlier artistic experiments, will go on view in September.Today, Ha is recognised as among the foremost Korean painters of his generation: part of an influential group of artists who came on to the scene in the 1970s and whose work was characterised by a spare simplicity of colour and material. In the 2000s, the movement was retrospectively named Dansaekhwa, which translates roughly as “monochrome painting”. By then, the artists – other important names include Lee Ufan and Park Seo-Bo – had begun to garner recognition outside their home country, a process that Bossier tells me has only accelerated over the past decade. (The Lisson show opens the day before Ha’s first ever North American museum retrospective, at the AsianArtMuseum in San Francisco.)At first glance, Ha’s pared-back abstractions – and the output of the Dansaekhwa artists more broadly – may seem to share significant overlap with the other examples of non-representational painting that proliferated around the globe in the second half of the 20th century. In particular, comparisons are often drawn to the work of US minimalists such as Robert Ryman, who famously restricted his palette to white and off-white paint. But there is a deep cultural specificity to Ha’s approach that is fundamental to understanding his art.View image in fullscreenHa Chong-Hyun.Photograph: Ha Chong-Hyun; Lisson GalleryHa was born in Sancheong in Korea in 1935, during the Japanese occupation. He lived in Japan as a child for several years before returning to Korea after liberation in 1945. “On our journey home, we encountered a violent storm at sea and I lost my grandmother and my young sibling,” he recalls. “Amid all the upheaval, I continued to draw. I remember making a portrait of Yi Jun, the Korean independence activist, which my teacher displayed on the classroom wall.” (We corresponded via email; Ha’s children translated between Korean and English.)In the turbulent decades that followed – the Korean war, postwar economic privation, a military dictatorship that didn’t end until 1988 – Ha developed an artistic language that responded to and expressed its historical circumstances. Abstraction, for him and other artists, was at least partly a way to rebel against the figurative style favoured by the state. The use of hemp as a support for his paintings, meanwhile, began as a matter of necessity. “In the poverty that followed the Korean war, conventional art supplies were difficult to obtain,” Ha explains. “Among the materials around us were coarse sacks that had carried grain and other relief supplies from abroad.”For Ha, his commitment to working back-to-front “has never meant simply repeating the same thing”. Over time, he has introduced – or reintroduced – a number of different elements to his practice: holding a flame to the surface to singe the paint, using wooden slats instead of hemp as the support, incorporating brighter colours such as red and blue. “I still believe, as I have always told my students, that ‘a painter should never allow the paint on his palette to dry’,” he says. “As long as my health allows me to stand in the studio, I want to keep working. There are still things I have not made, and things I have yet to discover.”Works by Ha Chong-Hyun will be on display at the Lisson Gallery, London,24 September to 7 NovemberReverse course: five works from the exhibitionWhite Paper on Urban Planning No5, 1968(main image)This work is from an early series executed between 1967 and 1969. “I remember how rapidly Seoul was changing at the time,” Ha says. “The city was emerging from the devastation of war: new roads were being laid out, new buildings were rising, and the environment around us was becoming increasingly geometric and architectural. I wanted to bring something of that order and energy into my painting.”View image in fullscreenPhotograph: George Darrell/Ha Chong-Hyun; Lisson GalleryWork 72-72(B), 1972Before he developed the back-pressure method, Ha’s work often incorporated common industrial materials such as barbed wire or metal springs. “The use of objects in these works is connected to the three-dimensional quality of his Conjunction paintings,” says Lisson Gallery’s Bossier.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenPhotograph: George Darrell/Ha Chong-Hyun; Lisson GalleryConjunction93-002, 1993“I have always believed that an artist should not simply see things as they appear, but should find another way of looking at and interpreting them,” says Ha. “Painters normally apply paint to the front of a canvas; I began to ask myself, almost instinctively, what might happen if I approached it from the other side.”View image in fullscreenPhotograph: George Darrell/Ha Chong-Hyun; Lisson GalleryConjunction 20-118, 2020Since around 2010, Ha has increased his use of colour – especially reds and blues – in his work. “For me, the continuity of Conjunction lies not in repetition, but in continuing to experiment within a language that has kept opening up new possibilities,” he says.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: George Darrell/Ha Chong-Hyun; Lisson GalleryConjunction 25-72, 2025Bossier points to a “meditative quality” of the intensely physical and repetitive back-pressure method. Meanwhile, the “hand tools” that Ha uses to manipulate the paint once it’s been pushed through the hemp include palette knives, sticks and combs.Explore more on these topicsArtExhibitionsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Freddie Meredith: Need a Light? review – one hilarious hour of cringe | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Watching a man labouring to strike up conversations in the smoking area of a nightclub proves not just funny but also touching and uplifting
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: Watching a man labouring to strike up conversations in the smoking area of a nightclub proves not just funny but also touching and uplifting
Content: A beta man than you … Freddie Meredith: Need a Light?Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA beta man than you … Freddie Meredith: Need a Light?Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewFreddie Meredith: Need a Light? review – one hilarious hour of cringePleasance Courtyard, EdinburghWatching a man labouring to strike up conversations in the smoking area of a nightclub proves not just funny but also touching and upliftingBrian LoganThu 27 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEver pretended to use your phone to avoid the shame of being Norman No-Mates at a party? Freddie Meredith’s new show is a 60-minute channelling of that experience, an hour-long cringe at a man labouring to strike up conversations in the smoking area of a nightclub.Meredith, a familiar face to viewers of Big Boys, Such Brave Girls and other TV series, has alighted on a familiar social type here, albeit one rarely so brilliantly depicted. His alter ego is a shy and insecure beta male desperately trying to look – well, alpha is out of his reach, but even basic social functioning would be an upgrade.He sounds like a dork, right? And so he is, in his wannabe hip dad-wear, with his fantasies about being in the audience on Top Gear and his furtive Amazon purchasing of “cool T-shirts for men”. But beyond the David Brent stylings is someone much more sympathetic, for whom we’re rooting by the show’s uplifting end.View image in fullscreenDrab tenderness … Freddie Meredith.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianMeredith performs the hour, all awkward grooviness, nervous laughter and duff small talk with the crowd (starring as his fellow clubbers), with a face that looks perpetually like it could burst into tears. But there’s something heroic in the effort. Social outcast he may be, but he’s doing his best to learn the route – all those codes and behaviours that come so easily to other people – back in.Kemah Bob: Love Child review – Miss Fortunate’s follow-up is a superbly playful origin storyRead more“Planning any house parties?” to one other raver, doesn’t quite cut it – but it prompts a wonderfully needy monologue on Meredith’s part, pledging to be the best house guest imaginable. “Can you come to the toilet with me?” Again, it’s not quite how things are done. But it leads to a choice routine involving urinals, men’s fragrances and (in due course) a Lady Gaga karaoke duet engineered to ensnare Meredith a new chum.Occasionally, there are sketches that stretch the conceit almost to breaking point. Always, we indulge them – because we’re so seduced by the drab tenderness with which Meredith constructs his world, a round-the-back-of-the-building refuge where a loner fails and fails again to learn social skills – and makes devoted friends of his audience while doing so.AtPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Owl at Home review – this Edinburgh fringe hoot is a wise choice for children | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Songs, physical comedy and clever design come together in Theatr Iolo’s adaptation of Arnold Lobel’s offbeat story, aimed at over-fives
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Songs, physical comedy and clever design come together in Theatr Iolo’s adaptation of Arnold Lobel’s offbeat story, aimed at over-fives
Content: A creature of habit … George Williams in Owl at Home.Photograph: Gilded BalloonView image in fullscreenA creature of habit … George Williams in Owl at Home.Photograph: Gilded BalloonEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewOwl at Home review – this Edinburgh fringe hoot is a wise choice for childrenGilded Balloon Teviot, EdinburghSongs, physical comedy and clever design come together in Theatr Iolo’s adaptation of Arnold Lobel’s offbeat story, aimed at over-fivesChris WiegandThu 27 Aug 2026 10.53 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 10.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArnold Lobel was a writer with a keen sense of the seasons.Frog and Toad Are Friends, one of my favourite books since childhood, has a wonderful story where the excitable Frog wakes up his grumpy friend Toad and tricks him into enjoying the dawn of spring with him. Those stories celebrate togetherness but Lobel’s collection Owl at Home is about aloneness and being at one with your surroundings – even when the arrival of winter brings a snowstorm blowing through your roost.With his hair gelled into tufts, George Williams plays Owl in this adaptation by Rina Vergano andTheatr Iolo, directed by Lee Lyford. We find Williams dozing in an armchair on Anisha Fields’ accomplished set, which retains the cosy essence of Lobel’s illustrations but is less twee. The roost functions as an equally eccentric character in itself, filled with contraptions, dark wooden furniture and a periscope to nervously keep an eye on the world outside.View image in fullscreenCosy essence of the original illustrations … Owl at Home, designed by Anisha Fields.Photograph: Kirsten McternanThe collection’s stories are supplemented with songs and physical comedy including a tail feather-shaking exercise routine and a tussle with a dust buster. There are many delightful details: Owl sleeps with an eye mask, over his horn-rimmed glasses, and swivels it around to become a sporty headband. Not bothered to chase his prey, he catches chocolate mice in traps and hangs them out to ripen; Williams is alarmingly good at producing the postprandial pellet. Children will recognise the trick of turning a half-eaten pancake into a smile or a crescent moon.Robot helpers and flying houses: Edinburgh fringe tips for familiesRead moreAimed at over-fives, the production is as offbeat and sweet as the book, the new material never jarring amid Lobel’s stories of the wind’s visit, the strange bumps in the blanket and filling a kettle with tears. The show captures his owlish wisdom about opening up to the world around you and the perils of being a creature of habit – young or old, feathered or not.AtGilded Balloon Teviot, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreChildren's theatreEdinburgh festivalChildren's books: 7 and underChildren and teenagersreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Yayoi Kusama obituary | Yayoi Kusama | The Guardian
description: Artist known for her dazzling polka-dotted paintings and infinity mirror room installations
Author: Christopher Masters
Headline: Artist known for her dazzling polka-dotted paintings and infinity mirror room installations
Content: Yayoi Kusama at the opening ceremony of the Yayoi Kusama Museum in Tokyo in 2017.Photograph: The Asahi Shimbun/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenYayoi Kusama at the opening ceremony of the Yayoi Kusama Museum in Tokyo in 2017.Photograph: The Asahi Shimbun/Getty ImagesYayoi KusamaObituaryYayoi Kusama obituaryArtist known for her dazzling polka-dotted paintings and infinity mirror room installationsChristopher MastersThu 27 Aug 2026 09.52 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 09.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Japanese artistYayoi Kusama, who has died aged 97, created an exhilarating oeuvre of polka-dotted paintings, stuffed cloth phalloi and provocative happenings, films and installations, as well as a curate’s egg of novels and poetry. Kusama’s autobiography, Infinity Net (2002), relates her work directly to the obsessions and neuroses from which she suffered throughout her life: “From my very earliest memories, I have felt imprisoned by the walls of my eyes and ears and heart, upon which have been emblazoned all manner of things – nature, the universe, people and blood and flowers…. The only way for me to elude these furtive appearances is to recreate them visually with paint, pen or pencil in an attempt to decipher what they are.”When she first arrived in New York in the late 1950s, critics and fellow artists praised her originality. Kusama’s friendDonald Judd, the minimalist artist, described her as transcending “whatever ... is oriental or American” but nonetheless emphasised her shallow pictorial space and other formal qualities associated with contemporary art in New York.Kusama characterised her own work in a letter to the American painterGeorgia O’Keeffeas “oriental mystic symbolism”. More recently, feminist writers such as Izumi Nakajima have discussed her highly original response to her identity as an Asian woman in a white male art world.Most interpretations of Kusama’s career have relied, at least partly, on examining her tortuous early life. She was born into a provincial bourgeois family that had made its fortune from cultivating nursery seedlings, at Matsumoto, in the mountainous Nagano prefecture north-west of Tokyo. Her father, Kamon, was a man of “extravagant and incorrigible profligacy”, she wrote, to which Kusama attributed many of her psychological problems. Her mother, Shigeru, “perpetually angry” and bitterly opposed to Yayoi becoming an artist, also played her part.View image in fullscreenVisitors walking through the artwork Infinity Mirrored Room during a preview of a Yayoi Kusama exhibition at the Museum Ludwig in Cologne, March 2026.Photograph: Martin Meissner/APKusama still managed to pursue her painting, compensating for the shortage of canvases in 40sJapanby reusing pieces of plant sacks and gaining inspiration from the brilliantly coloured flowers cultivated by her family. Her creativity was already linked to disturbing hallucinations: even the violets she depicted had a tendency to adopt human characteristics or to attach themselves to her.As she was to write in her poem Violet Obsession (1978), “One day suddenly my voice / became the voice of a violet / … The violets on the tablecloth break free / and crawl over my body /... O violets, little flowers – don’t talk to me / Give me back the voice that became a violet’s voice / I don’t want to be an adult – not yet.”This inability to distinguish herself from her surroundings was to be the principal reason for Kusama’s famous obsession with the polka dot. This apparently harmless motif became in her hands a weapon of “self-obliteration”, spreading like measles across much of her work. It created a powerful effect of formlessness and loss of individuality, whether appearing on paintings, sculptures or even the human body – her own or other people’s.Although generally associated with later phases in Kusama’s career, coloured dots had first appeared in a drawing of a woman, apparently her mother, which the budding artist made when she was 10 years old. By the early 50s Kusama was producing striking abstract watercolours such as Infinity Polka Dots (Red) of 1951, together with more obviously surrealist works that seemed to present simultaneous visions of both microscopic and cosmic reality.View image in fullscreenYayoi Kusama was in perfect accord with the zeitgeist of the 1960s.Photograph: Magnolia Pictures/Everett/ShutterstockNaturally enough for a youthful follower of surrealism, Kusama followed a disappointing period at the Kyoto Art Academy from 1948 to 1951 with an application to study in Paris. She almost went there, but instead the breakthrough of having solo exhibitions in Japan during the 50s spurred her towards an even bolder ambition – to move to America.This aspiration motivated Kusama to begin her long-lasting correspondence with O’Keeffe, who combined encouragement with a dash of realism about working in the US – “It seems to me very odd that you are so ambitious to show your painting here, but I wish the best for you.” The advice did not cool Kusama’s ardour, and eventually, in November 1957, she boarded a plane to Seattle, moving after six months to New York.Although initially living in extreme poverty, Kusama quickly made contact with key artistic figures, from the reclusive Joseph Cornell, who stimulated her long-lasting interest in collage, to Andy Warhol. For someone so apparently ill-adjusted, she was in perfect accord with the zeitgeist of the 1960s. Her Accumulation sculptures – mundane, often domestic objects covered with stuffed cloth penises – fitted neatly into early exhibitions of pop art, as well as expressing the sexual neurosis she blamed on her repressive upbringing and her father’s philandering.View image in fullscreenYayoi Kusama creating a work from her My Eternal Soul series displayed in Cologne, Germany, 2026.Photograph: Sonja Blom/AlamyEven more brilliantly, later in the decade Kusama became a star of the hippy movement, choreographing a succession of naked happenings and parties, which appear in her art-house movie Kusama’s Self-obliteration (1967). She supported her “make love, not war” message with her own psychedelic fashion designs, including a “Party Dress” accommodating up to 25 people and a “Homo Dress” with a strategic cut-out section. She offered to sleep with the US president Richard Nixon if he ended the Vietnam war.And then, in 1973, she went home to Japan. She tried her hand at art dealing but, within four years, checked herself into the psychiatric facility in Tokyo where she would live for the rest of her life. Despite a period of relative obscurity, she reasserted herself through a succession of autobiographical novels, from Manhattan Suicide Addict (1978) to The Psychological Hospital of Ants (1994). Her art, particularly her earlier work, began to climb in value, eventually exceeding the level of $10m at auction.Spectacular sculptures of vegetal and floral forms, adorning public sites such as the railway station in Lille, were accompanied in the last two decades by optically dazzling paintings made in Kusama’s studio opposite her clinic. Constellations of eyes and her own profile populate numerous luridly coloured canvases, some of which appeared in 2012 at the Victoria Miro Gallery andTate Modernin London, and then in New York, Paris and Madrid.View image in fullscreenVisitors to Yayoi Kusama: Infinity Mirror Rooms at Tate Modern in 2021.Photograph: Guy Bell/Rex/ShutterstockThe show culminated in a characteristic installation, an Infinity Mirrord Room, repeating an effect that Kusama had first created in 1965. Here the visitor was able to experience the artist’s most potent metaphor for the endlessness of the cosmos, a universe in which the individual’s identity is perpetually obliterated.More recently, this work was revivedin 2021for an even more successful exhibition at Tate, which also contained a room consisting of infinitely reflected, rotating chandeliers. Entitled Chandelier of Grief, it displayed the existential aspects of Kusama’s art. In contrast, her simultaneous collaborations with Louis Vuitton combined an assortment of polka-dot garments and accessories with a waving Kusama robot in the shop window.In 2006, she was awarded the Japanese Praemium Imperiale for painting, and in 2017 aYayoi Kusama Museumopened in Tokyo.Yayoi Kusama, artist and writer, born 22 March 1929; died 14 August 2026Explore more on these topicsYayoi KusamaJapanTate ModernobituariesShareReuse this content

title: BBC to bring back Top Gear amid speculation about show’s next presenters | Top Gear | The Guardian
description: Motoring series to return four years after Andrew ‘Freddie’ Flintoff suffered serious injuries in crash during filming
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Motoring series to return four years after Andrew ‘Freddie’ Flintoff suffered serious injuries in crash during filming
Content: But will the Stig come back too? The BBC has refused to comment yet on who will host the show upon its return.Photograph: Ben A Pruchnie/GettyView image in fullscreenBut will the Stig come back too? The BBC has refused to comment yet on who will host the show upon its return.Photograph: Ben A Pruchnie/GettyTop GearBBC to bring back Top Gear amid speculation about show’s next presentersMotoring series to return four years after Andrew ‘Freddie’ Flintoff suffered serious injuries in crash during filmingCaroline DaviesThu 27 Aug 2026 10.32 EDTFirst published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 07.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTop Gear,the long-running motoring show that has been off air since its co-hostAndrew “Freddie” Flintoffwas seriously injured in a crash during filming almost four years ago, is to return to the BBC, the broadcaster has confirmed.AfterFlintoff’s accidentat Dunsfold aerodrome in Surrey, the BBC said the series would be “rested” for the foreseeable future.The BBC’s director of entertainment, Ed Havard, confirmed the news of its return at a panel event at the Edinburgh TV festival on Thursday. “There has been a lot of speculation about this and we can confirm thatTop Gearis coming back,” he said.Havard refused to be drawn on who would host the show amid reports that the comedian and presenter – and a known car enthusiast –Jimmy Carrwas in the frame. “I’m not going to talk about talent today,” he replied to questions. “Jimmy would be a great host but I won’t be discussing that today.“We will have more information on Top Gear shortly,” Havard added.Carr was a guest on Top Gear in 2004, and has said: “It’s one of the biggest shows in the world. It’s a global phenomenon.”The former England rugby player and Celebrity Traitors starJoe Marleris also reportedly being considered to host.View image in fullscreenThe former England rugby player Joe Marler’s name has been mooted as a possible presenter.Photograph: Ian West/PAThe model Jodie Kidd is another rumoured contender. Kidd has appeared on Top Gear in the past, and after qualifying for a racing licence, began racing in Italy. She has also hosted various automotive shows including Channel 5’s The Classic Car Show, Chubb Insurance’s classic car podcast, and her own YouTube channel, Kidd in a Sweet Shop.View image in fullscreenJodie Kidd taking part in a rally in Brescia, Italy, in 2014.Photograph: Olycom SPA/RexOthers who have featured in speculation include the celebrity chef Gordon Ramsay, who has appeared on Top Gear several times and owns an extensive collection of cars, and the actor Rowan Atkinson, another car enthusiast who appeared during series 17, where he set a lap time of 1min 42.2sec, making him the fastest celebrity on the leaderboard at the time.Top Gear began in 1977 and became one of the BBC’s biggest hits in the hands of Jeremy Clarkson, Richard Hammond and James May in the 2000s.Clarkson’s contract was not renewed at the end of the 22nd season, after he punched a producer.He later issued a formal apology. Clarkson’s co-hosts also left after his departure, with the trio then signing up for another motoring show, The Grand Tour, on Amazon Prime Video.They were replaced by the broadcaster Chris Evans and the Friends star Matt LeBlanc. Evans left after just six episodes. The show also received criticism after LeBlanc and a rally driverperformed “doughnuts” near the Cenotaph war memorialin London’s Whitehall.View image in fullscreenPaddy McGuinness, Chris Harris and Andrew ‘Freddie’ Flintoff.Photograph: Lee Brimble/PAFlintoff, Paddy McGuinness and Chris Harris took over in 2018.Flintoff was taken to hospital with facial and rib injuries when the Morgan Super 3 he was driving – an open-topped three-wheeled car – flipped upside down and skidded on the tarmac before coming to a stop. The BBC later reached a financial settlement with the England cricket captain, an agreementreportedly worth about £9m. He has revealed he wasdeeply affected by the crashand did not leave his house for six months other than to attend medical appointments.View image in fullscreenFlintoff has said he suffers from PTSD as a result of the Top Gear crash.Photograph: Gareth Copley/GettyIn the Disney+ documentary Flintoff, released last year, the presenter admitted that after the accident, he did not think he had it in him to “get through”. Flintoff said his then three-and-a-half-year-old son Preston “wouldn’t come near me”. “I think it frightened him, my face; it frightened me. That was heartbreaking,” he said in the documentary.“I’ve got PTSD [post-traumatic stress disorder] and I get anxious, for periods of time. I just find myself crying for no particular reason.”Flintoff also said he relived the crash every night when he went to bed and described the experience as a “vivid” movie.Explore more on these topicsTop GearBBCEdinburgh International Television FestivalJimmy CarrFactual TVTelevisionAndrew FlintoffnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bronze age treasure stolen in four-minute Spanish museum heist | Art theft | The Guardian
description: Gold collection known as Treasure of Villena, worth at least €1.7m, is target of ‘very well planned’ raid
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: Gold collection known as Treasure of Villena, worth at least €1.7m, is target of ‘very well planned’ raid
Content: The Treasure of Villena comprises 29 bracelets, 11 bowls, three bottles and other miscellaneous pieces dating back to 1000BC.Photograph: Museum of Villena/EPAView image in fullscreenThe Treasure of Villena comprises 29 bracelets, 11 bowls, three bottles and other miscellaneous pieces dating back to 1000BC.Photograph: Museum of Villena/EPAArt theftBronze age treasure stolen in four-minute Spanish museum heistGold collection known as Treasure of Villena, worth at least €1.7m, is target of ‘very well planned’ raidPhilip Oltermannand agenciesThu 27 Aug 2026 11.47 EDTFirst published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 07.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThieves in Spain have raided the Treasure of Villena – a stunning collection of bronze age gold artefacts that has been described as the most important prehistoric trove inEurope– in the latest high-profile smash-and-grab heist on the continent.The raid on Thursday morning of the 66 mostly gold objects in the Spanish town of Villena lasted just minutes, officials said.“The alarm at the Villena Museum went off around 5.20am [4.20am BST],” a spokesperson for the town council said, adding that the thieves had left the building by 5.24am. The operation was “super-fast and super-professional”, the spokesperson said.“They’ve taken most of the treasure,” the mayor of Villena, Fulgencio Cerdán, told journalists, his voice breaking.View image in fullscreenThe collection has been held in a specially designated room in the Museum of Villena since May 2024.Photograph: Pablo Miranzo/EPALocal media said the few items the thieves had left behind included three silver vessels, a bracelet and some of the ornamentation of the bastón del reyezuelo, the “Kingfisher staff”, a prehistoric ceremonial scepter.Cerdán said: “We are absolutely devastated, I’m even trembling. The truth is that for those of us from Villena, this destroys us. It’s part of our heritage, of our wealth.”The treasure, which was discovered in 1963 by the archaeologist José María Soler in a vessel sunk in a dried-out riverbed in Villena, included 29 bracelets, 11 bowls, three bottles and other miscellaneous pieces dating back to about 1000BC. It immediately became the main attraction of a small architectural museum in the province of Alicante.Since May 2024, the hoard has been on display in a specially designated room in the newly opened, municipally owned Villena Museum.The unusual material of some of the items has long intrigued researchers. Though mainly gold, some pieces are also made of silver, iron, amber and a dark leaden material covered in a ferrous-looking oxide. A recent study published in the journalTrabajos de Prehistoriaclaimed that these items were probably forged from rare meteoritic iron.While the treasure’s value is incalculable, the gold alone is worth about €1.7m (£1.45m), according to the mayor.The thieves arrived in several vehicles and apparently entered the museum through a window, according to the Spanish government’s deputy representative in Alicante, Manuel Pineda.“All security systems were activated,” according to the Villena spokesperson, who insisted there had been “no failure” by the museum.Shortly before the robbery, another alarm went off at the city’s sports centre, and authorities were now investigating whether that was a diversion created by the thieves, the spokesperson added.Mauro Hernández, a professor of archaeology at the University of Alicante and an expert on the treasure, told the broadcaster Cadena SER that the operation showed signs of prior planning. “They had it very well planned,” Hernández said. “They knew how to do it, how to act and how to escape.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGuns, axes, explosives: violent museum heists are on the rise, says EuropolRead moreLast October, thieves broke into the Louvre Museum in Paris in broad daylight,escaping in less than eight minuteswith jewellery worth €88m. There have since been a series of brazen raids in institutions across Europe.Four works “of extraordinary value” by the Renaissance artist Antonello da Messinawere stolenfrom a museum in Sicily, Italy’s culture ministry said last Sunday.Two days earlier, Italian police said they hadrecovered paintingsby Renoir, Cézanne and Matisse worth more than $10.4m which were stolen from the Magnani-Rocca Foundation Museum near Parma.In a report published at the start of the week, the EU’s police agency Europol said that member states had detected a recent shift “towards violent and forceful methods” that could point to the involvement of new criminal networks focused on specific cultural artefacts.“Some thieves apprehended in recent cases appear to coordinate their efforts on an ad hoc basis, often recruited locally through social media and instant communication channels, without prior connections to each other,” the report said. “This differs from the usual structure of criminal networks involved in cultural goods trafficking, which typically operate in a core group organised around a leader.”Agence France-Presse contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsArt theftMuseumsSpainOrganised crimeEuropeHeritagenewsShareReuse this content

title: Hot ticket: UK’s first sauna theatre draws swimwear-clad audiences | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The 80-seat venue at Edinburgh fringe combines sauna rituals with theatre, music, storytelling … and sweat
Author: Robyn Vinter
Headline: The 80-seat venue at Edinburgh fringe combines sauna rituals with theatre, music, storytelling … and sweat
Content: The Sauna theatre brings together aufguss, a type of sauna ritual, with traditional art forms such as theatre, literature, music and poetry.Photograph: Victoria Haydn/Therme ManchesterView image in fullscreenThe Sauna theatre brings together aufguss, a type of sauna ritual, with traditional art forms such as theatre, literature, music and poetry.Photograph: Victoria Haydn/Therme ManchesterEdinburgh festival 2026Hot ticket: UK’s first sauna theatre draws swimwear-clad audiencesThe 80-seat venue at Edinburgh fringe combines sauna rituals with theatre, music, storytelling … and sweatRobyn VinterThu 27 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 00.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTucked away behind the Summerhall arts centre is the hottest new venue at theEdinburghfringe … quite literally. The Sauna theatre has proved popular among theatregoers at the world’s largest performing arts festival, with shows inside its purpose-built, 80-seat sauna drawing sweaty, swimwear-clad crowds.Visitors may be forgiven for thinking the sauna is a gimmick, especially at the fringe where absurd, experimental and ludicrous performances are not uncommon. This year they include a mandrinking his own urine, someonesinging the same song over and over,physical feats of exertionand several fully naked shows.But the reality is more wholesome, especially regarding nudity, which is not allowed at the venue, co-founded by the theatre makers James Grieve and Lucy Osborne.View image in fullscreenTheatregoers are asked to bring swimwear when they book.Photograph: Victoria Haydn/Therme Manchester“We’ve done a lot of research over the last few years and art and culture in saunas proliferates the world over,” Grieve said. “There’s a great tradition of storytelling, of folk music, in saunas.“Then there’s this incredible art form, aufguss, which is a sauna master infusing ice and water with essential oils, placing the infusion on the sauna stove and circulating the fragrant steam with towel-waving choreography. That’s usually accompanied by music and also storytelling, costume, lighting, sound. It’s basically a show in a sauna.”Deborah Carr, the head of the sauna, who trains professional sauna masters when she’s not at the fringe, said: “In the UK, this is the first sauna theatre, but we see them around the world – from Japan to Germany to Italy, [where] there is a sauna theatre that holds 320 people.“I think this is just emerging in the UK and seeing this here for the first time is really exciting, because it then plants a seed and it starts us growing.”View image in fullscreenAufguss involves placing an infusion on a stove and circulating the fragrant steam through choreography.Photograph: Victoria Haydn/Therme ManchesterInside are three tiers of wooden seating surrounding three stoves, which can heat the air to 90C (194F), professional-quality stage lighting and a (only slightly cooler) sound booth.Shows have built-in breaks, though audience members can leave at any point – and the braver ones can enter the cold plunge. Showers, mirrors and hairdryers make it more feasible for visitors to go about their day afterwards.The shows vary from morning raves to storytelling, theatre and music events. Mysteries of the Picts, at noon every day, features aufguss from two sauna masters performed to traditional folk music. Actors tell the story of ancient sweat houses thought to have provided community spaces inScotlandfor Celtic tribes in the late Roman period.Grieve said a performance that had worked especially well was an adaptation of Virginia Woolf’s The Waves. “Virginia Woolf talks a lot about heat and light and water. The aufguss masters perform rituals to that text and really help people feel like they’re inside the language, like they are feeling and sensing the language on their skin, through their nose, as well as listening to the actors perform it.”View image in fullscreenShows at the theatre range from raves to music events and storytelling.Photograph: Victoria Haydn/Therme ManchesterThe theatre’s organisers said the challenges had been around etiquette, such as ensuring people sit on towels. They said some attenders had turned up assuming it would be a metaphorical sauna, despite emails reminding visitors to bring a bathing suit.Those who arrive without swimsuits can borrow them – an offer many have, somewhat gamely, taken up.Grieve and Osborne hope to bring the venue back next year, when audiences may have a better understanding of what they have booked.“This has been a really exciting month for us to experiment with what’s possible in the sauna space,” Grieve said. “What we want to do is try to find the kind of work that only works in a sauna or that works best in a sauna. There are plenty of hot rooms in Edinburgh where you can see theatre.”View image in fullscreenThe theatre has received an enthusiastic response from audiences.Photograph: Mihaela BodlovicThe response had been amazing, Grieve added. “I think one of the great joys is seeing people leave the space having had an experience that’s made them feel better physically, emotionally. And that was something we really wanted to capture and harness.“We really believe that art and culture is good for you physically and mentally and that combined with sauna, maybe it becomes kind of exponentially good for you.”Carr said: “We see these lovely rosy cheeks and beaming faces as they go out. And then when people have come back, they’ve said: ‘I just felt so amazing. Not only did I enjoy it, I felt great for the rest of the day.’”Explore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalFringe theatreTheatreEdinburghScotlandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Busy Philipps reveals brain tumour diagnosis: ‘I’m grateful to be alive’ | Television | The Guardian
description: Actor says she had the ‘weirdest six months of my life’, after being diagnosed days after her Dawson’s Creek co-star James Van Der Beek died of cancer
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Actor says she had the ‘weirdest six months of my life’, after being diagnosed days after her Dawson’s Creek co-star James Van Der Beek died of cancer
Content: Busy Philipps in December 2025. The actor has revealed she had a brain tumour removed in March.Photograph: John Nacion/Variety/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBusy Philipps in December 2025. The actor has revealed she had a brain tumour removed in March.Photograph: John Nacion/Variety/Getty ImagesTelevisionBusy Philipps reveals brain tumour diagnosis: ‘I’m grateful to be alive’Actor says she had the ‘weirdest six months of my life’, after being diagnosed days after her Dawson’s Creek co-star James Van Der Beek died of cancerPress AssociationWed 26 Aug 2026 21.09 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 00.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBusy Philipps has revealed she had a brain tumour removed, which was diagnosed shortly after her Dawson’s Creek co-star James Van Der Beek died from bowel cancer.The 47-year-old, born Elizabeth Philipps, starred in the hit US teen drama as Audrey Liddell opposite Van Der Beek, whodied in February aged 48after being diagnosed with bowel cancer.The actortold Peopleshe is “grateful” that she is alive following a period she described as the “weirdest six months of my life”.Busy Philipps: ‘I’ve been on three big TV shows but was broke by the age of 28’Read moreKnown for Freaks And Geeks, Girls5eva and Cougar Town, Philipps said she did not present any obvious symptoms of having a tumour, such as seizures, and was reassured by her doctor that she did not need to have a scan, but felt she needed one regardless.After consulting a second doctor months later, she went through with a whole-body MRI screening in February, which led to the discovery of the grade 2 oligodendroglioma, a rare low-grade (slow-growing) tumour.In March she underwent a five-hour surgery, and a 2.6cm mass was removed from her brain.Speaking to People, Philipps said: “I didn’t know why I wanted to get this scan except for the fact that I just did.“We are frequently told by doctors that there is nothing to worry about [when] you kind of know that there’s something to worry about. There’s nothing to be afraid of in having information. It’s only empowering.”Philipps said that over the past two years she would tell friends that her “brain feels broken” and assumed certain behaviours were caused by perimenopause.Her doctor could not confirm whether it was related to the tumour or not.She said: “I wasn’t consciously aware that anything was really wrong, but there was something that was misfiring. Like, I could not get a handle on it. [And now] my brain does not feel broken any more.”Philipps debated cancelling the scan with her ex-husband, film-maker Marc Silverstein, as it came days after the death of her friend and former co-star Van Der Beek and just before an audition for a role in the upcoming legal drama Cupertino.She recounted: “He’s like, ‘Maybe it’s the best thing you could do for your friend this morning. Go get that scan.’”When neurologist Dr Orrin Devinsky told her the news, Philipps said she was “hyperventilating and trying to breathe”.Two days after the surgery, she was back home recovering and said she “wasn’t in pain at all” with more than 40 surgical staples in her forehead.Among the friends and family wishing her a swift recovery was Dawson’s Creek co-star Michelle Williams, who she said arranged “delicious” food service for her.Philipps soon started her “dream job” playing Natalia Boutella in Cupertino, but not long into filming the series she learned she had contracted a staphylococcus infection in her incision and needed debridement surgery.Despite this she said she felt grateful everything was caught early, adding: “What am I? The luckiest girl in the world?”Explore more on these topicsTelevisionCancerHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Met Orchestra/Nézet-Séguin review – messy bonbons and a hero’s triumph in a classy all-Strauss lineup | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: Yannick Nézet-Séguin polished up the Rosenkavalier suite then gave a exceptional reading of the composer’s self-congratulatory tone poem, while Elza van den Heever delivered a visceral account of Salome’s final scene
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Yannick Nézet-Séguin polished up the Rosenkavalier suite then gave a exceptional reading of the composer’s self-congratulatory tone poem, while Elza van den Heever delivered a visceral account of Salome’s final scene
Content: A magisterial fury in fuchsia … soprano Elza van den Heever with the Met Orchestra conducted by Yannick Nézet-Séguin.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouView image in fullscreenA magisterial fury in fuchsia … soprano Elza van den Heever with the Met Orchestra conducted by Yannick Nézet-Séguin.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouProms 2026ReviewMet Orchestra/Nézet-Séguin review – messy bonbons and a hero’s triumph in a classy all-Strauss lineupRoyal Albert Hall, LondonYannick Nézet-Séguin polished up the Rosenkavalier suite then gave an exceptional reading of the composer’s self-congratulatory tone poem, while Elza van den Heever delivered a visceral account of Salome’s final sceneClive PagetThu 27 Aug 2026 06.42 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 06.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArtistically ambitious and with an ego the size of a small planet,Richard Strausswas rarely backwards in coming forwards. When quizzed about the wisdom of depicting his 34-year-old self in music he brushed the matter aside, declaring himself no less interesting than Napoleon. The work in question, the self-congratulatory yet brilliantly conceived tone poem Ein Heldenleben, formed the second half of this all-Strauss programme. Before that, the Met Orchestra, here making their Proms debut, stayed on home turf with music from the operas.The Rosenkavalier suite, compiled by hand unknown, is frankly a mess, lurching from one bonbon to the next with never a thought for musical logic (the overblown ending is truly crass). Yannick Nézet-Séguin did a decent job of papering over the cracks, letting the music unfold naturally rather than forcing its ham-fisted transitions. The love scenes were the highlight here, the orchestra spacious and shapely. If the heart didn’t leap as it might, it was likely due to the absence of the human voice.South African soprano Elza van den Heever righted the balance. A magisterial fury in fuchsia, she delivered a visceral account of the final scene from Salome, running the gamut from implacable vengeance to unhinged lust. The voice was refulgent, her diction impressive, even if Nézet-Séguin allowed the orchestra to overwhelm her here and there.Ein Heldenleben, 50 minutes of one man’s triumph over artistic adversity, is symphonic music on a grand scale and the kind of late-romantic meat-and-potatoes Nézet-Séguin cut his teeth on before he took the opera job in New York. This was an exceptional reading, expansive yet resolute and with a welcome determination to embrace the score’s more tender moments. Persnickety woodwind and a duo of baleful tubas conjured up the composer’s carping critics while Benjamin Bowman’s sinuous solo violin invoked the hero’s capricious companion. Martial offstage brass and a tour de force orchestral battle preceded a glowing account of the hero’s works of peace and a perfectly judged ending.The playful exchange surrounding Van den Heever’s memory lapse in an otherwise radiant account of Strauss’s Zueignung only added to the impression of an undeniably class act.Available onBBC Sounds until 12 October. The Promscontinue until 12 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsProms 2026PromsFestivalsClassical musicRoyal Albert HallRichard StraussreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Dalliance review – a rare drama so beautifully written you will be instantly devoted  | Television | The Guardian
description: Hugo Weaving stars in this wonderful Australian series about old friends in their 60s. It is a feast of hilarity and heartbreak – and there needs to be more TV like it
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: Hugo Weaving stars in this wonderful Australian series about old friends in their 60s. It is a feast of hilarity and heartbreak – and there needs to be more TV like it
Content: Irreverence and honesty … from left, Georgie Parker as Rose, Hugo Weaving as Billy and Heather Mitchell as Dani in Dalliance.Photograph: Lisa Tomasetti/Paramount+View image in fullscreenIrreverence and honesty … from left, Georgie Parker as Rose, Hugo Weaving as Billy and Heather Mitchell as Dani in Dalliance.Photograph: Lisa Tomasetti/Paramount+TelevisionReviewDalliance review – a rare drama so beautifully written you will be instantly devotedHugo Weaving stars in this wonderful Australian series about old friends in their 60s. It is a feast of hilarity and heartbreak – and there needs to be more TV like itLucy ManganThu 27 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 11.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith Dalliance, television continues its brave expeditions into unknown narrative lands. It was first forced to venture into women’s stories (using female writers, directors, stars and, oh my goodness, sometimes it was just wall-to-wall womanity, you know?) in the post-Weinstein years. Previously unassailable figures were toppling like ninepins and investors needed to take refuge in those unlikely to have problematic pasts who were likely to tank projects the moment any reporter turned a beady eye upon them.That turned out quite well. Women were not as boring as we had been led to believe, and were often capable of anchoring quite interesting, intelligent or funny shows. Sometimes they were all three at the same time, even if they weren’t called Fleabag.That got commissioners wondering if they could try the same trick with age rather than sex as the undiscovered country. New Tricks walked so that The Split, Last Tango in Halifax, Happy Valley, The Thursday Murder Club and Ride or Die might run.Now to this illustrious list we may add the wonderful Dalliance, an Australian six-parter beautifully written by Pip Karmel, Chris Lee, Liz Doran and Jock Serong, and directed with requisite subtlety by Emma Jackon and Matt Saville. It stars Hugo Weaving as bonhomous retired cameraman Billy who is the catalyst for the reunion of enough old friends – all in their 60s – to provide viewers with a feast of storylines, hilarious and heartbreaking by turns, and all suffused with the kind of irreverence and honesty that makes you instantly devoted to the whole endeavour.Dani (Heather Mitchell) first meets Billy when he needs to hide under one of the tables she is catering on a ferry at a sailing event in Sydney Harbour. The man pursuing him (“Dickhead!”) is, he explains later, his brother Gary (David Wenham). It’s about money and an inheritance and Gary’s history as a jailbird and addict. They’re all right really. “Chalk and cheese,” says Gary later. “If chalk hated cheese’s guts.”View image in fullscreenIn at the deep end … Carolyn Bock as Adele and Georgie Parker as Rose in Dalliance.Photograph: Lisa Tomasetti/Paramount+To thank Dani for her aid, Billy places a bet for her on the next boat race. His long-odds pick duly romps home and he takes her back to his place to meet his wife Rose (Georgie Parker) and raise a glass to their good fortune. Billy falls asleep almost immediately. The women continue to bond over wine. Dani asks Rose if she can “borrow” Billy to use as her plus-one at an forthcoming do that promises, for unspecified reasons, to be a nightmare for her to attend alone. Rose seeks to clarify: “No sex?” “God no,” replies Dani. Rose agrees and so does Billy – though it hardly matters – when he wakes up.Their evening together unfolds through easy, unforced flashbacks during the remainder of the episodes, and in the meantime we get to know the rest of the gang. The guys – Billy’s best friend Rex (Russell Dykstra) who is happily coupled up with thirtysomething Dylan (Ryan Panizza), playboy Mani (Kirk Torrance), fully domesticated Luke (Wayne Blair) – are teammates from his rugby league days. Sarah (Catherine McClements) and Adele (Carolyn Bock), the latter married to Luke for 34 years, both date from the same era – as does Rose – and they have the rude, easy banter and rhythms that only decades of shared history can produce. Soon, Mani and Sarah are enjoying more literally rhythmic delights together, once they have peered closely enough at her handbag lube to check the use-by date is OK. It’s 2018, but as Sarah notes, what is there in it that can go off?Dalliance is not about plot. There are no murders nor mysteries to be investigated or suspects to be harangued – except the gentle reveal of what happened during Dani and Billy’s evening out. It’s a mood piece and an array of portraits (some more finely drawn than others – Adele perhaps the most underserved) of characters who have actually lived some life, been formed by meaningful experiences and come out the other side – at a later stage than we are used to seeing on our screens. And they and we are only better off for it.It’s a bit hard to talk about specifics without giving away a pivotal event, which reviewers have been asked not to do, so forgive any woolliness that creeps in. Good and bad decisions (sometimes marital. Sometimes on dating apps. Occasionally about a comeback tour) are made. People upset each other and find their way back to each other (“Do it again and I’m going to cut your balls off”). Grief touches everyone and life goes on. Dalliance is about the benefits of older age – the harvest you get to reap only after putting years of yourself into your friendships, your relationships, your work, your children, your life. All the things that can’t be rushed, can’t be forced, can’t be faked. It’s good.Dalliance is on Paramount+Explore more on these topicsTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Fightland is 50 Cent’s big and bloody boxing drama  | Television | The Guardian
description: The rapper executive-produces this story about a champion boxer out for revenge. Plus: a dream wedding turns into a nightmare in Ludwig. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: The rapper executive-produces this story about a champion boxer out for revenge. Plus: a dream wedding turns into a nightmare in Ludwig. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Throwing punches … Howard Charles and Marcus Luther Fleming in the ring for Fightland on Sky Atlantic.Photograph: Christopher Raphael/Christopher Raphael/© 2025 Starz, LLCView image in fullscreenThrowing punches … Howard Charles and Marcus Luther Fleming in the ring for Fightland on Sky Atlantic.Photograph: Christopher Raphael/Christopher Raphael/© 2025 Starz, LLCTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Fightland is 50 Cent’s big and bloody boxing dramaThe rapper executive-produces this story about a champion boxer out for revenge. Plus: a dream wedding turns into a nightmare in Ludwig. Here’s what to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Priya Elan,Hollie RichardsonandJack SealeThu 27 Aug 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFightland9pm, Sky Atlantic“Boxing is a criminal enterprise,” says Nicholas Pinnock’s slick crime kingpin Kingsley Marshall. “Always has been, always will be.” It’s a highly debatable claim but typical of this big, bloody and somewhat basic drama executive-produced by Curtis “50 Cent” Jackson, which is set at the nexus of pugilism and gangsterism. It stars Howard Charles as “Duke Kilroy”, a champion boxer in search of revenge after the murder of his brother. About as subtle as a punch in the face.Phil HarrisonDragons’ Den8pm, BBC OneAnother day in the Den and more Dragons to impress. This week includes a nervous husband-and-wife team with their worryingly expensive water-saving device, a health food entrepreneur who hasn’t made that much profit but has already had a grant from Sainbury’s, and a street art impresario who has gone viral.Priya ElanThe Big Deal with Steph McGovern8pm, BBC TwoThe business journalist’s surprisingly brutal art dealership competition lands in sunny Margate this week, where the five remaining pairs need to sell limited-edition prints to the public. Gavin gets off to a strong start: “I don’t even know what a print is.”Hollie RichardsonA House Through Time9pm, BBC TwoView image in fullscreenDavid Olusoga steps back in time.Photograph: Richard Ranken/BBC/Twenty Twenty ProductionsEvents take a dark turn as the 20th century arrives at the home in Calton Hill, Edinburgh. David Olusoga shows how the residence manifests the economics of the era – it’s now multiple-occupancy, which means overcrowding and trouble. There’s also an insight into the dangers of working in a prison.PHLudwig9pm, BBC OneIt’s murder on the dancefloor, as a dreamy wedding takes a nightmarish turn. Leave it to master-puzzler John (David Mitchell) who is now working as a crime scene consultant. But the fact that every wedding guest saw the victim creates a problem: “That’s too many variables!”HRHit Point9pm, U& DaveHoward Overman’s unusual crime thriller is heating up nicely, as compromised cop Leo continues to pretend to investigate crimes in which he is involved. The consequent bittersweetness of the sparking chemistry between Leo and his partner Bella is cannily written.Jack SealeExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout audiobook review – brilliant portrait of an existential crisis | Books | The Guardian
description: A teacher’s private anxieties are subtly combined with political events in this Booker-listed tale set in coastal Massachusetts
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: A teacher’s private anxieties are subtly combined with political events in this Booker-listed tale set in coastal Massachusetts
Content: Dread and ennui … Elizabeth Strout.Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDread and ennui … Elizabeth Strout.Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty ImagesAudiobook of the weekBooksReviewThe Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout audiobook review – brilliant portrait of an existential crisisA teacher’s private anxieties are subtly combined with political events in this Booker-listed tale set in coastal MassachusettsFiona SturgesThu 27 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 10.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArtie Dam is a much-loved history teacher from coastal Massachusetts famed for his white socks and old sneakers and who sees a growing hopelessness in his young students. Not only are they dispirited by the state of the world, but they also believe they won’t be able to achieve their professional dreams. Their feelings of dread and ennui are shared by Artie who is aghast at the imminent re-election of a cruel and divisive leader (who remains nameless).Artie is also lonely in the company of his wife, Evie, a therapist who comes from a wealthy family and is dismissive of her “soft” spouse. Artie realises he doesn’t truly know Evie, and she doesn’t care to know him. He traces their loss of connection to their son Rob’s car accident a decade ago in which Rob survived but his girlfriend Heather was killed. Such is Artie’s desolation that he contemplates suicide, if only he can find a way of doing it discreetly. But something happens while he is sailing in his boat that changes his mind. Later, a revelation from his son further shifts his perspective on his relationships.The Things We Never Say is the latest book from Elizabeth Strout which has been longlisted for this year’s Booker prize and which subtly binds together political events and private anxiety to portray a decent man in existential crisis. The reader is the actor Robert Petkoff who conveys Artie’s innate kindness and quiet despair. With that despair comes a realisation that “every single person [holds] within themselves a vast, unknowable universe”.Available via Penguin Audio, 6hr 35minFurther listeningLady Gregory’s ToothbrushColm Tóibín, Picador, 3hr 3minDerbhle Crotty reads the Brooklyn author’s 2003 essay on Augusta Gregory, the Irish playwright and folk historian who famously observed how ownership of a toothbrush separated the gentry from the peasant classes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories.
