title: Kolkhoz by Emmanuel Carrère review – intricate portrait of an elite French family | Autobiography and memoir | The Guardian
description: The author of The Adversary and Yoga unearths a history that includes the Nazis, Russia, and the Académie Française
Author: Blake Morrison
Headline: The author of The Adversary and Yoga unearths a history that includes the Nazis, Russia, and the Académie Française
Content: Hélène Carrère d’Encausse in 1983.Photograph: Micheline PELLETIER/Gamma-Rapho/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHélène Carrère d’Encausse in 1983.Photograph: Micheline PELLETIER/Gamma-Rapho/Getty ImagesBook of the dayAutobiography and memoirReviewKolkhoz by Emmanuel Carrère review – intricate portrait of an elite French familyThe author of The Adversary and Yoga unearths a history that includes the Nazis, Russia, and the Académie FrançaiseBlake MorrisonThu 27 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 09.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Emmanuel Carrère’s mother, Hélène, died in 2023, at the age of 94, President Macron spoke at her memorial. She had been “perpetual secretary” of the Académie Française, in effect its head, and 200 people gathered at Les Invalides in Paris to pay tribute. Emmanuel’s father, Louis, was there too, in a wheelchair, only half aware of what was going on. This 400-page memoir, translated into English by John Lambert, is a homage to both parents and the unlikely history that brought them together. It’s also an act of reparation towards Hélène, whom Emmanuel worshipped as a child but upset as an adult by publishing a book that she’d forbidden him to write.Hélène grew up in stateless poverty in Paris, the daughter of Georges Zourabichvili, whose parents had fled Georgia in 1921, and Nathalie von Pelken, who as a child had six governesses, one for each day excluding Sunday. Though “the magical world of the fallen Russian aristocracy” was the backdrop, conditions were tough, not least after Georges disappeared in 1944, murdered by partisans for alleged Nazi collaboration. Hélène was 15 at the time and unsuccessfully tried to hide the truth about George’s death from her younger brother, Nicolas.double quotation markCarrère’s mother wouldn’t have slept well if she’d known this book was comingShe was determined and highly ambitious. What she couldn’t excel at, she didn’t do. For a time she considered an acting career but found her metier as a Russian historian. It helped that she was charming and attractive, so much so that an Afghan pilot, on a flight from Tashkent to Paris via Tehran, first invited her to the cockpit, then landed the plane in Kabul in order to kidnap her. He kept her there for four days before a couple of US aid workers sneaked her away on a private plane.By then she was married to Louis, who worked for an insurance company and was often away on business trips. At home Hélène ruled the roost and let Emmanuel and his two sisters sleep around her bed, a setup she called “kolkhoz”, the name for collective farms in the USSR. There was no television or radio; the children were made to read. Her son’s reading was strenuous: from Jules Verne and Alexander Dumas, he moved on to Dostoevsky at 13. His mother brought out his softer side – whenever she went away he’d write long letters saying how “horribly” he missed her.He felt abandoned when she began receiving phone calls from a “Mr N” and had long furtive conversations with him. No less distraught, her husband threatened to kill himself. Hélène ended the affair to spare Louis but he “lost her love for ever” and moved from the marriage bed to a tiny room. Worse, she more or less stopped speaking to him, a habit that lasted to the end. When diagnosed with cancer and admitted to a palliative care home, she merely told him she’d be away at a conference.The mother-son relationship remained close until Emmanuel published A Russian Novel, which explored the story of her father, Georges, which she had asked him not to tell (“It’s my story, not yours. Leave him where he is”). Publication was “a family cataclysm”; she blamed her brother Nicolas for helping with it. Though she did eventually forgive Emmanuel, her loyalty to Russia divided them. A week before the invasion of Ukraine she described Putin as “a rational man”, committed to good relations with Europe. Dismayed, Emmanuel visited Georgia, where his cousin Salome Zourabichvili had become president. A trip to Ukraine followed. He remains violently opposed to Putin.What’s attractive about the book is its intimacy. If Hélène is a grand dame, her son enjoys the role of bon vivant, disclosing his drinking bouts, journalistic forays, failed relationships and blissful third marriage as well as his bipolar disorder. He’d like to write with “filial piety” and both his father’s genealogical research and his uncle Nicolas’s memoirs help him fill out the family story. But he also lets us in on his uncertainties as he proceeds: “what I’m hoping for is the unhoped for. We’ll see.”His mother loved order and completeness. And at her memorial Macron praised her for finishing the latest Académie dictionary – a 40-year task – with the wordzygomatique(an anatomical term). In reality, as she frustratedly told her son, they’d only reached zoo, with 62 more words to come, the last of them zz, onomatopoeia for sleep. She wouldn’t have slept well if she’d known this book was coming, but it’s an epic achievement and an honest, heartfelt account.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: Marketing meltdown: why has Andrew Garfield’s new film suddenly added Robin Hood? | Andrew Garfield | The Guardian
description: Paul Greengrass drama The Uprising was supposed to be a historical epic about the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381 – but a strange new campaign has inserted a surprising figure
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: Paul Greengrass drama The Uprising was supposed to be a historical epic about the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381 – but a strange new campaign has inserted a surprising figure
Content: Andrew Garfield in The Uprising.Photograph: Entertainment Pictures/AlamyView image in fullscreenAndrew Garfield in The Uprising.Photograph: Entertainment Pictures/AlamyAndrew GarfieldMarketing meltdown: why has Andrew Garfield’s new film suddenly added Robin Hood?Paul Greengrass drama The Uprising was supposed to be a historical epic about the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381 – but a strange new campaign has inserted a surprising figureStuart HeritageThu 27 Aug 2026 09.58 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 14.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNobody likes to have the full plot of a movie spoiled before they’ve even seen it. However, sometimes this can be taken to the extreme. Take the newPaul Greengrassmovie, The Uprising, for example. It is two weeks away from its US release and not only does nobody know the plot, but nobody seems to know what it is even about. Seriously, nobody at all. The film’s distributors just spent yesterday squabbling in public about whether Robin Hood was in it or not.Here’s what we know so far. Initially, all the trailers and promotional materials made The Uprising look like a film about the Peasants’ Revolt that tore through England in 1381. And this was very exciting, since the revolt was a thrilling moment in history that has been bizarrely underserved by Hollywood over the years. Most exciting of all, though, it sounded like it fit exactly into Greengrass’s wheelhouse: full of action and realism and political awareness.Hollywood encore: how ‘pro-shot’ Broadway shows became a major draw on the big screenRead moreBut that all changed this week, when the film’s US distributor, Focus Features,announcedthe film’sfull title on social media. What had once simply been The Uprising was now The Uprising: The Rise of Robin Hood. It added a new synopsis, reading: “Set against the true events of the Uprising that helped inspire the legend of Robin Hood, [Andrew Garfield’s character] forms an army of the people to face the King’s might in a fight for justice.”Needless to say, this was both confusing and frustrating. Frustrating because it sounded like a historically grounded and socially relevant film would now contain a character best known for once being played by a cartoon fox, and confusing because the stories of Robin Hood were set during the reign of Richard the Lionheart, who died nearly two centuries before the Peasants’ Revolt took place.Andrew Garfield’s character seemed to be at the centre of the mix-up. Officially credited as “The Ploughman”, we can assume that he has been named after William Langland’s poem Piers Plowman, which was written in the years leading up to the revolt. The poem is known for containing the first unambiguous literary reference to Robin Hood. It is also worth pointing out that, in 2022 when the film was firstannounced, The Uprising was set to be called The Hood.Realistically, several things might have happened here. The first is that Greengrass took a deeply uncharacteristic swing while making this film, and decided to augment the story of Wat Tyler with a time-traveling Robin Hood, blazing into the future to help the downtrodden people of England in their hour of need. The second is that he’s suggesting the Peasants’ Revolt helped reshape a mythical figure into a symbol of working-class resistance, at which point the distributors figured, “Screw it, let’s just tell everyone that Robin Hood is in it.”The Death of Robin Hood review – Hugh Jackman darkens a heroic tale in grim dramaRead moreThis backfired immediately. Not only because people were exasperated by the thought of yet another Robin Hood movie – not for nothing did this year’s A24 movieThe Death of Robin Hoodflop hard, recouping less than half of its production budget worldwide – but because the film’s UK distributor is adamant that the film has absolutely nothing to do with the guy at all.Contacted byMetroyesterday, Entertainment Film Distributors issued a statement reading: “The Uprising is a historical epic about the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381, not Robin Hood. The UK marketing campaign does not make any reference to Robin Hood. Marketing materials posted by other countries that may appear in the UK online and on social media referencing Robin Hood are not issued or approved by us.”Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onplatform.x.com. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueWhat we’re left with is a film that urgently needs to define exactly what it is before it comes out. As things stand, somebody is almost certainly going to feel conned.If the UK distributor is right, there will be those who hear this week’s new title, rush to the cinema in the hope of watching a Robin Hood film and leave disappointed because they were actually presented with a muddy meditation on class warfare based on a 700-year-old allegorical poem.But if the US distributor is right, then there will be those who rush to the cinema to watch a historically rigorous reenactment of one of the most important moments in British history and leave disappointed because Garfield turns up in a DeLorean halfway through, winks directly at the camera and then gets off with a busty maiden.The Uprising might be one of those things. It might be both. For all anyone knows, given the utter ineptitude of its own communications, it could even turn out to be Cloverfield 4 and climax with a scene where the peasants, the aristocrats, Robin Hood, King Arthur and Paddington Bear all team up to defeat a howling kaiju. At this point, who would even care?Explore more on these topicsAndrew GarfieldPaul GreengrassAction and adventure filmsDrama filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Idiots review – throwback bro comedy is an entertaining summer seat-filler | Movies | The Guardian
description: Dave Franco and O’Shea Jackson Jr lead a goofy roadtrip comedy that is just sharp enough to keep you strapped in
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: Dave Franco and O’Shea Jackson Jr lead a goofy roadtrip comedy that is just sharp enough to keep you strapped in
Content: O'Shea Jackson Jr and Dave Franco in Idiots.Photograph: Courtesy of IFCView image in fullscreenO'Shea Jackson Jr and Dave Franco in Idiots.Photograph: Courtesy of IFCMoviesReviewIdiots review – throwback bro comedy is an entertaining summer seat-fillerDave Franco and O’Shea Jackson Jr lead a goofy roadtrip comedy that is just sharp enough to keep you strapped inOwen MyersThu 27 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 13.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIdiots is billed as a return to the raunchy bro comedies of the 2000s like Pineapple Express and The Hangover and about halfway through there is a visual gag involving bodily functions that is so revolting, so unexpected and so genius that it comes close to them. For a moment, I was transported back to the mix of delight and disgust I felt upon watching a 90s Farrelly Brothers movie when I was far too young:How is this allowed?The Dog Stars review – Ridley Scott’s lethargic postapocalyptic drama is a misfireRead moreDescribed as an “earnest-dipshits-on-the-road screwball comedy” by director Macon Blair (I Don’t Feel at Home in This World Anymore, The Toxic Avenger), this R-rated indie comedy can’t entirely deliver on that enticingly deranged promise, but it has enough testosterone-fueled transgression to make its runtime breeze by. Dave Franco plays Mark, a doofus with a neck tattoo who expresses affection for his fellow man by slapping them on the jowls. When he is invited to vacate his job at a call center – which he has been coasting through by playing gory video games and sneaking shots of whiskey at his desk – he teams up with Davis (O’Shea Jackson Jr) for a dodgy under-the-table job involving transporting wayward teens to rehab. Their first charge is Sheridan (Mason Thames), a moody influencer who has made a name for himself by playing cruel stunts on members of the public like an off-brand Jake Paul. Like Harold & Kumar before it, the road trip is an obvious but effective ruse for Idiots’s freeform, THC-addled approach to storytelling which finds the trio jumping from country diner to crummy motel to a Slavic granny’s living room as Sheridan attempts to derail his passage to rehab.The film has been over a decade in development but it’s hard to resist the leads’ natural-feeling, infectious chemistry. That’s perhaps due to the fact that they have worked together before in various configurations: Jackson and Franco in the short-lived Quibi TV show The Now; Franco and Thames in 2025 weepie Regretting You. Jackson is particularly memorable as a version of the kind of softhearted hustler he played inIngrid Goes West, and Kiernan Shipka steals most of her scenes as a badass eastern European stripper who teams up with the gang after they partake of her … services. I am of course referring to a lapdance set to a heavy metal soundtrack where Shipka stares at Franco like she is burning a hole into his soul.The cast’s strength lets Macon’s film get away with some winning stupidity, such as when Davis is reprimanded by his pastor, played by Killer Mike, for taking a church group of kids to see a movie with full frontal shots of “dongs”. (The film turns out to be Lars Von Trier’sAntichrist.) Sheridan has some great lines that parody the broken-brained slang of lookmaxxing forums: the character is essentially a Clavicular proxy, sneering “you are beta cuck trash” at one adversary. There’s space for a little more insight about the psychology of internet clout-chasing than Idiots provides: it has far less to say on this than dark comedies like Quentin Dupieux’sThe Piano Accident, or indeed Ingrid Goes West. All the same, it is satisfying to see Sheridan face the consequences of his chosen path to fame as the film turns into an all-out brawl thanks to a run-in with a crustpunk gang led by Peter Dinklage as Karl “Koko” Sandoz and Nicholas Braun playing a wannabe rapper with a face tattoo and gold grills.As the stakes intensify, the film grows increasingly muddled, and Idiots begins to feel like it is going round in circles. I am sure that director Blair didn’t intend a micro distributor like IFC to pick this up – surely it was picturing a wider release comparable to Franco’s Neighbors given its relatively big-name actors, puerile humor (complimentary) and the fact that it changed its original title of Shitheads to something more commercially viable – though it should be said, far less memorable. There isn’t much space for laughs at the end as the film struggles to tie up its loose ends. You don’t remember the classic bro comedies for the “I love you man” bear hugs, you remember them for their zany set pieces and whipsmart dialogue set to become immortalized as broski memes for evermore.Idiots is out in the US on 28 August and in the UK on 2 October with an Australian release to be announcedExplore more on these topicsFilmComedy filmsPeter DinklageComedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Colony review – zombies return to the mall with a fresh and frenzied range of scares | Horror films | The Guardian
description: This time the ranks of the undead have acquired a hive mind, making them even more formidable adversaries. Can a maverick academic save the day?
Author: Laurence Phelan
Headline: This time the ranks of the undead have acquired a hive mind, making them even more formidable adversaries. Can a maverick academic save the day?
Content: Unhappy shopper … Jun Ji-hyun in Colony.Photograph: Everett/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenUnhappy shopper … Jun Ji-hyun in Colony.Photograph: Everett/ShutterstockHorror filmsReviewColony review – zombies return to the mall with a fresh and frenzied range of scaresThis time the ranks of the undead have acquired a hive mind, making them even more formidable adversaries. Can a maverick academic save the day?Laurence PhelanThu 27 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 11.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is another frenzied K-zombie action-horror from Yeon Sang-ho,the director ofTrain to BusanandPeninsula. Colony is frontloaded with 10 minutes of sciencey exposition and setup during which a biotech CEO mentions maze-solving slime mould and the pioneering work of the entomologist William Wheeler onthe hive mindsof ant colonies. Then the CEO is injected with a disgruntled former employee’s bright green liquid tech – it always needs to be bright green in such circumstances – and becomes the first victim of a bio-terror attack that traps a small cross-section of South Korean society in a tower block with hordes of fast-moving rabid flesh-munchers. An hour and three quarters of goopy, bloody mayhem ensue.An upscale shopping mall occupies the lower floors of the tower, and it takes some nerve to give your zombie film much the same setting as Dawn of the Dead, the masterwork of the godfather of the genreGeorge A Romero. Thankfully Colony can boast an innovation: these zombies have a hive mind, an emergent collective intelligence that makes them more formidable adversaries than your average braindead stumbler. The moment that one of the infected notices you and screams, as in Invasion of the Bodysnatchers, they all turn and attack.And as they do, spasmodically jerking in unison, all angular limbs and unnatural angles, or while they writhe and entwine as they pile upon and devour their latest victim, the importance of movement choreographer Jeon Young is clearer than ever. A collaborator on each of Sang-ho’s zombie films, but this time working with a company of South Korea’s top contemporary dancers, Young makes many of the action and gore scenes resemble something you might see on stage at Sadler’s Wells. Michael Jackson’s Thriller video might have done it first but Colony does it better, more scarily and on an epic scale.As in every zombie movie, the non-infected must collaborate to have any chance of survival. Thankfully a couple of them were attendees of the biotech conference at the start of the film, so Professor Se-jeong (Jun Ji-hyun) becomes the de facto leader of the group and may just be able to outsmart even these massed ranks of collectively non-stupid zombies. She isn’t set up as the most likable character: honest to a fault, possibly somewhere on the spectrum and without much time for social niceties. But then conformism, bureaucratic groupthink and mindless techno-consumerism are the villains here; the heroes are the outcasts and free-thinkers.Colony is in UK and Irish cinemas from 28 AugustExplore more on these topicsHorror filmsSouth KoreaZombiesAction and adventure filmsScience fiction and fantasy filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: A Slow Fire review – hope flickers in Simon Stephens’ postapocalyptic bunker drama | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Two men shelter from catastrophe in this Beckettian tale of memory, companionship and survival, which is intelligently performed but light on tension
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Two men shelter from catastrophe in this Beckettian tale of memory, companionship and survival, which is intelligently performed but light on tension
Content: Hope in the dark … Ross Gaynor (left) and Ian Toner in A Slow Fire at Jermyn Street theatre, London.Photograph: Alex BrennerView image in fullscreenHope in the dark … Ross Gaynor (left) and Ian Toner in A Slow Fire at Jermyn Street theatre, London.Photograph: Alex BrennerTheatreReviewA Slow Fire review – hope flickers in Simon Stephens’ postapocalyptic bunker dramaJermyn Street theatre, LondonTwo men shelter from catastrophe in this Beckettian tale of memory, companionship and survival, which is intelligently performed but light on tensionArifa AkbarThu 27 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 06.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJermyn Street’s basement theatre provides the perfect space for Simon Stephens’ postapocalyptic play about two men hiding in a bunker after an unnamed global catastrophe. Several of Beckett’s plays have been performed on this stage in recent years and these characters are distinctly Beckettian. Ashton (Ross Gaynor) and Reece (Ian Toner) may be the last men on Earth; they spend their time rehearsing the same stories, sometimes singing and, ultimately, waiting. But for what?The difference between Beckett’s men and Stephens’ is the emphasis of hope over despair, although the two converge at times. Ashton and Reece play memory games, it seems, enacting scenes from their former lives. These are filled with optimism and promise: a declaration of love, a moment between father and son, the announcement of a pregnancy. One man is a porter, the other a professor. In ordinary life, they might have little in common but here they become receptacles for each other’s most precious memories.There is no sight of the post-diluvial landscape. Instead, there is a mattress, a camping stove and a record player, the high winds and ominous churn of machinery suggesting the threats above ground (great sound design). Occasional reports come from the outside: they worry about the theft of a nearby track. Does it mean they are literally coming to the end of the road?View image in fullscreenEnd of the road … Ian Toner in A Slow Fire at Jermyn Street theatre, London.Photograph: Alex BrennerThe production, which premiered at Glass Mask theatre in Dublin earlier this year and is again directed by Rex Ryan,is in no rush to reveal its world and the games played within it, making you work to imagine your own apocalypse outside.There are some arresting moments and both actors give strong performances. Sometimes, their role-play turns desolate; at others, they tenderly savour a past memory with gentle humour (that occasionally lacks bite). A third man, Presley (Fionn Ó Loingsigh), and a surprise character, Mary (Holly Demaine), enter this space, the latter bringing a powerful monologue full of shock and horror at what has happened outside, spoken almost in a single breath.Ultimately, these interlopers bring real (as opposed to re-enacted) hope alongside a sense of threat as Presley arrives with a gun. But their intrigues do not contain enough of a story arc or offer sufficient dramatic tension. Too many meaningful silences slow the pace and get in the way of building momentum. Sometimes, messages are spelled out (“humans never heed warnings”, says one character, reflecting on natural disasters, climate catastrophe and human-made destruction). But there are reflective and lyrical moments too and a strongly resonant overarching idea, with intelligence in both the performances and the script.AtJermyn Street theatre, London, until 26 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreSimon StephensJermyn Street TheatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Song & Dance album review – Jacques Forestier’s impressive debut has persuasive rhythmic poise | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The Canadian violinist’s album definitely does what it says on the tin: from Bartók to Ernst, there is a quiet and beguiling eloquence to his playing
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: The Canadian violinist’s album definitely does what it says on the tin: from Bartók to Ernst, there is a quiet and beguiling eloquence to his playing
Content: Promising … Jacques Forestier.Photograph: Ryan ParkerView image in fullscreenPromising … Jacques Forestier.Photograph: Ryan ParkerClassical musicReviewSong & Dance album review – Jacques Forestier’s impressive debut has persuasive rhythmic poiseJacques Forestier/Boris Kusnezow(Warner Classics)The Canadian violinist’s album definitely does what it says on the tin: from Bartók to Ernst, there is a quiet and beguiling eloquence to his playingErica JealThu 27 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 11.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePerhaps the most promising thing about this impressive debut album fromJacques Forestier, the young Canadian violinist who tied in first place at the 2024 Joseph Joachim Competition, is the way it lives up to its title.View image in fullscreenJacques Forestier and Boris Kusnezow: Song & Dance album cover.Photograph: Warner ClassicsThere’s a swing to the way he and the pianistBoris Kusnezowplay Bartók’s six Romanian Folk Dances that extends even into the quiet movements, which sound distant and beguiling. Wieniawski’s Polonaise de Concert comes across as a dance rather than just a flashy showpiece. Bach’s D minor Sarabande is framed by movements from Ysaÿe’s solo Sonatas. All have persuasive rhythmic poise.As for the songs, he shapes long-breathed lines in three numbers from Gershwin’s Porgy and Bess – arranged by Jascha Heifetz, seemingly less as showpieces, more because Heifetz wished he were able to sing them himself. Brahms reused his own song melodies in his Sonata No 1; there’s the occasional corner that is arbitrarily turned as played by Forestier, but otherwise it’s a quietly eloquent, lyrical performance. Perhaps the most impressive track is for Forestier alone: Heinrich Ernst’s Grand Caprice, basically an arrangement of Schubert’s song Erlkönig. Forestier, keeping the interweaving threads untangled and the pace urgent, voices its drama beautifully.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com. title: Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy review – picture-postcard retelling of haunting Minoan myth | Games | The Guardian
description: The medieval franchise is transplanted to Crete, conjuring action-adventure magic from familiar ingredients
Author: Lewis Gordon
Headline: The medieval franchise is transplanted to Crete, conjuring action-adventure magic from familiar ingredients
Content: A swashbuckling hero … Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy.Illustration: Asobo StudioView image in fullscreenA swashbuckling hero … Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy.Illustration: Asobo StudioGamesReviewResonance: A Plague Tale Legacy review – picture-postcard retelling of haunting Minoan mythPlayStation 5, Xbox Series S/X, PC; Asobo StudioThe medieval franchise is transplanted to Crete, conjuring action-adventure magic from familiar ingredientsLewis GordonThu 27 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 12.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe path in Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy is a familiar one. Amid ancient ruins and sun-dappled gorges, a young woman, Sophia, dutifully treads the same footsteps as a Minoan warrior from millennia ago, one with whom she seems to share a visionary connection. The “resonance” between these two characters is made clear by their echoing actions – a crank pushed in the bronze age that still works in the medieval present, for example. Through these spliced timelines, it becomes clear that Sophia, compelled by her supernatural gift, possesses little agency. Destiny beckons her forwards.This is a smart meta concept for a game that, at its most basic level, boils down to keeping your left thumb planted firmly on the analogue stick, always pushing Sophia onwards in linear fashion. You jostle her through ornate corridors rendered as higgledy-piggledy pirate camps and cobbled Venetian streets. For the greater part of the game, you propel her through the Minoan remains of Crete, which harbour a dark and terrible secret. It is classic third-person action-adventure fare, building on the template laid down by the likes ofTomb Raiderand then refined and complicated by titles such asThe Last of Us. Little, from an interactive perspective, surprises: you dash, vault and swing between teetering podiums, squeeze through tiny gaps in rock and crouch behind conveniently placed walls to avoid enemies.View image in fullscreenImmersed in the bronze age … Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy.Illustration: Asobo StudioYet the Bordeaux-based studio Asobo conjures magic from the familiar. Sophia, a supporting character from the second game in the A Plague Tale series, carries this swashbuckling adventure with aplomb. She is spiky and confident, the daughter of a wealthy mother and a smuggler father. The game starts with her as a young child, recently escaped from abuse in a nunnery, before cutting to roughly a decade in the future. Now in her 20s, Sophia is a capable, cut-throat fighter, on the hunt for the treasure that lurks deep inside the extensive cave network of Crete – the home, according to Greek mythology, of the bull-headed Minotaur.In tone, Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy is a long way off the dour machismo ofChristopher Nolan’s recent Odyssey adaptation. Rather than brooding, greyscale landscapes, Asobo delivers a Crete that, at least initially, seems lifted directly from holiday brochures: soft sandstone cliffs, swallows dancing in the evening light, vivid green vegetation tangling around crumbling statues. Some of the most striking sights arrive via the Minoan frescoes: their deep oranges and eye-popping yellows have not faded but remain ebulliently bright.View image in fullscreenWorthy of a holiday brochure … Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy.Illustration: Asobo StudioIt is always a treat when the game pivots to this classical time period, briefly putting us in control of the warrior and letting us soak up the vibrant atmosphere through their eyes: crowds baying for blood; stands draped in textile finery; magenta-coloured flowers strewn across mosaic floors.A Plague Tale: Requiem review – rat-infested sequel raises stakes and spectacleRead moreBut, slowly, the world and story darken, though Asobo’s fascination with light – a means of warding off hordes of rats in prior A Plague Tale games – remains. Sophia carries a sphere that can reflect and refract light, crucial for solving environmental puzzles that often involve rotating supersized lenses to redirect beams. But these puzzles, like the platforming, are somewhat rudimentary, causing you to only briefly pause and ponder without ever yielding oh-so-satisfying “aha” moments. Rarely is there more than one solution or the opportunity to get creative: rather, you must follow the logic clearly signposted by the designers.Although stealth is sometimes an option, often our champion must engage in hand-to-hand combat. The most memorable fights occur towards the game’s conclusion, in which swirling light causes calcified, zombie-like figures to disintegrate into dust, Sophia teeing up their demise with lethal slashes of her sword. These are some of the most dynamic melee encounters in the game’s roughly 12-hour run time: a balletic, show-stopping dance of light and movement.Sophia may traipse a path similar to that of countless treasure-hunting, action-adventure video game classics – but for all the overfamiliar design choices, there is enough verve in the beguiling presentation and lively, compellingly drawn characters to elevate this beyond mere retread. Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy succeeds, in large part, because of Sophia, a heroine who confronts history head on, before finally breaking free of it in apocalyptically spectacular style.Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy is released 27 AugustExplore more on these topicsGamesPCXbox series S/XAction gamesAdventure gamesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Architourism in France: the retro futurist seaside town near Montpellier that’s out of this world | France holidays | The Guardian
description: With buildings inspired by Mayan pyramids and featuring ‘intergalactic curves’, La Grande-Motte is a great alternative beach resort for fans of modern architecture
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: With buildings inspired by Mayan pyramids and featuring ‘intergalactic curves’, La Grande-Motte is a great alternative beach resort for fans of modern architecture
Content: The sport harbour in the futuristic seaside town of La Grande-Motte.Photograph: Michael Runkel/Robert Harding/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe sport harbour in the futuristic seaside town of La Grande-Motte.Photograph: Michael Runkel/Robert Harding/Getty ImagesFrance holidaysArchitourism in France: the retro futurist seaside town near Montpellier that’s out of this worldBuilt in the 60s and 70s to curb a holiday exodus to Spain, with apartments inspired by Mayan pyramids and featuring ‘intergalactic curves’, La Grande-Motte is having another moment in the sun with fans of modern architectureMark C O’FlahertyThu 27 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 02.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy dream holiday is a trip back in time. Not to see the results of seismic Pompeii or 15th-century Machu Picchu – although I love both – but somewhere created specifically between the mid 1950s and 1970s, when cities were getting weird. I love postwar architourism, exploring urban planning at its most frenzied and optimistic. I have relished trips to Niemeyer’s Brasília and Le Corbusier’s Chandigarh in India, where the monumental and visionary modernist architecture and interiors are at odds with the minimal population. So La Grande-Motte, the retro futurist folly of a resort town on the southern coast of France, a 30-minute drive from Montpellier, had long been on my “must visit” list.The tourist board of this Occitanie seaside town likes to flag up some superficial parallels between it and the aforementioned cities, but this isn’t a high-concept capital city or administrative hub. It was built in the late 1960s and early 1970s purely to persuade the French to stop going south to the Costa Brava in Spain. As part of an initiative by the French government, a stretch of windswept mosquito-infested coast between Montpellier and Perpignan, including Gruissan and Port Leucate, was reimagined as an alternative to the Côte d’Azur with several new-build beach towns. La Grande-Motte would be the weirdest project. It was made for fun. It’s also well positioned to visit the nearby salt marshes and 13th-century walled-in town of Aigues-Mortes, for when you want to feel as if you’ve ticked a few more holiday boxes.The mastermind behind the town’s architecture, Jean Balladur, took inspiration from temples and Mesoamerican pyramids from the first century, imagining what the 21st century would look like in the 1970s. Why shouldn’t modernist apartments be arranged in the shape of a Maya pyramid, or an intergalactic curve? I rented a tiny studio with my husband in the Incas building for part of my trip, and while there was nothing in the way of high design about the interior, being on that terrace immersed us in a timewarp.View image in fullscreenShops and apartments facing the main port.Photograph: Mark C O’FlahertyWalking around Point Zéro (named for being the site of the earliest construction), home to La Grande-Motte’s main beach, all looks fairly standard: families playing on the sand, couples drinking cocktails outside cafes. The beach gained a Blue Flag award for environmental management and water quality in 2025. But the place is unique: the ferris wheel is solar powered and the buildings suggest you’re on another planet entirely – there are no rectangular blocks and few right angles to be seen. The urban planning has been driven by pedestrian pathways and cycle routes, punctuated by thousands of trees.double quotation markIt seems a renaissance is under way, as the grandchildren of people who first bought apartments here are discovering itOn the beach there are concrete sculptures by artistJoséphine Chevry, which look like the tips of the wartime sound mirrors in Dungeness, Kent. Chevry created them to help shape the dunes (AKA “the big mound”) but also to serve as functional wind breakers and shade when Point Zéro was created. They’re now mostly buried in the sand. Time has moved on but they will for ever be core to the town’s concept.View image in fullscreenThe beach at Le Couchant seen through one of the town’s many sculptures.Photograph: Hemis/AlamyThe place has had cyclical fortunes. As with many seaside towns, it fell from grace in the 1980s. It was gauche. In 2014 the fashion designer Simon Porte Jacquemus created a nostalgic collection and book in homage to the town and talked to AnOther Magazineof its “trashy reputation”, but he also said he found it “inspiring and exciting” and remembered his holidays there as a child. And it seems a renaissance is under way as the grandchildren of people who first bought apartments here are discovering it.double quotation markThe balconies jut out like theatre boxes and create an optical illusion of the building being slantedI’d recommend the fabulously vintage three-starHotel Le Quetzal(doubles from €114 room-only) as an interesting base. It feels brilliantly 1970s, being part of the original wave of development in the town, but was refurbished a few years ago so the essentials are fresh and modern. Its design is as interesting as anywhere in town: the balconies jut out like theatre boxes and create an optical illusion of the building being slanted. There’s no restaurant but people microwave meals in the lobby or bring back a margherita from nearbyL’Atelier de la Pizzato have on their balcony.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA couple of days by the pool here are great, fending off seagulls from your pain au chocolate at breakfast and watching stray cats wander around the loungers; the same families have been coming for years. Nearby,L’innatenduis a better restaurant than anything on the seafront (I particularly recommend the squid with black rice), although the most enjoyable meal I had was a bunch of simple marinated skewers atLa Guinguette des Alizés, opposite the seafront carousel on Avenue du Couchant that looks like a piece of pop art.View image in fullscreenBalladur’s architecture seems to anticipate the 21st century from the 1970s viewpoint.Photograph: Remi A/Getty ImagesStrolling around La Grande-Motte’s apartment blocks was as fascinating to me as a visit to the Colosseum. I walked through the open-air theatre that looks like a derelict World’s Fair site but is used for shows regularly, around the elegant white bow shape of Saint-Augustin’s church, down to the water and the Big Pyramid apartment complex facing the yachts on the dock, and to the low and curved buildings of Le Couchant. I spent hours photographing stairwells and walkways, and the hundreds of balconies that make the town the sum of its geometric parts – graphic beauty reminiscent of the Bauhaus, Saul Bass posters and Verner Panton furniture. La Grande-Motte is a sunny, gleaming white vision of a future that we could never live up to. Or perhaps deserve.Explore more on these topicsFrance holidaysCultural tripsCity breaksEurope holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: High in cocoa, high on nostalgia: the chocolate I love most now | Chocolate | The Guardian
description: Including, to my surprise, a 100% cacao bar
Author: Annalisa Barbieri
Headline: Including, to my surprise, a 100% cacao bar
Content: M&S retro chocolate bars from the 1980s: calledNow!,Jet,SparksandCoconut Grove.Photograph: Karen Thomas/M&SView image in fullscreenM&S retro chocolate bars from the 1980s: calledNow!,Jet,SparksandCoconut Grove.Photograph: Karen Thomas/M&SGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The chocolate diariesChocolateHigh in cocoa, high on nostalgia: the chocolate I love most nowIncluding, to my surprise, a 100% cacao bar …Annalisa BarbieriThu 27 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlthough I’mun peu fatiguéeof chocolates in bonbon shape with coloured cocoa-butter splashes atop, I appreciate this is the way many chocolates truffles are made. Overcoming that prejudice, I tucked into a box ofScoffchocolates. They were beautifully fresh tasting – they are made in batches throughout the year and the latest batch has just been let loose. I liked every one of the nine flavours I tested, from lemon to malted milk. But the ingredient list is long and a bit mainstream; a cleaner, more artisan approach and this would be a winning brand.View image in fullscreenScoff chocolates: truffles for the truffle-weary.Photograph: Gem Clack/PRMarks & Spencer has brought out some 1980s classics in original packaging for those wanting to go full Rivals: look out forNow!,Jet,SparksandCoconut Groveand see which chocolate classics they remind you of. My testers loved them.View image in fullscreenM&S Now! bar.My more everyday chocolate, as I am a high cocoa-content woman, has beenWillie’s 100% Cacaowith pistachio and date or raisin and hazelnut. I am not generally a fan of 100% cacao (it can only be called chocolate if sugar is also an ingredient) and I once described the bulk of the hundred percenters as tasting like you’ve woken up after a night out with your face in the ashtray (Firetree 100% is the exception). But these, from Willie’s Cacao, very much make the cut. An absolute joy of a dark chocolate and, boy, do you appreciate the sweetness of the raisins when you come across them.Date for your dairy: 26 and 27 September sees one of my favourite festivals – theAldeburgh Food and Drink Fairin my glorious Suffolk. Various wonderful chocolate makers will be there, as well as lots of other food and drink. The atmosphere is always jolly and you may spot me walking around in my chocolate cord flares.Explore more on these topicsChocolateThe chocolate diariesFoodShareReuse this content

title: Honey, I shrunk the wine: why miniature bottles are big again | Wine | The Guardian
description: Whether they’re consumed as a considered glass for one or something to sip on a short trip, miniature wine bottles are back with a bang
Author: Mina Holland
Headline: Whether they’re consumed as a considered glass for one or something to sip on a short trip, miniature wine bottles are back with a bang
Content: Wine miniatures: instant, easy drinking with a focus on fun.Photograph: Laithwaites/PRView image in fullscreenWine miniatures: instant, easy drinking with a focus on fun.Photograph: Laithwaites/PRGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.WineHoney, I shrunk the wine: why miniature bottles are big againWhether they’re consumed as a considered glass for one or something to sip on a short trip, miniature wine bottles are back with a bangMina HollandThu 27 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the 1920s, the London wine merchant Berry Bros & Rudd was asked to create a wine cellar for adoll’s house, commissioned by Queen Mary, to showcase the best of British craftsmanship. Designed by Edwin Lutyens, it had running water, electricity, a library of tiny books and, naturally, a wine cellar stocked with 1,200 miniature bottles, including vintage ports, an 1889 Montrachet and top-tier bordeaux. These days, the doll’s house resides in Windsor Castle, but Berry Bros has a replica of that cellar in its own Mayfair cellar, complete with 5ml bottles of those same wines.It is fair to say that this is not representative of the calibre of wine one generally finds in miniature bottles, a format associated with air travel and what I once called “journey juice” – ie, a drop that would last me the six stops from home to London Victoria on a Friday night. Google “miniature bottles of wine” and you’ll overwhelmingly be served examples from the very biggest wine brands in the world. This is also true ofcanned wines, although I’d argue there’s more interesting wine going into cans than small bottles.However! There are times when a mini bottle, which is usually somewhere between 200ml and 250ml, is just the ticket; when you’re the only one drinking and want just a glass, say, or maybe you’re sipping fizz and don’t want a larger bottle to lose its bubbles. For both reasons, champagne is ideal in miniature. What’s not to love about a cold, dry, biscuity and very sparkly solo glass of Lanson Le Black Création or Pommery Pink Pop? It’s cute, it’s camp and it’ll cost you a third of the price of a full bottle for those evenings when one (generous) glass is enough.They mostly come in plastic bottles, so minis are also good for a picnic. It’s no coincidence, then, that Marks & Spencer – summer’s temple to the picnic – should have a good selection. Also unsurprising is the disproportionate presence of rosé in mini bottles – the standouts being M&S’s Finca Miguel Cava Rosado, a sprightly, red fruit-forward friend to any fizz-loving prosecco sceptics, and Côteaux Varois en Provence, which is simple but unfailingly delicious. I also think the same store’s Rosso di Puglia is a winner fresh out of a cooler: juicy and food-versatile. Laithwaites, too, has a good selection of minis, including its very popular Cabalié wines from Languedoc-Roussillon. The white, in particular, is a peachy viognier blend, at once rich and fresh.None of these is wine to challenge you, but if you want instant, easy drinking with a focus on fun, stock up your fridge, or even your doll’s house.Four mini marvelsLanson Le Black Création£13.15 (200ml) Sainsbury’s, 12.5%. A classic non-vintage champagne that always hits the spot. Drink straight from the bottle for extra loucheness.M&S Côteaux Varois en Provence£4 (250ml) Ocado, 12.5%. Everything you want from Provençal rosé – a dry, strawberries and cream delight in a voluptuous mini bouteille.Cabalié Blanc 2024£3.99 (187ml) Laithwaites, 12%. Viognier, muscat and colombard have a party so you can, too.M&S Finca Miguel Cava Rosado Brut£3.50 (200ml) Ocado, 11.5%. An impressive, bubbly blend of Catalonian grape trepat with pinot noir – it cries out for picnic tapas.Explore more on these topicsWineFoodPicnicsFrench food and drinkSpanish food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for Richard Olney’s saffron and tomato rice | Food | The Guardian
description: Laborious to harvest and extortionately priced, the sunset-coloured stigmas of the saffron crocus have an extraordinarily warm, pungent taste. Fortunately, however, a little goes a very long way …
Author: Rachel Roddy
Headline: Laborious to harvest and extortionately priced, the sunset-coloured stigmas of the saffron crocus have an extraordinarily warm, pungent taste. Fortunately, however, a little goes a very long way …
Content: Rachel Roddy's take on Richard Olney’s saffron and tomato rice.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The Guardian.View image in fullscreenRachel Roddy's take on Richard Olney’s saffron and tomato rice.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The Guardian.A kitchen in RomeFoodRachel Roddy’s recipe for Richard Olney’s saffron and tomato riceLaborious to harvest and extortionately priced, the sunset-coloured stigmas of the saffron crocus have an extraordinarily warm, pungent taste. Fortunately, however, a little goes a very long way …Rachel RoddyThu 27 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe saffron crocus has six lilac-purple flowers, three yellow stamens and three orange-red stigmas that extend beyond the petals like the wiry antennae of an insect. The thread-like stigmas have to be picked only by hand when the flowers are fully open, a laborious, finickety job that hasn’t changed much since ancient times. Then, to avoid the colour and flavour fading, the stigmas need to be dried very quickly, a process that reduces their weight by about 80%. Tens of thousands of fiery-looking filaments are required to produce half a kilogram of the dried threads, which make the “hay” or powder we know as saffron and explains the exorbitant cost. Fortunately, just a few threads of this precious spice go a long way.Native to Crete, Iran and south-west Asia, the saffron crocus has been cultivated since the dawn of civilisation for its medicinal properties, as well as for use in cosmetics, perfume, food and as a dye. According to Alan Davidson inThe Oxford Companion to Food, the Moguls brought the use of saffron from Persia to India, in particular Kashmir; meanwhile, in the westward direction, the Arabs were cultivating saffron in Spain by AD960, although it was not until the 13th century that cultivation spread to Italy, France, Germany and England, particularly Essex. In his bookThe Last Food of England, Marwood Yeatman describes the “orderly strips of purple flowers inches apart in beds of up to 10ft wide” growing in a field outside the prosperous, half-timbered Essex wool town of Chipping Walden. “The women (‘crokers’) stooped to lift the crop on damp and dewy September mornings.” By the early 1500s, Chipping Walden had been renamed Saffron Walden.To preserve the colour and flavour, the stigma must be dried immediately without damage. In hotter, drier countries, this was – and still is – done outside in the shade. An alternative method is to use mesh trays over charcoal, while in England kilns were used, and the resulting threads or “chives”were sold either as hay saffron or pressed between weighted boards. In a year-long project by the University of Cambridge, researchers found documents from as late as 1871 recording thefts of saffron from warehouses and druggists. But, just a few decades later, while a few individuals continued to grow saffron for their own use, commercial cultivation in Britain had ceased.These days,growers such as David Smale, a geophysicist by training, are cultivating English saffron commercially, and it is Smale’s advice I followed this week when I madeRichard Olney’s recipe for buttered saffron rice and slivers of ripe, carefully peeled tomatoes: a delicate, delicious dish that can be served with poached chicken, fish or hard-boiled eggs.Remember, to release their sunset colour and extraordinarily warm, pungent, slightly metallic taste and hay-like fragrance, the saffron threads need to be soaked and infused. Smale notes that, “after infusing, the strands should be very pale and the colour should have leached into the liquid”, adding that “it takes just 10 or so saffron strands” for an exquisite effect.Saffron rice with tomatoServes450g butter3 tbsp olive oil1 medium onion, peeled and finely dicedSalt300g long-grainrice6-10 saffron strands, soaked in 2 tsp just-warm water500mllight vegetable stock, or water500g fresh tomatoes– ripe, flavoursome ones, ideallyIn a heavy-based casserole or saute pan with a lid, melt the butter and oil over a medium-low heat, add the onion and a pinch of salt, then cook, stirring regularly, for about 10 minutes, until the onion softens but remains pale.Add the rice and the saffron with its soaking water and stir for a minute until all the grains glisten. Add the water or stock, stir a few times, then turn down the heat to the gentlest simmer, cover and cook for 18-20 minutes, until the rice is tender.While the rice is cooking, peel the tomatoes by immersing them in boiling water for five minutes, then draining and dunking them in cold water, at which point the skins should pull away easily. Quarter the tomatoes, brush away the seeds and cut the flesh into thin strips or small cubes.When the rice is cooked, pull it off the heat and leave to sit for 10 minutes, during which time it will dry and swell. Finally, stir in the tomatoes and season with salt to taste.Explore more on these topicsFoodA kitchen in RomeItalian food and drinkRiceTomatoesMain courseStarterVegetablesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Why we’re all hooked on tinned fish  | Food | The Guardian
description: Sardines, mackerel, herring, pilchards, sprats and anchovies ... canning only makes the umami flavour better. They’re my top choice for pasta
Author: Rachel Roddy
Headline: Sardines, mackerel, herring, pilchards, sprats and anchovies ... canning only makes the umami flavour better. They’re my top choice for pasta
Content: Good in a crisis … Rachel Roddy's spaghetti with tinned sardines, anchovy, capers, chilli and lemon.Photograph: Rita Platts/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGood in a crisis … Rachel Roddy's spaghetti with tinned sardines, anchovy, capers, chilli and lemon.Photograph: Rita Platts/The GuardianFeastFoodWhy we’re all hooked on tinned fishSardines, mackerel, herring, pilchards, sprats and anchovies ... canning only makes the umami flavour better. They’re my top choice for pastaSign up here for our weekly food newsletter, FeastRachel RoddyThu 27 Aug 2026 08.10 EDTLast modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 08.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIcan’t find it, despite having spent the past 35 minutes looking, but somewhere in the house isThe Crisis Cook Book. It’s a standard paperback, postbox-red with white writing on the cover, and full of recipes from chefs includingRowley Leigh,Heston BlumenthalandJeremy Lee. Not having found it, I needed Amazon to tell me it was published in 2007 and compiled by Nick Lander, at the time the Financial Times’ restaurant correspondent. He asked 28 chefs to donate three recipes – their favourite starter, main course and dessert – and proceeds from the book went to the national homelessness charity Crisis.The reason I needed (and still need – it is now a mission) to find the book is because inside it is Rowley’s recipe for pasta with tinned sardines, fennel, chilli and lemon zest. It’s a recipe that I have made so many times, and for so many years, that I don’t need to look at the book; but, equally, because I’ve made it so many times and so much time has passed, I have no idea how far I have drifted from the original, and want to check. I’ve even written aboutthis recipein my weekly Guardian column, without referring to the book or even mentioning Rowley! Not that a store-cupboard version of the Sicilianpasta con le sarde(pasta with sardines and wild fennel) is owned by anyone, although Rowley did teach me.So here I am, setting the record straight, Rowley taught me to – and this is approximate – soften thinly sliced red onion, fennel and red chilli in lots of olive oil, add a tin of sardines (mashed), then toss the lot with al dente pasta, minced parsley and enough lemon zest to scent the pasta and the kitchen. It’s a meal that is not only deeply delicious but also thrifty, because a small amount of fish goes a long way.In short, tinned fish rules. It gives a product with a notoriously short life an extremely long one, thus drastically reducing the risk of food waste. Sardines, mackerel, herring, pilchards, sprats and anchovies are my tinned fish of choice – tasty, rich in essential omega 3 fatty acids and, if watchfully sourced, sustainable. That sourcing is very important, though (sardine stocksin some parts of the world are struggling), so I’d recommend keeping an eye onthe Marine Conservation Society’s Good Fish Guide. The other thing about tinned fish is the deep umami flavour that can develop during the curing and canning process, especially when the fish is preserved in a good-tasting brine or oil.View image in fullscreenFlexible and thrifty … Rachel’s potato and tinned fish cakes.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianAnd now, more than ever, it’s easier to find fish preserved in these delicious brines and oils thanks to enterprises such as Mitch Tonks’sRockfishin the West Country andSea Sistersin Dorset, both of which take great care with their canning, and to exceptional producers such asGiribizziandLa Belle-Iloise. Not to mention The Tinned Fish Market, which has stalls in Old Spitalfields and Borough markets in London (andan online shop) dedicated to excellent tinned fish. All of which is encouraging supermarkets to keep up.Back to recipes. Yotam Ottolenghi also has a play on the classic Sicilian sardine pasta, usingmackerel fillets, za’atar and lime, served with linguine; another Yotam recipe forconchiglie with tinned smoked oystersis a template that can be adapted to just about any tinned fish you happen to have in the cupboard. Anna Berrill, meanwhile, uses tinned sardines instead of anchovies for hertomato, caper and olive puttanesca, which she serves with polenta, as well as in a great-sounding sardine, caper, chive and celery salad.I generally use sardines in my recipe forpotato and tinned fishcakes, but mackerel, herring, pilchards and sprats all work. Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall’stinned mackerel patéis equally flexible, and yes to his quick-pickled onions, too! Hugh, a tinned fish champion, also suggests a sardine omelette (his daughter’s recipe) and mixing sardines with canned white beans and thinly sliced red onionfor a store-cupboard salad, as well as reminding us they’re tasty just piled on toast. I agree – it is always a good idea to have a tin or two of sardines in the cupboard. Now where is that bloody book?My week in foodView image in fullscreenAn alternative taste test … Marcus Ansell, AKA Tinned Fish Reviews, with his trusty sidekick, King Arthur.Photograph: Lucy Ansell/SWNSCan do|In keeping with the tinned fish theme, Marcus Ansell – known to his millions of Instagram, YouTube and TikTok followers asTinned Fish Reviewsand usually found wearing a fez – opens, decants and taste tests cans of fish. Calm to the extreme, even when appalled or ecstatic about the contents of the tin, he is a joy to watch and learn from. As is his dog, King Arthur.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFeastRecipes from all our star cooks, seasonal eating ideas and restaurant reviews. Get our best food writing every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDear diaries|This week, I have been cooking fromThom Eagle’s Allotment Diaries, which isn’t a cookbook, nor does it contain recipes. Rather, it is a record of a year on an allotment and his thoughts on growing, which are inseparable from those about family, grief, the seasons, and how he might slice, cook and flavour whatever he has picked. In turn, he has sent me into the kitchen with a reminder that a short phrase about courgette “stewed as filling for an omelette” can often be more helpful and inspiring than a long recipe. A stunning book.Wrap up warm|My son this week reminded me how great chickpea flourpancakesare. I’d recommend a batter made from 250g chickpea flour, 450ml cold water and a big pinch of salt, so it’s the consistency of smooth single cream. Leave it to rest, then fried as you would pancakes, they should be firm but floppy, and frilly at the edges. The flavour is like a pancake crossed with hummus and they’re fantastic with some stir-fried greens and a big blob of ricotta.If you want to read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive Feast in your inbox every Thursday.Explore more on these topicsFoodFeastFishSeafoodMain courseSnacksnewslettersShareReuse this content
